items.title: HTML Introduction
items.excerpt: What HTML is, what a web page is made of, and your first complete HTML page that you can edit and run right away.
items.content:
HTML is the language every web page is built with. When you open any website, your browser receives HTML and turns it into the headings, paragraphs, links and images you see. If you want to build websites, HTML is the first thing to learn, and it is also the easiest.

In this lesson you will learn what HTML is, how it works, and you will write your first web page.

What is HTML?

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.

  • HyperText means text that contains links to other pages. Links are what turn separate pages into the web.
  • Markup means you "mark up" ordinary text with labels, called tags, that tell the browser what each piece of text is: a heading, a paragraph, a link, a list.
  • Language means it follows rules, so every browser understands it the same way.

HTML is not a programming language. It has no calculations, no conditions and no loops. It only describes the structure of a page. That's why beginners can learn it in a few days.

Your first HTML page

Here is a complete web page. Click Try it Yourself to open it in the editor, change the text, and press Run.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <title>My First Page</title>
</head>
<body>

  <h1>Hello, world!</h1>
  <p>This is my first web page.</p>

</body>
</html>

The browser shows a big heading and a paragraph underneath. The tags themselves, the words in angle brackets, are never shown. They only tell the browser how to display the content.

How the example works

Every line has a job:

  • <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser this is a modern HTML document.
  • <html> is the root element. Everything else goes inside it.
  • <head> holds information about the page, such as its title. It is not shown on the page itself.
  • <title> sets the text shown in the browser tab and in search results.
  • <body> holds everything that is visible on the page.
  • <h1> is a main heading.
  • <p> is a paragraph.

You'll learn each of these in detail in the next lessons. For now, notice the pattern: most content sits between an opening tag like <p> and a closing tag like </p>. The closing tag has a forward slash.

What does a browser do with HTML?

  1. You visit a web address.
  2. The server sends back an HTML file, which is plain text.
  3. The browser reads the tags from top to bottom.
  4. It builds the page you see on screen.

You can see the HTML of any page yourself: right-click a page and choose View page source (or press Ctrl + U). Try it on this page.

HTML, CSS and JavaScript

Almost every website uses three languages together:

  • HTML gives the page its structure: headings, paragraphs, images, links.
  • CSS controls the look: colours, fonts, spacing, layout.
  • JavaScript adds behaviour: buttons that react, menus that open, content that updates.

A simple way to remember it: HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the clothes, and JavaScript is the movement. This tutorial starts with HTML because the other two are built on top of it.

What you need

Nothing to buy and nothing to install:

  • A text editor to write HTML. Any computer already has one (Notepad on Windows, TextEdit on Mac), and the next lesson shows a better free one.
  • A web browser to view the result: Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari.

You can also practise directly on this site: every example has a Try it Yourself button.

Exercise

Open the first example with Try it Yourself and make these changes, pressing Run after each one:

  1. Change the heading to your own name.
  2. Change the paragraph to say why you want to learn web development.
  3. Add a second paragraph below the first one. (Hint: copy the whole <p>…</p> line.)

If all three show up on the right, you have just edited your first web page.

Summary

  • HTML is the language that describes the structure of web pages.
  • Content is marked up with tags, usually in pairs like <p> and </p>.
  • Every page has the same basic outline: <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head> and <body>.
  • HTML handles structure, CSS handles style, JavaScript handles behaviour.

In the next lesson you'll set up a free code editor and create an HTML file on your own computer.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Editors
items.excerpt: Write HTML on your own computer: create your first .html file in Notepad or TextEdit, then set up VS Code, the free editor most developers use.
items.content:
You can write HTML in any program that saves plain text. In this lesson you'll create a real HTML file on your computer, open it in your browser, and then set up Visual Studio Code, the free editor most web developers use every day.

Option 1: The editor you already have

Every computer comes with a simple text editor. It's enough for your first page.

On Windows (Notepad)

  1. Open the Start menu, type Notepad and open it.
  2. Type or paste the page below.
  3. Click File → Save As.
  4. Choose a folder (for example, Desktop).
  5. Set Save as type to All files.
  6. Name the file index.html and set Encoding to UTF-8.
  7. Click Save.

On Mac (TextEdit)

TextEdit saves rich text by default, which breaks HTML. Change that first:

  1. Open TextEdit → Settings (or Preferences).
  2. On the New Document tab, select Plain text.
  3. On the Open and Save tab, tick Display HTML files as HTML code instead of formatted text.
  4. Create a new document, type the page below, and save it as index.html.

Here is the page to type:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My Computer Page</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>It works!</h1>
  <p>I wrote this file on my own computer.</p>
</body>
</html>

Open the file in a browser

Find index.html in the folder where you saved it and double-click it. It opens in your default browser and shows your heading and paragraph.

Every time you change the file:

  1. Save it in the editor (Ctrl + S, or Cmd + S on Mac).
  2. Switch to the browser and refresh (F5, or Cmd + R on Mac).

That save-and-refresh loop is how you'll work through this whole tutorial.

Option 2: Visual Studio Code (recommended)

Notepad works, but a code editor makes HTML much easier. Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is free, works on Windows, Mac and Linux, and is used by most professional web developers.

What it does for you:

  • Colours your code, so tags, text and attributes are easy to tell apart.
  • Auto-completes tags: type <p and it suggests the rest.
  • Closes tags for you, so you don't forget </p>.
  • Emmet shortcut: in a new .html file, type ! and press Tab to get a full page outline instantly.

Set it up

  1. Download VS Code from the official site, code.visualstudio.com, and install it.
  2. Create a folder for your practice files, for example html-practice.
  3. In VS Code choose File → Open Folder and select that folder.
  4. Click the New File icon and name it index.html.
  5. Type ! then press Tab. VS Code writes the page outline for you.
  6. Add <h1>Hello from VS Code</h1> inside the <body>, then save.

Live Server: refresh automatically

The Live Server extension reloads the browser every time you save:

  1. Click the Extensions icon on the left (four squares).
  2. Search for Live Server and click Install.
  3. Right-click index.html and choose Open with Live Server.

Now every save updates the browser by itself, with no manual refresh needed.

Practising on VitalStack

Every example in these lessons has a Try it Yourself button. It opens an editor right here in your browser: change the code on the left, press Run, and see the result on the right. It's the quickest way to test a small idea. For anything you want to keep, use your own files.

Common mistakes

  • The page shows the code instead of the result. The file was saved as .txt or rich text. Make sure the name ends in .html and the format is plain text.
  • Strange characters (Ã© instead of é). Save the file as UTF-8 and keep the <meta charset="UTF-8"> line in the <head>.
  • Changes don't appear. You forgot to save, or to refresh the browser.

Exercise

  1. Create a folder called html-practice with an index.html file inside it.
  2. Write a page with your name as the <h1> and one paragraph about yourself.
  3. Open it in the browser, change the paragraph, save, and refresh to see the update.

Summary

  • HTML files are plain text files ending in .html.
  • You can write them in Notepad or TextEdit, but VS Code is free and much easier.
  • Open the file in a browser to see the result; save and refresh after every change.
  • Save files as UTF-8 to avoid broken characters.

Next, you'll learn what each part of the basic page structure means.

items.title: HTML Basic Structure
items.excerpt: The outline every HTML page shares: doctype, html, head, title, meta tags and body, what each one does and the mistakes to avoid.
items.content:
Every HTML page, from a one-line test to a huge website, starts from the same outline. Once you know it, you can start any new page in seconds and understand the source of pages you find online.

The complete outline

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>Page title shown in the tab</title>
</head>
<body>

  <h1>Visible content goes here</h1>
  <p>Everything inside body appears on the page.</p>

</body>
</html>

Let's go through it line by line.

The doctype

<!DOCTYPE html>

The very first line tells the browser to use modern HTML (HTML5). Without it, browsers fall back to an old "quirks mode" where some layouts and styles behave differently. It is not a tag and has no closing part. Just put it at the top of every page.

The html element

<html lang="en">
  ...
</html>

<html> is the root: every other element lives inside it. The lang attribute says which language the page is written in. Screen readers use it to pronounce words correctly, and search engines use it to show your page to the right readers. Use en for English and hi for Hindi.

The head: information about the page

The <head> holds details about the page. Nothing here appears in the page itself.

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>HTML Basic Structure</title>
</head>
  • <meta charset="UTF-8"> sets the character encoding, so letters like é, ñ and Hindi or emoji characters display correctly. Keep it as the first line inside <head>.
  • <meta name="viewport" ...> makes the page fit phone screens instead of showing a tiny desktop version. Every page you build should have it.
  • <title> sets the text in the browser tab, in bookmarks, and as the clickable headline in Google results. Make it short and describe the page.

Later you'll also put links to CSS files and other page information in the head.

The body: everything visible

<body>
  <h1>Welcome</h1>
  <p>Hello! This text is visible.</p>
</body>

Headings, paragraphs, images, links, tables and forms all go inside <body>. A page has exactly one <head> and one <body>.

Indentation keeps code readable

Browsers ignore extra spaces and line breaks in your code, so these two are identical to the browser:

<body><h1>Title</h1><p>Text</p></body>
<body>
  <h1>Title</h1>
  <p>Text</p>
</body>

The second is far easier for people to read. Indent the contents of an element by two spaces, so you can see at a glance what is inside what.

Comments

Comments are notes for yourself or other developers. The browser skips them.

<!-- This is a comment. It does not appear on the page. -->
<p>This paragraph does appear.</p>

Use comments to explain sections of a long page, or to temporarily hide some HTML while testing.

Common mistakes

  • Content in the head. Visible content belongs in <body>. If you put a paragraph in <head>, the browser quietly moves it into the body to repair the page, so it may look fine while your HTML is actually invalid.
  • Forgetting the viewport meta tag. The page looks fine on a computer but tiny on phones.
  • Two body elements. Keep exactly one; put all content inside it.
  • Missing doctype. The page may look slightly different in each browser.

Exercise

Open the complete outline with Try it Yourself and:

  1. Change the <title> to "My Practice Page". (The tab title isn't visible in the editor's result, but it will be in your own files.)
  2. Add a comment above the heading that says what the page is for.
  3. Add a second heading with <h2> and a paragraph under it.
  4. Change lang="en" to lang="hi" and add a short Hindi sentence in a new paragraph.

Summary

  • Start every page with <!DOCTYPE html>.
  • <html lang="…"> wraps everything and states the language.
  • <head> holds information about the page: charset, viewport and title.
  • <body> holds everything the reader sees.
  • Indent nested elements and use <!-- comments --> to keep code readable.

Next, you'll look closely at elements: opening tags, closing tags and how to nest them.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Elements
items.excerpt: How HTML elements work: opening and closing tags, content, nesting elements correctly, empty elements like br and img, and block versus inline.
items.content:
A web page is made of elements. Each heading, paragraph, link and image is one element. In this lesson you'll learn how elements are written, how they fit inside each other, and the few rules that keep a page from breaking.

Anatomy of an element

Most elements have three parts:

<p>This is a paragraph.</p>
  • <p> is the opening tag: the element's name in angle brackets.
  • This is a paragraph. is the content.
  • </p> is the closing tag: the same name with a forward slash.

Together, the opening tag, the content and the closing tag form one element. People often say "tag" when they mean element; the meaning is usually clear from context.

Some elements you'll use constantly

<h1>Main heading</h1>
<h2>Smaller heading</h2>
<p>A paragraph of text.</p>
<a href="https://example.com">A link</a>
<strong>Important text</strong>
<em>Emphasised text</em>

You'll learn each of these properly in later lessons. Open the example with Try it Yourself to see how each one looks.

Nesting elements

Elements can contain other elements. This is called nesting:

<p>Learning <strong>HTML</strong> is <em>fun</em>.</p>

Here <strong> and <em> sit inside the paragraph. The whole page is nested too: <body> is inside <html>, headings and paragraphs are inside <body>.

The one rule of nesting

Close elements in the reverse order you opened them. The last one opened is the first one closed.

<!-- Correct -->
<p>This is <strong>very important</strong>.</p>

<!-- Wrong: strong opened inside p, but p closes first -->
<p>This is <strong>very important.</p></strong>

Browsers try to repair wrong nesting, but each browser repairs it differently, and the result is often not what you meant. Correct nesting avoids those surprises. VS Code's auto-closing and indentation make wrong nesting easy to spot.

Empty elements

Some elements have no content and therefore no closing tag. They're called empty (or void) elements:

<p>First line<br>Second line</p>
<hr>
<img src="https://picsum.photos/200/120" alt="A random sample photo">
  • <br> inserts a line break inside text.
  • <hr> draws a horizontal line, used to separate sections.
  • <img> displays an image; you'll learn its src and alt attributes in the next lesson.

You may see these written as <br /> in older code. Both forms work in HTML5; this tutorial uses the shorter <br>.

Don't skip closing tags

Browsers often show a page correctly even when you forget a closing tag:

<p>First paragraph
<p>Second paragraph

It looks fine here, but missing closing tags cause hard-to-find layout bugs as pages grow, especially once you add CSS. Always close every element that has a closing tag.

Upper or lower case?

<P> and <p> mean the same thing; tag names are not case-sensitive. The convention, and what you'll see in almost all modern code, is lowercase. Stick to it.

Block and inline elements

Elements display in one of two basic ways:

  • Block elements start on a new line and take the full width available: <h1> to <h6>, <p>, <div>, <ul>, <table>.
  • Inline elements stay inside the line of text and take only the space they need: <a>, <strong>, <em>, <span>, <img>.
<p>This paragraph is a block.</p>
<p>So is this one. It starts on a new line.</p>
<p>Inline elements like <strong>strong</strong> and <a href="#">links</a> stay within the line.</p>

Two generic elements have no meaning of their own and are used to group content for styling later: <div> (block) and <span> (inline). You'll use them a lot once you start CSS.

Exercise

Use Try it Yourself on any example above and build this:

  1. An <h1> with the title "My Favourite Things".
  2. A paragraph that contains one word in <strong> and one in <em>.
  3. A <hr> line.
  4. A paragraph with a line break (<br>) in the middle.
  5. Check your nesting: every element closes in the reverse order it opened.

Summary

  • An element is usually an opening tag, content and a closing tag.
  • Elements can be nested; close them in reverse order.
  • Empty elements like <br>, <hr> and <img> have no closing tag.
  • Always close elements, and write tag names in lowercase.
  • Block elements start on a new line; inline elements flow within text.

Next, you'll learn attributes, which give elements extra information, like where a link goes or which image to show.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Attributes
items.excerpt: Attributes give elements extra information: href for links, src and alt for images, lang, title, id and class, with the rules for writing them correctly.
items.content:
Tags tell the browser what something is. Attributes add the details: where a link goes, which image to show, what language the page is in. Almost every real page uses them, so this lesson covers the ones you'll need most.

What an attribute looks like

<a href="https://www.example.com">Visit Example</a>
  • Attributes always go inside the opening tag.
  • They're written as name="value": here the name is href and the value is the web address.
  • An element can have several attributes, separated by spaces.

href: where a link goes

The <a> (anchor) element creates a link. Its href attribute holds the destination:

<p><a href="https://developer.mozilla.org">Read the MDN Web Docs</a></p>
<p><a href="about.html">About this site</a></p>
<p><a href="https://developer.mozilla.org" target="_blank">Open MDN in a new tab</a></p>
  • A full web address (https://…) links to another site.
  • A file name like about.html links to a page in the same folder.
  • target="_blank" opens the link in a new tab. Use it sparingly; readers generally prefer to choose that themselves.

src and alt: showing an image

<img> needs two attributes:

<img src="https://picsum.photos/320/180" alt="A sample landscape photo" width="320" height="180">
  • src (source) is the address of the image file.
  • alt (alternative text) describes the image. Screen readers read it aloud for blind users, it appears if the image fails to load, and search engines use it to understand the image. **Always write an alt.** If an image is purely decorative, use an empty one: alt="".
  • width and height (in pixels) let the browser reserve space before the image loads, so the page doesn't jump around.

lang: the page language

<html lang="en">

As you saw in the structure lesson, lang on the <html> element states the page's language. You can also mark a single phrase in another language:

<p>The word for thank you in Hindi is <span lang="hi">धन्यवाद</span>.</p>

title: extra information on hover

<p><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is easy to learn.</p>

The title attribute shows a small tooltip when you hover over the element with a mouse. It's handy for abbreviations, but don't put important information only in a title: it isn't visible on phones.

id and class: names for styling and scripts

<h2 id="contact">Contact us</h2>
<p class="note">Replies within two days.</p>
<p class="note">We read every message.</p>
  • id gives one element a unique name. No two elements on a page may share an id. You can link straight to it: <a href="#contact">Jump to contact</a>.
  • class gives a shared name to any number of elements, so CSS can style them all at once.

You'll use id and class constantly in the CSS and JavaScript tutorials.

style: quick inline styling

<p style="color: green; font-size: 20px;">This text is green and larger.</p>

The style attribute applies CSS directly to one element. It's fine for quick experiments, but real pages keep their styles in CSS files, which you'll learn in the CSS tutorial.

Rules for writing attributes

  • Use lowercase names: href, not HREF.
  • Always quote values: href="page.html". Quotes are required as soon as a value contains a space, so quoting every value avoids mistakes.
  • Use double quotes normally. If the value itself contains double quotes, wrap it in single quotes: title='She said "hi"'.
  • Boolean attributes need no value. Their presence alone turns them on:
<input type="checkbox" checked> I agree
<button disabled>Not available yet</button>

Exercise

Open any example with Try it Yourself and build a small profile card:

  1. An <h2> with your name and id="profile".
  2. An image with src="https://picsum.photos/200", a meaningful alt text, and width="200".
  3. A paragraph that contains a link to your favourite website, opening in a new tab.
  4. An abbreviation with a title, for example <abbr title="Cascading Style Sheets">CSS</abbr>.
  5. A link at the top of the page that jumps to #profile.

Summary

  • Attributes add information to elements and always go in the opening tag.
  • They're written as name="value"; use lowercase names and quote every value.
  • Key attributes: href (links), src and alt (images), lang, title, id, class, style.
  • Always give images a useful alt text.

Next up: headings and paragraphs, and how to structure the text of a page so it's easy to read.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Headings
items.excerpt: The six heading levels from h1 to h6, how to build a clear outline with them, and why headings matter for readers, screen readers and Google.
items.content:
Headings are the titles and subtitles of a page. Readers scan them to decide what to read, screen readers use them to jump around, and search engines use them to understand what each part of the page is about. Getting headings right is one of the easiest ways to make a page better.

Six levels of headings

HTML has six heading elements, from <h1> (most important) to <h6> (least important):

<h1>Heading level 1</h1>
<h2>Heading level 2</h2>
<h3>Heading level 3</h3>
<h4>Heading level 4</h4>
<h5>Heading level 5</h5>
<h6>Heading level 6</h6>

Browsers show <h1> largest and boldest, and each level after it a little smaller. But the size is only the default look. What really matters is the level, because it describes how important the heading is and where it sits in the page's outline.

Headings build an outline

Think of a page like a book. The <h1> is the book title, each <h2> is a chapter, and each <h3> is a section inside a chapter.

<h1>Healthy Breakfast Ideas</h1>

<h2>Quick breakfasts</h2>
<h3>Overnight oats</h3>
<p>Mix oats with milk and leave them in the fridge.</p>
<h3>Banana toast</h3>
<p>Toast, peanut butter and a sliced banana.</p>

<h2>Weekend breakfasts</h2>
<h3>Vegetable omelette</h3>
<p>Eggs, onions, tomatoes and spinach.</p>

If you read only the headings, you understand the whole page: the topic, the two groups, and the dishes in each. That's the test of a good heading structure.

Rules for a clean outline

One h1 per page

The <h1> is the main title of the page. Use it once. On a blog, it is the post title; on a lesson page like this one, it is the lesson name.

Don't skip levels

Go from <h2> to <h3>, not from <h2> straight to <h5>. Skipping levels confuses screen reader users, who often navigate by heading level.

<!-- Avoid -->
<h2>Our services</h2>
<h5>Web design</h5>

<!-- Better -->
<h2>Our services</h2>
<h3>Web design</h3>

Going back up is fine: after an <h3> you can start a new <h2> section.

Choose headings by meaning, not by size

Never pick <h4> just because you like its smaller size. Pick the level that fits the outline, and change the size later with CSS. You'll learn how in the CSS lessons.

Headings and accessibility

Many blind and low-vision users browse with a screen reader. A common habit is to press a key that jumps from heading to heading, like skimming. A page with clear headings is quick to explore; a page with no headings is one long wall of text read aloud from top to bottom.

Headings and search engines

Google reads your headings to understand the topics on the page. A heading like <h2>How to boil eggs</h2> tells it far more than a bold paragraph that says the same thing. Write headings for people first: short, specific and descriptive. That's also what works best for search.

Don't use headings just to make text big or bold

<!-- Wrong: this isn't a title, just a sentence someone wanted to stand out -->
<h3>Free delivery on all orders today!</h3>

If the text isn't a title for the content that follows, use a paragraph and make it stand out with <strong> or CSS instead.

Common mistakes

  • Several h1 elements on one page for decoration. Keep one main title.
  • Skipping levels (h2 → h4) to get a smaller font.
  • Using headings for styling text that isn't a title.
  • Vague headings like "Section 2" or "More info". Say what the section contains.

Exercise

Open the breakfast example with Try it Yourself and:

  1. Add a third <h2> section called "Breakfasts for kids" with two <h3> dishes.
  2. Write one paragraph under each new dish.
  3. Read only the headings out loud. Does the outline make sense on its own?
  4. Change one <h3> into <h5> and notice how the outline now "jumps". Change it back.

Summary

  • HTML has six heading levels, <h1> to <h6>.
  • Headings form an outline: one <h1>, then <h2> sections, then <h3> sub-sections.
  • Don't skip levels and don't choose a level for its size.
  • Good headings help readers, screen reader users and search engines.

Next, you'll learn about paragraphs, line breaks and horizontal rules.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Paragraphs
items.excerpt: How the p element works, why browsers ignore your extra spaces, and when to use line breaks, horizontal rules and pre for preformatted text.
items.content:
Most of the text on the web lives in paragraphs. In this lesson you'll learn how the <p> element works, how browsers treat spaces and line breaks in your code, and three related elements: <br>, <hr> and <pre>.

The p element

A paragraph starts with <p> and ends with </p>:

<p>This is the first paragraph. It can be as long as you like.</p>
<p>This is the second paragraph. Browsers add space above and below each one.</p>

Each paragraph is a block: it starts on a new line and takes the full width available. The browser adds a margin before and after it, so paragraphs are visually separated without any extra work.

Browsers collapse white space

This surprises almost every beginner. Extra spaces and line breaks in your HTML code are ignored. Any run of spaces, tabs and new lines is shown as a single space.

<p>
  This     paragraph
  has lots of      spaces
  and line breaks      in the code.
</p>

In the browser, this shows as one normal line of text: "This paragraph has lots of spaces and line breaks in the code."

This is actually useful: you can indent and wrap your code however you like to keep it readable, and the page still looks clean.

Line breaks with br

To break a line inside a paragraph without starting a new paragraph, use <br>:

<p>
  VitalStack<br>
  Learn to code, one lesson at a time<br>
  contact@example.com
</p>

<br> is an empty element: it has no closing tag. Use it where a line break is part of the content, such as addresses, poems or song lyrics.

Don't use several <br> tags to create space between blocks. That's a job for separate paragraphs or for CSS margins.

<!-- Avoid -->
<p>First idea.<br><br><br>Second idea.</p>

<!-- Better -->
<p>First idea.</p>
<p>Second idea.</p>

Horizontal rules with hr

<hr> marks a change of topic between paragraphs. Browsers draw it as a horizontal line.

<p>That's everything about the morning schedule.</p>
<hr>
<p>Now let's look at the afternoon.</p>

Like <br>, it has no closing tag. Use it for a thematic break, not as decoration. If you just want a line for looks, add a border with CSS later.

Preformatted text with pre

Sometimes spaces and line breaks do matter, for example in ASCII art, poems laid out in a special way, or plain-text output. The <pre> element keeps every space and line break exactly as you typed it, and shows the text in a monospace font.

<pre>
Name      Score
Asha        92
Rohan       87
Meera       95
</pre>

The columns line up because nothing is collapsed. <pre> is also commonly used together with <code> to show blocks of program code.

Choosing the right element

Common mistakes

  • Expecting Enter to make a new line. Pressing Enter in your code does nothing on the page. Use a new <p> or a <br>.
  • **Using <br><br> for spacing.** Make separate paragraphs instead.
  • **Putting a heading or list inside <p>.** A paragraph can only contain text and inline elements. The browser will close the paragraph early and your layout will break.
  • **Forgetting the closing </p>.** Browsers often guess correctly, but not always. Close every paragraph.

Exercise

  1. Write three short paragraphs about your favourite food.
  2. Add your (made-up) postal address using one paragraph and <br> tags.
  3. Separate two topics with an <hr>.
  4. Make a small table of three friends and their ages using <pre>, and line up the columns with spaces.

Summary

  • <p> creates a paragraph; browsers add space around it.
  • Extra spaces and new lines in your code collapse into one space.
  • <br> breaks a line inside a block; <hr> marks a change of topic.
  • <pre> keeps spacing exactly as written, in a monospace font.

Next, you'll learn how to make text bold, italic, highlighted and more with text formatting elements.
items.subject: html

items.title: What Is Artificial Intelligence? A Plain-English Guide
items.excerpt: What AI really is, how it differs from normal software, the main types of AI, where you already use it every day, and what it can and can't do.
items.content:
Short answer: artificial intelligence (AI) is software that performs tasks we normally associate with human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognising images or making predictions, by learning patterns from data instead of following only hand-written rules.

That one idea, learning from data, is what separates modern AI from ordinary programs. This guide explains it without jargon, with examples you already use every day.

Normal software vs AI

A normal program follows rules a programmer wrote:

def shipping_cost(total):
    if total >= 500:
        return 0
    return 40

Every decision is spelled out. This works well when the rules are clear.

Now try writing rules to answer "is there a cat in this photo?". Ears, whiskers, fur… but cats come in every colour, angle, lighting and pose, partly hidden behind sofas. Nobody can write those rules.

AI takes a different approach. Instead of rules, you give it thousands of examples (photos labelled "cat" and "not cat"), and a learning algorithm adjusts a mathematical model until it gets the answers right. The result is a program whose "rules" were learned, not written.

Key terms, untangled

Artificial intelligence is the broad goal: machines doing "intelligent" tasks.

Machine learning (ML) is the main way we achieve it today: systems that learn from data. Spam filters, product recommendations and fraud detection are classic ML.

Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers, loosely inspired by the brain. It powers image recognition, speech recognition and translation.

Generative AI creates new content (text, images, audio, code) instead of only classifying or predicting. Chatbots and image generators are generative AI.

Large language models (LLMs) are generative models trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word. They power AI chat assistants and coding assistants. See our guide How Large Language Models Work.

Think of them as nested circles: AI ⊃ machine learning ⊃ deep learning ⊃ generative AI and LLMs.

How a model learns (the core idea)

Here's machine learning in five steps, using house prices as an example:

  1. Collect data: thousands of past sales with size, location, age, and the price they sold for.
  2. Choose a model: a mathematical function with adjustable numbers called parameters (or weights).
  3. Train: show the model examples. It guesses a price, compares it with the real price, and nudges its parameters to reduce the error. Repeat millions of times.
  4. Test: check the model on houses it has never seen, to make sure it learned general patterns rather than memorising.
  5. Use it: give it a new house and it predicts a price. This step is called inference.

Modern language models follow the same idea at an enormous scale: billions of parameters, trained on vast amounts of text, to predict the next piece of text.

Types of machine learning

  • Supervised learning: learning from labelled examples ("this email is spam"). Used for classification and prediction.
  • Unsupervised learning: finding structure in unlabelled data, like grouping customers with similar buying habits.
  • Reinforcement learning: learning by trial and error with rewards, like an AI learning a game by playing it millions of times. It's also used to fine-tune chat assistants based on human feedback.

AI you already use every day

  • Search engines understanding what you mean, not just your exact words.
  • Maps predicting traffic and arrival times.
  • Email spam filters and smart replies.
  • Phones unlocking with your face, improving photos, transcribing voice messages.
  • Streaming and shopping recommendations.
  • Banks flagging unusual transactions.
  • Translation apps.
  • Chat and coding assistants that answer questions and write drafts.

What AI is good at, and where it fails

Strengths:

  • Finding patterns in huge amounts of data far faster than people.
  • Working with messy inputs: language, images, audio.
  • Producing drafts, summaries and suggestions instantly.

Weaknesses:

  • It can be confidently wrong. Language models can produce fluent text that is false, often called hallucination, because they generate likely-sounding text rather than looking facts up.
  • It reflects its data. If training data contains biases or gaps, the model will too.
  • It doesn't truly understand the world the way people do, even when it sounds like it does.
  • It struggles outside what it has seen: unusual situations, very recent events (unless connected to live information), and tasks needing reliable step-by-step precision.

A practical rule: use AI to go faster, and use your own judgement to check what matters.

Narrow AI vs general AI

Every AI system in use today is narrow AI: built for specific kinds of tasks, even if those tasks are broad, like conversation. Artificial general intelligence (AGI), an AI that can learn and do any intellectual task a human can, is a research goal and a subject of much debate. Experts disagree on whether and when it might arrive.

Why this matters for programmers

AI doesn't replace the need to understand programming; it changes how you work:

  • AI assistants can write first drafts of code, explain errors and generate tests, but someone must judge whether the code is correct, secure and maintainable.
  • Building AI-powered features (search, chatbots, recommendations) is now a normal part of software development, usually by calling AI models through an API.
  • Fundamentals like data structures, debugging, SQL and clear thinking are what let you use AI tools well instead of being misled by them.

If you're starting out, our Python course is the most direct path toward working with AI.

Frequently asked questions

Is AI the same as machine learning?

No. AI is the broad goal; machine learning is the main technique used to reach it today. Almost all modern AI products are built with machine learning.

Does AI think like a human?

No. Models process numbers and patterns. They can imitate human-like answers very well, but they don't have experiences, goals or understanding in the human sense.

Do I need advanced maths to work with AI?

To use AI models and build applications with them: no, solid programming is enough. To research or train new models from scratch: yes, linear algebra, probability and calculus help a lot.

Will AI take programming jobs?

It's changing them. Routine code is faster to produce, so the value shifts to understanding problems, designing systems, reviewing and testing, and knowing the domain. People who combine programming fundamentals with AI tools are in a strong position.

What should I learn first?

Python basics, then working with data (lists, dictionaries, files, JSON, SQL), then calling AI models through APIs. Theory can come alongside as your curiosity grows.

Summary

  • AI is software that performs "intelligent" tasks, mostly by learning patterns from data.
  • Machine learning, deep learning, generative AI and LLMs are nested layers of the same idea.
  • Models are trained on examples, tested on new data, and then used for predictions.
  • AI is powerful but can be confidently wrong and biased; human judgement still matters.
  • For programmers, AI is a tool and a new kind of feature to build, and fundamentals make you better at both.

items.title: HTML Text Formatting
items.excerpt: Bold, italic, highlighted, small, deleted, inserted, subscript and superscript text, and the difference between strong and b, em and i.
items.content:
HTML has a set of small elements that change how a few words look or what they mean: important words, emphasis, highlighted text, chemical formulas and more. These are inline elements: they sit inside a line of text instead of starting a new block.

Strong and em: meaning

<p><strong>Warning:</strong> turn off the power before opening the case.</p>
<p>I <em>really</em> want to learn JavaScript this month.</p>
  • <strong> marks text as important. Browsers show it in bold.
  • <em> marks emphasis, the stress you'd put on a word when speaking. Browsers show it in italics.

Screen readers can change their voice for these elements, and search engines understand that the words matter. Emphasis changes meaning, too: "I *really* want" is different from "*I* really want".

B and i: style without extra importance

<p>The <b>Pro</b> plan includes everything in Basic.</p>
<p>The word <i lang="fr">bonjour</i> means hello.</p>
  • <b> makes text bold without saying it is important, e.g. product names or key words in a summary.
  • <i> sets text apart without emphasis: foreign words, technical terms, names of ships or books, thoughts.

Rule of thumb: if you'd stress it when reading aloud, use <em>; if it's important, use <strong>. If it only needs to look different, use <b> or <i>.

Highlighted, small, deleted and inserted text

<p>Search results for <mark>flexbox</mark> in this lesson.</p>
<p><small>Prices include tax.</small></p>
<p>Price: <del>₹999</del> <ins>₹499</ins></p>
  • <mark> highlights text that is relevant right now, like search matches. It gets a yellow background by default.
  • <small> is for side comments and fine print: copyright notes, legal text.
  • <del> shows text that was removed (drawn with a line through it).
  • <ins> shows text that was added (underlined).

<del> and <ins> are perfect for showing price drops or edits to a document.

Subscript and superscript

<p>Water is H<sub>2</sub>O.</p>
<p>E = mc<sup>2</sup></p>
<p>Today is the 1<sup>st</sup> of the month.</p>
  • <sub> lowers the text: chemical formulas, maths indices.
  • <sup> raises the text: powers, footnote numbers, ordinals like 1st.

Code, keyboard keys and abbreviations

These are very useful on a programming site:

<p>Use the <code>console.log()</code> function to print a value.</p>
<p>Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>S</kbd> to save.</p>
<p><abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr> is easy to learn.</p>
  • <code> marks a piece of computer code (shown in a monospace font).
  • <kbd> marks keys the user should press.
  • <abbr> marks an abbreviation; the title shows the full form when you hover over it.

Quotations

<p>As the saying goes, <q>practice makes perfect</q>.</p>

<blockquote cite="https://www.w3.org/">
  <p>The Web is for everyone.</p>
</blockquote>
  • <q> is a short quote inside a sentence; the browser adds the quotation marks.
  • <blockquote> is a longer quote shown as its own indented block. The cite attribute can point to the source.

Nesting formatting elements

You can combine them, as long as you close them in the reverse order:

<p><strong>Note: <em>do not</em> skip this step.</strong></p>

Common mistakes

  • **Using <b> for important warnings.** Use <strong> so the importance is in the code, not just the look.
  • Underlining normal text. Readers expect underlined text to be a link. Avoid <u> except for special cases like marking spelling errors.
  • Overusing bold. If everything is bold, nothing stands out. Pick a few words.
  • Wrong nesting like <strong><em>text</strong></em>. Close the inner element first.

Exercise

Write a short "product card" using only paragraphs and formatting:

  1. Product name in <b>, old price in <del> and new price in <ins>.
  2. One important note with <strong> and one emphasised word with <em>.
  3. A fine-print line with <small>.
  4. A tip that says to press Ctrl + P to print, using <kbd>.
  5. Bonus: write the formula for carbon dioxide (CO2) with <sub>.

Summary

  • <strong> = important, <em> = emphasis; <b> and <i> only change the look.
  • <mark>, <small>, <del>, <ins>, <sub> and <sup> cover most other formatting needs.
  • <code>, <kbd> and <abbr> are handy for technical writing.
  • Use <q> and <blockquote> for quotations.

Next, you'll learn the most important element of the web: links.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Links
items.excerpt: Create links with the a element: absolute and relative URLs, opening links in a new tab safely, linking to a section, email and phone links, and writing good link text.
items.content:
Links are what make the web a *web*. With one element, <a>, you can connect a page to any other page in the world, to a section of the same page, to an email address or to a phone number.

The a element

<a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/">MDN Web Docs</a>
  • <a> stands for anchor.
  • href (hypertext reference) is the address the link goes to.
  • The text between the tags is what the reader sees and clicks.

By default, browsers show unvisited links blue and underlined, and visited links purple. You'll restyle them with CSS later.

Absolute and relative URLs

An absolute URL contains the full address, including https:// and the domain. Use it to link to other websites:

<a href="https://www.python.org/">Python's official site</a>

A relative URL is a path from the current page. Use it for pages on your own site:

<a href="about.html">About (same folder)</a>
<a href="blog/first-post.html">First post (inside the blog folder)</a>
<a href="../index.html">Home (one folder up)</a>
<a href="/contact/">Contact (from the site root)</a>
  • No slash at the start: relative to the current folder.
  • ../ goes up one folder.
  • A slash at the start (/contact/) starts from the root of the website.

Relative links keep working if you move the whole site to another domain, which is why sites use them internally.

Opening a link in a new tab

<a href="https://github.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">GitHub</a>

target="_blank" opens the link in a new tab. Add rel="noopener noreferrer" so the new page can't control your page through JavaScript (modern browsers do this automatically, but it's still a good habit).

Use new tabs sparingly. Readers can open a new tab themselves; forcing it can be confusing, especially on phones. A good rule: open in a new tab only when leaving the page would lose the reader's work, e.g. a link inside a half-filled form.

Linking to a section of a page

Give an element an id, then link to it with #:

<a href="#faq">Jump to the FAQ</a>

<!-- ... lots of content ... -->

<h2 id="faq">Frequently asked questions</h2>

Clicking the link scrolls straight to the heading. You can also combine it with a page address: href="guide.html#faq". The "On this page" box on VitalStack lessons works exactly like this.

Email and phone links

<a href="mailto:contact@example.com">Email us</a>
<a href="tel:+911234567890">Call us</a>

mailto: opens the reader's email app with the address filled in. tel: starts a call on phones. Note that email addresses in page code can be collected by spam bots, so many sites use a contact form instead.

Download links

<a href="files/cheatsheet.pdf" download>Download the cheat sheet</a>

The download attribute asks the browser to save the file instead of opening it.

Write link text that makes sense on its own

Screen reader users often list all the links on a page, and search engines use link text to understand the target page. "Click here" tells them nothing.

<!-- Avoid -->
<p>To learn about images, <a href="html-images.html">click here</a>.</p>

<!-- Better -->
<p>Next, learn how to <a href="html-images.html">add images to a page</a>.</p>

The title attribute

<a href="html-forms.html" title="Lesson 15: HTML Forms">Forms</a>

title shows a small tooltip on hover. It's a nice extra, but don't put important information only there: phone users and many screen reader users never see it.

Common mistakes

  • **Missing https://** in external links: href="google.com" is treated as a file in your own folder.
  • "Click here" link text. Describe the destination instead.
  • Spaces in file names like my page.html. Use hyphens: my-page.html.
  • **Linking to an id that doesn't exist** or has different spelling. #FAQ and #faq are different.

Exercise

  1. Make a link to your favourite website that opens in the same tab.
  2. Make a second link that opens in a new tab with the safe rel value.
  3. Add three <h2> sections with ids, and a small "table of contents" at the top with links to each.
  4. Add an email link that says "Write to me".

Summary

  • <a href="...">text</a> creates a link.
  • Use absolute URLs for other sites and relative URLs inside your own site.
  • #id links jump to a section; mailto: and tel: start emails and calls.
  • Write link text that describes where the link goes.

Next, you'll add pictures to your pages with images.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Images
items.excerpt: Add images with the img element, write useful alt text, set width and height, choose the right file format and make images load fast with lazy loading.
items.content:
Images make pages friendlier and easier to understand. In this lesson you'll add images with <img>, describe them for people who can't see them, and learn the habits that keep pages fast.

The img element

<img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1025/400/300" alt="A small dog wrapped in a blanket" width="400" height="300">
  • src (source) is the address of the image file, absolute or relative, just like a link.
  • alt (alternative text) describes the image.
  • width and height give the image's size in pixels.

<img> is an empty element: no closing tag.

Alt text: the most important attribute

Alt text is read aloud by screen readers, shown if the image fails to load, and used by search engines to understand the picture. Write what a person would need to know if they couldn't see it.

<!-- Too vague -->
<img src="chart.png" alt="chart">

<!-- Useful -->
<img src="chart.png" alt="Bar chart: Python is the most used language in the survey at 49%, JavaScript second at 41%">

Tips for good alt text:

  • Be specific and short; one sentence is usually enough.
  • Don't start with "Image of" or "Picture of". Screen readers already say it's an image.
  • If an image is pure decoration (a background swirl, a divider), use an empty alt: alt="". Screen readers then skip it. Never leave the attribute out completely.
  • If the image contains text, include that text in the alt.

Width and height prevent jumping pages

When a page loads, text often appears before images. If the browser doesn't know an image's size, it can't reserve space, so the text jumps down when the image arrives. Annoying for readers, and Google measures it as a quality signal ("layout shift").

Setting width and height to the image's real size lets the browser reserve the right space from the start. With CSS you can still make the image responsive later (max-width: 100%; height: auto;), and the browser keeps the correct proportions.

Image file formats

Large images are the most common reason pages load slowly. Resize a photo to the size it will actually be shown (there's no point sending a 4000-pixel photo for a 400-pixel box) and compress it.

Lazy loading

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Sunset over the sea" width="800" height="533" loading="lazy">

loading="lazy" tells the browser to load the image only when the reader scrolls near it. Use it for images further down the page. Don't use it for the main image at the top; that one should load right away.

Images as links

Put an <img> inside an <a> to make it clickable:

<a href="https://www.w3.org/">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/0/200/120" alt="Visit the W3C website" width="200" height="120">
</a>

When the image is the only content of a link, its alt text becomes the link text, so describe where the link goes.

Figures with captions

<figure>
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1043/400/260" alt="A wooden desk with a laptop and a notebook" width="400" height="260">
  <figcaption>My study setup: one laptop, one notebook, no distractions.</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure> groups an image with its caption (<figcaption>). The caption is visible to everyone; the alt describes the image itself. They usually say different things.

Common mistakes

  • Missing alt attribute. Always include it, even if it's empty for decoration.
  • Wrong path. src="Images/Photo.JPG" and images/photo.jpg are different files on most servers. Paths are case-sensitive.
  • Huge files. Resize and compress before uploading.
  • Using images of text for headings or buttons. Real text is sharper, searchable and translatable.

Exercise

  1. Add an image from https://picsum.photos/id/237/300/200 with good alt text, and width and height.
  2. Wrap it in a <figure> with a caption.
  3. Make the image a link to any website.
  4. Add a second image further down with loading="lazy".

Summary

  • <img src="..." alt="..." width="..." height="..."> adds an image.
  • Alt text describes the image; use alt="" only for decoration.
  • Width and height stop the page from jumping while it loads.
  • Choose the right format, keep files small, and lazy-load images lower on the page.

Next, you'll organise content with ordered, unordered and description lists.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Lists
items.excerpt: Unordered, ordered and description lists, nested lists, numbering options and why navigation menus are built from lists.
items.content:
Lists are everywhere: shopping lists, steps in a recipe, features of a product, the menu at the top of a website. HTML has three kinds of lists, and choosing the right one makes your content clearer for everyone.

Unordered lists

Use <ul> when the order doesn't matter. Each item goes in an <li> (list item):

<h3>Things to pack</h3>
<ul>
  <li>Laptop and charger</li>
  <li>Water bottle</li>
  <li>Notebook</li>
</ul>

Browsers show each item with a bullet point.

Ordered lists

Use <ol> when the order matters, such as steps or rankings:

<h3>Make a cup of tea</h3>
<ol>
  <li>Boil water.</li>
  <li>Add tea leaves and let them brew for 3 minutes.</li>
  <li>Add milk and sugar.</li>
  <li>Strain into a cup.</li>
</ol>

The browser numbers the items automatically. If you add or remove a step, the numbers update by themselves.

Changing the numbering

<ol> has a few useful attributes:

<ol type="A">
  <li>Option A</li>
  <li>Option B</li>
</ol>

<ol start="5">
  <li>This item is number 5</li>
  <li>This one is 6</li>
</ol>

<ol reversed>
  <li>Third place</li>
  <li>Second place</li>
  <li>Winner</li>
</ol>
  • type can be 1 (default), A, a, I or i.
  • start sets the first number.
  • reversed counts down.

Description lists

Use <dl> for pairs of terms and descriptions, like a glossary or a list of details:

<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>The language that gives a web page its structure.</dd>

  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>The language that controls how the page looks.</dd>

  <dt>JavaScript</dt>
  <dd>The language that makes the page interactive.</dd>
</dl>
  • <dl> is the description list.
  • <dt> is the term.
  • <dd> is the description of that term.

Nested lists

A list item can contain another list. Put the inner list inside the <li>, before its closing tag:

<ul>
  <li>Frontend
    <ul>
      <li>HTML</li>
      <li>CSS</li>
      <li>JavaScript</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Backend
    <ul>
      <li>Python</li>
      <li>SQL</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

Browsers indent nested lists and change the bullet style for each level.

Lists for navigation menus

Almost every website menu is a list of links inside a <nav> element:

<nav>
  <ul>
    <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/tutorials/">Tutorials</a></li>
    <li><a href="/blog/">Blog</a></li>
    <li><a href="/contact-us/">Contact</a></li>
  </ul>
</nav>

A menu *is* a list of choices, so this is the right meaning. Screen readers also announce "list, 4 items", which helps users know how big the menu is. With CSS you'll later remove the bullets and lay the links out in a row.

What can go inside a list

  • <ul> and <ol> may only contain <li> elements directly.
  • An <li> can contain almost anything: text, links, images, paragraphs, even other lists.
<!-- Wrong: text directly inside ul -->
<ul>
  Fruits
  <li>Apple</li>
</ul>

<!-- Right -->
<h4>Fruits</h4>
<ul>
  <li>Apple</li>
</ul>

Common mistakes

  • Typing bullet characters (• or -) at the start of paragraphs instead of using a real list.
  • **Closing the <li> before the nested list**, which places the inner list outside the item.
  • **Using <ol> for things with no order**, or <ul> for steps that must be followed in order.
  • **Putting headings or paragraphs directly in <ul>** without an <li>.

Exercise

  1. Make an unordered list of five programming languages.
  2. Make an ordered list with the steps to send an email.
  3. Create a nested list: three countries, each with two cities.
  4. Make a description list with three computer terms of your choice and their meanings.
  5. Build a small <nav> menu of four links using a list.

Summary

  • <ul> for unordered lists, <ol> for ordered lists, <li> for each item.
  • type, start and reversed change how ordered lists are numbered.
  • <dl>, <dt> and <dd> create description lists.
  • Nest a list inside an <li>; navigation menus are lists of links.

Next, you'll organise data in rows and columns with tables.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Tables
items.excerpt: Build tables with table, tr, th and td; add headers, captions and sections; merge cells with colspan and rowspan; and know when not to use a table.
items.content:
Tables show data in rows and columns: timetables, price lists, results, comparisons. HTML tables are built from a handful of elements that fit together like a grid.

A first table

<table>
  <tr>
    <th>Name</th>
    <th>Language</th>
    <th>Score</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Asha</td>
    <td>Python</td>
    <td>92</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Rohan</td>
    <td>JavaScript</td>
    <td>87</td>
  </tr>
</table>
  • <table> wraps the whole table.
  • <tr> (table row) creates a row.
  • <th> (table header) is a heading cell, shown bold and centred.
  • <td> (table data) is a normal cell.

Every row should have the same number of cells. By default, tables have no borders. You'll add them with CSS; for a quick test you can add border="1" to the <table> tag.

Captions

A <caption> gives the table a title. It must be the first thing inside <table>:

<table border="1">
  <caption>Class test results, March</caption>
  <tr>
    <th>Name</th>
    <th>Score</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Meera</td>
    <td>95</td>
  </tr>
</table>

Screen readers announce the caption before reading the table, so users know what they're about to hear.

Table sections: thead, tbody, tfoot

For larger tables, group the rows into sections:

<table border="1">
  <caption>Monthly expenses</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Item</th>
      <th>Cost (₹)</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Rent</td>
      <td>12,000</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Internet</td>
      <td>700</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Food</td>
      <td>6,500</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
  <tfoot>
    <tr>
      <th>Total</th>
      <td>19,200</td>
    </tr>
  </tfoot>
</table>
  • <thead> holds the header rows.
  • <tbody> holds the main data.
  • <tfoot> holds summary rows such as totals.

These sections make the structure clear, make styling easier, and let browsers repeat the header on every printed page.

Row headers and the scope attribute

Headers can label rows as well as columns. scope tells assistive technology which way a header points:

<table border="1">
  <tr>
    <th scope="col">Day</th>
    <th scope="col">Morning</th>
    <th scope="col">Evening</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th scope="row">Monday</th>
    <td>HTML</td>
    <td>Exercise</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <th scope="row">Tuesday</th>
    <td>CSS</td>
    <td>Reading</td>
  </tr>
</table>

Merging cells: colspan and rowspan

colspan makes a cell stretch across several columns; rowspan makes it stretch down several rows.

<table border="1">
  <tr>
    <th>Time</th>
    <th>Monday</th>
    <th>Tuesday</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>9:00</td>
    <td colspan="2">Team meeting (both days)</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>10:00</td>
    <td rowspan="2">Workshop</td>
    <td>Coding</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>11:00</td>
    <td>Review</td>
  </tr>
</table>

When a cell spans, the rows it covers have fewer <td> elements. In the last row above there are only two cells, because "Workshop" from the row before is still taking up the Monday column.

When not to use a table

Long ago, people built whole page layouts out of tables. Don't. Tables are for tabular data only: information that naturally has rows and columns. For page layout, use CSS Flexbox and Grid (you'll learn both in the CSS course). Layout tables confuse screen readers and are very hard to make work on phones.

Common mistakes

  • Different numbers of cells per row, which makes columns misalign.
  • **Using <td> for headings** with bold text instead of <th>.
  • **Putting the <caption> anywhere except first** inside <table>.
  • Forgetting to remove cells when using colspan or rowspan.
  • Using tables for layout.

Exercise

  1. Build a table of your weekly timetable: days as rows, three time slots as columns.
  2. Add a caption and <thead> / <tbody> sections.
  3. Use scope="row" on the day names.
  4. Merge two cells with colspan for an activity that lasts two slots.
  5. Add a <tfoot> row that counts the number of study sessions.

Summary

  • <table>, <tr>, <th> and <td> build the grid.
  • <caption>, <thead>, <tbody> and <tfoot> give it structure.
  • scope clarifies header direction; colspan and rowspan merge cells.
  • Use tables only for data, never for page layout.

Next, you'll meet the two general-purpose containers: div and span.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Div and Span
items.excerpt: Block and inline elements explained, and how the generic div and span containers group content for styling and scripting.
items.content:
So far, every element you've used has a meaning: a heading, a paragraph, a link. Sometimes you just need a container to group things together so you can style or move them. That's what <div> and <span> are for. To use them well, you first need to understand block and inline elements.

Block elements

A block element starts on a new line and stretches across the full width available. Paragraphs, headings, lists and tables are all block elements.

<h3>A heading</h3>
<p>A paragraph.</p>
<p>Another paragraph.</p>

Each one sits on its own line, stacked from top to bottom.

Inline elements

An inline element stays inside the flow of text. It only takes as much width as its content and doesn't start a new line. Links, <strong>, <em>, <code> and <img> are inline.

<p>This sentence has a <a href="#">link</a>, some <strong>bold text</strong> and <code>code</code> in it.</p>

All of these stay on the same line as the surrounding text.

A simple rule: block elements can contain inline elements, but inline elements shouldn't contain block elements. For example, don't put a <p> inside a <strong>.

The div element

<div> (division) is a generic block container. It has no meaning and no default style; it simply groups other elements.

<div style="background: #eef6ff; padding: 16px; border-radius: 8px;">
  <h3>Tip of the day</h3>
  <p>Save your work often. Press Ctrl + S.</p>
</div>

Here the div groups a heading and a paragraph into one box so they can share a background colour. The style attribute adds a little CSS; you'll learn proper ways to do this in the CSS course.

Divs are used for:

  • Grouping elements to style them together (cards, boxes, columns).
  • Building page layouts with CSS Flexbox or Grid.
  • Giving JavaScript one element to show, hide or update.

The span element

<span> is a generic inline container. Use it to style or target a few words inside a line of text:

<p>Your order status: <span style="color: green; font-weight: bold;">Delivered</span></p>
<p>Total: <span id="total">₹0</span></p>

The first span colours one word. The second gives JavaScript a handle: a script could find #total and update the price without touching the rest of the paragraph.

Div vs span

Use meaningful elements first

Div and span have no meaning. Before reaching for them, ask: is there an element that describes this content?

<!-- Avoid: a div pretending to be a heading -->
<div style="font-size: 24px; font-weight: bold;">Our team</div>

<!-- Better -->
<h2>Our team</h2>

HTML also has meaningful containers like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section> and <footer>. You'll learn them in the Semantic Elements lesson. Use those when they fit; use a div only when nothing else does.

Similarly, never build a clickable "button" from a div or span. Use a real <button>, which works with the keyboard and screen readers automatically.

A small card layout

<div style="border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 8px; padding: 16px; max-width: 280px;">
  <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/20/280/160" alt="A laptop on a desk" width="280" height="160">
  <h3>Learn HTML</h3>
  <p>20 lessons · <span style="color: #2563eb;">Beginner</span></p>
  <a href="#">Start learning</a>
</div>

One div wraps the whole card; one span highlights a single word inside the text.

Common mistakes

  • "Divitis": wrapping everything in many layers of divs. Keep the structure as simple as possible.
  • Divs instead of headings, lists or buttons. Use the element with the right meaning.
  • Putting a div inside a span or a paragraph. A block can't go inside inline content.

Exercise

  1. Create two "tip boxes" with divs, each with a different background colour, a heading and a paragraph.
  2. In a sentence, use spans to colour the words "red", "green" and "blue" in their own colours.
  3. Build a profile card for yourself like the example above.

Summary

  • Block elements start on a new line and fill the width; inline elements stay in the text.
  • <div> is a generic block container; <span> is a generic inline container.
  • Neither has any meaning, so use meaningful elements first.
  • Divs and spans are mainly used as hooks for CSS and JavaScript.

Next, you'll learn how to name elements with classes and ids.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Classes and IDs
items.excerpt: Name elements with the class and id attributes, use them from CSS and JavaScript, and learn the naming rules that keep a project tidy.
items.content:
As pages grow, you need a way to say "these five boxes should look the same" or "this one element is the shopping cart". The class and id attributes give elements names that CSS and JavaScript can use.

The class attribute

A class is a label you can give to any number of elements:

<style>
  .note {
    background: #fff7d6;
    border-left: 4px solid #f2b705;
    padding: 8px 12px;
  }
</style>

<p class="note">Remember to save your file before refreshing the browser.</p>
<p>A normal paragraph.</p>
<p class="note">File names are case-sensitive on most servers.</p>

The CSS rule .note (with a dot) styles every element that has class="note". Change the rule once, and every note on the site changes.

Several classes on one element

Separate class names with spaces:

<style>
  .btn { padding: 8px 16px; border-radius: 6px; border: none; }
  .btn-primary { background: #2563eb; color: white; }
  .btn-large { font-size: 20px; }
</style>

<button class="btn btn-primary">Save</button>
<button class="btn btn-primary btn-large">Sign up</button>
<button class="btn">Cancel</button>

This is how most real-world CSS works: small, reusable classes combined on each element.

The id attribute

An id is a unique name: only one element on a page may have a given id.

<style>
  #site-title { color: #2563eb; }
</style>

<h1 id="site-title">VitalStack</h1>

In CSS, an id is selected with #. Ids have three main uses:

  • Links to a section: <a href="#pricing"> jumps to id="pricing".
  • JavaScript: document.getElementById("cart") finds exactly one element.
  • Forms: a <label for="email"> is connected to the input with id="email".

Class vs id

A good habit: use classes for styling and keep ids for links, forms and JavaScript. Id rules in CSS are very "strong" and hard to override later, which you'll understand in the CSS Selectors lesson.

Classes and ids in JavaScript

<p id="greeting">Hello!</p>
<button class="change">Change greeting</button>

<script>
  document.querySelector(".change").addEventListener("click", function () {
    document.getElementById("greeting").textContent = "Welcome to VitalStack!";
  });
</script>

Click the button and the paragraph text changes. The script found the button by its class and the paragraph by its id. You'll learn this properly in the JavaScript course.

Naming rules and good habits

  • Names are case-sensitive: Note and note are different.
  • Don't use spaces inside one name (a space means "two classes"). Use hyphens: main-menu, card-title.
  • Don't start a name with a number.
  • Name things by what they are, not how they look: .warning is better than .red-text, because you might change the colour to orange next year.
  • Keep names short, lowercase and consistent across the site.

Common mistakes

  • The same id twice on a page. Links and JavaScript will only find the first one.
  • **Using . or # in the HTML attribute.** Write class="note", not class=".note". The dot belongs in CSS only.
  • **Writing class="btn" class="large".** Only the first one counts. Use class="btn large".
  • Naming by appearance, which makes names lie after a redesign.

Exercise

  1. Create a .card class with a border and padding, and use it on three divs.
  2. Add a second class .featured with a different background, and apply it to one of the cards as well.
  3. Give your page a heading with id="top" and add a "Back to top" link at the bottom.
  4. Change the button example so the button's text also changes after it's clicked.

Summary

  • class labels any number of elements; select them in CSS with .name.
  • id names one unique element; select it with #name.
  • An element can have many classes, separated by spaces.
  • Use classes for styling, ids for links, labels and JavaScript.

Next, you'll start collecting information from users with HTML forms.
