items.title: How to Start Learning to Code: A Realistic Roadmap
items.excerpt: A realistic plan for complete beginners: choosing your first language, setting up, a month-by-month roadmap, daily habits, getting unstuck and avoiding tutorial hell.
items.content:
Short answer: pick one goal (websites or data/automation), learn the matching first language (HTML, CSS and JavaScript for websites, Python for data and automation), practise a little every day, and start building small projects within your first month. Expect basic skills in about 3 months and job-ready skills in 6–12 months of steady practice.

Millions of people start learning to code; many give up within weeks, not because it's too hard, but because they lack a plan. Here's one.

Step 1: Choose a direction (not forever, just for now)

Your first language matters less than sticking with one long enough to get good. Choose based on what excites you:

If you're unsure, start with web basics (instant visual results, very motivating) or Python (simple syntax, huge range of uses). Both are excellent first choices, and skills transfer between languages.

Step 2: Set up (one evening)

  • For web: a browser and VS Code. That's it. You can even start in the browser with our Try it Yourself editor.
  • For Python: install Python and VS Code (our installation guide), or start online with Google Colab.

Don't spend weeks choosing the "perfect" setup. Any reasonable editor works.

Step 3: Follow one structured path

Jumping between random videos leaves gaps. Pick one course and finish it. On VitalStack:

  • Web path: HTML (20 lessons) → CSS (20) → JavaScript (25)
  • Data path: Python (20 lessons) → SQL (15)

Each course ends with a project that ties everything together.

A realistic first 6 months

Based on about 1 hour a day:

Some people go faster, some slower. What matters is that you keep going.

Daily habits that make the difference

Practise every day, even briefly

Thirty minutes daily beats five hours on Sunday. Coding is a skill like a musical instrument: regular practice builds it; cramming doesn't.

Type the code, don't just read it

Reading code feels like learning; typing, running and changing it is learning. Do every example and exercise.

Break things on purpose

Change a value, delete a bracket, rename a variable, and see what happens. Errors teach you how the language works.

Keep a learning log

At the end of each session, write two lines: what you learned and what confused you. Reviewing the log weekly shows real progress, which is great for motivation.

How to get unstuck

Being stuck is normal; every developer is stuck daily. A process:

  1. Read the error message, especially the last line. It usually says what's wrong and where.
  2. Explain the problem out loud (to a friend, a rubber duck, or in writing). Often you'll spot the issue while explaining.
  3. Check your assumptions with console.log() or print(): is that variable really what you think it is?
  4. Search the exact error message online.
  5. Ask for a hint from an AI assistant or a community, not the full solution (how to use AI for learning).
  6. Take a break. Seriously: the answer often appears after a walk.

Escaping "tutorial hell"

Tutorial hell is watching course after course but feeling unable to build anything alone. The cure:

  • Build something after every few lessons, without following a video.
  • Start tiny: a tip calculator, a quiz, a page about your hobby.
  • Add your own feature to every tutorial project.
  • Accept that it's hard. The discomfort of building alone is exactly where learning happens.

Beginner project ideas

Web:

  • Personal profile or portfolio page.
  • A recipe page with a list of ingredients that can be ticked off.
  • A tip calculator or unit converter.
  • A quiz with a score at the end.
  • A to-do list that saves to local storage.

Python:

  • A number-guessing game.
  • A password generator (using the secrets module).
  • An expense tracker that saves to JSON.
  • A script that renames or organises files in a folder.
  • A weather or quote fetcher using a public API.

Learn Git early

Git tracks changes to your code and GitHub shares it. Learn the basics by month 2 or 3; it's essential for every developer job and makes your portfolio visible. See Git and GitHub for Beginners.

Join a community

Learning alone is harder. Join a local meetup, a Discord or forum for learners, or study with a friend. Sharing progress keeps you accountable, and explaining things to others deepens your own understanding.

Common mistakes

  • Switching languages every few weeks. Depth beats breadth at the start.
  • Waiting until you "know enough" to build. Build from week 2.
  • Comparing yourself to others' highlight reels. Compare yourself to where you were last month.
  • Copying code without understanding it, especially from AI.
  • Skipping the boring basics. Variables, loops and functions are the foundation of everything.

Frequently asked questions

Am I too old to learn to code?

No. People successfully start at 30, 40, 50 and beyond. What matters is consistent practice, not age.

Do I need to be good at maths?

For web development and most programming: basic arithmetic and logical thinking are enough. Data science, games and AI research use more maths, which you can learn when you need it.

Do I need an expensive computer?

No. Any computer from the last several years can run a browser, VS Code and Python. You can even start on free online editors.

Free or paid courses?

Many excellent resources are free, including all VitalStack courses. Paid courses can add structure, feedback or certificates, but they're not required.

When can I get a job?

With focused daily practice, many people become job-ready in 6–12 months. You'll need fundamentals, 2–4 good portfolio projects (how to build them), Git, and interview practice.

Summary

  • Choose a direction: web (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) or data/automation (Python).
  • Follow one structured path and finish it.
  • Practise daily, type everything, and build small projects from the first month.
  • Get unstuck with a process, escape tutorial hell by building, and learn Git early.

items.title: HTML Forms
items.excerpt: How forms collect information: the form element, action and method, labels, text inputs, the name attribute and submit buttons.
items.content:
Every sign-up page, search box, contact page and checkout is a form. Forms let visitors send information to a website. In this lesson you'll build a complete basic form and understand what happens when it's submitted.

A first form

<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="name">Your name</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name">

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email">

  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

That's a working form with two fields and a button. Let's look at each part.

The form element

<form> wraps all the fields that are sent together. Its two most important attributes are:

  • action: the URL that receives the data. If you leave it out, the form submits to the current page.
  • method: how the data is sent, get or post.

GET or POST?

A search form is a perfect GET form:

<form action="https://www.google.com/search" method="get">
  <label for="q">Search Google</label>
  <input type="search" id="q" name="q">
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

Type a word and submit: you'll see ?q=yourword added to the address.

Labels

A <label> describes a field. Connect it to the field by making the label's for match the input's id:

<label for="city">City</label>
<input type="text" id="city" name="city">

Why this matters:

  • Clicking the label puts the cursor in the field, a bigger target on phones.
  • Screen readers read the label when the field gets focus. Without it, the user just hears "edit text" and has to guess.

You can also wrap the input inside the label, which connects them without for/id:

<label>City <input type="text" name="city"></label>

The name attribute

name is the key the data is sent with. A field without a name is not sent at all.

If someone types "Asha" into <input name="name"> and "asha@example.com" into <input name="email">, the server receives:

name=Asha&email=asha%40example.com

The id is for the page (labels, CSS, JavaScript); the name is for the server. They often have the same value, which is fine.

Placeholder and value

<label for="phone">Phone</label>
<input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone" placeholder="98765 43210">

<label for="country">Country</label>
<input type="text" id="country" name="country" value="India">
  • placeholder shows a light example inside an empty field. It disappears when the user types, so it should never replace the label.
  • value sets the starting content of the field. The user can change it.

Textarea for longer text

<label for="message">Message</label>
<textarea id="message" name="message" rows="5" cols="40"></textarea>

<textarea> is a multi-line text box. It has a closing tag; any text between the tags becomes its starting value.

Buttons

<button type="submit">Send</button>
<button type="reset">Clear form</button>
<button type="button">Does nothing by itself</button>
  • submit sends the form (this is the default for a button inside a form).
  • reset clears all fields back to their starting values; rarely useful, and easy to click by mistake.
  • button does nothing unless JavaScript gives it a job.

Grouping with fieldset and legend

<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Delivery address</legend>
    <label for="street">Street</label>
    <input type="text" id="street" name="street">
    <label for="pin">PIN code</label>
    <input type="text" id="pin" name="pin">
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Continue</button>
</form>

<fieldset> draws a box around related fields, and <legend> gives the group a title that screen readers announce.

Common mistakes

  • No labels, only placeholders. The hint vanishes as soon as the user types.
  • **Missing name** on a field, so its value is never sent.
  • **for and id that don't match** exactly (they're case-sensitive).
  • Sending passwords with GET, which puts them in the address bar and browser history.

Exercise

Build a "Contact us" form with:

  1. Name and email fields, each with a label.
  2. A subject field with a placeholder example.
  3. A message <textarea>.
  4. A submit button that says "Send message".
  5. Group name and email in a <fieldset> with the legend "Your details".

Submit it with method="get" and look at the URL to see exactly what would be sent.

Summary

  • <form> wraps fields; action says where data goes, method says how.
  • Use GET for searches, POST for anything private or that changes data.
  • Every field needs a <label> and a name.
  • <textarea> handles long text; <button type="submit"> sends the form.

Next, you'll learn all the input types: checkboxes, radio buttons, dropdowns, dates and built-in validation.
items.subject: html

items.title: HTML Form Inputs
items.excerpt: Every common input type, from email, number and date to checkboxes, radio buttons and dropdowns, plus built-in validation with required, min, max and pattern.
items.content:
The <input> element changes completely depending on its type. One attribute turns a plain text box into a date picker, a slider or a checkbox. Choosing the right type gives users the right keyboard on their phone and gives you free validation.

Text-like inputs

<form>
  <label for="u">Username</label>
  <input type="text" id="u" name="username"><br><br>

  <label for="e">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="e" name="email"><br><br>

  <label for="p">Password</label>
  <input type="password" id="p" name="password"><br><br>

  <label for="t">Phone</label>
  <input type="tel" id="t" name="phone"><br><br>

  <label for="w">Website</label>
  <input type="url" id="w" name="website"><br><br>

  <button>Send</button>
</form>
  • email checks for an @ and shows an email keyboard on phones.
  • password hides the characters.
  • tel shows a number pad on phones (it doesn't check the format, because phone formats differ by country).
  • url checks for a full web address.

Numbers, ranges and dates

<label for="qty">Quantity (1–10)</label>
<input type="number" id="qty" name="qty" min="1" max="10" value="1"><br><br>

<label for="vol">Volume</label>
<input type="range" id="vol" name="volume" min="0" max="100" step="5"><br><br>

<label for="dob">Date of birth</label>
<input type="date" id="dob" name="dob"><br><br>

<label for="time">Meeting time</label>
<input type="time" id="time" name="time"><br><br>

<label for="fav">Favourite colour</label>
<input type="color" id="fav" name="colour" value="#2563eb">

min, max and step limit what can be chosen. Date and time inputs show the device's own calendar or clock picker.

Checkboxes

Checkboxes let users pick any number of options:

<p>Which languages do you know?</p>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="langs" value="html"> HTML</label><br>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="langs" value="css" checked> CSS</label><br>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="langs" value="js"> JavaScript</label>
  • value is what gets sent when the box is ticked (if you leave it out, the browser sends "on").
  • checked ticks the box from the start.
  • Unticked boxes send nothing.

Radio buttons

Radio buttons let users pick exactly one option from a group. Buttons with the **same name** form one group:

<p>Choose a plan:</p>
<label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="free" checked> Free</label><br>
<label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="pro"> Pro</label><br>
<label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="team"> Team</label>

Clicking one automatically un-selects the others. If each radio had a different name, they'd all be selectable at once, the most common radio-button bug.

Dropdowns with select

<label for="course">Course</label>
<select id="course" name="course">
  <option value="">Choose a course…</option>
  <option value="html">HTML</option>
  <option value="css">CSS</option>
  <option value="js" selected>JavaScript</option>
</select>

Use <optgroup label="..."> to group long lists, and add multiple to let users pick several options (though checkboxes are usually easier for that).

File uploads and hidden fields

<label for="cv">Upload your CV (PDF)</label>
<input type="file" id="cv" name="cv" accept=".pdf">

<input type="hidden" name="source" value="newsletter">

A form with a file input must use method="post" and enctype="multipart/form-data". Hidden inputs send a value the user doesn't see, such as which page the form came from.

Built-in validation

The browser can check fields before the form is sent, with no JavaScript:

<form>
  <label for="n">Name (required)</label>
  <input type="text" id="n" name="name" required minlength="2"><br><br>

  <label for="age">Age (13–120)</label>
  <input type="number" id="age" name="age" min="13" max="120"><br><br>

  <label for="pin">PIN code (6 digits)</label>
  <input type="text" id="pin" name="pin" pattern="[0-9]{6}" title="Six digits, e.g. 400001"><br><br>

  <button>Submit</button>
</form>

Try submitting it empty or with wrong values: the browser stops and shows a message.

  • required: the field can't be empty.
  • minlength / maxlength: text length limits.
  • min / max: number and date limits.
  • pattern: a regular expression the value must match; describe the format in title or near the field.

Important: browser validation helps users, but anyone can bypass it. A server must always check the data again.

Other useful attributes

  • disabled: the field can't be used and isn't sent.
  • readonly: the field can't be changed but is sent.
  • autocomplete="email" (or name, tel, street-address…): lets the browser fill in saved details.
  • autofocus: puts the cursor in this field when the page loads (use once, at most).

Common mistakes

  • Radio buttons with different names, so more than one can be selected.
  • **Using type="text" for everything**, missing the right phone keyboards and free checks.
  • Trusting browser validation alone. Always validate on the server too.
  • **Checkboxes without value**, so the server receives "on" with no idea which option it was.

Exercise

Build a course registration form with:

  1. Name (required), email (type email, required) and age (13–100).
  2. A dropdown of three courses.
  3. Radio buttons for "Morning" or "Evening" batch.
  4. Checkboxes for "I have a laptop" and "Send me updates".
  5. A start date picker.

Try to submit it with empty and wrong values and read the browser's messages.

Summary

  • The type attribute turns <input> into the right control for each kind of data.
  • Checkboxes allow many choices; radio buttons with the same name allow one.
  • <select> creates a dropdown from <option> elements.
  • required, min, max, minlength and pattern give free validation, but the server must check again.

Next, you'll learn semantic elements that describe the structure of a whole page.

items.title: HTML Semantic Elements
items.excerpt: Describe the parts of a page with header, nav, main, article, section, aside and footer, and see why meaningful HTML helps readers and search engines.
items.content:
"Semantic" means "related to meaning". A semantic element tells the browser what its content is, not just how to show it. <h1> and <p> are semantic; <div> isn't. HTML has a set of semantic elements for the big parts of a page: the header, the menu, the main content, the sidebar and the footer.

The page layout elements

Most websites follow the same pattern:

<body>
  <header>
    <h1>My Coding Blog</h1>
    <nav>
      <ul>
        <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/blog/">Blog</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about/">About</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </header>

  <main>
    <article>
      <h2>How I learned HTML in 30 days</h2>
      <p>It started with one simple page…</p>
    </article>
  </main>

  <aside>
    <h3>Popular posts</h3>
    <ul>
      <li><a href="#">10 CSS tips</a></li>
    </ul>
  </aside>

  <footer>
    <p><small>© My Coding Blog</small></p>
  </footer>
</body>

Without any CSS this looks the same as a pile of divs, but the code now describes the page.

What each element means

header

Introductory content: a site logo and title, or the heading area of an article. A page can have several headers: one for the site and one inside each article.

nav

A block of major navigation links: the main menu, a table of contents, pagination. Not every group of links needs <nav>; footer links to legal pages, for example, usually don't.

main

The main content of the page, the part that's unique to it. There should be only one visible <main> per page, and it shouldn't include things repeated on every page like the site header, menu or footer.

article

A self-contained piece of content that would make sense on its own, even if copied to another site: a blog post, a news story, a product card, a forum post, a comment.

section

A thematic group of content, usually with its own heading: "Features", "Pricing", "FAQ". If you can't think of a heading for it, you probably want a <div> instead.

aside

Content that's related but not essential: a sidebar, a "did you know?" box, related links, ads.

footer

The closing part of a page or an article: copyright, contact details, related links, author info.

Article or section?

A simple test: would it make sense on its own? Then it's an <article>. Is it one part of something bigger? Then it's a <section>. They can also be nested both ways:

<article>
  <h2>Getting Started with Python</h2>
  <section>
    <h3>Installing Python</h3>
    <p>Download it from python.org…</p>
  </section>
  <section>
    <h3>Your first program</h3>
    <p>Open your editor and type print("Hello")…</p>
  </section>
</article>

Other useful semantic elements

<p>Published on <time datetime="2026-03-14">14 March</time></p>

<details>
  <summary>What is a semantic element?</summary>
  <p>An element whose name describes the meaning of its content.</p>
</details>

<address>
  Written by Asha. Contact: <a href="mailto:asha@example.com">asha@example.com</a>
</address>
  • <time> marks a date or time; datetime gives it in a format computers understand.
  • <details> and <summary> create a collapsible box with no JavaScript. Great for FAQs.
  • <address> holds contact information for the author or owner.
  • <figure> and <figcaption>, from the images lesson, are semantic too.

Why semantic HTML matters

  • Accessibility. Screen readers announce landmarks like "navigation" and "main", and let users jump straight to them. A "skip to content" experience comes almost for free.
  • Search engines understand which part is the real content and which part is the menu or footer.
  • Readable code. </article> tells you far more than the seventh </div> in a row.
  • Reader modes in browsers use these elements to show a clean version of your page.

Common mistakes

  • **More than one <main>** on a page.
  • **Wrapping everything in <section>**, even blocks with no heading. Use <div> for pure styling groups.
  • **Using <aside> for main content**, just because it's displayed in a side column.
  • Forgetting headings inside sections and articles.

Exercise

Take any page you've built in this course (or start a new one) and:

  1. Wrap the title and menu in <header> and <nav>.
  2. Put the main content in <main> with one <article> and two <section>s inside it.
  3. Add an <aside> with three related links.
  4. Add a <footer> with a copyright line.
  5. Add a FAQ with two <details> boxes.

Summary

  • Semantic elements describe meaning: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <aside>, <footer>.
  • One <main> per page; <article> stands alone; <section> is a themed part with a heading.
  • <time>, <details>/<summary> and <address> add meaning to smaller pieces.
  • Semantic HTML helps accessibility, search engines and your own code.

Next, you'll add audio and video to your pages.

items.title: HTML Media (Audio and Video)
items.excerpt: Play sound and video with the audio and video elements, offer several file formats, add captions, and embed YouTube videos with iframe.
items.content:
Before HTML5, playing a video on a web page needed a plugin like Flash. Today the browser does it on its own with two elements: <video> and <audio>. In this lesson you'll use both, add captions, and embed videos from YouTube.

The video element

<video src="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-videos/flower.mp4"
       width="400" height="225" controls>
  Your browser does not support the video element.
</video>
  • src is the video file.
  • controls shows the play button, timeline and volume. Without it, the user has no way to start the video.
  • width and height reserve space, just like with images.
  • The text inside the tags only appears in very old browsers that can't play video.

Useful video attributes

<video src="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-videos/flower.mp4"
       width="400" height="225"
       controls muted loop playsinline
       poster="https://picsum.photos/id/106/400/225"
       preload="metadata">
</video>
  • poster: an image shown before the video starts.
  • muted: starts with sound off.
  • loop: starts again at the end.
  • autoplay: starts playing by itself. Browsers only allow this if the video is also muted, because surprise sound is annoying.
  • playsinline: on iPhones, plays inside the page instead of going full-screen.
  • preload: none, metadata (just the length and size) or auto. Use none or metadata to save your readers' mobile data.

Several formats with source

Not every browser supports every format. You can list several files and the browser picks the first one it can play:

<video width="400" height="225" controls>
  <source src="movie.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="movie.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Sorry, your browser can't play this video.
</video>

Today MP4 (H.264) plays in every modern browser, so a single MP4 file is usually enough. WebM files are often smaller, so listing WebM first and MP4 as a fallback is a common pattern.

The audio element

<audio controls src="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-audio/t-rex-roar.mp3">
  Your browser does not support the audio element.
</audio>

<audio> works just like <video>, with controls, loop, muted, preload and <source> elements. MP3 plays everywhere.

Captions and subtitles with track

Captions help deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers, people watching without sound (most mobile viewers), and people who speak another language.

<video width="400" height="225" controls>
  <source src="lesson.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track src="lesson-en.vtt" kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  <track src="lesson-hi.vtt" kind="subtitles" srclang="hi" label="Hindi">
</video>

Caption files use the simple WebVTT format:

WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:04.000
Welcome to the HTML video lesson.

00:00:04.000 --> 00:00:08.000
Today we'll add captions to a video.

Embedding YouTube videos with iframe

Video files are large, and streaming them from your own hosting can be slow and expensive. For long videos, upload them to YouTube and embed them with an <iframe> (an element that shows another web page inside yours):

<iframe width="400" height="225"
        src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID"
        title="Lesson video: HTML basics"
        loading="lazy"
        allow="accelerometer; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture"
        allowfullscreen></iframe>

Replace VIDEO_ID with the code from the video's address (the part after watch?v=). YouTube's Share → Embed button gives you this code ready-made.

  • title describes the frame for screen readers. Always add it.
  • loading="lazy" delays loading until the reader scrolls near it, which saves a lot of data.
  • youtube-nocookie.com is YouTube's privacy-friendlier version that doesn't set tracking cookies until the user plays the video.

Good practice with media

  • Never autoplay with sound.
  • Provide captions for videos with speech and a transcript for audio such as podcasts. Transcripts also help search engines understand the content.
  • Keep files small: compress videos and use a sensible resolution (720p is plenty for most lesson clips).
  • Don't put essential information *only* in a video. Some readers can't or won't play it.

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting controls**, which leaves an un-playable box.
  • **Autoplay without muted**: the browser blocks it.
  • Huge video files on cheap hosting, which make pages slow. Use YouTube or a video host.
  • **An iframe without a title.**

Exercise

  1. Add the flower video with controls, a poster image and preload="metadata".
  2. Make a muted, looping version without controls, like a background clip.
  3. Add the audio example.
  4. Embed any YouTube video using its Share → Embed code, and add a title and loading="lazy".

Summary

  • <video> and <audio> play media without plugins; add controls.
  • Use <source> for several formats and <track> for captions.
  • Autoplay only works muted, and should be rare.
  • Embed long videos from YouTube with an <iframe> that has a title.

items.title: HTML Accessibility Basics
items.excerpt: Make pages everyone can use: who relies on accessibility, keyboard access, alt text, labels, contrast, headings, landmarks and when to use ARIA.
items.content:
Accessibility (often shortened to a11y: "a", eleven letters, "y") means building pages that everyone can use, including people who are blind, have low vision, are deaf, can't use a mouse, or have trouble reading. The good news: if you've followed this course, you're already doing most of it, because accessible HTML is mostly *correct* HTML.

Who benefits

  • Screen reader users (blind or low vision) hear the page read aloud and navigate by headings, links and landmarks.
  • Keyboard users (people with motor disabilities, power users) move through the page with Tab, Enter and the arrow keys.
  • People who zoom the page to 200% or more.
  • Deaf and hard-of-hearing users rely on captions and transcripts.
  • Everyone else, sometimes: a broken arm, bright sunlight on a phone screen, a slow connection, a noisy train.

Accessible sites also tend to rank better in search, because search engines "read" pages in a similar way to screen readers.

1. Use the right element

The single biggest rule. Native elements come with built-in keyboard support and meaning:

<!-- Bad: looks like a button, but keyboard users can't reach or press it -->
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

<!-- Good: focusable, works with Enter and Space, announced as "button" -->
<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

Use <button> for actions, <a href> for going somewhere, headings for titles, lists for lists.

2. Text alternatives

<img src="team.jpg" alt="Our five team members at the 2025 hackathon">
<img src="divider.png" alt="">

Every image needs alt: a description for meaningful images, empty for decoration. Videos need captions; audio needs a transcript.

3. Label every form field

<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">

A placeholder is not a label. Error messages should be in text near the field and say how to fix the problem ("Enter an email like name@example.com"), not just turn the field red.

4. A clear heading structure

One <h1>, then <h2> and <h3> in order. Many screen reader users jump from heading to heading to find what they need, just as sighted users skim.

5. Landmarks

<header>…</header>
<nav aria-label="Main">…</nav>
<main>…</main>
<footer>…</footer>

Semantic layout elements become landmarks that screen readers list and jump to. If you have two <nav>s, give each an aria-label so users can tell them apart.

6. Keyboard access and focus

Try this now: put your mouse away and press Tab to move through any website. You should:

  • Reach every link, button and field, in a logical order.
  • Always see where you are (the focus outline).
  • Be able to activate everything with Enter or Space.

Never remove the focus outline with CSS (outline: none) unless you replace it with another clear style.

A skip link lets keyboard users jump past the menu:

<a href="#main" class="skip-link">Skip to content</a>
<header>…long menu…</header>
<main id="main">…</main>

7. Colour and contrast

  • Text needs enough contrast with its background: at least 4.5:1 for normal text. Light grey on white often fails. Browser developer tools can check contrast for you.
  • Never use colour alone to carry meaning. "Fields in red are required" fails for colour-blind users; add a word or symbol: "Email (required)".

8. Language and page title

<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>Contact us · VitalStack</title>
</head>

lang makes screen readers use the right pronunciation. A unique, descriptive <title> is the first thing a screen reader announces on a new page.

9. ARIA: only when HTML isn't enough

ARIA attributes add extra information for assistive technology:

<button aria-label="Close menu">✕</button>
<button aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="menu">Menu</button>
<p role="alert">Your message has been sent.</p>
  • aria-label gives a name to an element with no visible text, like an icon button.
  • aria-expanded tells users whether a menu is open.
  • role="alert" makes a screen reader announce a message immediately.

The first rule of ARIA: don't use ARIA if a native element does the job. A <button> is better than <div role="button">. Wrong ARIA is worse than none.

Quick checklist

  • ☐ Every image has suitable alt text.
  • ☐ Every form field has a label.
  • ☐ Headings are in order; one <h1>.
  • ☐ Everything works with the keyboard, and focus is visible.
  • ☐ Text contrast is strong enough; colour is never the only signal.
  • ☐ lang and a unique <title> are set.
  • ☐ Videos have captions.

Common mistakes

  • Clickable divs and spans instead of buttons and links.
  • Removing focus outlines for looks.
  • "Click here" links and icon buttons with no name.
  • Adding ARIA everywhere instead of using the right HTML.

Exercise

  1. Take your form from the Form Inputs lesson and check every field has a working label (click each label: the field should get focus).
  2. Use only the Tab key to fill in and submit the form.
  3. Add a "Skip to content" link to your semantic page from lesson 17.
  4. Find an icon-only button (like ✕) and give it an aria-label.

Summary

  • Accessible HTML is mostly correct, semantic HTML.
  • Alt text, labels, headings, landmarks and visible focus cover most needs.
  • Check contrast and never use colour alone.
  • Use ARIA only when native HTML can't express what you need.

items.title: HTML Project: Build a Personal Profile Page
items.excerpt: Put the whole HTML course into practice by building a complete, accessible personal profile page step by step, ready to style in the CSS course.
items.content:
Time to use everything you've learned. In this project you'll build a complete personal profile page: a header with a menu, an about section, a skills list, a projects table, a contact form and a footer. It's pure HTML for now; in the CSS course you'll make it beautiful.

What you'll build

The finished page has:

  1. A header with your name and a navigation menu that jumps to each section.
  2. An "About me" section with a photo and a short introduction.
  3. A "Skills" section with a nested list.
  4. A "Projects" table.
  5. A "Contact" form.
  6. A FAQ with collapsible answers.
  7. A footer.

Work step by step. After each step, check the result with Try it Yourself or in your own editor.

Step 1: The skeleton

Start with the basic structure from lesson 3 and the semantic layout from lesson 17:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>Asha Verma · Web Developer</title>
</head>
<body>
  <a href="#main">Skip to content</a>

  <header>
    <h1>Asha Verma</h1>
    <p>Beginner web developer from Pune</p>
    <nav aria-label="Main">
      <ul>
        <li><a href="#about">About</a></li>
        <li><a href="#skills">Skills</a></li>
        <li><a href="#projects">Projects</a></li>
        <li><a href="#contact">Contact</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </header>

  <main id="main">
    <!-- sections go here -->
  </main>

  <footer>
    <p><small>© Asha Verma. Built with plain HTML.</small></p>
  </footer>
</body>
</html>

Replace the name, city and title with your own (or invent a character). Notice the menu links point to ids you'll create next.

Step 2: About me

Inside <main>, add the first section:

<section id="about">
  <h2>About me</h2>
  <figure>
    <img src="https://picsum.photos/id/64/240/240" alt="Asha smiling, sitting at a desk with a laptop" width="240" height="240">
    <figcaption>Learning to code, one lesson a day.</figcaption>
  </figure>
  <p>Hi! I'm Asha. I started learning web development in January and I'm <strong>building one small project every week</strong>.</p>
  <p>Before coding, I worked in <em>customer support</em>, which taught me to explain things clearly. Now I want to build websites that are <mark>simple and easy to use</mark>.</p>
</section>

You used: a heading, a figure with an image and caption, paragraphs, and text formatting.

Step 3: Skills

<section id="skills">
  <h2>Skills</h2>
  <ul>
    <li>Frontend
      <ul>
        <li>HTML: semantic pages, forms, tables</li>
        <li>CSS: learning now</li>
      </ul>
    </li>
    <li>Tools
      <ul>
        <li>VS Code</li>
        <li>Browser developer tools</li>
      </ul>
    </li>
  </ul>

  <h3>Learning plan</h3>
  <ol>
    <li>Finish the HTML course</li>
    <li>Learn CSS layout with Flexbox and Grid</li>
    <li>Start JavaScript</li>
  </ol>
</section>

An unordered list for skills (no order), an ordered list for the plan (order matters).

Step 4: Projects table

<section id="projects">
  <h2>Projects</h2>
  <table border="1">
    <caption>Things I've built so far</caption>
    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th scope="col">Project</th>
        <th scope="col">What I learned</th>
        <th scope="col">Link</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr>
        <th scope="row">Recipe page</th>
        <td>Headings, lists and images</td>
        <td><a href="#">View</a></td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <th scope="row">Timetable</th>
        <td>Tables with colspan</td>
        <td><a href="#">View</a></td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <th scope="row">This profile</th>
        <td>Putting it all together</td>
        <td><a href="#main">You're here</a></td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
</section>

Step 5: Contact form

<section id="contact">
  <h2>Contact me</h2>
  <form action="https://example.com/contact" method="post">
    <fieldset>
      <legend>Your details</legend>
      <p>
        <label for="name">Name</label><br>
        <input type="text" id="name" name="name" autocomplete="name" required>
      </p>
      <p>
        <label for="email">Email</label><br>
        <input type="email" id="email" name="email" autocomplete="email" required>
      </p>
    </fieldset>

    <p>Reason for contacting:</p>
    <p>
      <label><input type="radio" name="reason" value="project" checked> A project</label><br>
      <label><input type="radio" name="reason" value="hello"> Just saying hello</label>
    </p>

    <p>
      <label for="message">Message</label><br>
      <textarea id="message" name="message" rows="5" cols="40" required minlength="10"></textarea>
    </p>

    <button type="submit">Send message</button>
  </form>
</section>

Labels on every field, the right input types, validation, and grouped radio buttons.

Step 6: FAQ

<section id="faq">
  <h2>FAQ</h2>
  <details>
    <summary>Are you available for freelance work?</summary>
    <p>Small HTML and CSS projects, yes. Use the contact form.</p>
  </details>
  <details>
    <summary>How long have you been coding?</summary>
    <p>Since <time datetime="2026-01">January 2026</time>.</p>
  </details>
</section>

Step 7: Check your work

Go through this checklist:

  • ☐ Every menu link jumps to the right section.
  • ☐ Only one <h1>; headings go h2 → h3 without skipping.
  • ☐ Every image has alt text, width and height.
  • ☐ Every form field has a label; submitting empty fields shows browser messages.
  • ☐ You can reach every link and field using only the Tab key.
  • ☐ No ids are repeated.

For a final check, paste your page into the free W3C Markup Validator (validator.w3.org, "Validate by Direct Input"). It lists any mistakes in your HTML; fix them until it shows no errors.

Ideas to extend it

  • Add a "Currently learning" section with a short <blockquote> from a favourite programmer.
  • Add a short YouTube video introducing yourself, with loading="lazy" and a title.
  • Make a second page, projects.html, and link between the two pages.

What you've learned in this course

Over 20 lessons you've gone from "what is HTML?" to a complete, accessible, semantic page. You can now structure text, links, images, lists, tables, forms and media, and you know how to make pages that work for everyone.

Summary

  • A complete page combines structure, content and forms inside semantic landmarks.
  • Check menus, headings, alt text, labels and keyboard access before calling it done.
  • The W3C validator is a free way to find mistakes.

Next comes the CSS course, where you'll take this exact page and give it colours, fonts, spacing and a modern layout.

items.title: CSS Introduction
items.excerpt: What CSS is, how a CSS rule is built from a selector and declarations, and why separating style from HTML makes websites easier to build and change.
items.content:
HTML gives a page its structure: headings, paragraphs, lists, forms. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how that structure looks: colours, fonts, spacing, layout, even animations. Every good-looking website you've ever used is HTML plus CSS.

Before and after CSS

Here is a small page with no CSS at all:

<h1>VitalStack</h1>
<p>Learn to code, one lesson at a time.</p>
<a href="#">Start learning</a>

It works, but it looks plain. Now the same HTML with a few lines of CSS:

<style>
  body {
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
    background: #f5f7fb;
    padding: 32px;
  }
  h1 {
    color: #2563eb;
  }
  a {
    display: inline-block;
    background: #2563eb;
    color: white;
    padding: 10px 18px;
    border-radius: 8px;
    text-decoration: none;
  }
</style>

<h1>VitalStack</h1>
<p>Learn to code, one lesson at a time.</p>
<a href="#">Start learning</a>

Open it with Try it Yourself. The HTML didn't change at all; CSS changed the font, the background, the heading colour, and turned a plain link into a button.

Anatomy of a CSS rule

h1 {
  color: #2563eb;
  font-size: 32px;
}
  • h1 is the selector: which elements the rule applies to.
  • Everything inside { } is the declaration block.
  • color: #2563eb; is a declaration, made of a property (color) and a value (#2563eb), separated by a colon and ending with a semicolon.

A rule can have as many declarations as you like. Put each on its own line to keep it readable.

What "cascading" means

Several rules can apply to the same element. The cascade is the set of rules that decides which one wins. In short:

  1. More specific selectors beat less specific ones (an id beats a class, a class beats an element name).
  2. If two rules are equally specific, the one that comes later wins.
<style>
  p { color: gray; }
  p { color: green; }
</style>
<p>What colour am I?</p>

The paragraph is green, because the second rule comes later. You'll learn the full details in the Selectors lesson.

Inheritance

Some properties, mainly text-related ones like color, font-family and line-height, are inherited: children take them from their parent. That's why setting a font on body changes the font of the whole page. Box-related properties such as border, padding and background are not inherited.

Why keep style separate from HTML

You *could* style every element with a style attribute, but separating CSS from HTML has big advantages:

  • Change once, update everywhere. One stylesheet can style hundreds of pages. Change a colour in one place and the whole site updates.
  • Cleaner HTML that only describes content.
  • Faster sites: the browser downloads the stylesheet once and caches it.
  • Different looks for different devices (phone, desktop, print) from the same HTML.

CSS comments

/* Main heading colour */
h1 {
  color: #2563eb; /* brand blue */
}

Comments start with /* and end with */. CSS has no // single-line comments.

Common mistakes

  • Missing semicolons. color: red font-size: 20px; breaks both declarations. End every declaration with ;.
  • Missing closing brace }, which can break every rule after it.
  • Spelling property names wrong (colour instead of color). The browser silently ignores properties it doesn't know.
  • Spaces in values where they don't belong, like 20 px. Write 20px.

Exercise

Open the "after" example with Try it Yourself and:

  1. Change the heading colour to any colour you like.
  2. Change the background of the page to white.
  3. Make the button's corners fully round with border-radius: 999px;.
  4. Add a rule for p that sets font-size: 18px; and color: #444;.

Summary

  • CSS controls how HTML looks: colours, fonts, spacing and layout.
  • A rule = selector + declaration block; a declaration = property + value.
  • The cascade decides which rule wins; some properties are inherited.
  • Keeping CSS separate from HTML makes sites easier to change and faster.

Next, you'll learn the three ways to add CSS to a page.

items.title: How to Write Better AI Prompts: A Practical Guide
items.excerpt: A practical framework for writing prompts that get useful answers from AI assistants, with before-and-after examples for coding, writing, learning and data tasks.
items.content:
Short answer: a good prompt gives the AI what a smart new colleague would need: the goal, the context, the constraints, the format you want, and ideally an example. Vague prompts get generic answers; specific prompts get useful ones.

AI assistants are only as helpful as the instructions they receive. This guide gives you a simple framework and real before-and-after examples you can adapt today.

Why prompts matter

A language model predicts a likely response to your text (see How Large Language Models Work). If your prompt could mean ten different things, you'll get an average of all ten. If it's precise, the most likely response is the one you actually want.

Compare:

Weak:   Write about Python.

Strong: Write a 150-word introduction to Python for a complete beginner
        who wants to analyse sales data in Excel. Mention one thing Python
        does better than Excel, avoid jargon, and end with a suggested first step.

The second prompt answers every question the AI would otherwise guess: who it's for, how long, what to include, what tone, how to end.

The framework: G-C-C-F-E

Goal: what do you want?

Start with the task in one clear sentence. Use action verbs: *explain, write, fix, compare, summarise, list, rewrite, review*.

Context: what does it need to know?

Who's the audience? What have you already tried? What's the situation? The AI knows nothing about your project, your level or your constraints unless you say so.

Constraints: what are the rules?

Length, tone, language, things to avoid, tools or versions to use: "Use only the standard library", "no more than 5 bullet points", "keep my original meaning".

Format: how should the answer look?

Bullet list, table, numbered steps, code only, JSON with specific keys, an email ready to send. If you'll paste the answer somewhere, say how it needs to look.

Example: show what good looks like

One short example often beats a paragraph of description. Show the style, structure or output you want.

You don't need all five every time. For quick questions, goal plus context is often enough. For anything you'll reuse or publish, use all five.

Before and after: coding

Weak:
My code doesn't work, fix it.
[code]

Strong:
This Python function should return the average of a list of numbers,
but it crashes with "ZeroDivisionError" when the list is empty.

[code]

1. Explain in one sentence why it crashes.
2. Fix it so an empty list returns 0.
3. Keep the function name and signature the same.
4. Add two quick test cases using assert.

What changed: the expected behaviour, the exact error, the constraint (same signature) and the output format (explanation, fix, tests).

Tip: always paste the exact error message and say what you expected to happen. "It doesn't work" forces the AI to guess.

Before and after: learning a concept

Weak:
Explain recursion.

Strong:
I'm learning JavaScript and understand loops and functions, but recursion
confuses me. Explain recursion using a real-life analogy first, then a
simple JavaScript example that counts down from 5, then show me the same
thing as a loop so I can compare. Finish with one practice exercise
(without the answer).

Asking for an analogy, a comparison with something you already know, and an exercise turns the AI into a tutor instead of an encyclopaedia.

Before and after: writing

Weak:
Write an email to my manager about leave.

Strong:
Write a short, polite email to my manager, Priya, asking for leave on
the 14th and 15th for a family wedding. I've already finished the report
due that week and Rohan has agreed to cover urgent messages. Tone: friendly
but professional. Under 120 words. Include a subject line.

The details make the email ready to send, instead of a template full of [brackets].

Before and after: data tasks

Weak:
Analyse this data.

Strong:
Below is CSV data of monthly sales (columns: month, region, revenue).
1. Which region grew the most from the first to the last month, in %?
2. Are there any months that look like errors or outliers?
3. Give the answer as a short table, then 2–3 sentences of insight.
If something can't be determined from the data, say so instead of guessing.

[data]

The last line is important: give the AI permission to say "I don't know". It reduces made-up answers.

Techniques that work

Assign a role (lightly)

"Act as a senior Python reviewer" or "You're a patient tutor for beginners" sets the tone and depth. It helps, but specifics about the task matter more than the role.

Ask for steps before the answer

For reasoning problems, "work through this step by step, then give the final answer" often improves accuracy, and lets you see where it went wrong.

Break big tasks into smaller prompts

Instead of "build me a complete website", go step by step: plan the pages → write the HTML for the home page → add the CSS → add the contact form. You stay in control and can correct course early.

Iterate: the first answer is a draft

Reply with what to change: "Shorter", "more examples", "use a table", "the second point is wrong because…". Conversation is part of prompting.

Ask it to ask you questions

"Before you answer, ask me up to 3 questions about anything that's unclear." Great for plans, designs and anything personal.

Use delimiters for pasted content

Separate instructions from material with clear markers:

Summarise the article between the triple quotes in 5 bullet points
for a busy executive.

"""
[article text]
"""

This helps the model tell your instructions apart from the content.

Prompts to save and reuse

Code review:
Review this [language] code for bugs, security issues and readability.
List problems in order of importance, with a fix for each. Don't rewrite
the whole file. [code]

Explain an error:
I got this error: [error]. Here's the code: [code]. Explain what it means
in plain English, the most likely cause, and how to fix it.

Study plan:
Create a [n]-week plan to learn [topic] for someone who knows [current
skills] and has [hours] hours a week. Include weekly goals and one small
project per week.

Summarise:
Summarise the text below in [n] bullet points for [audience]. Keep numbers
and names exact. [text]

Limits to remember

  • Check facts and code. A great prompt reduces errors but doesn't remove them. Run the code; verify claims that matter.
  • Don't paste secrets (passwords, API keys, private customer data) into AI tools unless your organisation allows it.
  • Your judgement is the final step, especially for anything published, legal, medical or financial.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need special "magic words"?

No. Clear, specific, complete instructions beat tricks. Write as you would to a capable colleague who knows nothing about your situation.

Should prompts be long?

As long as needed, no longer. Add details that change the answer; skip filler like "please kindly".

Why do I get different answers to the same prompt?

Models use some randomness when generating text. If you need consistency, be more specific, give an example of the exact format, or ask for a fixed structure.

Is prompt engineering a real job skill?

Yes, as part of other jobs. Developers building AI features, writers, analysts and support teams all benefit from writing clear prompts. It's really the skill of clear communication.

Summary

  • Good prompts include Goal, Context, Constraints, Format and an Example.
  • Paste exact errors, define the audience, and specify the output format.
  • Break big tasks into steps, iterate on drafts, and let the AI ask clarifying questions.
  • Give permission to say "I don't know", and always verify important output.

items.title: How to Add CSS
items.excerpt: The three ways to add CSS (inline styles, internal style elements and external stylesheets), when to use each one, and which wins when they conflict.
items.content:
There are three places you can write CSS: directly on an element, in a <style> element inside the page, or in a separate .css file. Real websites mostly use the third, but you'll meet all three.

1. Inline styles

Add a style attribute to one element:

<p style="color: crimson; font-weight: bold;">This paragraph is styled inline.</p>
<p>This one isn't.</p>

Inline styles affect only that one element. They're handy for a quick test, or when a script changes one element's style, but they have big downsides:

  • You can't reuse them; every element needs its own copy.
  • They mix content and design, making HTML hard to read.
  • They're very hard to override from a stylesheet.

2. Internal stylesheet

Put rules inside a <style> element, usually in the <head>:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>Internal CSS</title>
  <style>
    body { font-family: Georgia, serif; }
    h1 { color: teal; }
    p { line-height: 1.6; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Internal stylesheet</h1>
  <p>Every paragraph on this page gets the same line height.</p>
  <p>Including this one.</p>
</body>
</html>

The rules apply to the whole page. This is fine for a single-page project, an email template or a quick demo (the examples in these lessons use it so they run in Try it Yourself). But the styles can't be shared with other pages.

3. External stylesheet (the normal way)

Write the CSS in its own file, for example styles.css:

/* styles.css */
body {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  margin: 0;
}
h1 {
  color: #2563eb;
}

Then link it from the <head> of every page:

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My site</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
  • rel="stylesheet" says what kind of file it is.
  • href is the path to the file, relative or absolute, just like a link.

Benefits:

  • One file styles the whole site. Change it once and every page updates.
  • Faster: the browser downloads styles.css once and reuses it from its cache on every other page.
  • Clean HTML with no styling mixed in.

A typical project folder looks like this:

my-site/
├── index.html
├── about.html
└── css/
    └── styles.css

With that structure, the link is <link rel="stylesheet" href="css/styles.css">.

Several stylesheets

You can link more than one file. They're applied in order, so later files can override earlier ones:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/base.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/theme.css">

Many sites also load web fonts this way, for example a stylesheet from Google Fonts.

Which one wins?

When the same property is set in more than one place for the same element and with equal selector strength, the order decides:

  1. Browser default styles (weakest)
  2. External and internal stylesheets, in the order they appear in the page
  3. Inline style attributes (strongest)
<style>
  p { color: blue; }
</style>
<p style="color: green;">I'm green: the inline style wins.</p>
<p>I'm blue.</p>

There's also !important, which forces a declaration to win (color: red !important;). Avoid it: it makes CSS very hard to manage, because the only way to beat it is another !important.

When to use which

Common mistakes

  • **Wrong path in href**, so the stylesheet never loads and the page looks unstyled. Check the browser's developer tools (F12 → Network) for a red 404.
  • **Writing <style> tags inside a .css file.** A CSS file contains only CSS.
  • **Using <link> in the body.** Put stylesheets in the <head> so the page doesn't flash unstyled.
  • **Overusing !important.**

Exercise

  1. Create a folder with index.html and css/styles.css on your computer.
  2. Link the stylesheet and set a background colour on body and a colour on h1.
  3. Create about.html, link the same stylesheet, and check both pages share the design.
  4. Add an inline style to one paragraph and confirm it beats the stylesheet.

Summary

  • CSS can be inline (style attribute), internal (<style>) or external (<link> to a .css file).
  • External stylesheets are the standard for real websites.
  • Later rules beat earlier ones; inline styles beat stylesheets; avoid !important.

Next, you'll learn how selectors choose which elements a rule styles.

items.title: CSS Selectors
items.excerpt: Element, class, id, group, descendant, child, attribute and pseudo-class selectors, plus specificity, the rule that decides which style wins.
items.content:
A selector is the part of a CSS rule that chooses which elements to style. Learning selectors well is the key to writing short, clean CSS. This lesson covers the selectors you'll use every day and the rule that settles conflicts: specificity.

Basic selectors

<style>
  p { color: #444; }                 /* element (type) selector */
  .highlight { background: #fff3b0; } /* class selector */
  #intro { font-size: 20px; }        /* id selector */
  * { box-sizing: border-box; }      /* universal selector: every element */
</style>

<p id="intro">This is the introduction.</p>
<p>A normal paragraph with a <span class="highlight">highlighted phrase</span>.</p>
<p class="highlight">A whole highlighted paragraph.</p>
  • Element: p matches every <p>.
  • Class: .highlight matches every element with class="highlight".
  • Id: #intro matches the one element with id="intro".
  • Universal: * matches everything.

You can combine an element and a class with no space: p.highlight matches only paragraphs that have the class.

Grouping selectors

Separate selectors with commas to give them the same styles:

h1, h2, h3 {
  font-family: Georgia, serif;
  color: #1e293b;
}

Combinators: selecting by position

<style>
  article p { color: green; }      /* descendant: any p inside article */
  ul > li { font-weight: bold; }   /* child: only direct li children of ul */
  h2 + p { font-style: italic; }   /* adjacent sibling: the p right after an h2 */
</style>

<article>
  <h2>Article title</h2>
  <p>First paragraph (green and italic).</p>
  <p>Second paragraph (green only).</p>
</article>

<ul>
  <li>Direct child (bold)
    <ol><li>Nested item: not a direct child of ul, so its text isn't bold</li></ol>
  </li>
</ul>
  • A B (space): B anywhere inside A.
  • A > B: B directly inside A.
  • A + B: B immediately after A, with the same parent.
  • A ~ B: any B after A with the same parent.

Note: the nested item's text is still bold because font-weight is inherited from its parent <li>; the selector itself didn't match it.

Attribute selectors

a[target="_blank"] { color: purple; }     /* exact value */
input[type="email"] { border-color: blue; }
a[href^="https"] { font-weight: bold; }   /* value starts with */
a[href$=".pdf"] { color: crimson; }       /* value ends with */

These are great for forms and for styling links by their destination.

Pseudo-classes: state and position

A pseudo-class starts with a colon and selects elements in a certain state or position:

<style>
  a:hover { color: crimson; }
  button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid orange; }
  input:invalid { border: 2px solid red; }
  li:first-child { color: green; }
  li:last-child { color: blue; }
  li:nth-child(even) { background: #f1f5f9; }
  p:not(.note) { color: #555; }
</style>

<a href="#">Hover over me</a>
<p><button>Tab to me</button></p>
<p><input type="email" placeholder="Type an invalid email"></p>
<ul>
  <li>First</li><li>Second</li><li>Third</li><li>Fourth</li>
</ul>
<p class="note">A note</p>
<p>Not a note</p>

:nth-child(even) (or odd, 3, 3n) is perfect for striped table rows. :not() excludes elements.

Pseudo-elements

A pseudo-element starts with two colons and styles a part of an element:

p::first-line { font-weight: bold; }
.required::after { content: " *"; color: red; }
::selection { background: #2563eb; color: white; }

::before and ::after insert decorative content. They need the content property, even if it's empty (content: "").

Specificity: which rule wins

When two rules conflict, the more specific selector wins, no matter which comes first. Think of it as a score with three columns:

Compare from the left: one id beats any number of classes, and one class beats any number of elements. If the scores are equal, the later rule wins. Inline styles beat all of these.

<style>
  #title { color: blue; }
  .heading { color: green; }
  h1 { color: red; }
</style>
<h1 id="title" class="heading">I'm blue: the id is most specific</h1>

Practical advice: style with classes, keep selectors short, and avoid ids in CSS. Low, even specificity makes your CSS predictable.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the dot or hash: highlight { } looks for a <highlight> element.
  • Adding a space by accident: p .note (note inside p) is not p.note (p that has class note).
  • Long chains like body div.main ul li a, which are fragile and hard to override.
  • **Fighting specificity with !important** instead of simplifying selectors.

Exercise

  1. Make every second row of a list grey with :nth-child(even).
  2. Colour links that open in a new tab differently with an attribute selector.
  3. Add a red asterisk after every label with class required using ::after.
  4. Write two conflicting rules and predict which wins, then test it.

Summary

  • Element, .class, #id and * are the basic selectors; commas group them.
  • Combinators (space, >, +, ~) select by position.
  • Pseudo-classes (:hover, :nth-child) select by state; pseudo-elements (::before) style parts.
  • Specificity decides conflicts: ids > classes > elements; then the later rule wins.

items.title: CSS Colors
items.excerpt: Colour names, hex codes, rgb, hsl and transparency, how to pick a small colour palette, and how to check text contrast.
items.content:
Colour is one of the first things people notice about a website. CSS gives you several ways to write the same colour, and knowing them all makes it easy to copy colours from design tools and adjust them.

Where colours are used

<style>
  .demo {
    color: white;              /* text colour */
    background-color: #2563eb; /* background */
    border: 4px solid #1e40af; /* border colour */
    padding: 16px;
  }
</style>
<div class="demo">Text, background and border colours</div>

color always means the text colour. Backgrounds and borders have their own properties.

Colour names

p { color: tomato; }
h1 { color: navy; }

CSS knows about 140 names like red, teal, gold, slategray and rebeccapurple. They're easy to read but limited, so real designs use the formats below.

Hex codes

h1 { color: #2563eb; }
p  { color: #333; }   /* short form of #333333 */

A hex colour is # followed by three pairs of hexadecimal digits (0–9, a–f) for red, green and blue. 00 means none of that colour; ff means full.

  • #000000 is black, #ffffff is white.
  • #ff0000 is pure red, #00ff00 green, #0000ff blue.
  • If each pair has two equal digits, you can shorten it: #336699 → #369.

Hex is the format you'll copy most often from design tools like Figma.

rgb()

h1 { color: rgb(37, 99, 235); }

The same red-green-blue idea, with numbers from 0 to 255. rgb(37, 99, 235) is exactly the same colour as #2563eb.

hsl(): the most human-friendly format

.primary { color: hsl(221, 83%, 53%); }
  • Hue (0–360): the position on the colour wheel. 0 is red, 120 green, 240 blue.
  • Saturation (0–100%): from grey to full colour.
  • Lightness (0–100%): 0% is black, 50% normal, 100% white.

HSL makes it easy to create shades of one colour: keep the hue, change the lightness.

<style>
  .shade { padding: 10px; color: white; }
  .s1 { background: hsl(221, 83%, 30%); }
  .s2 { background: hsl(221, 83%, 45%); }
  .s3 { background: hsl(221, 83%, 60%); }
  .s4 { background: hsl(221, 83%, 75%); color: #111; }
</style>
<div class="shade s1">Dark</div>
<div class="shade s2">Medium</div>
<div class="shade s3">Light</div>
<div class="shade s4">Lighter</div>

Transparency

Add a fourth value for alpha (opacity), from 0 (invisible) to 1 (solid):

<style>
  .photo {
    background: url("https://picsum.photos/id/1018/400/200") center/cover;
    height: 200px;
    display: flex;
    align-items: end;
  }
  .caption {
    background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.6);
    color: white;
    padding: 12px;
    width: 100%;
  }
</style>
<div class="photo"><div class="caption">A dark see-through caption over a photo</div></div>

You can write transparency as rgb(0 0 0 / 0.6), rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6), hsl(221 83% 53% / 0.5) or an 8-digit hex like #2563eb80. They all work in modern browsers.

There's also the opacity property, but it makes the whole element see-through, including its text. To fade only a background, use a transparent colour instead.

currentColor and transparent

  • transparent is fully see-through.
  • currentColor means "the current text colour". It's useful for borders and icons that should match the text: border: 2px solid currentColor;.

Choosing a palette

Most good websites use very few colours:

  • One brand colour for links, buttons and highlights.
  • Neutrals (near-black, greys, off-white) for text and backgrounds.
  • Status colours: green for success, red for errors, yellow/orange for warnings.

Use pure black (#000) for text sparingly; a very dark grey like #1f2937 is softer to read.

Contrast matters

Text must stand out from its background. The accessibility guideline (WCAG) asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Light grey text on white often fails. In Chrome or Firefox, open developer tools (F12), click a text element's colour swatch, and the colour picker shows the contrast ratio.

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting the #** in hex codes: color: 2563eb; is ignored.
  • Low-contrast text, like #aaa on white.
  • **Using opacity to fade a background**, which fades the text too.
  • Too many colours. Pick a small palette and reuse it.

Exercise

  1. Write the same colour as a name, hex, rgb and hsl and put four boxes side by side to compare.
  2. Create five shades of green by changing only the lightness in hsl().
  3. Add a semi-transparent caption over an image.
  4. Check the contrast of your text with your browser's developer tools.

Summary

  • color is text colour; background-color and border-color are separate.
  • Write colours as names, hex (#2563eb), rgb() or hsl().
  • Add alpha for transparency; opacity fades the whole element.
  • Use a small palette and keep text contrast at 4.5:1 or higher.

Next, you'll style backgrounds with colours, images and gradients.

items.title: CSS Backgrounds
items.excerpt: Background colours, images, repeat, position, size, cover and contain, gradients and the background shorthand, with a hero banner example.
items.content:
Backgrounds turn plain boxes into banners, cards and sections. In this lesson you'll use colours, images and gradients as backgrounds and control exactly how images are sized and placed.

Background colour

<style>
  .box { background-color: #e0f2fe; padding: 20px; }
</style>
<div class="box">A light blue box</div>

Background images

<style>
  .pattern {
    background-image: url("https://picsum.photos/id/1080/120/120");
    height: 240px;
  }
</style>
<div class="pattern"></div>

url() takes the path to the image. By default the image repeats in both directions to fill the box. That's useful for patterns but usually not what you want for photos.

Unlike <img>, a background image has no alt text and is invisible to screen readers. Use backgrounds only for decoration; if the image matters to the content, use an <img> element.

background-repeat

.a { background-repeat: no-repeat; } /* show it once */
.b { background-repeat: repeat-x; }  /* only horizontally */
.c { background-repeat: repeat-y; }  /* only vertically */

background-position

.hero { background-position: center; }
.logo-corner { background-position: right bottom; }
.custom { background-position: 20px 40px; }  /* x then y */

You can use keywords (top, bottom, left, right, center), lengths or percentages.

background-size: cover and contain

This is the property you'll use most:

<style>
  .frame {
    width: 260px;
    height: 160px;
    border: 2px solid #94a3b8;
    margin-bottom: 12px;
    background: url("https://picsum.photos/id/1015/600/300") no-repeat center #f1f5f9;
  }
  .cover { background-size: cover; }
  .contain { background-size: contain; }
</style>
<div class="frame cover"></div>
<div class="frame contain"></div>
  • cover scales the image to fill the whole box, cropping the edges if needed. Perfect for hero banners.
  • contain scales it to fit inside the box completely, which can leave empty space.
  • You can also give exact sizes: background-size: 100px auto;.

Gradients

Gradients are backgrounds made by CSS itself, so they need no image file:

<style>
  .g { height: 80px; margin-bottom: 10px; border-radius: 8px; }
  .g1 { background: linear-gradient(#2563eb, #7c3aed); }
  .g2 { background: linear-gradient(to right, #f97316, #facc15); }
  .g3 { background: linear-gradient(135deg, #10b981 0%, #3b82f6 50%, #8b5cf6 100%); }
  .g4 { background: radial-gradient(circle, #fde68a, #f59e0b); }
</style>
<div class="g g1"></div>
<div class="g g2"></div>
<div class="g g3"></div>
<div class="g g4"></div>
  • linear-gradient(direction, colour1, colour2, ...) blends in a straight line. The direction can be to right, to bottom left or an angle like 135deg.
  • Percentages after colours (colour stops) control where each colour sits.
  • radial-gradient() blends outward from a centre.

Several backgrounds at once

You can layer backgrounds, separated by commas. The first one is on top. A common trick is a dark gradient over a photo so white text stays readable:

<style>
  .hero {
    background:
      linear-gradient(rgb(0 0 0 / 0.55), rgb(0 0 0 / 0.55)),
      url("https://picsum.photos/id/1044/900/400") center / cover no-repeat;
    color: white;
    padding: 80px 24px;
    text-align: center;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  .hero h1 { margin: 0 0 8px; }
</style>
<section class="hero">
  <h1>Learn to code for free</h1>
  <p>Short lessons, real examples, no sign-up needed.</p>
</section>

The background shorthand

All background properties can be set in one line:

.hero {
  background: #1e293b url("hero.jpg") center / cover no-repeat;
}

The order is flexible, but the size must come straight after the position, separated by /. Any part you leave out goes back to its default, which can accidentally reset something you set earlier.

background-attachment

background-attachment: fixed; keeps the image still while the page scrolls (a "parallax" feel). It's often ignored on phones and can make scrolling slow, so use it sparingly.

Common mistakes

  • **Wrong image path in url(). Paths in a CSS file are relative to the CSS file**, not the HTML page.
  • Forgetting the box needs a height. An empty div with a background image has zero height and shows nothing.
  • White text on a busy photo without a dark overlay.
  • Important images as backgrounds, which screen readers can't see.

Exercise

  1. Create a 300 × 200 box with a photo background using cover.
  2. Add a gradient overlay and white centred text on top.
  3. Make a striped button with linear-gradient(to right, ...).
  4. Try contain instead of cover and note the difference.

Summary

  • background-color, background-image, -repeat, -position and -size control backgrounds.
  • cover fills and crops; contain fits without cropping.
  • linear-gradient() and radial-gradient() create backgrounds with no image file.
  • Layer a gradient over a photo to keep text readable.

Next, you'll draw borders, rounded corners and shadows.

items.title: CSS Borders
items.excerpt: Border width, style and colour, single sides, the border shorthand, rounded corners with border-radius, circles, outlines and box shadows.
items.content:
Borders draw lines around elements. Together with rounded corners and shadows, they're how you make cards, buttons, inputs and avatars look finished.

The three parts of a border

<style>
  .b {
    border-width: 3px;
    border-style: solid;
    border-color: #2563eb;
    padding: 12px;
  }
</style>
<p class="b">A 3px solid blue border.</p>

A border needs a style to appear. Without border-style, there's no border at all, even if you set a width and colour.

Border styles

<style>
  .s { border-width: 4px; border-color: #334155; padding: 8px; margin: 8px 0; }
</style>
<p class="s" style="border-style: solid;">solid</p>
<p class="s" style="border-style: dashed;">dashed</p>
<p class="s" style="border-style: dotted;">dotted</p>
<p class="s" style="border-style: double;">double</p>
<p class="s" style="border-style: groove;">groove</p>
<p class="s" style="border-style: none;">none</p>

In real designs you'll use solid 95% of the time, and occasionally dashed for things like "drop a file here" areas.

The border shorthand

Write all three parts on one line, in any order:

.card { border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; }

This is how you'll almost always write borders.

Individual sides

<style>
  .note {
    border-left: 5px solid #f59e0b;
    background: #fffbeb;
    padding: 12px 16px;
  }
  .title {
    border-bottom: 2px solid #2563eb;
    padding-bottom: 6px;
  }
</style>
<h2 class="title">Section title with an underline</h2>
<p class="note">A note with a coloured bar on the left.</p>

Use border-top, border-right, border-bottom and border-left to style one side. A left border on a tinted box is a classic "note" or "tip" style.

Rounded corners with border-radius

<style>
  .r { background: #dbeafe; padding: 16px; margin-bottom: 10px; }
  .r1 { border-radius: 6px; }
  .r2 { border-radius: 20px; }
  .r3 { border-radius: 999px; text-align: center; }
  .r4 { border-radius: 20px 0 20px 0; }
</style>
<div class="r r1">Slightly rounded (6px)</div>
<div class="r r2">Very rounded (20px)</div>
<div class="r r3">Pill shape (999px)</div>
<div class="r r4">Opposite corners only</div>
  • One value rounds all four corners.
  • Four values go clockwise from the top-left: top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left.
  • A very large value like 999px makes a "pill", perfect for tags and buttons.

border-radius works even without a border: it rounds the background too.

Circles

A square with border-radius: 50% becomes a circle:

<style>
  .avatar {
    width: 120px;
    height: 120px;
    border-radius: 50%;
    object-fit: cover;
    border: 4px solid white;
    box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.25);
  }
</style>
<img class="avatar" src="https://picsum.photos/id/64/240/240" alt="Profile photo">

object-fit: cover stops the photo from being squashed if it isn't square.

Box shadows

<style>
  .card {
    max-width: 280px;
    padding: 20px;
    border-radius: 12px;
    background: white;
    box-shadow: 0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.12);
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  body { background: #f1f5f9; padding: 24px; }
</style>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Card title</h3>
  <p>A soft shadow makes the card float above the page.</p>
</div>

box-shadow: x-offset y-offset blur colour;

  • Positive x moves the shadow right; positive y moves it down.
  • A bigger blur makes it softer.
  • Use a transparent black for natural shadows. Strong, dark shadows look dated.
  • Add a fourth length for spread, and the keyword inset for an inner shadow.

Outline: a border that takes no space

button:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #f59e0b;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

An outline looks like a border but doesn't take up space and doesn't move anything. Browsers use it to show keyboard focus. If you restyle focus, use outline, never just remove it.

Common mistakes

  • No border-style, so the border never appears.
  • **border-radius: 50% on a rectangle**, which makes an oval, not a circle. Make width and height equal first.
  • Heavy shadows like 5px 5px 5px black. Keep shadows soft and subtle.
  • Removing focus outlines with outline: none and nothing in their place.

Exercise

  1. Style a "warning" box with a thick orange left border and a pale orange background.
  2. Make a pill-shaped tag that says "Beginner".
  3. Turn a photo into a round avatar with a white border and soft shadow.
  4. Build a card with rounded corners and a subtle shadow, and give it a bigger shadow on hover with .card:hover.

Summary

  • A border needs width, style and colour; the border shorthand sets all three.
  • border-top, -right, -bottom, -left style one side.
  • border-radius rounds corners; 50% on a square makes a circle.
  • box-shadow adds depth; outline is for focus and takes no space.

Next, you'll control the space around and inside elements with margin and padding.
