items.title: Installing Java and Running Programs
items.excerpt: Install the JDK on Windows, Mac or Linux, compile and run with javac and java, try code instantly in JShell, and set up IntelliJ IDEA or VS Code for Java.
items.content:
Let's get Java running on your computer. You will install the JDK, compile a program from the terminal, try JShell, and set up an editor.

Step 1: Install the JDK

Download a free JDK build. Eclipse Temurin 21 (LTS) from adoptium.net is a great choice. Oracle JDK 21 also works.

  • Windows: download the .msi installer and tick "Set JAVA_HOME variable" and "Add to PATH".
  • Mac: download the .pkg, or run brew install --cask temurin@21.
  • Linux (Ubuntu): sudo apt install openjdk-21-jdk.

Step 2: Check the installation

Open a new terminal (Command Prompt / PowerShell on Windows) and run:

java -version
javac -version

You should see something like openjdk version "21.0.4". If you see "command not found", the JDK's bin folder is not on your PATH. Reinstall with the PATH option ticked, or add it manually.

Step 3: Compile and run from the terminal

Create a folder, and a file named Greeting.java inside it:

public class Greeting {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String name = "Asha";
        System.out.println("Welcome to Java, " + name + "!");
    }
}

In the terminal, go to that folder and run:

javac Greeting.java      # creates Greeting.class (bytecode)
java Greeting            # runs it on the JVM (no .class extension!)

Output:

Welcome to Java, Asha!

Shortcut: run a single file directly

Since Java 11 you can skip the javac step for single-file programs:

java Greeting.java

Java compiles it in memory and runs it. Perfect for practice.

Step 4: JShell, Java's playground

JShell (Java 9+) lets you type Java and see results immediately, with no class or main needed:

jshell
jshell> int a = 7
a ==> 7

jshell> a * 6
$2 ==> 42

jshell> "java".toUpperCase()
$3 ==> "JAVA"

jshell> /exit

Use JShell to test small ideas quickly.

Step 5: Choose an editor (IDE)

In IntelliJ: New Project → Java → choose JDK 21 → Create. Right-click the src folder → New → Java Class, type Main, then type psvm and press Tab: IntelliJ writes the main method for you. Type sout + Tab for System.out.println().

Learn these IntelliJ shortcuts early: psvm (main method), sout (println), Alt+Enter (quick fix), Ctrl+Alt+L (format code), Shift+F10 (run).

Command-line arguments

The String[] args in main receives words typed after the class name:

public class Args {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("You passed " + args.length + " arguments");
        for (String a : args) {
            System.out.println("- " + a);
        }
    }
}
java Args.java red green
You passed 2 arguments
- red
- green

Reading compiler errors

Java's compiler tells you the file, the line and the problem:

Greeting.java:4: error: ';' expected
        System.out.println("Hi")
                                ^
1 error

Read the first error first: later errors are often caused by it. Line 4, a semicolon is missing.

Common mistakes

  • Running java Greeting.class (wrong) instead of java Greeting.
  • An old Java version on the PATH: check java -version and javac -version show the same version.
  • Saving the file as Greeting.java.txt on Windows (turn on "show file extensions").

Exercise

  1. Install the JDK and confirm java -version works.
  2. Write About.java that prints three facts about you, then compile and run it with javac and java.
  3. In JShell, calculate how many seconds are in a day.
  4. Modify Args.java to print the arguments in reverse order.
Hint for 4

Loop from args.length - 1 down to 0: for (int i = args.length - 1; i >= 0; i--).

Summary

  • Install a JDK (Temurin 21), then check with java -version.
  • javac File.java compiles; java ClassName runs. java File.java does both for single files.
  • JShell is a quick playground; IntelliJ IDEA is the most popular IDE.

Next: variables and data types, the building blocks of every program.

items.title: Java Variables and Data Types
items.excerpt: Declare variables, learn Java's eight primitive types, String, var, constants with final, type casting, integer overflow and naming rules, with clear examples.
items.content:
A variable is a labelled box that holds a value. In Java every box has a fixed type: a box for whole numbers can't hold text. This strictness catches mistakes before your program even runs.

Declaring variables

public class Variables {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int age = 21;                 // type name = value;
        double price = 499.99;
        String city = "Pune";
        boolean isStudent = true;
        char grade = 'A';

        age = 22;                     // change the value (same type)
        System.out.println(city + " " + age + " " + price + " " + isStudent + " " + grade);
    }
}

Output:

Pune 22 499.99 true A

The pattern is always type name = value;. You can declare first and assign later: int score; score = 90; but a local variable must have a value before you read it.

The 8 primitive types

In practice you'll mostly use **int, long, double, boolean, char**.

  • long literals end in L, float literals end in f.
  • Underscores make big numbers readable: 1_000_000.
  • char uses single quotes 'A'; String uses double quotes "A".

String is not primitive

String is a class (that's why it starts with a capital S). It holds text and has many useful methods:

String name = "Vital Stack";
System.out.println(name.length());        // 11
System.out.println(name.toUpperCase());   // VITAL STACK

You'll learn Strings in depth in the Strings lesson.

Primitive vs reference: what's in the box?

A primitive variable holds the value itself. A reference variable (like a String or any object) holds an address pointing to an object in memory (the heap). Play the animation to see it:

This difference explains many Java behaviours later, like why == on Strings can surprise you.

var: let Java infer the type

Since Java 10, inside methods you can write var and Java works out the type from the value:

var count = 10;          // int
var total = 99.5;        // double
var msg = "Hello";       // String

The type is still fixed: count = "ten"; is an error. Use var when the type is obvious from the right side.

Constants with final

final double GST_RATE = 0.18;
final int MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS = 3;
// GST_RATE = 0.12;   // error: cannot assign a value to final variable

Constants are written in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.

Type casting

Widening (small → big) happens automatically. Narrowing (big → small) needs an explicit cast and may lose data:

public class Casting {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int marks = 87;
        double asDouble = marks;            // widening: 87.0
        double avg = 78.9;
        int rounded = (int) avg;            // narrowing: 78 (decimal dropped, not rounded!)
        long big = 3_000_000_000L;
        int broken = (int) big;             // overflow: -1294967296
        System.out.println(asDouble + " " + rounded + " " + broken);
        System.out.println(Math.round(avg));   // 79: proper rounding
    }
}

Output:

87.0 78 -1294967296
79

Integer division and overflow

System.out.println(7 / 2);       // 3   (int / int = int)
System.out.println(7 / 2.0);     // 3.5 (one double makes it double)
int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE;     // 2147483647
System.out.println(max + 1);     // -2147483648: overflow wraps around!

When counting money, views or IDs that may exceed 2 billion, use long. For exact money calculations (no rounding errors), professionals use BigDecimal.

Naming rules and conventions

  • Names can contain letters, digits, _ and $, but can't start with a digit.
  • Can't be a keyword (class, int, public…).
  • Convention: camelCase for variables (totalPrice, isLoggedIn).
  • Choose meaningful names: studentCount, not sc.

Default values

Fields in a class get defaults (0, 0.0, false, null). Local variables inside methods do not: reading one before assigning is a compile error.

Common mistakes

  • int price = 99.5; → error: possible lossy conversion. Use double.
  • long l = 3000000000; → error: integer number too large. Add L.
  • Expecting (int) 9.99 to be 10. It's 9.
  • char c = "A"; → double quotes make a String. Use 'A'.

Exercise

  1. Create variables for a product: name, price, quantity, inStock. Print a sentence using all four.
  2. Calculate the total cost (price × quantity) and the total with 18% GST.
  3. Store your height in metres as double and print it in centimetres as an int.
  4. What does System.out.println(10 / 4 + 10 % 4); print? Guess first, then run it.
Hint for 4

10 / 4 is integer division = 2, and 10 % 4 is the remainder = 2. So the answer is 4.

Interview corner

  • How many primitive types does Java have? Eight: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean.
  • Is String a primitive? No, it's a class in java.lang; variables hold references to String objects.
  • What happens on int overflow? It silently wraps around to the negative side. Use Math.addExact to get an exception instead.

Summary

  • Variables have a fixed type: type name = value;.
  • Eight primitives; int, long, double, boolean, char are the everyday ones.
  • var infers types, final makes constants, casting converts between types.
  • Watch for integer division and overflow.

Next: operators and expressions to calculate and compare.

items.title: Java Operators and Expressions
items.excerpt: Arithmetic, assignment, comparison, logical, increment and ternary operators in Java, operator precedence, short-circuit evaluation and the Math class.
items.content:
Operators are the symbols that do work on values: add, compare, combine conditions. You'll use them in every line of logic you write.

Arithmetic operators

% is incredibly useful: n % 2 == 0 checks for even numbers, n % 10 gives the last digit.

public class Digits {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int n = 4729;
        System.out.println("Last digit: " + n % 10);        // 9
        System.out.println("Without last: " + n / 10);      // 472
        System.out.println("Is even? " + (n % 2 == 0));     // false
    }
}

Assignment and compound assignment

int score = 10;
score += 5;   // score = score + 5  → 15
score -= 3;   // 12
score *= 2;   // 24
score /= 5;   // 4
score %= 3;   // 1

Increment and decrement

int a = 5;
int b = a++;   // b = 5, then a becomes 6  (post-increment)
int c = ++a;   // a becomes 7, then c = 7  (pre-increment)
System.out.println(a + " " + b + " " + c);   // 7 5 7

Post (a++) uses the old value then increments; pre (++a) increments first. Interviewers love asking this. In real code, use a++ on its own line to keep things clear.

Comparison operators

All return a boolean:

Use == for primitives only. To compare Strings or other objects, use .equals(). You'll see exactly why in the Strings lesson.

Logical operators

int age = 20;
boolean hasId = true;
boolean canEnter = age >= 18 && hasId;      // true
boolean discount = age < 12 || age > 60;    // false
System.out.println(canEnter + " " + discount + " " + !canEnter);

Short-circuit evaluation

&& stops as soon as the left side is false; || stops as soon as the left side is true. This protects you from errors:

String name = null;
if (name != null && name.length() > 3) {   // safe: length() never runs when name is null
    System.out.println("Long name");
}

The ternary operator

A one-line if/else that returns a value:

int marks = 72;
String result = marks >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";
System.out.println(result);   // Pass

Format: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. Great for simple choices; use a normal if for anything complex.

Operator precedence

Like maths, some operators go first:

  1. () brackets
  2. ++ -- ! (unary)
  3. * / %
  4. + -
  5. < > <= >=
  6. == !=
  7. &&
  8. ||
  9. ?:
  10. = += …
System.out.println(2 + 3 * 4);       // 14, not 20
System.out.println((2 + 3) * 4);     // 20
System.out.println("Sum: " + 2 + 3); // Sum: 23 (text joining goes left to right!)
System.out.println("Sum: " + (2 + 3)); // Sum: 5

When in doubt, add brackets. They make code clearer for humans too.

The Math class

public class MathDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Math.max(12, 30));      // 30
        System.out.println(Math.min(12, 30));      // 12
        System.out.println(Math.abs(-7));          // 7
        System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 10));       // 1024.0
        System.out.println(Math.sqrt(144));        // 12.0
        System.out.println(Math.round(4.5));       // 5
        System.out.println(Math.ceil(4.1));        // 5.0
        System.out.println(Math.floor(4.9));       // 4.0
        int dice = (int) (Math.random() * 6) + 1;  // 1 to 6
        System.out.println(dice >= 1 && dice <= 6);  // true
    }
}

Common mistakes

  • if (x = 5) → assignment, not comparison. Java gives a compile error for ints (good!). Use ==.
  • Expecting 5 / 2 to be 2.5. Use 5 / 2.0 or cast one side to double.
  • Mixing & with &&: single & doesn't short-circuit.
  • "Total: " + a + b joins text instead of adding. Wrap the sum in brackets.

Exercise

  1. Given seconds = 3725, print it as 1 h 2 min 5 s using / and %.
  2. Write an expression that is true when a year is a leap year: divisible by 4 and not by 100, unless divisible by 400.
  3. Use the ternary operator to print "Adult" or "Minor".
  4. Predict the output: int x = 3; int y = x++ + ++x; What are x and y?
Hint for 2

(year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0

Hint for 4

x++ gives 3 (x becomes 4), ++x makes x 5 and gives 5. So y = 8, x = 5.

Interview corner

  • **i++ vs ++i?** Post-increment returns the old value; pre-increment returns the new one.
  • **&& vs &?** && short-circuits; & always evaluates both sides (and also works as bitwise AND on ints).
  • **What is "5" + 3 + 2?** "532". And 3 + 2 + "5"? "55". Evaluation is left to right.

Summary

  • Arithmetic: + - * / %; watch for integer division.
  • Comparisons return booleans; logical &&, ||, ! combine them with short-circuiting.
  • Ternary ?: picks between two values; brackets beat memorising precedence.
  • Math has max, min, abs, pow, sqrt, round, random and more.

Next: Strings, the most used class in Java.

items.title: Java Strings
items.excerpt: Create and use Strings in Java, the most useful String methods, why == fails and equals() works, the string pool, immutability, StringBuilder and text blocks.
items.content:
Text is everywhere: names, emails, messages, JSON. In Java, text is handled by the String class. Strings look simple, but they have a few surprises that every Java interview asks about.

Creating Strings

String course = "Java";                 // string literal (recommended)
String other = new String("Java");      // forces a new object (rarely needed)
String empty = "";

Useful String methods

public class StringMethods {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s = "  Learn Java at VitalStack  ";
        String t = s.trim();                              // remove spaces at both ends
        System.out.println(t);                            // Learn Java at VitalStack
        System.out.println(t.length());                   // 24
        System.out.println(t.toUpperCase());              // LEARN JAVA AT VITALSTACK
        System.out.println(t.charAt(0));                  // L
        System.out.println(t.indexOf("Java"));            // 6
        System.out.println(t.contains("Stack"));          // true
        System.out.println(t.substring(6, 10));           // Java  (end index excluded)
        System.out.println(t.replace("Java", "Spring"));  // Learn Spring at VitalStack
        System.out.println(t.startsWith("Learn"));        // true
        System.out.println(String.join("-", "a", "b", "c"));  // a-b-c
        String[] words = t.split(" ");
        System.out.println(words.length);                 // 4
        System.out.println("".isEmpty() + " " + "  ".isBlank());  // true true
    }
}

Indexes start at 0. substring(start, end) includes start but excludes end.

== vs equals(): the classic trap

== on objects compares addresses (is it the same object?). .equals() compares content (same characters?). Watch it happen:

public class Compare {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String a = "java";
        String b = "java";
        String c = new String("java");
        System.out.println(a == b);          // true: both point to the same pooled literal
        System.out.println(a == c);          // false: c is a separate object
        System.out.println(a.equals(c));     // true: same characters
        System.out.println("JAVA".equalsIgnoreCase(a));   // true
    }
}

**Rule: always compare Strings with .equals().** a == b being true above is an optimisation (the string pool: Java reuses identical literals), not something to rely on.

Write "admin".equals(role) instead of role.equals("admin"). If role is null, the first form returns false; the second crashes with NullPointerException.

Strings are immutable

A String can never change. Methods like toUpperCase() return a new String:

String name = "asha";
name.toUpperCase();              // result thrown away!
System.out.println(name);        // asha
name = name.toUpperCase();       // keep the new String
System.out.println(name);        // ASHA

Why immutable? It makes Strings safe to share between threads, safe as HashMap keys, and lets the string pool reuse them.

StringBuilder: build text efficiently

Because Strings are immutable, += in a loop creates a new String every time. For many changes, use StringBuilder:

public class Builder {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
            sb.append(i).append(i < 5 ? ", " : "");
        }
        System.out.println(sb);                    // 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
        System.out.println(sb.reverse());          // 5 ,4 ,3 ,2 ,1
        StringBuilder word = new StringBuilder("level");
        System.out.println(word.reverse().toString().equals("level"));   // true: palindrome
    }
}

StringBuilder is mutable: append, insert, delete, reverse change the same object. (StringBuffer is the older, thread-safe, slower version.)

Formatting text

String name = "Ravi";
double total = 1234.5;
String msg = String.format("Hi %s, your total is ₹%.2f", name, total);
System.out.println(msg);                     // Hi Ravi, your total is ₹1234.50
System.out.println("%s scored %d%%".formatted("Neha", 92));   // Neha scored 92%

%s = text, %d = whole number, %.2f = decimal with 2 places, %% = a percent sign.

Text blocks (Java 15+)

For multi-line text like JSON or SQL, use triple quotes:

String json = """
        {
          "course": "Java",
          "lessons": 16
        }
        """;
System.out.print(json);

Looping over characters

public class CountVowels {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String text = "VitalStack teaches Java";
        int vowels = 0;
        for (char ch : text.toLowerCase().toCharArray()) {
            if ("aeiou".indexOf(ch) >= 0) vowels++;
        }
        System.out.println("Vowels: " + vowels);   // Vowels: 8
    }
}

Converting to and from Strings

int n = Integer.parseInt("42");          // "42" → 42
double d = Double.parseDouble("3.5");    // "3.5" → 3.5
String s1 = String.valueOf(99);          // 99 → "99"
String s2 = "" + 99;                     // also works

Integer.parseInt("abc") throws NumberFormatException. You'll learn to handle that in the Exceptions lesson.

Common mistakes

  • Comparing with == instead of .equals().
  • Forgetting Strings are immutable: calling s.trim() without saving the result.
  • substring end index off by one.
  • Building big strings with += inside loops: use StringBuilder.

Exercise

  1. Check if a word is a palindrome (ignore case).
  2. Count how many times the letter a appears in "Java and JavaScript are different".
  3. Turn "vital stack java course" into "Vital Stack Java Course".
  4. Mask an email: "asha.kumar@gmail.com" → "a*****@gmail.com".
Hint for 3

Split on spaces, then for each word take w.substring(0, 1).toUpperCase() + w.substring(1) and join with a StringBuilder.

Hint for 4

Find the @ with indexOf("@"). Keep the first character, add "*".repeat(at - 1), then add substring(at).

Interview corner

  • Why are Strings immutable in Java? Security (paths, URLs can't be changed after checks), thread safety, caching of hashCode and the string pool.
  • String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer? String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and fast; StringBuffer is mutable and synchronized (thread-safe but slower).
  • **How many objects does new String("java") create?** Up to two: the pooled literal "java" (if not already in the pool) and the new object on the heap.

Summary

  • Strings are immutable objects with many helpful methods.
  • Compare content with .equals(), never ==.
  • Use StringBuilder for building text in loops, String.format for formatting, text blocks for multi-line text.

Next: reading user input and printing formatted output.
items.subject: java

items.title: Java User Input with Scanner
items.excerpt: Read numbers and text from the keyboard with Scanner, avoid the nextInt/nextLine trap, validate input, and print neat output with printf.
items.content:
Programs become interesting when they react to the user. In Java, the easiest way to read keyboard input is the Scanner class.

Reading input with Scanner

import java.util.Scanner;

public class Hello {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);

        System.out.print("Your name: ");
        String name = in.nextLine();

        System.out.print("Your age: ");
        int age = in.nextInt();

        System.out.println("Hi " + name + ", next year you'll be " + (age + 1));
        in.close();
    }
}
Your name: Asha Kumar
Your age: 21
Hi Asha Kumar, next year you'll be 22
  • import java.util.Scanner; brings the class in (it's not in java.lang).
  • new Scanner(System.in) reads from the keyboard.

The nextInt() + nextLine() trap

System.out.print("Age: ");
int age = in.nextInt();          // user types 21 and presses Enter
System.out.print("City: ");
String city = in.nextLine();     // returns "" immediately!

nextInt() reads 21 but leaves the Enter (newline) behind. The next nextLine() reads that empty leftover. Fix: call in.nextLine(); once after nextInt() to consume it, or read every line with nextLine() and convert:

int age = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine().trim());

Reading everything with nextLine() and converting yourself is the safest habit. It avoids the trap completely.

Validating input

If the user types abc where you expect a number, nextInt() throws InputMismatchException. Check first:

import java.util.Scanner;

public class SafeInput {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);
        System.out.print("Enter marks (0-100): ");
        while (!in.hasNextInt()) {
            System.out.print("Numbers only, try again: ");
            in.next();                      // throw away the bad token
        }
        int marks = in.nextInt();
        System.out.println(marks >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail");
    }
}

Printing with printf

printf formats output neatly, great for tables and bills:

public class Bill {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] items = {"Notebook", "Pen set", "Backpack"};
        double[] prices = {120, 250.5, 1899};
        double total = 0;
        System.out.printf("%-10s %10s%n", "Item", "Price");
        for (int i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
            System.out.printf("%-10s %10.2f%n", items[i], prices[i]);
            total += prices[i];
        }
        System.out.printf("%-10s %10.2f%n", "TOTAL", total);
    }
}
Item            Price
Notebook       120.00
Pen set        250.50
Backpack      1899.00
TOTAL         2269.50

A mini program: simple calculator

import java.util.Scanner;

public class Calculator {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);
        System.out.print("First number: ");
        double a = Double.parseDouble(in.nextLine());
        System.out.print("Operator (+ - * /): ");
        String op = in.nextLine().trim();
        System.out.print("Second number: ");
        double b = Double.parseDouble(in.nextLine());

        double result = switch (op) {
            case "+" -> a + b;
            case "-" -> a - b;
            case "*" -> a * b;
            case "/" -> a / b;
            default -> Double.NaN;
        };
        System.out.printf("%.2f %s %.2f = %.2f%n", a, op, b, result);
    }
}

(You'll learn switch properly in the next lesson.)

Other ways to read input

  • BufferedReader with InputStreamReader: faster, used in competitive programming.
  • Command-line args: values passed when starting the program.
  • Files: covered in the File I/O lesson.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting import java.util.Scanner;.
  • The nextInt() then nextLine() empty-line trap.
  • Creating a new Scanner inside a loop: create one and reuse it.
  • Closing a Scanner on System.in and then trying to read again: closing it closes the keyboard stream too.

Exercise

  1. Ask for length and width, then print the area and perimeter of a rectangle.
  2. Ask for a temperature in Celsius and print Fahrenheit with one decimal place.
  3. Ask for 3 subject marks and print the total, the average (2 decimals) and the grade.
  4. Print a multiplication table for a number the user enters, nicely aligned with printf.
Hint for 4

System.out.printf("%2d x %2d = %3d%n", n, i, n * i); inside a loop from 1 to 10.

Summary

  • Scanner reads from System.in: nextLine, nextInt, nextDouble, hasNextInt.
  • Avoid the nextInt + nextLine trap by reading lines and parsing them.
  • printf with %d, %.2f, %s, %-10s and %n makes output neat.

Next: making decisions with if, else and switch.

items.title: Java If, Else and Switch
items.excerpt: Make decisions in Java with if, else if, else, nested conditions, the classic switch statement and the modern switch expression with arrows and yield.
items.content:
Programs need to make decisions: is the password correct? Is the cart empty? Did the student pass? Conditions let your code take different paths.

if and else

public class Grades {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int marks = 76;

        if (marks >= 90) {
            System.out.println("Grade A+");
        } else if (marks >= 75) {
            System.out.println("Grade A");
        } else if (marks >= 60) {
            System.out.println("Grade B");
        } else if (marks >= 40) {
            System.out.println("Grade C");
        } else {
            System.out.println("Fail");
        }
    }
}

Output: Grade A. Java checks from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true.

  • The condition must be a boolean. if (marks) is an error in Java (unlike JavaScript or Python).
  • Braces are optional for a single statement, but always use them. It prevents bugs when you add a second line later.

Combining conditions

int age = 19;
boolean hasTicket = true;
boolean vip = false;

if ((age >= 18 && hasTicket) || vip) {
    System.out.println("Welcome to the concert!");
}

Nested if

boolean loggedIn = true;
String role = "admin";

if (loggedIn) {
    if ("admin".equals(role)) {
        System.out.println("Open admin dashboard");
    } else {
        System.out.println("Open user dashboard");
    }
} else {
    System.out.println("Please sign in");
}

Deep nesting gets hard to read. A cleaner style is the guard clause: handle the "exit early" cases first.

static String dashboard(boolean loggedIn, String role) {
    if (!loggedIn) return "Please sign in";
    if ("admin".equals(role)) return "Admin dashboard";
    return "User dashboard";
}

The classic switch statement

When comparing one value against many fixed options, switch is cleaner than a long else if chain:

int day = 3;
switch (day) {
    case 1:
        System.out.println("Monday");
        break;
    case 2:
        System.out.println("Tuesday");
        break;
    case 3:
        System.out.println("Wednesday");
        break;
    default:
        System.out.println("Another day");
}

**Don't forget break!** Without it, Java "falls through" and runs the next cases too:

int n = 1;
switch (n) {
    case 1: System.out.println("one");
    case 2: System.out.println("two");      // also printed!
    default: System.out.println("many");    // also printed!
}

switch works with int, char, String, enums (and their wrapper types).

The modern switch expression (Java 14+)

Arrows -> never fall through, and the switch can return a value:

public class Seasons {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String month = "OCT";
        String season = switch (month) {
            case "DEC", "JAN", "FEB" -> "Winter";
            case "MAR", "APR", "MAY" -> "Summer";
            case "JUN", "JUL", "AUG", "SEP" -> "Monsoon";
            case "OCT", "NOV" -> "Post-monsoon";
            default -> "Unknown";
        };
        System.out.println(season);    // Post-monsoon
    }
}
  • Several labels share one case: case "DEC", "JAN", "FEB".
  • No break needed.
  • Need several statements? Use a block and yield:
int fee = switch (plan) {
    case "student" -> 0;
    case "pro" -> {
        int base = 499;
        yield base - 50;     // yield returns the value from a block
    }
    default -> 999;
};

Prefer the arrow form in new code. It's shorter, safer (no forgotten break) and the compiler checks that every enum value is covered.

Pattern matching for switch (Java 21)

Java 21 can switch on the type of an object:

static String describe(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case Integer i when i > 100 -> "big number " + i;
        case Integer i -> "number " + i;
        case String s -> "text of length " + s.length();
        case null -> "nothing";
        default -> "something else";
    };
}

You'll use this more after the OOP course.

Common mistakes

  • if (x = 5) instead of if (x == 5).
  • Comparing Strings with == in conditions: use .equals().
  • A semicolon after the condition: if (ok); { ... } makes the block run always!
  • Forgetting break in classic switch.
  • Order of else if matters: put the most specific conditions first (>= 90 before >= 75).

Exercise

  1. Read a number and print whether it's positive, negative or zero, and whether it's even or odd.
  2. Read three numbers and print the largest using only if/else.
  3. Electricity bill: first 100 units ₹5 each, next 100 units ₹7, above 200 units ₹10. Calculate the bill for any number of units.
  4. Use a switch expression to convert a number 1-7 into a day name.
Hint for 3

For 250 units: 100 × 5 + 100 × 7 + 50 × 10. Use Math.min or an if/else chain to split units into slabs.

Interview corner

  • What types can switch work on? byte, short, char, int, their wrappers, String, enums, and (Java 21) any type with pattern matching.
  • What is fall-through? In classic switch, without break execution continues into the next case.
  • Switch statement vs expression? A statement performs actions; an expression produces a value (with -> or yield).

Summary

  • if / else if / else picks the first true branch; conditions must be boolean.
  • Use guard clauses to avoid deep nesting.
  • Classic switch needs break; the modern arrow switch returns values and never falls through.

Next: loops, to repeat work without repeating code.

items.title: Java Loops
items.excerpt: Repeat work with for, while, do-while and the enhanced for-each loop, control loops with break and continue, nested loops for patterns, and avoid infinite loops.
items.content:
Loops repeat code. Printing 1,000 invoices, checking every item in a cart, retrying a failed login: all loops. Java has four kinds.

The for loop

Use for when you know how many times to repeat:

public class Table {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int n = 7;
        for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
            System.out.println(n + " x " + i + " = " + (n * i));
        }
    }
}

A for has three parts: for (start; condition; update).

  1. int i = 1 runs once at the beginning.
  2. i <= 10 is checked before each round; if false, the loop ends.
  3. i++ runs after each round.

Counting down or in steps:

for (int i = 10; i >= 1; i--) { System.out.print(i + " "); }       // 10 9 8 ... 1
for (int i = 0; i <= 20; i += 5) { System.out.print(i + " "); }    // 0 5 10 15 20

The while loop

Use while when you don't know how many rounds you'll need, only the stopping condition:

public class DigitSum {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int n = 98765, sum = 0;
        while (n > 0) {
            sum += n % 10;   // take the last digit
            n /= 10;         // drop the last digit
        }
        System.out.println(sum);   // 35
    }
}

The do-while loop

do-while checks the condition after the body, so it always runs at least once. Perfect for menus:

import java.util.Scanner;

public class Menu {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);
        int choice;
        do {
            System.out.println("1. Start quiz  2. Scores  0. Exit");
            choice = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());
            System.out.println("You chose " + choice);
        } while (choice != 0);
    }
}

The enhanced for (for-each)

To visit every item in an array or collection, for-each is simplest:

int[] marks = {78, 92, 65, 88};
int total = 0;
for (int m : marks) {
    total += m;
}
System.out.println("Average: " + (double) total / marks.length);   // 80.75

Read it as "for each m in marks". You don't get the index, and you can't modify the array through m. Use a normal for when you need the index.

break and continue

  • break exits the loop immediately.
  • continue skips the rest of this round and moves to the next.
public class FirstMultiple {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int i = 1; i <= 50; i++) {
            if (i % 3 != 0) continue;        // skip non-multiples of 3
            if (i % 7 == 0) {
                System.out.println("First multiple of 3 and 7: " + i);   // 21
                break;
            }
        }
    }
}

Nested loops

A loop inside a loop. The inner loop finishes all its rounds for each round of the outer loop:

public class Stars {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int rows = 4;
        for (int r = 1; r <= rows; r++) {
            for (int c = 1; c <= r; c++) {
                System.out.print("* ");
            }
            System.out.println();
        }
    }
}
* 
* * 
* * * 
* * * *

Pattern programs like this are very common in fresher interviews and college exams. Nested loops over n items run n × n times, which is O(n²). See the DSA course's Big-O lesson for why that matters.

Labelled break

To exit both loops at once, label the outer loop:

outer:
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < 5; j++) {
        if (i * j == 6) {
            System.out.println("Found " + i + " x " + j);
            break outer;
        }
    }
}

Infinite loops

int i = 0;
while (i < 5) {
    System.out.println(i);
    // forgot i++ → runs forever!
}

Always make sure something inside the loop moves it towards the stopping condition. while (true) with a break inside is fine when used on purpose (servers, game loops).

Which loop when?

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one: i <= arr.length instead of i < arr.length → ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
  • Semicolon after the loop header: for (...); makes an empty loop.
  • Changing the loop variable inside a for body: confusing, avoid.

Exercise

  1. Print all even numbers from 1 to 50 in one line.
  2. Calculate the factorial of 10 with a loop (use long).
  3. Print the first 15 Fibonacci numbers.
  4. Check whether a number is prime (loop up to the square root).
  5. Print this pyramid for 4 rows:
   *
  ***
 *****
*******
Hint for 4

Loop i from 2 while i * i <= n. If n % i == 0, it's not prime.

Hint for 5

Row r has rows - r spaces then 2 * r - 1 stars.

Interview corner

  • while vs do-while? do-while runs the body at least once; while may run zero times.
  • Can you use for-each to remove items from a list? No: it throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use an Iterator's remove() or list.removeIf(...).
  • Print 1 to 100 without a loop? Recursion: void print(int n) { if (n > 100) return; System.out.println(n); print(n + 1); }.

Summary

  • for for counted loops, while for condition loops, do-while for at-least-once, for-each for collections.
  • break exits, continue skips a round, labels break outer loops.
  • Nested loops multiply work: n × n rounds.

Next: arrays, to store many values in one variable.

items.title: Java Arrays
items.excerpt: Store many values in one variable with Java arrays, loop over them, find max and average, use 2D arrays for grids, and save time with the Arrays utility class.
items.content:
Imagine storing marks for 60 students in 60 separate variables. Impossible to manage! An array stores many values of the same type under one name, in numbered slots.

Creating arrays

int[] marks = {78, 92, 65, 88, 71};       // values known up front
String[] cities = new String[3];          // 3 empty slots: null, null, null
double[] prices = new double[4];          // 4 slots, all 0.0
cities[0] = "Delhi";
cities[1] = "Mumbai";
cities[2] = "Chennai";
  • Indexes start at 0; the last index is length - 1.
  • marks.length (no brackets: it's a field, not a method) gives the size.
  • The size is fixed once created. Need a growing list? Use ArrayList (Collections lesson).
  • New arrays get default values: 0, 0.0, false, or null for objects.
index:   0    1    2    3    4
marks: [ 78 | 92 | 65 | 88 | 71 ]

Reading and looping

public class Marks {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] marks = {78, 92, 65, 88, 71};
        System.out.println("First: " + marks[0] + ", last: " + marks[marks.length - 1]);

        int total = 0, best = marks[0];
        for (int i = 0; i < marks.length; i++) {
            total += marks[i];
            if (marks[i] > best) best = marks[i];
        }
        System.out.println("Total " + total + ", best " + best + ", average " + (double) total / marks.length);
    }
}
First: 78, last: 71
Total 394, best 92, average 78.8

Accessing marks[5] here throws **ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException**, the most common array bug.

The Arrays helper class

java.util.Arrays has ready-made tools:

import java.util.Arrays;

public class ArraysDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] nums = {42, 7, 19, 3, 25};
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(nums));        // [42, 7, 19, 3, 25]
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(nums));        // [3, 7, 19, 25, 42]
        System.out.println(Arrays.binarySearch(nums, 19)); // 2 (array must be sorted)
        int[] copy = Arrays.copyOf(nums, 3);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(copy));        // [3, 7, 19]
        int[] filled = new int[4];
        Arrays.fill(filled, 9);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(filled));      // [9, 9, 9, 9]
        System.out.println(Arrays.stream(nums).sum());    // 96
    }
}

Printing an array directly (System.out.println(nums)) shows something like [I@1b6d3586, the type and a hash. Use Arrays.toString(nums).

Arrays are references

An array variable holds a reference. Assigning it doesn't copy the array; both names point to the same one:

int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
int[] b = a;          // same array, two names
b[0] = 99;
System.out.println(a[0]);    // 99!
int[] c = a.clone();  // a real copy
c[1] = 50;
System.out.println(a[1]);    // 2

Comparing with a == c checks whether they're the same array object. To compare contents, use Arrays.equals(a, c).

Reversing an array in place

The classic two-pointer technique (see the DSA course for more):

int[] arr = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
for (int l = 0, r = arr.length - 1; l < r; l++, r--) {
    int tmp = arr[l];
    arr[l] = arr[r];
    arr[r] = tmp;
}
// arr is now [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

2D arrays: grids and tables

A 2D array is an array of arrays: rows and columns.

public class Grid {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[][] scores = {
            {80, 75, 90},    // student 0
            {60, 85, 70},    // student 1
        };
        System.out.println(scores[1][2]);          // 70: row 1, column 2
        for (int r = 0; r < scores.length; r++) {
            int sum = 0;
            for (int c = 0; c < scores[r].length; c++) {
                sum += scores[r][c];
            }
            System.out.println("Student " + r + " total: " + sum);
        }
    }
}
70
Student 0 total: 245
Student 1 total: 215

Use 2D arrays for game boards, seating charts, matrices and images.

Arrays and methods

You can pass arrays into methods and return them:

static int max(int[] values) {
    int best = values[0];
    for (int v : values) if (v > best) best = v;
    return best;
}

Since the method gets a reference, it can change the caller's array.

Common mistakes

  • Using i <= arr.length in loops (off by one).
  • Forgetting arrays have fixed size.
  • arr.length() with brackets (that's for Strings). Arrays use arr.length.
  • Assuming b = a copies the array.

Exercise

  1. Find the second largest number in an array.
  2. Count how many numbers in an array are even.
  3. Rotate an array left by one position: [1,2,3,4] → [2,3,4,1].
  4. Add two 3×3 matrices and print the result.
  5. Check if an array is sorted in ascending order.
Hint for 1

Keep two variables, first and second. When you find a bigger number, the old first becomes second.

Hint for 3

Save arr[0], shift every element one place left, then put the saved value at the end.

Interview corner

  • Default value of an int array element? 0. Of a String array element? null.
  • Can you change an array's size? No. Create a new one (Arrays.copyOf) or use ArrayList.
  • Where are arrays stored? On the heap; the variable holds a reference.
  • **Time to access arr[i]?** O(1): Java computes the memory address directly.

Summary

  • Arrays hold a fixed number of same-type values, indexed from 0.
  • Loop with for (index needed) or for-each.
  • Arrays.toString, sort, copyOf, fill, equals save time.
  • Array variables are references; 2D arrays are arrays of arrays.

Next: methods, to organise code into reusable pieces.
items.subject: java

items.title: Java Methods
items.excerpt: Write reusable Java methods with parameters and return values, understand pass-by-value, overload methods, use varargs and watch recursion on the call stack.
items.content:
A method is a named block of code that does one job. Instead of copying the same 10 lines in five places, you write a method once and call it five times. Methods make programs shorter, clearer and easier to fix.

Defining and calling a method

public class Methods {
    static int square(int n) {        // define
        return n * n;
    }

    static void greet(String name) {  // no return value
        System.out.println("Namaste, " + name + "!");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        greet("Riya");                         // call
        int result = square(9);                // call and keep the result
        System.out.println(result);            // 81
        System.out.println(square(3) + square(4));   // 25
    }
}

Anatomy: static int square(int n)

  • static: belongs to the class, so main (also static) can call it without an object. (You'll learn about non-static methods in the OOP course.)
  • int: the return type. void means "returns nothing".
  • square: the name, in camelCase, usually a verb.
  • (int n): parameters: inputs the method needs.
  • return n * n; sends a value back and ends the method.

Multiple parameters and early return

static double finalPrice(double price, int discountPercent) {
    if (discountPercent <= 0) return price;           // early return
    return price - price * discountPercent / 100.0;
}

static boolean isEligible(int age, boolean hasId) {
    return age >= 18 && hasId;
}

Pass by value

Java always passes a copy of the value. For primitives, the method gets a copy of the number:

static void tryToChange(int x) {
    x = 100;
}

int a = 5;
tryToChange(a);
System.out.println(a);   // 5: the original is untouched

For objects and arrays, the copied value is the reference. So the method can modify the object it points to, but can't make the caller's variable point somewhere else:

static void addBonus(int[] marks) {
    marks[0] += 5;           // changes the caller's array
}

Method overloading

Several methods can share a name if their parameter lists differ:

static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
static int add(int a, int b, int c) { return a + b + c; }
static double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; }

add(2, 3);        // 5   → first version
add(2, 3, 4);     // 9   → second
add(2.5, 1.5);    // 4.0 → third

Java picks the version by the arguments. A different return type alone is not enough to overload.

Varargs: any number of arguments

static int sum(int... nums) {        // nums is an int[]
    int total = 0;
    for (int n : nums) total += n;
    return total;
}

sum();              // 0
sum(4, 5);          // 9
sum(1, 2, 3, 4);    // 10

String.format and printf use varargs, that's how they accept any number of values.

Scope: where variables live

Variables declared inside a method (or block) exist only there:

static void demo() {
    int x = 10;
    if (x > 5) {
        int y = 20;      // y only exists inside this if-block
    }
    // System.out.println(y);   // error: cannot find symbol
}

Recursion: a method calling itself

A recursive method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version, until it hits a base case. Each call gets its own frame on the call stack. Play the animation to watch frames being pushed and popped:

public class Factorial {
    static long factorial(int n) {
        if (n <= 1) return 1;            // base case: stop here
        return n * factorial(n - 1);     // recursive case
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(factorial(5));   // 120
        System.out.println(factorial(20));  // 2432902008176640000
    }
}

Without a base case, calls pile up until Java throws **StackOverflowError**.

Think of recursion as a stack of plates: each call adds a plate; the base case starts removing them, and each plate's result is used by the one below.

Good method habits

  • One job per method. If you need "and" to describe it, split it.
  • Short: aim for under ~20 lines.
  • Clear names: calculateGst, isValidEmail, printReceipt.
  • Return values rather than printing inside: easier to test and reuse.

Common mistakes

  • Missing return in a non-void method (compile error: missing return statement).
  • Code after return (unreachable statement error).
  • Calling a non-static method from main without an object.
  • Expecting a method to change a primitive variable passed to it.

Exercise

  1. Write isEven(int n) returning boolean.
  2. Write max(int a, int b, int c).
  3. Write countDigits(long n).
  4. Write a recursive power(int base, int exp).
  5. Write a recursive sumDigits(int n): sumDigits(1234) = 10.
  6. Overload area: one for a circle (radius), one for a rectangle (length, width).
Hint for 4

Base case: exp == 0 returns 1. Otherwise base * power(base, exp - 1).

Hint for 5

n % 10 + sumDigits(n / 10), with base case n == 0 returns 0.

Interview corner

  • Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? Always pass-by-value. For objects, the value passed is a copy of the reference.
  • Overloading vs overriding? Overloading = same name, different parameters, same class (compile time). Overriding = subclass redefines a parent method with the same signature (runtime). See the OOP course.
  • What causes StackOverflowError? Recursion that's too deep or never reaches a base case.

Summary

  • Methods have a return type, a name and parameters; return sends a value back.
  • Java is pass-by-value; objects are passed as copies of references.
  • Overloading reuses a name with different parameters; varargs accepts any count.
  • Recursion uses the call stack and needs a base case.

Next: collections, the dynamic lists and sets that real Java programs use every day.

items.title: Java ArrayList and Collections
items.excerpt: Use ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet and TreeSet, understand how an ArrayList grows, generics, wrapper classes, autoboxing, iterating safely and the Collections utility class.
items.content:
Arrays have a fixed size. Real apps need lists that grow and shrink: a shopping cart, a list of students, search results. Java's Collections Framework provides ready-made data structures for this.

The big picture

                 Collection
          ┌──────────┼──────────┐
         List        Set        Queue
   ArrayList     HashSet      ArrayDeque
   LinkedList    LinkedHashSet PriorityQueue
                 TreeSet
       Map (separate): HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap
  • List: ordered, allows duplicates, access by index.
  • Set: no duplicates.
  • Queue/Deque: add at one end, remove from the other.
  • Map: key → value pairs (next lesson).

ArrayList: the list you'll use most

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Cart {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> cart = new ArrayList<>();
        cart.add("Notebook");
        cart.add("Pen");
        cart.add("Backpack");
        cart.add(1, "Pencil");                 // insert at index 1
        System.out.println(cart);              // [Notebook, Pencil, Pen, Backpack]
        System.out.println(cart.get(2));       // Pen
        System.out.println(cart.size());       // 4
        System.out.println(cart.contains("Pen"));   // true
        cart.set(0, "Diary");                  // replace
        cart.remove("Pencil");                 // remove by value
        cart.remove(0);                        // remove by index
        System.out.println(cart);              // [Pen, Backpack]
        for (String item : cart) {
            System.out.println("- " + item);
        }
    }
}
  • List<String> uses generics: the list only accepts Strings, checked at compile time.
  • new ArrayList<>(): the empty <> (diamond) lets Java infer the type.
  • Declaring the variable as List (the interface) and creating an ArrayList is good practice: you can switch implementation later.

How ArrayList grows

Inside, an ArrayList is a normal array. When it's full, Java creates a bigger array (about 1.5×) and copies everything over. Watch it:

That's why add() at the end is fast on average (O(1)), while add(0, x) or remove(0) shifts every element (O(n)).

Wrapper classes and autoboxing

Collections can't hold primitives. Use the wrapper classes: Integer, Double, Boolean, Character, Long…

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>();
nums.add(5);             // autoboxing: int 5 → Integer
int first = nums.get(0); // unboxing: Integer → int

Trap: list.remove(1) on a List<Integer> removes the element at index 1. To remove the value 1, write list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)).

Another trap: compare Integer objects with .equals(), not ==. == only works by accident for small values (-128 to 127 are cached).

LinkedList

A LinkedList stores nodes that point to each other. Adding/removing at the ends is O(1), but get(i) must walk the chain: O(n). In practice, ArrayList is faster for most uses; reach for ArrayDeque when you need a queue or stack.

Sets: no duplicates

import java.util.*;

public class Tags {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> raw = List.of("java", "spring", "java", "sql", "spring");
        Set<String> unique = new HashSet<>(raw);           // fast, no order guaranteed
        Set<String> inOrder = new LinkedHashSet<>(raw);    // keeps insertion order
        Set<String> sorted = new TreeSet<>(raw);           // sorted
        System.out.println(unique.size());     // 3
        System.out.println(inOrder);           // [java, spring, sql]
        System.out.println(sorted);            // [java, spring, sql]
        System.out.println(unique.add("java"));   // false: already there
    }
}

HashSet lookups (contains) are O(1) on average, which makes sets perfect for "have I seen this before?" checks.

Iterating and removing safely

Removing inside a for-each throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use removeIf or an Iterator:

List<Integer> marks = new ArrayList<>(List.of(35, 80, 22, 90, 41));
marks.removeIf(m -> m < 40);               // [80, 90, 41]

Iterator<Integer> it = marks.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next() > 85) it.remove();       // [80, 41]
}

The Collections utility class

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(5, 2, 9, 1));
Collections.sort(nums);                    // [1, 2, 5, 9]
Collections.reverse(nums);                 // [9, 5, 2, 1]
Collections.shuffle(nums);                 // random order
System.out.println(Collections.max(nums)); // 9
List<String> fixed = Collections.unmodifiableList(new ArrayList<>(List.of("a")));

List.of(...) creates an immutable list: calling add on it throws UnsupportedOperationException. Wrap it in new ArrayList<>(...) when you need to change it.

Sorting objects

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ravi", "Anu", "Mohammed", "Zoya"));
names.sort(Comparator.comparing(String::length));            // by length
names.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());                       // Z to A

You'll see Comparator and lambdas (m -> m < 40) in detail in the Streams lesson.

Common mistakes

  • List<int>: not allowed. Use List<Integer>.
  • Modifying a List.of(...) list.
  • Removing inside for-each.
  • Using LinkedList "because inserts are fast" and then calling get(i) in a loop (O(n²)).

Exercise

  1. Store 5 student names in an ArrayList, add one, remove one, and print the list sorted.
  2. Remove duplicates from [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 5] while keeping the original order.
  3. Find the common elements of two lists using sets (retainAll).
  4. Remove all names shorter than 4 letters with removeIf.
Hint for 2

new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(list)) keeps the first occurrence of each value in order.

Interview corner

  • ArrayList vs LinkedList? Array-backed vs node-based. ArrayList wins for random access and is usually faster overall.
  • ArrayList vs array? ArrayList grows dynamically and only holds objects; arrays are fixed-size and can hold primitives.
  • Default capacity of ArrayList? 10 (allocated on first add); it grows by about 50% when full.
  • HashSet vs TreeSet? HashSet: O(1) average, no order. TreeSet: O(log n), sorted.
  • What is fail-fast? Iterators throw ConcurrentModificationException if the collection is changed structurally during iteration (except through the iterator).

Summary

  • Use List<T> list = new ArrayList<>() by default; Set for uniqueness.
  • ArrayList grows by copying into a bigger array; adding at the end is amortised O(1).
  • Collections hold objects: wrappers and autoboxing bridge primitives.
  • Use removeIf or an Iterator to remove while looping.

Next: HashMap, the key-value structure behind caches, counters and lookups.

items.title: Java HashMap and Maps
items.excerpt: Store key-value pairs with HashMap, LinkedHashMap and TreeMap, count frequencies with merge and getOrDefault, iterate entries, and see how hashCode picks a bucket.
items.content:
A Map stores key → value pairs, like a dictionary: word → meaning, roll number → student, product ID → price. Looking up a value by its key is extremely fast. Maps are one of the most used structures in real Java code and in interviews.

HashMap basics

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class Prices {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Integer> price = new HashMap<>();
        price.put("apple", 120);
        price.put("banana", 40);
        price.put("mango", 150);
        price.put("apple", 130);                     // same key: value replaced

        System.out.println(price.get("mango"));       // 150
        System.out.println(price.get("grapes"));      // null: key not found
        System.out.println(price.getOrDefault("grapes", 0));   // 0
        System.out.println(price.containsKey("banana"));       // true
        System.out.println(price.size());             // 3
        price.remove("banana");
        System.out.println(price.keySet());           // keys (order not guaranteed)
    }
}
  • Keys are unique; put with an existing key replaces the value.
  • get returns null for missing keys. Prefer getOrDefault.
  • HashMap allows one null key and many null values.

Looping over a map

Map<String, Integer> stock = new HashMap<>(Map.of("pen", 50, "book", 12, "bag", 3));

for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : stock.entrySet()) {
    System.out.println(e.getKey() + " → " + e.getValue());
}

stock.forEach((item, qty) -> {
    if (qty < 5) System.out.println("Low stock: " + item);
});

Use entrySet() when you need both key and value; it avoids a second lookup per key.

The counting pattern

Counting how often things appear is the most common map use, in real code and interviews:

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class WordCount {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String text = "java is fun and java is powerful and java is everywhere";
        Map<String, Integer> count = new TreeMap<>();      // sorted by key
        for (String w : text.split(" ")) {
            count.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);               // add 1, or start at 1
        }
        System.out.println(count);
    }
}
{and=2, everywhere=1, fun=1, is=3, java=3, powerful=1}

merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) means "if the key is new, store 1; otherwise add 1 to the old value". The older style is count.put(w, count.getOrDefault(w, 0) + 1);.

Grouping with computeIfAbsent

Map<Character, List<String>> byLetter = new TreeMap<>();
for (String name : List.of("Asha", "Arjun", "Bala", "Chitra", "Bhavna")) {
    byLetter.computeIfAbsent(name.charAt(0), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(name);
}
// {A=[Asha, Arjun], B=[Bala, Bhavna], C=[Chitra]}

How HashMap works inside

A HashMap is an array of buckets. To store a key, Java:

  1. Calls key.hashCode() to get a number.
  2. Mixes the bits and uses it to choose a bucket index.
  3. Stores the entry there. Two keys in the same bucket (a collision) are chained in a list (or a balanced tree if the bucket gets long, since Java 8).

When the map is 75% full (the load factor), it doubles its buckets and redistributes entries. Watch real hashCode() values pick buckets, including the famous collision "Aa" vs "BB":

On average get and put are O(1). That's why maps power caches, indexes and lookups.

If you use your own class as a key, you must override both equals() and hashCode() consistently. Otherwise two "equal" keys land in different buckets and get returns null. The OOP course covers this.

HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap

TreeMap also has handy navigation: firstKey(), lastKey(), floorKey(x), ceilingKey(x), headMap, tailMap.

Immutable maps

Map<String, String> capitals = Map.of("India", "New Delhi", "Japan", "Tokyo");
// capitals.put("France", "Paris");   // UnsupportedOperationException

Common mistakes

  • Expecting HashMap to keep insertion order. Use LinkedHashMap.
  • Calling get(key) and unboxing a null to int: int n = map.get("x"); throws NullPointerException if missing.
  • Mutable objects as keys: if a key's fields change after insertion, its hash changes and it gets "lost".
  • Modifying a map while iterating with for-each.

Exercise

  1. Count the frequency of each character in "programming".
  2. Find the first non-repeating character in a string (hint: LinkedHashMap).
  3. Given a list of (name, city) pairs, group names by city.
  4. Two Sum: given an array and a target, return the indexes of two numbers that add up to the target, in O(n) using a map.
Hint for 2

Count with a LinkedHashMap, then loop over its entries and return the first with count 1.

Hint for 4

For each number x, check if target - x is already in the map (value → index). If not, store x.

Interview corner

  • How does HashMap work internally? Array of buckets; hashCode → bucket index; collisions chained (treeified after 8 entries per bucket); resize at 0.75 load factor.
  • HashMap vs Hashtable? Hashtable is old and synchronized, and allows no null keys/values. Use HashMap, or ConcurrentHashMap for threads.
  • Why must equals and hashCode be consistent? Equal objects must have equal hash codes, or lookups fail.
  • Time complexity of get? O(1) average; O(log n) worst case in a treeified bucket since Java 8.

Summary

  • Maps store unique keys with values; HashMap gives O(1) average lookups.
  • getOrDefault, merge, computeIfAbsent make counting and grouping easy.
  • LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order; TreeMap keeps keys sorted.
  • Keys need consistent equals and hashCode.

Next: exceptions, how Java handles errors without crashing.

items.title: Java Exception Handling
items.excerpt: Handle errors gracefully with try, catch and finally, understand checked vs unchecked exceptions, throw and throws, try-with-resources and custom exceptions.
items.content:
Things go wrong: a user types "abc" instead of a number, a file is missing, the network drops. Without handling, Java prints a scary stack trace and the program stops. Exception handling lets you catch the problem and respond gracefully.

What an exception looks like

public class Crash {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] marks = {80, 90};
        System.out.println(marks[5]);
        System.out.println("This never prints");
    }
}
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 5 out of bounds for length 2
	at Crash.main(Crash.java:4)

Read stack traces from the top: the exception type, the message, then where it happened (file and line).

try and catch

Put risky code in try; handle problems in catch. Step through the animation and try ten / 2 and 10 / 2 too:

public class SafeDivide {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] inputs = {"10", "abc", "0"};
        for (String s : inputs) {
            try {
                int n = Integer.parseInt(s);
                System.out.println("100 / " + n + " = " + (100 / n));
            } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
                System.out.println("'" + s + "' is not a number");
            } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
                System.out.println("Can't divide by zero");
            } finally {
                System.out.println("-- checked " + s);
            }
        }
    }
}
100 / 10 = 10
-- checked 10
'abc' is not a number
-- checked abc
Can't divide by zero
-- checked 0
  • When an exception happens, Java skips the rest of the try and jumps to the first matching catch.
  • finally runs always: success, exception, even after return. Use it for cleanup.
  • Catch several types in one block with |: catch (NumberFormatException | ArithmeticException e).

The exception family tree

Throwable
├── Error                  (serious JVM problems: OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError; don't catch)
└── Exception
    ├── IOException, SQLException, ...      ← checked
    └── RuntimeException                    ← unchecked
        ├── NullPointerException
        ├── ArithmeticException
        ├── ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
        ├── NumberFormatException (via IllegalArgumentException)
        └── IllegalStateException

Checked vs unchecked

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;

public class ReadFile {
    static String load(String file) throws IOException {     // "I might throw this"
        return Files.readString(Path.of(file));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            System.out.println(load("notes.txt"));
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("Could not read file: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

throw: raise your own exception

static void withdraw(double balance, double amount) {
    if (amount <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
    }
    if (amount > balance) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient balance");
    }
    System.out.println("Withdrawn " + amount);
}
  • throw (singular, inside a method) raises an exception.
  • throws (plural, in the method signature) declares what might be thrown.

Custom exceptions

Create meaningful exceptions for your domain:

public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {
    private final double shortBy;

    public InsufficientFundsException(double shortBy) {
        super("Insufficient funds, short by ₹" + shortBy);
        this.shortBy = shortBy;
    }

    public double getShortBy() { return shortBy; }
}

Extend Exception for checked, RuntimeException for unchecked. Most modern frameworks (like Spring) prefer unchecked exceptions.

try-with-resources

Files, database connections and network sockets must be closed. try (...) closes them automatically, even on error:

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.FileReader;
import java.io.IOException;

public class FirstLine {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"))) {
            System.out.println(reader.readLine());
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("Problem: " + e.getMessage());
        }   // reader.close() is called automatically
    }
}

Any class implementing AutoCloseable works here.

Best practices

  • Catch specific exceptions, not Exception or Throwable.
  • Never swallow exceptions silently: catch (Exception e) {} hides bugs. At least log them.
  • Validate early: check inputs and throw IllegalArgumentException with a clear message.
  • Don't use exceptions for normal flow (like ending a loop). They're slower and confusing.
  • Keep the cause when wrapping: throw new ServiceException("Save failed", e);.

NullPointerException is the most common Java exception. Avoid it by checking for null, using Objects.requireNonNull, returning empty lists instead of null, or Optional (Streams lesson). Java 14+ even tells you exactly which variable was null.

Common mistakes

  • Catching Exception before a more specific one (compile error: already caught).
  • Using finally to return a value (it overrides the try's return or hides exceptions).
  • Forgetting to close resources (use try-with-resources).

Exercise

  1. Read two numbers as Strings, divide them, and handle bad numbers and division by zero with clear messages.
  2. Write validateAge(int age) that throws IllegalArgumentException if age is negative or above 150.
  3. Create a checked InvalidMarksException and throw it when marks are outside 0-100.
  4. What does this print? try { return 1; } finally { System.out.println("finally"); }
Hint for 4

It prints "finally" and then the method returns 1. finally runs before the method actually returns.

Interview corner

  • Checked vs unchecked? Checked must be caught or declared (compile-time check); unchecked extends RuntimeException and doesn't.
  • throw vs throws? throw raises an exception object; throws declares it in the signature.
  • Does finally always run? Almost: except if the JVM exits (System.exit) or crashes.
  • Error vs Exception? Errors are serious JVM problems you shouldn't catch; exceptions are conditions your program can handle.
  • What is try-with-resources? A try that automatically closes AutoCloseable resources.

Summary

  • try risky code, catch specific exceptions, finally for cleanup.
  • Checked exceptions must be handled or declared; unchecked usually signal bugs.
  • throw your own exceptions with clear messages; create custom ones for your domain.
  • try-with-resources closes files and connections automatically.

Next: lambdas and streams, modern Java's way to process data.

items.title: Java Lambdas and Streams
items.excerpt: Write short functions with lambdas and method references, process collections with the Stream API (filter, map, sorted, collect, groupingBy) and avoid nulls with Optional.
items.content:
Java 8 changed how Java code looks. Lambdas let you pass small functions around, and Streams let you process collections in a clear "pipeline" style: filter this, transform that, collect the result. Every modern Java codebase and Spring Boot project uses them.

From loop to stream

Find the names of students who scored above 75, in upper case, sorted:

// The classic loop way
List<String> result = new ArrayList<>();
for (Student s : students) {
    if (s.marks() > 75) {
        result.add(s.name().toUpperCase());
    }
}
Collections.sort(result);

// The stream way
List<String> result = students.stream()
        .filter(s -> s.marks() > 75)
        .map(s -> s.name().toUpperCase())
        .sorted()
        .toList();

The stream version reads like the problem statement.

Lambdas

A lambda is a short anonymous function: parameters -> body.

x -> x * 2                          // one parameter
(a, b) -> a + b                     // two parameters
() -> System.out.println("Hi")      // no parameters
s -> {                              // a block body needs return
    String t = s.trim();
    return t.toUpperCase();
}

A lambda can be used wherever Java expects a functional interface, an interface with exactly one abstract method:

Method references

When a lambda just calls one existing method, use :::

names.forEach(s -> System.out.println(s));
names.forEach(System.out::println);          // same thing

names.stream().map(s -> s.toUpperCase());
names.stream().map(String::toUpperCase);     // same thing

A complete stream example

import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class StreamDemo {
    record Student(String name, String city, int marks) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Student> students = List.of(
            new Student("Asha", "Pune", 88),
            new Student("Ravi", "Delhi", 72),
            new Student("Meera", "Pune", 95),
            new Student("Karan", "Delhi", 64),
            new Student("Zoya", "Mumbai", 81)
        );

        List<String> toppers = students.stream()
                .filter(s -> s.marks() >= 80)
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(Student::marks).reversed())
                .map(Student::name)
                .toList();
        System.out.println(toppers);                         // [Meera, Asha, Zoya]

        double avg = students.stream().mapToInt(Student::marks).average().orElse(0);
        System.out.println(avg);                             // 80.0

        Map<String, List<String>> byCity = students.stream()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Student::city, TreeMap::new,
                         Collectors.mapping(Student::name, Collectors.toList())));
        System.out.println(byCity);     // {Delhi=[Ravi, Karan], Mumbai=[Zoya], Pune=[Asha, Meera]}

        Map<String, Long> countByCity = students.stream()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Student::city, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
        System.out.println(countByCity);                     // {Delhi=2, Mumbai=1, Pune=2}

        boolean anyFail = students.stream().anyMatch(s -> s.marks() < 40);
        System.out.println(anyFail);                         // false

        String names = students.stream().map(Student::name).collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
        System.out.println(names);                           // Asha, Ravi, Meera, Karan, Zoya
    }
}

(record creates a simple data class in one line. You'll meet records properly in the OOP course.)

How a stream pipeline works

  1. Source: list.stream(), Arrays.stream(arr), Stream.of(...), IntStream.range(0, 10).
  2. Intermediate operations (lazy, return a new stream): filter, map, sorted, distinct, limit, skip, flatMap, peek.
  3. Terminal operation (runs the pipeline): toList, collect, forEach, count, sum, reduce, anyMatch, findFirst, min, max.

Nothing runs until the terminal operation. And a stream can be used only once.

int sumOfSquaresOfEvens = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10)
        .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
        .map(n -> n * n)
        .sum();                 // 4 + 16 + 36 + 64 + 100 = 220

reduce

reduce combines all elements into one:

int product = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).reduce(1, (a, b) -> a * b);   // 120

Optional: a box that may be empty

Methods like findFirst and max return Optional, because there might be no result:

Optional<Student> best = students.stream().max(Comparator.comparingInt(Student::marks));
System.out.println(best.map(Student::name).orElse("nobody"));   // Meera

Optional<Student> fromChennai = students.stream().filter(s -> s.city().equals("Chennai")).findFirst();
System.out.println(fromChennai.isPresent());                     // false

Use orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, map, ifPresent instead of calling get() blindly. Optional makes "might be missing" explicit and prevents NullPointerExceptions.

Don't overuse streams. A simple loop is fine and sometimes clearer, especially when you need indexes, early exits with complex logic, or checked exceptions.

Common mistakes

  • Reusing a stream after a terminal operation: IllegalStateException.
  • Changing external variables inside a lambda (they must be effectively final).
  • Using peek or map for side effects like saving to a database.
  • Optional.get() without checking: defeats the purpose.

Exercise

Given List<Integer> nums = List.of(5, 12, 7, 3, 18, 12, 9, 4);

  1. Collect the even numbers into a list.
  2. Get the distinct numbers sorted in descending order.
  3. Find the sum of numbers greater than 6.
  4. Find the second largest distinct number.
  5. Given a list of words, build a map of word length → list of words.
Hint for 4

nums.stream().distinct().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).skip(1).findFirst()

Hint for 5

words.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length))

Interview corner

  • What is a functional interface? An interface with exactly one abstract method (optionally marked @FunctionalInterface), so it can be implemented with a lambda.
  • map vs flatMap? map transforms each element to one element; flatMap transforms each element to a stream and flattens them into one stream.
  • Intermediate vs terminal operations? Intermediate are lazy and return streams; terminal trigger processing and produce a result.
  • Stream vs Collection? A collection stores data; a stream processes data once, lazily, without storing it.

Summary

  • Lambdas are short functions; method references (Class::method) are even shorter.
  • Streams: source → intermediate operations → terminal operation.
  • filter, map, sorted, collect(groupingBy), reduce cover most needs.
  • Optional represents a value that might be missing.

Next: reading and writing files.
