items.title: Java File Handling
items.excerpt: Read and write text files in Java with the modern Files and Path API, process big files line by line, append data, list folders, and handle CSV files safely.
items.content:
Programs often need to save data that survives after they close: reports, logs, settings, CSV exports. Java's modern java.nio.file API (Path and Files) makes file handling short and safe.

Paths

A Path represents a file or folder location:

import java.nio.file.Path;

Path file = Path.of("data", "students.csv");    // data/students.csv (works on every OS)
System.out.println(file.getFileName());          // students.csv
System.out.println(file.toAbsolutePath());       // full path on your computer

Relative paths are resolved from the folder where you run the program.

Writing and reading a whole file

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.List;

public class Notes {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path path = Path.of("notes.txt");

        Files.writeString(path, "Learn Java\nPractise daily\n");          // create or overwrite
        Files.writeString(path, "Build projects\n", StandardOpenOption.APPEND);  // add to the end

        String all = Files.readString(path);                              // whole file as one String
        System.out.print(all);

        List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(path);                    // one String per line
        System.out.println(lines.size() + " lines");                      // 3 lines

        Files.write(path, List.of("one", "two", "three"));                // write a list of lines
        System.out.println(Files.exists(path) + " " + Files.size(path) + " bytes");
    }
}

Output:

Learn Java
Practise daily
Build projects
3 lines
true 14 bytes

throws IOException on main is fine for small scripts. In real apps, catch IOException and show a helpful message.

Big files: read line by line

readAllLines loads everything into memory. For a 2 GB log file, stream it instead:

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class ErrorCount {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(Path.of("server.log"))) {
            long errors = lines.filter(l -> l.contains("ERROR")).count();
            System.out.println("Errors: " + errors);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("Could not read log: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Files.lines reads lazily, one line at a time, so memory stays tiny. Put it in try-with-resources so the file is closed.

BufferedReader and BufferedWriter

The classic approach, still common in older code and useful for fine control:

import java.io.*;
import java.nio.file.*;

public class CopyUpper {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Files.writeString(Path.of("in.txt"), "hello\nworld\n");
        try (BufferedReader in = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of("in.txt"));
             BufferedWriter out = Files.newBufferedWriter(Path.of("out.txt"))) {
            String line;
            while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) {     // null = end of file
                out.write(line.toUpperCase());
                out.newLine();
            }
        }
        System.out.print(Files.readString(Path.of("out.txt")));   // HELLO WORLD on two lines
    }
}

Working with a CSV file

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;

public class CsvReport {
    record Sale(String product, int qty, double price) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path csv = Path.of("sales.csv");
        Files.write(csv, List.of("product,qty,price", "Pen,10,15.5", "Book,3,220", "Bag,1,1499"));

        List<Sale> sales = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String line : Files.readAllLines(csv).subList(1, 4)) {     // skip the header
            String[] p = line.split(",");
            sales.add(new Sale(p[0], Integer.parseInt(p[1]), Double.parseDouble(p[2])));
        }
        double total = sales.stream().mapToDouble(s -> s.qty() * s.price()).sum();
        System.out.printf("Total sales: ₹%.2f%n", total);    // Total sales: ₹2314.00
    }
}

Real CSV files can contain commas inside quotes, so for production use a library like OpenCSV or Apache Commons CSV.

Folders

Path dir = Path.of("reports");
Files.createDirectories(dir);                       // creates parent folders too, no error if it exists
Files.writeString(dir.resolve("may.txt"), "Report");
try (var files = Files.list(dir)) {
    files.forEach(f -> System.out.println(f.getFileName()));
}
Files.copy(dir.resolve("may.txt"), dir.resolve("may-backup.txt"), StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
Files.deleteIfExists(dir.resolve("may-backup.txt"));

Always specify the character encoding when files may contain Hindi, emojis or ₹: Files.readString(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8). The Files methods already default to UTF-8, but older FileReader code may not.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the file path is relative to where you run the program, not where the .java file is.
  • Reading huge files with readAllLines (OutOfMemoryError).
  • Not closing streams: use try-with-resources.
  • Overwriting a file when you meant to append: pass StandardOpenOption.APPEND.

Exercise

  1. Write a program that saves 5 to-do items to todo.txt and then reads and numbers them.
  2. Count the words in a text file.
  3. Read marks.csv (name,marks) and write result.csv with an extra Pass/Fail column.
  4. Append a timestamped line (LocalDateTime.now()) to log.txt every time the program runs.
Hint for 2

Read the whole file, then text.trim().split("\\s+").length. \\s+ splits on any run of spaces or new lines.

Interview corner

  • **Files.readAllLines vs Files.lines?** The first loads everything into a List; the second returns a lazy Stream, better for large files.
  • Why use buffered streams? They read/write in chunks, reducing slow disk operations.
  • What is serialization? Converting an object to bytes (e.g. ObjectOutputStream) to save or send it. Modern apps usually prefer JSON.

Summary

  • Path.of(...) points to files; Files reads, writes, copies and deletes.
  • writeString/readString for small files; Files.lines in try-with-resources for big ones.
  • Append with StandardOpenOption.APPEND; create folders with createDirectories.

Next: put everything together in a project.

items.title: Java Project: Student Grade Manager
items.excerpt: Build a complete console app in Java that adds students, calculates grades, shows toppers with streams, and saves everything to a CSV file. Uses every concept from this course.
items.content:
Time to build something real. You'll make a Student Grade Manager: a menu-driven console app that stores students, calculates grades, shows statistics, and saves data to a file so it's still there next time. This project uses records, collections, maps, streams, exceptions, file handling and Scanner.

What it does

=== Student Grade Manager ===
1. Add student
2. List students
3. Statistics
4. Search by name
5. Save and exit
Choose: 1
Name: Asha
Marks (0-100): 91
Saved Asha (A+)

Step 1: The data

A record is perfect for simple data. We add a method to calculate the grade:

record Student(String name, int marks) {
    String grade() {
        if (marks >= 90) return "A+";
        if (marks >= 75) return "A";
        if (marks >= 60) return "B";
        if (marks >= 40) return "C";
        return "F";
    }
}

Step 2: The full program

Save as GradeManager.java and run with java GradeManager.java.

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class GradeManager {

    record Student(String name, int marks) {
        String grade() {
            if (marks >= 90) return "A+";
            if (marks >= 75) return "A";
            if (marks >= 60) return "B";
            if (marks >= 40) return "C";
            return "F";
        }
    }

    private static final Path FILE = Path.of("students.csv");
    private static final List<Student> students = new ArrayList<>();
    private static final Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        load();
        while (true) {
            System.out.println("\n=== Student Grade Manager ===");
            System.out.println("1. Add student\n2. List students\n3. Statistics\n4. Search by name\n5. Save and exit");
            String choice = ask("Choose: ");
            switch (choice) {
                case "1" -> addStudent();
                case "2" -> listStudents();
                case "3" -> statistics();
                case "4" -> search();
                case "5" -> { save(); System.out.println("Bye!"); return; }
                default -> System.out.println("Please choose 1-5.");
            }
        }
    }

    static String ask(String prompt) {
        System.out.print(prompt);
        return in.hasNextLine() ? in.nextLine().trim() : "5";
    }

    static void addStudent() {
        String name = ask("Name: ");
        if (name.isEmpty() || name.contains(",")) {
            System.out.println("Name can't be empty or contain commas.");
            return;
        }
        int marks;
        try {
            marks = Integer.parseInt(ask("Marks (0-100): "));
            if (marks < 0 || marks > 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("out of range");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {   // NumberFormatException is a subclass
            System.out.println("Marks must be a whole number from 0 to 100.");
            return;
        }
        Student s = new Student(name, marks);
        students.add(s);
        System.out.println("Saved " + s.name() + " (" + s.grade() + ")");
    }

    static void listStudents() {
        if (students.isEmpty()) { System.out.println("No students yet."); return; }
        System.out.printf("%-15s %5s %5s%n", "Name", "Marks", "Grade");
        students.stream()
                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Student::name, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER))
                .forEach(s -> System.out.printf("%-15s %5d %5s%n", s.name(), s.marks(), s.grade()));
    }

    static void statistics() {
        if (students.isEmpty()) { System.out.println("No students yet."); return; }
        IntSummaryStatistics st = students.stream().mapToInt(Student::marks).summaryStatistics();
        System.out.printf("Students: %d | Average: %.1f | Highest: %d | Lowest: %d%n",
                st.getCount(), st.getAverage(), st.getMax(), st.getMin());

        List<String> toppers = students.stream()
                .filter(s -> s.marks() == st.getMax())
                .map(Student::name).toList();
        System.out.println("Topper(s): " + String.join(", ", toppers));

        Map<String, Long> byGrade = students.stream()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Student::grade, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
        byGrade.forEach((g, n) -> System.out.println(g + ": " + "*".repeat(n.intValue()) + " " + n));
    }

    static void search() {
        String q = ask("Search: ").toLowerCase();
        students.stream()
                .filter(s -> s.name().toLowerCase().contains(q))
                .forEach(s -> System.out.println(s.name() + " → " + s.marks() + " (" + s.grade() + ")"));
    }

    static void load() {
        if (!Files.exists(FILE)) return;
        try {
            for (String line : Files.readAllLines(FILE)) {
                String[] p = line.split(",");
                if (p.length == 2) students.add(new Student(p[0], Integer.parseInt(p[1].trim())));
            }
            System.out.println("Loaded " + students.size() + " students.");
        } catch (IOException | NumberFormatException e) {
            System.out.println("Could not load saved data: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    static void save() {
        List<String> lines = students.stream().map(s -> s.name() + "," + s.marks()).toList();
        try {
            Files.write(FILE, lines);
            System.out.println("Saved " + lines.size() + " students to " + FILE);
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.out.println("Could not save: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

How it works

  • **record Student**: an immutable data class with a grade() method (OOP in action).
  • **List<Student>**: the in-memory store.
  • Switch expression with arrows for the menu.
  • Exceptions: invalid marks are caught, so the app never crashes on bad input.
  • Streams: sorting, statistics (summaryStatistics), grouping by grade with TreeMap for sorted output.
  • Files: data loads at start and saves on exit as CSV.

Sample statistics output:

Students: 4 | Average: 76.5 | Highest: 91 | Lowest: 52
Topper(s): Asha
A: * 1
A+: * 1
B: * 1
C: * 1

Make it yours: challenges

  1. Edit and delete: add menu options to update a student's marks and remove a student.
  2. Multiple subjects: store a Map<String, Integer> of subject → marks and compute the average.
  3. Duplicate check: don't allow two students with the same name (case-insensitive).
  4. Report file: export a nicely formatted report.txt.
  5. Rank list: print students with their rank (ties share the same rank).
Hint for 3

Before adding, check students.stream().anyMatch(s -> s.name().equalsIgnoreCase(name)).

Hint for 5

Sort by marks descending. Keep the previous marks and rank; if marks are equal, reuse the rank, otherwise rank = position + 1.

Put this project on GitHub with a README and a screenshot of the output. Recruiters look for small, complete, working projects, not tutorials copied line by line.

What's next?

You now know core Java. Continue with:

  1. Java OOP: classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism and interfaces, with animations.
  2. DSA: arrays, hashing, recursion and interview patterns.
  3. Servlet, JPA and Spring Boot: build real web back-ends.

Summary

  • You built a complete menu-driven app with data persistence.
  • It combined records, collections, streams, exceptions, file I/O and input handling.
  • Extending projects with your own features is the best way to master Java.

items.title: What is Object-Oriented Programming?
items.excerpt: Understand OOP with real-life analogies, see how a class becomes many objects in an animation, and meet the four pillars: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction.
items.content:
So far you've written programs as a list of steps. That works for small programs. But a banking app, Swiggy or an online course site has thousands of moving parts. Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) organises code around objects: things that hold their own data and know how to do their own work.

The real-life idea

Look around you. Everything is an object:

  • A phone has data (brand, battery level, contacts) and behaviour (call, charge, take photo).
  • A bank account has data (owner, balance) and behaviour (deposit, withdraw).
  • A student has data (name, roll number, marks) and behaviour (attend class, take exam).

OOP lets you model software the same way. Instead of loose variables and functions, you build objects that bundle data (fields) and behaviour (methods) together.

Class vs object

  • A class is a blueprint: it describes what every object of that kind has and can do.
  • An object is one real thing built from the blueprint, with its own values.

Think of a cookie cutter (class) and cookies (objects). One cutter, many cookies, each can have different toppings. Play the animation: one Dog class, three different dogs.

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog rex = new Dog();       // create an object with new
        rex.name = "Rex";
        rex.age = 3;

        Dog bella = new Dog();     // another object, separate data
        bella.name = "Bella";
        bella.age = 5;

        rex.bark();                // Rex says Woof!
        bella.bark();              // Bella says Woof!
    }
}

class Dog {
    String name;            // field (data)
    int age;

    void bark() {           // method (behaviour)
        System.out.println(name + " says Woof!");
    }
}

new Dog() creates a new object in memory. Each object has its own copy of the fields: changing rex.age never touches bella.

Why OOP?

That's why Java, C#, Kotlin, Python and TypeScript all support OOP, and why every Java interview asks about it.

The four pillars (a preview)

  1. Encapsulation: keep data private and change it only through methods with rules. *An ATM lets you withdraw, but never lets you edit the bank's balance directly.*
  2. Inheritance: a new class reuses and extends an existing one. *A SavingsAccount is an Account with interest.*
  3. Polymorphism: one call, many behaviours. *animal.speak() makes a dog bark and a cat meow.*
  4. Abstraction: show what something does, hide how. *You press the brake pedal without knowing hydraulics.*

Each pillar gets its own lesson with an animation in this course.

Thinking in objects

Before writing code, ask:

  1. What are the nouns? (Student, Course, Enrollment, Teacher) → candidate classes.
  2. What does each know? (name, email, fee) → fields.
  3. What does each do? (enroll, pay, complete lesson) → methods.
  4. How are they related? (a Course has Lessons; a Teacher is a User) → composition and inheritance.

Practise by modelling things around you: a cricket match, a movie ticket booking, a library. Write the class names, fields and methods on paper before coding. Interviewers often ask exactly this ("design a parking lot").

Common mistakes

  • Thinking class = object. The class is the plan; objects are built from it with new.
  • Making everything public and changing fields from anywhere (breaks encapsulation).
  • Creating huge "god classes" that do everything. Keep each class focused on one job.

Exercise

  1. List 3 fields and 3 methods for each: MobilePhone, Movie, ShoppingCart.
  2. Write a Car class with brand, speed and methods accelerate() and brake(). Create two cars and call their methods.
  3. Identify the classes in this statement: "A customer places an order containing products and pays using UPI or card."
Hint for 3

Nouns: Customer, Order, Product, Payment (with UpiPayment and CardPayment as kinds of Payment).

Interview corner

  • What is OOP? A programming style that organises software into objects combining data and behaviour, built on encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction.
  • Class vs object? A class is a blueprint/template; an object is an instance of it in memory with its own state.
  • Is Java 100% object-oriented? No, because of primitive types (int, double…) and static members.

Summary

  • OOP models software as objects with fields (data) and methods (behaviour).
  • A class is the blueprint; new creates objects, each with its own data.
  • Four pillars: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction.

Next: classes and objects in depth, including how objects live in memory.
items.subject: java-oop

items.title: Java Classes and Objects
items.excerpt: Write classes with fields, methods and constructors, use the this keyword, see objects and references on the heap in an animation, and learn what null means.
items.content:
In this lesson you'll write proper classes with constructors, understand this, and see exactly what happens in memory when you create objects.

A class with a constructor

Setting every field by hand (rex.name = "Rex") is repetitive and error-prone. A constructor sets up the object as it's created:

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student a = new Student("Asha", 1, 88.5);
        Student b = new Student("Ravi", 2, 35);
        System.out.println(a.describe());   // 1: Asha (88.5) PASS
        System.out.println(b.describe());   // 2: Ravi (35.0) FAIL
    }
}

class Student {
    String name;
    int rollNo;
    double marks;

    Student(String name, int rollNo, double marks) {   // constructor: same name as class, no return type
        this.name = name;
        this.rollNo = rollNo;
        this.marks = marks;
    }

    boolean hasPassed() {
        return marks >= 40;
    }

    String describe() {
        return rollNo + ": " + name + " (" + marks + ")" + (hasPassed() ? " PASS" : " FAIL");
    }
}
  • A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type (not even void).
  • It runs automatically when you call new Student(...).
  • If you write no constructor, Java gives you a free default constructor with no parameters. Once you write any constructor, the free one disappears.

The this keyword

Inside a class, this means "the current object". In the constructor, this.name = name; means "set this object's name field to the name parameter". Without this, the parameter would hide the field and name = name; would do nothing useful.

this is also used to call another constructor (constructor chaining):

class Product {
    String title;
    double price;
    int stock;

    Product(String title, double price) {
        this(title, price, 0);       // call the 3-argument constructor
    }

    Product(String title, double price, int stock) {
        this.title = title;
        this.price = price;
        this.stock = stock;
    }
}

Objects live on the heap

Local variables live on the stack (one frame per method call). Objects created with new live on the heap. A variable like Student a doesn't hold the object; it holds a reference (like an address) to it. Step through:

This explains a lot:

Student x = new Student("Meera", 3, 91);
Student y = x;            // copies the reference, NOT the object
y.marks = 50;
System.out.println(x.marks);   // 50.0: x and y point to the same object
System.out.println(x == y);    // true: same object

null: a reference to nothing

Student s = null;          // points to no object
System.out.println(s == null);   // true
s.describe();              // NullPointerException!

Calling a method on null is the famous NullPointerException. Make sure a reference points to an object before using it.

Garbage collection

When no variable refers to an object anymore, it becomes garbage. Java's garbage collector automatically frees that memory. You never call delete like in C++.

Student temp = new Student("Temp", 9, 0);
temp = null;   // the old object is now unreachable → eligible for garbage collection

Instance methods use the object's data

Methods without static are instance methods: they work on a particular object's fields. That's why you call them on an object: a.describe(). Inside, marks means this.marks.

class Counter {
    int count;
    void increment() { count++; }     // changes THIS object's count
}

Counter c1 = new Counter(), c2 = new Counter();
c1.increment(); c1.increment(); c2.increment();
System.out.println(c1.count + " " + c2.count);   // 2 1

toString: printing objects nicely

Printing an object shows something like Student@1b6d3586 unless you override toString():

@Override
public String toString() {
    return "Student{name=" + name + ", marks=" + marks + "}";
}

Now System.out.println(a) prints Student{name=Asha, marks=88.5}. You'll learn more about @Override in the inheritance lesson.

One file, many classes?

A .java file can contain only one public class, named like the file. Other non-public classes may be in the same file (handy for practice, like above), but in real projects each class gets its own file inside packages (folders like com.vitalstack.school).

Common mistakes

  • Writing void Student(...): with a return type it's a method, not a constructor!
  • Forgetting this. when the parameter has the same name as the field.
  • Using an object before new (NullPointerException).
  • Assuming y = x copies the object.

Exercise

  1. Create a Book class with title, author, price and a constructor. Add applyDiscount(int percent).
  2. Create a Rectangle class with area() and perimeter() methods. Create three rectangles and print the biggest area.
  3. Create a BankAccount with owner and balance, and methods deposit and withdraw (refuse if the balance is too low).
  4. Predict the output, then run it:
Counter a = new Counter();
Counter b = a;
a.increment();
b.increment();
System.out.println(a.count);
Hint for 4

a and b refer to the same Counter object, so both increments change one count. It prints 2.

Interview corner

  • What is a constructor? A special method that initialises a new object; same name as the class, no return type, called by new.
  • Can a constructor be private? Yes: used in singletons and factory methods so others can't create objects freely.
  • Where are objects stored? On the heap; references to them can be on the stack (local variables) or in other objects' fields.
  • What is garbage collection? The JVM automatically reclaiming memory of objects that are no longer reachable.

Summary

  • Classes have fields, methods and constructors; new calls the constructor.
  • this refers to the current object and can chain constructors.
  • Objects live on the heap; variables hold references; null means no object.
  • Unreachable objects are cleaned up by the garbage collector.

Next: more constructor tricks and the static keyword.

items.title: Java Static Members and Constructor Overloading
items.excerpt: Learn the difference between static and instance members, shared counters, static utility methods, static blocks, constructor overloading and initialisation order.
items.content:
Some data belongs to each object (every student has their own name). Some belongs to the class as a whole (the total number of students, the school's name). The static keyword marks class-level members.

Instance vs static fields

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student a = new Student("Asha");
        Student b = new Student("Ravi");
        Student c = new Student("Meera");
        System.out.println(Student.count);               // 3
        System.out.println(c.id + " " + c.name);          // 3 Meera
        System.out.println(Student.school);               // VitalStack Academy
    }
}

class Student {
    static String school = "VitalStack Academy";   // one copy, shared by all
    static int count = 0;                           // shared counter

    String name;                                    // one copy per object
    int id;

    Student(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        count++;                                    // update the shared counter
        this.id = count;                            // give each student a unique id
    }
}
 Class area (one copy)           Heap (one per object)
 ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐
 │ school = "Vital…"    │        │ name = "Asha" │ │ name = "Ravi" │ ...
 │ count  = 3           │        │ id   = 1      │ │ id   = 2      │
 └──────────────────────┘        └───────────────┘ └───────────────┘

Access static members through the class name: Student.count. (Java also allows a.count, but that's misleading, so avoid it.)

Static methods

A static method belongs to the class and doesn't need an object. It cannot use instance fields or this, because there's no particular object.

class MathUtils {
    static int square(int x) { return x * x; }
    static boolean isPrime(int n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;
        for (int i = 2; (long) i * i <= n; i++) if (n % i == 0) return false;
        return true;
    }
}

int s = MathUtils.square(12);         // 144
boolean p = MathUtils.isPrime(97);    // true

That's why main is static: the JVM calls it before any object exists. And it's why Java's own utility classes are static: Math.max(), Arrays.sort(), Integer.parseInt().

Constants: static final

class Config {
    static final double GST_RATE = 0.18;
    static final int MAX_CART_ITEMS = 50;
}

static final means one shared copy that never changes: perfect for constants.

Constructor overloading

Give users several ways to create an object:

class Pizza {
    String size;
    String crust;
    int toppings;

    Pizza() {                                   // all defaults
        this("Medium", "Thin", 0);
    }

    Pizza(String size) {                        // choose size only
        this(size, "Thin", 0);
    }

    Pizza(String size, String crust, int toppings) {   // full control
        this.size = size;
        this.crust = crust;
        this.toppings = toppings;
    }

    double price() {
        double base = switch (size) {
            case "Small" -> 199;
            case "Large" -> 449;
            default -> 299;
        };
        return base + toppings * 49;
    }
}

new Pizza().price();                       // 299.0
new Pizza("Large").price();                // 449.0
new Pizza("Small", "Cheese burst", 3).price();   // 346.0

Chaining with this(...) keeps the real setup code in one place. this(...) must be the first line of a constructor.

Static blocks and initialisation order

A static { } block runs once, when the class is first loaded. Instance initialiser blocks { } run before every constructor:

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Demo();
        new Demo();
    }
}

class Demo {
    static { System.out.println("1. static block (class loaded)"); }
    { System.out.println("2. instance block"); }
    Demo() { System.out.println("3. constructor"); }
}
1. static block (class loaded)
2. instance block
3. constructor
2. instance block
3. constructor

Common mistakes

  • Using an instance field inside a static method: "non-static variable cannot be referenced from a static context". Create an object, or make the method non-static.
  • Making fields static "to make the error go away": then every object shares one value, a serious bug.
  • Overusing static: it makes code hard to test. Prefer objects for anything with state.

Exercise

  1. Add a static counter to a Car class that counts how many cars were created.
  2. Create a Temperature utility class with static cToF and fToC methods.
  3. Create an Order class whose constructor assigns ids like ORD-1001, ORD-1002… using a static counter.
  4. Give a Ticket class three constructors: (movie), (movie, seat), (movie, seat, price). Chain them.
Hint for 3

static int next = 1001; then in the constructor this.id = "ORD-" + next++;

Interview corner

  • Why is main static? So the JVM can call it without creating an object.
  • Can a static method access instance variables? Not directly; it has no this. It needs an object reference.
  • Can we override a static method? No. A subclass can declare one with the same signature (hiding), but there's no runtime polymorphism.
  • When does a static block run? Once, when the class is loaded by the JVM.

Summary

  • Static members belong to the class (one copy); instance members belong to each object.
  • Static methods can't use this; use them for utilities.
  • static final makes constants.
  • Overload constructors and chain them with this(...) as the first statement.

Next: encapsulation, protecting your object's data.

items.title: Java Encapsulation
items.excerpt: Protect object data with private fields, getters, setters and validation, learn the four access modifiers, packages, and build immutable classes, with a live bank-account animation.
items.content:
Imagine anyone in your program could write account.balance = -50000;. Bugs would be everywhere and impossible to trace. Encapsulation means hiding an object's data and only allowing changes through methods that enforce the rules.

The ATM analogy

At an ATM you can deposit and withdraw, but you can't open the machine and edit the bank's database. The ATM checks your PIN, your balance, the daily limit. Your object should work the same way: private data, public methods with checks.

Private fields, public methods

Try different operations in the animation, including withdrawing too much and depositing a negative amount:

public class BankAccount {
    private final String owner;     // private: only this class can touch it
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(String owner, double opening) {
        if (opening < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Opening balance can't be negative");
        this.owner = owner;
        this.balance = opening;
    }

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        balance += amount;
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
        if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");
        balance -= amount;
    }

    public double getBalance() { return balance; }      // read-only access
    public String getOwner() { return owner; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BankAccount acc = new BankAccount("Asha", 1000);
        acc.deposit(500);
        acc.withdraw(200);
        System.out.println(acc.getOwner() + ": " + acc.getBalance());   // Asha: 1300.0
        try {
            acc.withdraw(5000);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("Blocked: " + e.getMessage());           // Blocked: Insufficient funds
        }
    }
}

From outside the class, acc.balance = -50000; is now a compile error. The only ways to change the balance are deposit and withdraw, and both validate.

Getters and setters

  • A getter (getBalance(), or isActive() for booleans) returns a field's value.
  • A setter (setEmail(...)) changes it, ideally with validation.
public class User {
    private String email;

    public String getEmail() { return email; }

    public void setEmail(String email) {
        if (email == null || !email.contains("@")) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid email");
        }
        this.email = email.trim().toLowerCase();
    }
}

Don't auto-generate a setter for every field. Ask "should outsiders change this?" A bank balance should have deposit/withdraw, not setBalance. An id should have no setter at all.

The four access modifiers

Rule of thumb: fields private, methods public only if needed, everything else as restricted as possible.

Packages

Packages are folders that group related classes and control visibility:

package com.vitalstack.bank;          // first line of the file

import java.util.List;                 // use classes from other packages

public class BankAccount { ... }

The file lives in com/vitalstack/bank/BankAccount.java. Package names are lowercase, usually your domain reversed.

Immutable classes

The safest objects are those that can't change after creation. Like String, they are automatically thread-safe and can be shared freely.

public final class Money {                 // final: no subclass can break the rules
    private final long paise;              // final fields: set once
    private final String currency;

    public Money(long paise, String currency) {
        this.paise = paise;
        this.currency = currency;
    }

    public Money plus(Money other) {       // returns a NEW object instead of changing this one
        return new Money(this.paise + other.paise, currency);
    }

    public long getPaise() { return paise; }
}

Recipe for immutability: final class, private final fields, no setters, return new objects for changes, and make defensive copies of mutable things like lists (List.copyOf(list)).

Defensive copies

public class Course {
    private final List<String> lessons;

    public Course(List<String> lessons) {
        this.lessons = List.copyOf(lessons);      // caller's later changes don't affect us
    }

    public List<String> getLessons() {
        return lessons;                           // List.copyOf is already unmodifiable
    }
}

Without the copy, a caller could keep a reference to the list and change your object's insides.

Common mistakes

  • Public fields "for convenience".
  • Setters with no validation, making encapsulation pointless.
  • Returning internal mutable lists directly.
  • Getters with side effects (a getter should not change state).

Exercise

  1. Create a Student class with private name and marks; the setter must reject marks outside 0-100.
  2. Create Thermostat with a private temperature that can only be changed by increase()/decrease() within 16-30 °C.
  3. Make an immutable Point class with x, y and a move(dx, dy) method returning a new Point.
  4. Create a Playlist class that holds songs in a private list, with addSong, removeSong and a getSongs that returns an unmodifiable view.
Hint for 4

Return Collections.unmodifiableList(songs) or List.copyOf(songs) from getSongs().

Interview corner

  • What is encapsulation? Bundling data with the methods that operate on it and restricting direct access (private fields + controlled public methods).
  • Encapsulation vs abstraction? Encapsulation hides data (how state is protected); abstraction hides complexity (what an object does vs how).
  • How to create an immutable class? final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies, return new objects for changes.
  • protected vs default? protected also allows access from subclasses in other packages.

Summary

  • Keep fields private; expose behaviour through validated public methods.
  • Access modifiers: private < package-private < protected < public.
  • Immutable objects (final fields, no setters) are simple and thread-safe.
  • Make defensive copies of mutable data going in and out.

Next: inheritance, building new classes on top of existing ones.

items.title: Java Inheritance
items.excerpt: Reuse code with extends, override methods with @Override, call parent code with super, see method lookup climb the class hierarchy in an animation, and learn when to prefer composition.
items.content:
Many classes share common parts. A Dog, a Cat and a Cow all eat and sleep. Instead of writing eat() three times, put it in an Animal class once and let the others inherit it. That's inheritance: a new class (child/subclass) builds on an existing one (parent/superclass).

extends

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Puppy p = new Puppy();
        p.speak();   // Woof!           (from Dog)
        p.sleep();   // naps all day    (Puppy's own)
        p.eat();     // eats food       (from Animal)
        p.fetch();   // fetches the ball (from Dog)
    }
}

class Animal {
    void eat()   { System.out.println("eats food"); }
    void sleep() { System.out.println("sleeps"); }
    void speak() { System.out.println("makes a sound"); }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void speak() { System.out.println("Woof!"); }     // replace the parent's version
    void fetch() { System.out.println("fetches the ball"); }   // add something new
}

class Puppy extends Dog {
    @Override
    void sleep() { System.out.println("naps all day"); }
}

How Java finds the method

When you call p.speak(), Java starts at the object's actual class and walks up the hierarchy until it finds the method. Pick an object and a method in the animation and watch the search climb:

Try Cat + fetch: the search reaches the top without finding it. In real Java, that's a compile error, because the compiler checks that the method exists for the variable's type.

Overriding and @Override

A subclass overrides a method by defining one with the same name and parameters. Always add @Override: the compiler then checks that you really are overriding something. If you mistype speek(), you get an error instead of a silent bug.

Rules for overriding:

  • Same name and parameter list.
  • Return type the same (or a subtype).
  • Access can't be more restrictive (a public method can't become private).
  • private, static and final methods can't be overridden.

super: talk to the parent

super calls the parent's version of a method or constructor:

public class Payroll {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Employee e = new Employee("Ravi", 50000);
        Manager m = new Manager("Asha", 80000, 200000);
        System.out.println(e.describe());   // Ravi earns ₹600000.0
        System.out.println(m.describe());   // Asha earns ₹1160000.0 (manager)
    }
}

class Employee {
    protected String name;
    protected double salary;

    Employee(String name, double salary) {
        this.name = name;
        this.salary = salary;
    }

    double annualPay() { return salary * 12; }

    String describe() { return name + " earns ₹" + annualPay(); }
}

class Manager extends Employee {
    private final double bonus;

    Manager(String name, double salary, double bonus) {
        super(name, salary);            // must be the first line: build the Employee part
        this.bonus = bonus;
    }

    @Override
    double annualPay() {
        return super.annualPay() + bonus;    // reuse the parent's calculation
    }

    @Override
    String describe() { return super.describe() + " (manager)"; }
}
  • If the parent has no no-argument constructor, the child must call super(...) explicitly.
  • Notice that describe() in Employee calls annualPay(), and for a Manager the overridden version runs. That's polymorphism, the next lesson.

The Object class

Every class in Java secretly extends java.lang.Object. That's where toString(), equals(), hashCode() and getClass() come from. You'll override them in a later lesson.

Types of inheritance in Java

Single:        A ← B
Multilevel:    A ← B ← C          (Animal ← Dog ← Puppy)
Hierarchical:  A ← B, A ← C       (Animal ← Dog, Animal ← Cat)
Multiple:      A, B ← C           ✗ not allowed with classes

Java does not allow a class to extend two classes (the "diamond problem": if both parents have speak(), which one wins?). A class can, however, implement many interfaces.

final: stop inheritance

final class Rupee { }            // no class can extend Rupee
class Shape {
    final double PI = 3.14159;
    final void draw() { }        // subclasses can't override draw()
}

Composition: "has a" vs "is a"

Use inheritance only for true is-a relationships: a Manager is an Employee. For has-a, put one object inside another:

class Engine {
    void start() { System.out.println("Engine started"); }
}

class Car {
    private final Engine engine = new Engine();   // Car HAS an Engine
    void drive() {
        engine.start();
        System.out.println("Car is moving");
    }
}

class Car extends Engine would be wrong: a car isn't an engine. Favour composition over inheritance: it's more flexible, and deep inheritance trees become hard to change.

A quick test: say it out loud. "A Puppy is a Dog" ✅ inheritance. "A Car is an Engine" ❌ composition.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting super(...) when the parent has only constructors with parameters.
  • Accidentally overloading instead of overriding (different parameters) without @Override.
  • Using inheritance just to reuse a couple of methods (use composition or a helper class).
  • Deep hierarchies (more than 2-3 levels) that are hard to follow.

Exercise

  1. Create Vehicle (brand, move()), then Car and Bike that override move().
  2. Create Account with withdraw(), and SavingsAccount that overrides it to keep a minimum balance of ₹1000.
  3. Create Shape with area() returning 0, then Circle and Square that override it.
  4. Model a Library that has a list of Books (composition), with addBook and findByAuthor.
Hint for 2

In SavingsAccount.withdraw, check balance - amount >= 1000 and then call super.withdraw(amount).

Interview corner

  • Why doesn't Java support multiple inheritance of classes? To avoid the diamond problem and complexity. Interfaces provide multiple inheritance of type.
  • Can a constructor be inherited? No. But a child constructor calls a parent constructor with super(...) (implicitly super() if you don't).
  • What is method overriding? A subclass providing its own implementation of a parent method with the same signature, chosen at runtime.
  • Composition vs inheritance? Inheritance = is-a, tight coupling; composition = has-a, flexible. Prefer composition.

Summary

  • extends lets a class inherit fields and methods; Java searches up the hierarchy to find a method.
  • Override with @Override; call the parent with super.
  • Java has single class inheritance; every class extends Object.
  • Prefer composition for has-a relationships.

Next: polymorphism, where inheritance really pays off.

items.title: Java Polymorphism
items.excerpt: One call, many behaviours. See dynamic method dispatch in an animation, compare compile-time overloading with runtime overriding, upcasting, downcasting, instanceof and pattern matching.
items.content:
Polymorphism means "many forms". The same method call does different things depending on the actual object. It lets you write code that works with a general type (Animal) and still get specific behaviour (Woof!, Meow!). It's the most powerful idea in OOP and a favourite interview topic.

One loop, many behaviours

Add or remove animals in the input and watch each object answer the same speak() call differently:

import java.util.List;

public class Zoo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Animal> zoo = List.of(new Dog(), new Cat(), new Cow(), new Dog());
        for (Animal a : zoo) {
            System.out.println(a.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + a.speak());
        }
    }
}

abstract class Animal {
    abstract String speak();
}
class Dog extends Animal { String speak() { return "Woof!"; } }
class Cat extends Animal { String speak() { return "Meow!"; } }
class Cow extends Animal { String speak() { return "Moo!"; } }
Dog: Woof!
Cat: Meow!
Cow: Moo!
Dog: Woof!

The loop doesn't know or care which animal it has. Add a Duck class tomorrow and this loop doesn't change. That's the real benefit: code that's open for new types without editing old code.

Upcasting: a parent reference to a child object

Animal a = new Dog();     // upcasting: always safe, automatic
a.speak();                // "Woof!": the Dog's version runs
  • The variable type (Animal) decides which methods you're allowed to call (checked at compile time).
  • The object type (Dog) decides which version actually runs (decided at runtime).

This runtime choice is called dynamic method dispatch (or late binding).

Compile-time vs runtime polymorphism

class Printer {
    void print(int n)    { System.out.println("int: " + n); }
    void print(String s) { System.out.println("text: " + s); }
}
new Printer().print(5);       // int: 5      (chosen at compile time)
new Printer().print("hi");    // text: hi

Downcasting and instanceof

Sometimes you need the specific type back, for example to call fetch() which only Dog has:

Animal a = new Dog();
// a.fetch();               // compile error: Animal has no fetch()

if (a instanceof Dog) {
    Dog d = (Dog) a;        // downcasting: explicit
    d.fetch();
}

Casting to the wrong type throws ClassCastException at runtime, so check with instanceof first.

Pattern matching (Java 16+)

Shorter and safer: test and cast in one step:

if (a instanceof Dog d) {
    d.fetch();              // d is already a Dog here
}

And with switch (Java 21):

String sound = switch (a) {
    case Dog d -> "dog says " + d.speak();
    case Cat c -> "cat says " + c.speak();
    default -> "unknown animal";
};

If your code is full of instanceof checks, it's a sign you should move that behaviour into the classes as an overridden method. Let polymorphism do the work.

A practical example: payments

public class Checkout {
    static void pay(Payment p, double amount) {          // works for ANY payment type
        System.out.printf("%s: pay ₹%.2f (fee ₹%.2f)%n", p.name(), amount + p.fee(amount), p.fee(amount));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (Payment p : new Payment[] { new Upi(), new Card(), new NetBanking() }) {
            pay(p, 1000);
        }
    }
}

interface Payment {
    double fee(double amount);
    String name();
}

class Upi implements Payment {
    public double fee(double amount) { return 0; }
    public String name() { return "UPI"; }
}

class Card implements Payment {
    public double fee(double amount) { return amount * 0.02; }
    public String name() { return "Card"; }
}

class NetBanking implements Payment {
    public double fee(double amount) { return 10; }
    public String name() { return "Net banking"; }
}
UPI: pay ₹1000.00 (fee ₹0.00)
Card: pay ₹1020.00 (fee ₹20.00)
Net banking: pay ₹1010.00 (fee ₹10.00)

Adding Wallet payments later means adding one class. pay() never changes. Spring, Hibernate and most frameworks are built on exactly this idea.

What is NOT polymorphic

  • Fields: a.name uses the variable's type, not the object's. (Another reason to keep fields private.)
  • Static methods: chosen by the reference type (method hiding, not overriding).
  • Private and final methods: can't be overridden.

Common mistakes

  • Expecting overloading to pick a method based on the object's runtime type (it uses the declared type).
  • Downcasting without instanceof → ClassCastException.
  • Long if (x instanceof A) ... else if (x instanceof B) chains instead of overriding.

Exercise

  1. Create Shape with area() and perimeter(), subclasses Circle, Rectangle, Triangle. Put them in a list and print the total area.
  2. Create Notification with send(String msg), implemented by EmailNotification, SmsNotification and PushNotification. Send one message through all of them.
  3. Predict the output:
class A { void show() { System.out.println("A"); } }
class B extends A { void show() { System.out.println("B"); } }
A obj = new B();
obj.show();
Hint for 3

The object is a B, and show() is overridden, so it prints "B" even though the variable type is A.

Interview corner

  • What is polymorphism? The ability of one interface (method call, reference type) to represent many forms (behaviours of different classes).
  • Types in Java? Compile-time (overloading) and runtime (overriding / dynamic dispatch).
  • What is dynamic method dispatch? The JVM picks the overridden method based on the actual object at runtime.
  • Can you achieve polymorphism with interfaces? Yes, that's the most common way in modern Java.

Summary

  • Polymorphism: one call, behaviour decided by the real object.
  • Overloading = compile-time; overriding = runtime (dynamic dispatch).
  • Upcasting is automatic; downcast safely with instanceof pattern matching.
  • Polymorphic code accepts new types without changes.

Next: abstraction with abstract classes.

items.title: Java Abstraction and Abstract Classes
items.excerpt: Hide complexity with abstraction, write abstract classes and abstract methods, use the template method pattern, and learn when to choose an abstract class over an interface.
items.content:
When you drive a car, you use the steering wheel, accelerator and brake. You don't think about fuel injection or ABS sensors. Abstraction means showing what something does and hiding how it does it. In Java, abstraction is built with abstract classes and interfaces.

Abstract classes

An abstract class is a partial blueprint: it can't be instantiated on its own, and it can declare abstract methods (no body) that subclasses must implement.

public class Shapes {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Shape s = new Shape("x");     // error: Shape is abstract
        Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(2), new Rectangle(3, 4) };
        for (Shape s : shapes) System.out.println(s.describe());
    }
}

abstract class Shape {
    private final String name;

    Shape(String name) { this.name = name; }

    abstract double area();              // no body: every shape MUST provide one

    String describe() {                  // normal method shared by all shapes
        return String.format("%s with area %.2f", name, area());
    }
}

class Circle extends Shape {
    private final double r;
    Circle(double r) { super("Circle"); this.r = r; }
    @Override double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}

class Rectangle extends Shape {
    private final double w, h;
    Rectangle(double w, double h) { super("Rectangle"); this.w = w; this.h = h; }
    @Override double area() { return w * h; }
}
Circle with area 12.57
Rectangle with area 12.00
  • An abstract class can have fields, constructors and normal methods.
  • A concrete subclass must implement all abstract methods (or be abstract itself).
  • You can't write new Shape(...), but you can have Shape variables pointing to subclasses.

Template method pattern

A powerful use of abstract classes: the parent defines the steps of an algorithm, and subclasses fill in the details.

public class Reports {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new SalesReport().generate());
        System.out.println(new AttendanceReport().generate());
    }
}

abstract class ReportGenerator {
    // the template: fixed order of steps (final so subclasses can't break it)
    public final String generate() {
        return header() + "\n" + body() + "\n" + footer();
    }

    protected String header() { return "=== VitalStack Report ==="; }
    protected abstract String body();                 // each report decides this
    protected String footer() { return "Generated automatically"; }
}

class SalesReport extends ReportGenerator {
    protected String body() { return "Sales this week: ₹1,24,500"; }
}

class AttendanceReport extends ReportGenerator {
    protected String body() { return "Attendance: 92%"; }
    @Override protected String footer() { return "Sent to HR"; }
}
=== VitalStack Report ===
Sales this week: ₹1,24,500
Generated automatically
=== VitalStack Report ===
Attendance: 92%
Sent to HR

Spring uses this pattern a lot (JdbcTemplate, AbstractController…).

Abstraction in everyday Java

You already use abstraction constantly:

  • List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();: you program against List without knowing how ArrayList manages its array.
  • Files.readString(path) hides OS file system details.
  • System.out.println hides how text reaches your screen.

Abstract class vs interface

Rule of thumb: start with an interface. Use an abstract class when subclasses need to share fields or common code. Often you'll use both: an interface for the contract and an abstract class with shared code that implements it.

Common mistakes

  • Trying to instantiate an abstract class.
  • Forgetting to implement an abstract method (compile error: "is not abstract and does not override abstract method").
  • Abstract classes with no abstract methods and no shared code: probably not needed.
  • Over-abstracting too early. Abstract when you see real duplication.

Exercise

  1. Create an abstract Employee with abstract calculatePay(), and FullTimeEmployee (monthly salary) and Contractor (hours × rate) subclasses. Print total payroll.
  2. Create an abstract Game with a template play() method: start(), takeTurns(), end(). Implement Cricket and Chess versions.
  3. Can an abstract class have a constructor? Write a small example to check.
Hint for 3

Yes. It runs when a subclass object is created, through super(...). Use it to initialise the shared fields.

Interview corner

  • What is abstraction? Hiding implementation details and exposing only essential behaviour.
  • Can an abstract class have a constructor? Yes; it's called via super() from subclasses.
  • Can an abstract class have no abstract methods? Yes; it just can't be instantiated.
  • Can a method be both abstract and final? No: abstract must be overridden, final can't be.
  • Abstract class vs interface? See the table: state and constructors vs multiple implementation and capabilities.

Summary

  • Abstraction shows what, hides how.
  • Abstract classes can't be instantiated and may force subclasses to implement abstract methods.
  • The template method pattern fixes the steps and lets subclasses fill in details.
  • Prefer interfaces for capabilities; abstract classes for shared state and code.

Next: interfaces in depth.

items.title: Java Interfaces
items.excerpt: Define contracts with interfaces, implement several at once, use default and static methods, Comparable and Comparator, functional interfaces and programming to an interface.
items.content:
An interface is a contract: a list of methods a class promises to provide. Any class that implements the interface can be used wherever that interface is expected. Interfaces are everywhere in Java: List, Comparable, Runnable, and every Spring service.

Defining and implementing

public class InterfaceDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(2), new Rectangle(3, 4) };
        double total = 0;
        for (Shape s : shapes) {
            System.out.println(s.label());
            total += s.area();
        }
        System.out.printf("Total area: %.2f%n", total);
    }
}

interface Shape {
    double area();                      // public and abstract automatically
    default String label() {            // a default method has a body
        return getClass().getSimpleName() + " (" + String.format("%.2f", area()) + ")";
    }
}

class Circle implements Shape {
    private final double r;
    Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
    public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}

class Rectangle implements Shape {
    private final double w, h;
    Rectangle(double w, double h) { this.w = w; this.h = h; }
    public double area() { return w * h; }
}
Circle (12.57)
Rectangle (12.00)
Total area: 24.57

Change the sizes in the animation and watch one area() call reach different classes:

  • Interface methods are public abstract by default. The implementing method must be public.
  • A class can implement many interfaces: class Duck implements Flyer, Swimmer.
  • Interfaces can extend other interfaces.

Multiple interfaces

interface Flyer   { default String move() { return "flies"; } }
interface Swimmer { String swim(); }

class Duck implements Flyer, Swimmer {
    public String swim() { return "paddles"; }
}

Duck d = new Duck();
System.out.println(d.move() + " and " + d.swim());   // flies and paddles

If two interfaces have the same default method, the class must override it and choose (Flyer.super.move()). That's how Java avoids the diamond problem.

Static methods and constants

interface Gst {
    double RATE = 0.18;                       // public static final constant
    static double withGst(double price) {     // called as Gst.withGst(100)
        return price * (1 + RATE);
    }
}

Comparable: natural ordering

Implement Comparable<T> so objects can be sorted:

import java.util.*;

public class Ranking {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Student> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
            new Student("Asha", 88), new Student("Ravi", 95), new Student("Meera", 72)));
        Collections.sort(list);
        System.out.println(list);                                        // [Ravi=95, Asha=88, Meera=72]
        list.sort(Comparator.comparing(s -> s.name));                   // a different order on demand
        System.out.println(list);                                        // [Asha=88, Meera=72, Ravi=95]
    }
}

class Student implements Comparable<Student> {
    final String name;
    final int marks;
    Student(String name, int marks) { this.name = name; this.marks = marks; }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Student other) {        // negative: this first; positive: other first
        return Integer.compare(other.marks, this.marks);   // higher marks first
    }

    @Override public String toString() { return name + "=" + marks; }
}
  • Comparable: one natural order built into the class.
  • Comparator: any number of external orders: Comparator.comparing(...), .reversed(), .thenComparing(...).

Functional interfaces and lambdas

An interface with exactly one abstract method is a functional interface, and can be implemented with a lambda:

@FunctionalInterface
interface DiscountRule {
    double apply(double price);
}

DiscountRule festive = price -> price * 0.8;
DiscountRule flat100 = price -> Math.max(0, price - 100);
System.out.println(festive.apply(1000) + " " + flat100.apply(1000));   // 800.0 900.0

Runnable, Comparator, Predicate, Function are all functional interfaces.

Programming to an interface

Declare variables, parameters and return types as interfaces, not concrete classes:

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();            // ✅ can switch to LinkedList later
ArrayList<String> names2 = new ArrayList<>();      // ❌ locked in

In Spring Boot you'll write interface CourseRepository and Spring creates the implementation for you. Your services depend only on the interface, which makes them easy to test with fake implementations.

Interfaces describe capabilities ("can be compared", "can be paid with", "can be saved"). Name them as adjectives or roles: Comparable, Payable, Searchable, PaymentGateway.

Common mistakes

  • Making the implementing method package-private (it must be public).
  • Putting state in interfaces (only constants are allowed).
  • Creating an interface for every single class "just because": add one when you have, or truly expect, multiple implementations, or for testing boundaries.
  • compareTo using subtraction (a - b) with big numbers can overflow. Use Integer.compare.

Exercise

  1. Create Playable with play() and stop(); implement it in Song and Video.
  2. Make a Product class Comparable by price, then sort with a Comparator by name and by rating.
  3. Create PaymentGateway with pay(double), implement RazorpayGateway and PaytmGateway (just print messages), and a Checkout class that accepts any gateway in its constructor.
  4. Create a Validator<T> functional interface and write lambdas that validate an email and a phone number.
Hint for 3

class Checkout { private final PaymentGateway gateway; Checkout(PaymentGateway g) { gateway = g; } }. This is dependency injection, which Spring automates.

Interview corner

  • Can an interface have method bodies? Yes: default and static methods (Java 8+) and private methods (Java 9+).
  • Interface vs abstract class? Interfaces: no instance state, multiple implementation. Abstract classes: state, constructors, single inheritance.
  • What is a marker interface? An interface with no methods (e.g. Serializable) that tags a class.
  • Comparable vs Comparator? Comparable: natural order inside the class (compareTo). Comparator: separate ordering objects (compare).

Summary

  • Interfaces are contracts; classes implements them, and can implement many.
  • Default and static methods add behaviour without breaking implementers.
  • Comparable gives natural ordering; Comparator gives custom orderings.
  • Program to interfaces for flexible, testable code.

items.title: Java equals, hashCode and toString
items.excerpt: Override the Object methods correctly. Learn why == differs from equals, the equals-hashCode contract, what breaks in HashMap and HashSet when you get it wrong, and a clean toString.
items.content:
Every Java class inherits three important methods from Object: toString(), equals() and hashCode(). Their default versions are rarely what you want for your own classes, and getting equals/hashCode wrong causes some of the sneakiest bugs in Java.

toString: readable objects

class Book {
    String title; String author;
    Book(String title, String author) { this.title = title; this.author = author; }
}

System.out.println(new Book("Wings of Fire", "A. P. J. Abdul Kalam"));
// Book@6d06d69c   ← class name + hash: useless

Override it:

@Override
public String toString() {
    return "Book{title='" + title + "', author='" + author + "'}";
}
// Book{title='Wings of Fire', author='A. P. J. Abdul Kalam'}

toString is used by println, string concatenation, debuggers and logs. Always override it for data classes.

== vs equals

  • == asks: are these the same object (same address)?
  • equals() asks: are these objects meaningfully equal (same content)?

The default Object.equals is just ==. So two different Book objects with the same title and author are not equal until you override equals. (You saw the same issue with Strings and the string pool.)

Overriding equals correctly

import java.util.Objects;

class Book {
    private final String isbn;
    private final String title;

    Book(String isbn, String title) { this.isbn = isbn; this.title = title; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;                          // same object
        if (!(o instanceof Book other)) return false;        // null or different type
        return isbn.equals(other.isbn);                      // compare what defines identity
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(isbn);                           // same fields as equals!
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() { return title + " [" + isbn + "]"; }
}

Note the parameter type is Object, not Book. Writing equals(Book o) overloads instead of overriding, and collections will never call it. @Override catches that mistake.

The contract

  1. Reflexive: a.equals(a) is true.
  2. Symmetric: if a.equals(b) then b.equals(a).
  3. Transitive: if a.equals(b) and b.equals(c) then a.equals(c).
  4. Consistent: same result every time if nothing changed.
  5. a.equals(null) is false.
  6. **If a.equals(b), then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode().** (The reverse isn't required: different objects may share a hash.)

Why hashCode matters: the HashSet bug

HashMap and HashSet first use hashCode() to pick a bucket, then equals() to compare inside it (revisit the HashMap animation in the Java course). If you override equals but not hashCode, two equal objects usually land in different buckets:

import java.util.*;

public class HashBug {
    static class Point {
        final int x, y;
        Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
            return o instanceof Point p && p.x == x && p.y == y;
        }
        // hashCode NOT overridden!
    }

    static class FixedPoint {
        final int x, y;
        FixedPoint(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
            return o instanceof FixedPoint p && p.x == x && p.y == y;
        }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Set<Point> broken = new HashSet<>();
        broken.add(new Point(1, 2));
        System.out.println(broken.contains(new Point(1, 2)));     // false (almost always)!

        Set<FixedPoint> fixed = new HashSet<>();
        fixed.add(new FixedPoint(1, 2));
        System.out.println(fixed.contains(new FixedPoint(1, 2))); // true
    }
}

Rules of thumb

  • **Always override equals and hashCode together, using the same fields**.
  • Use fields that don't change (an id, ISBN, email). If a field used in hashCode changes while the object is in a HashSet, the object gets "lost" in the wrong bucket.
  • Use Objects.equals(a, b) for null-safe field comparison and Objects.hash(...) for hashCode.
  • Let your IDE generate them (IntelliJ: Alt+Insert → equals() and hashCode()), or use a record, which does it for you.

Records do it automatically

record Point(int x, int y) { }

Point a = new Point(1, 2), b = new Point(1, 2);
System.out.println(a.equals(b));             // true
System.out.println(a.hashCode() == b.hashCode());   // true
System.out.println(a);                        // Point[x=1, y=2]

Records generate equals, hashCode and toString from their components. More in the next lesson.

JPA/Hibernate entities are a special case: their id may be null until saved. Many teams compare entities by id only when it's not null, or by a natural business key. You'll see this in the JPA course.

Common mistakes

  • equals(Book other) instead of equals(Object o) (overloading, not overriding).
  • Overriding equals without hashCode.
  • Using mutable fields in hashCode.
  • Using getClass() != o.getClass() vs instanceof inconsistently across a hierarchy (pick one approach).

Exercise

  1. Create an Employee class where two employees are equal if they have the same employee id. Add both to a HashSet and check its size.
  2. Remove the hashCode override and test again. What changes?
  3. Write a Money class (amount in paise + currency) with proper equals, hashCode and toString like ₹12.50.
  4. Rewrite Money as a record and compare the amount of code.
Hint for 1

Two new Employee(101, "Asha") objects should give a set of size 1 only when both equals and hashCode use the id.

Interview corner

  • What's the contract between equals and hashCode? Equal objects must have equal hash codes. Unequal objects may share a hash code.
  • What happens if you override only equals? HashMap/HashSet lookups fail for equal objects because they land in different buckets.
  • Can two different objects have the same hashCode? Yes, that's a collision; equals decides.
  • Why make keys immutable? If a key's hash changes after insertion, the map can't find it.

Summary

  • Override toString for readable output.
  • == compares references; equals compares meaning.
  • Override equals(Object) and hashCode() together using the same immutable fields.
  • Records generate all three automatically.

items.title: Java Records, Enums and Sealed Classes
items.excerpt: Modern Java OOP features. Write data classes in one line with records, model fixed sets of values with enums (fields, methods, switch), and control inheritance with sealed classes.
items.content:
Modern Java (16 to 21) added features that make OOP code shorter and safer. You'll see them in every new Spring Boot project and in interviews for Java 17/21 roles.

Records: data classes in one line

Before records, a simple class holding a name and price needed a constructor, getters, equals, hashCode and toString: 40+ lines. Now:

record Product(String name, double price) { }

That one line gives you:

  • private final fields name and price
  • a constructor new Product("Pen", 20)
  • accessors name() and price() (no get prefix)
  • equals, hashCode and toString
public class RecordDemo {
    record Product(String name, double price) {
        Product {                                   // compact constructor: validation
            if (price < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("price < 0");
            name = name.trim();
        }
        double withGst() { return price * 1.18; }   // records can have methods
        static Product free(String name) { return new Product(name, 0); }   // and static factories
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Product p = new Product("  Notebook ", 120);
        System.out.println(p);                      // Product[name=Notebook, price=120.0]
        System.out.println(p.name() + " " + p.withGst());
        System.out.println(p.equals(new Product("Notebook", 120)));   // true
        System.out.println(Product.free("Sticker"));                   // Product[name=Sticker, price=0.0]
    }
}

Records are immutable and can't extend other classes (they can implement interfaces). Use them for DTOs (data sent to/from APIs), results, keys and values. In Spring Boot, request and response bodies are often records.

Enums: a fixed set of values

When something can only be one of a few values (days, order statuses, user roles), use an enum instead of Strings or ints:

enum OrderStatus { PLACED, PACKED, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED }

OrderStatus s = OrderStatus.SHIPPED;
System.out.println(s);                 // SHIPPED
System.out.println(s.ordinal());       // 2 (position, starts at 0)
System.out.println(OrderStatus.valueOf("PACKED"));   // String → enum
for (OrderStatus st : OrderStatus.values()) System.out.print(st + " ");

With Strings, a typo like "SHIPED" compiles and causes bugs. With enums, the compiler catches it.

Enums with fields and methods

Enums are full classes:

public class PlanDemo {
    enum Plan {
        FREE(0, 3), PRO(499, 50), TEAM(1999, 500);

        private final int monthlyPrice;
        private final int maxProjects;

        Plan(int monthlyPrice, int maxProjects) {      // enum constructors are private
            this.monthlyPrice = monthlyPrice;
            this.maxProjects = maxProjects;
        }

        int yearlyPrice() { return monthlyPrice * 10; }   // 2 months free
        boolean allows(int projects) { return projects <= maxProjects; }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Plan p = Plan.PRO;
        System.out.println(p + " costs ₹" + p.yearlyPrice() + "/year");   // PRO costs ₹4990/year
        System.out.println(Plan.FREE.allows(5));                            // false
    }
}

Switch on enums

String message = switch (status) {
    case PLACED, PACKED -> "Getting your order ready";
    case SHIPPED -> "On the way";
    case DELIVERED -> "Enjoy!";
    case CANCELLED -> "Refund in 3-5 days";
};

With the arrow switch, if you forget a constant the compiler complains: no default needed. Enums are also the simplest correct way to make a singleton (enum AppConfig { INSTANCE; }).

When storing enums in a database with JPA, use @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING). The default (ORDINAL) stores 0, 1, 2… and breaks if you ever reorder the constants.

Sealed classes: controlled inheritance (Java 17)

Sometimes you want a closed set of subtypes: a payment is UPI, Card or Cash, and nothing else. sealed lists exactly who may extend:

sealed interface Payment permits Upi, Card, Cash { }
record Upi(String vpa) implements Payment { }
record Card(String last4, String network) implements Payment { }
record Cash() implements Payment { }

Combined with pattern-matching switch, the compiler knows all the cases:

public class SealedDemo {
    sealed interface Payment permits Upi, Card, Cash { }
    record Upi(String vpa) implements Payment { }
    record Card(String last4, String network) implements Payment { }
    record Cash() implements Payment { }

    static String receipt(Payment p) {
        return switch (p) {                                   // no default needed: all cases covered
            case Upi u -> "Paid via UPI " + u.vpa();
            case Card c -> "Paid by " + c.network() + " card ****" + c.last4();
            case Cash c -> "Paid in cash";
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(receipt(new Upi("asha@okicici")));
        System.out.println(receipt(new Card("4242", "Visa")));
        System.out.println(receipt(new Cash()));
    }
}
Paid via UPI asha@okicici
Paid by Visa card ****4242
Paid in cash

If someone adds a Wallet type to permits later, every switch that doesn't handle it becomes a compile error, so nothing is forgotten.

Subclasses of a sealed type must be final, sealed or non-sealed. Records are implicitly final.

Which to use?

Common mistakes

  • Trying to add mutable fields or setters to a record (fields are final).
  • Using ordinal() for business logic or storage.
  • Comparing enums with .equals() (works, but == is preferred and null-safe for enums).

Exercise

  1. Create record Address(String city, String pin) that rejects PIN codes that aren't 6 digits.
  2. Create an enum Planet with mass and radius, and a method for surface gravity.
  3. Create an enum TrafficLight with a next() method (RED → GREEN → YELLOW → RED).
  4. Model Shape as a sealed interface with Circle, Square and Triangle records, and write area(Shape s) with a pattern-matching switch.
Hint for 3

TrafficLight next() { return values()[(ordinal() + 1) % values().length]; } with constants declared in order RED, GREEN, YELLOW.

Interview corner

  • What is a record? A concise immutable data carrier; Java generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.
  • Can an enum have a constructor? Yes, always private; called once per constant.
  • Why are enums good singletons? The JVM guarantees one instance per constant, and they're safe against reflection and serialization tricks.
  • What problem do sealed classes solve? They restrict which classes can extend a type, enabling exhaustive pattern matching.

Summary

  • Records: immutable data in one line, with validation in compact constructors.
  • Enums: type-safe constants that can have fields, methods and exhaustive switches.
  • Sealed types: a closed hierarchy the compiler can check.
