items.title: The N+1 Query Problem and How to Fix It
items.excerpt: Watch one query turn into N+1 in an animation, measure it with Hibernate statistics, and fix it with JOIN FETCH, entity graphs, @BatchSize and DTO projections. The most asked Hibernate interview question.
items.content:
Your page lists 100 authors with their book counts. Locally it's fast. In production, with real data, it takes 4 seconds. The logs show 101 queries for one page. Welcome to the N+1 problem, the number one Hibernate performance issue and the number one Hibernate interview question.

What N+1 means

  1. 1 query loads the list of N authors.
  2. Then, for each author, accessing a lazy relationship (a.getBooks()) fires 1 more query.

Total: N + 1 queries. With 5 authors that's 6; with 500 it's 501 round trips to the database.

Change the number of authors and switch between lazy loading and JOIN FETCH:

The code looks innocent, which is why the problem is so common:

List<Author> authors = em.createQuery("select a from Author a", Author.class).getResultList();
for (Author a : authors) {
    System.out.println(a.getName() + ": " + a.getBooks().size());   // a query per author!
}

It often hides inside templates, JSON serialisation or toString(), far from the original query.

Measure it

Turn on Hibernate statistics and count the SQL statements. The demo below loads 5 authors with three books each, four different ways:

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

@Entity
public class Author {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String name;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "author", cascade = CascadeType.ALL)
    private List<Book> books = new ArrayList<>();

    protected Author() { }
    public Author(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public void add(Book b) { books.add(b); b.author = this; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public List<Book> getBooks() { return books; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Book {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    Author author;

    protected Book() { }
    public Book(String title) { this.title = title; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

public record AuthorBooks(String name, long books) { }
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.stat.Statistics;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class Main {
    static EntityManagerFactory emf;

    static void measure(String label, Function<EntityManager, List<Author>> query) {
        Statistics stats = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
        stats.clear();
        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        long totalBooks = 0;
        for (Author a : query.apply(em)) totalBooks += a.getBooks().size();
        em.close();
        System.out.printf("%-22s %2d queries (%d books)%n", label, stats.getPrepareStatementCount(), totalBooks);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics().setStatisticsEnabled(true);
        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
            Author a = new Author("Author " + i);
            for (int j = 1; j <= 3; j++) a.add(new Book("Book " + i + "." + j));
            em.persist(a);
        }
        em.getTransaction().commit();
        em.close();

        measure("lazy loading (N+1)", e -> e.createQuery("select a from Author a", Author.class).getResultList());

        measure("JOIN FETCH", e -> e.createQuery(
                "select a from Author a join fetch a.books", Author.class).getResultList());

        measure("entity graph", e -> {
            EntityGraph<Author> g = e.createEntityGraph(Author.class);
            g.addAttributeNodes("books");
            return e.createQuery("select a from Author a", Author.class)
                    .setHint("jakarta.persistence.fetchgraph", g).getResultList();
        });

        EntityManager dto = emf.createEntityManager();
        emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics().clear();
        List<AuthorBooks> rows = dto.createQuery(
                "select new com.vitalstack.AuthorBooks(a.name, count(b)) from Author a left join a.books b group by a.name",
                AuthorBooks.class).getResultList();
        System.out.printf("%-22s %2d queries (%d rows)%n", "DTO projection",
                emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics().getPrepareStatementCount(), rows.size());
        dto.close();
        emf.close();
    }
}

Output:

lazy loading (N+1)      6 queries (15 books)
JOIN FETCH              1 queries (15 books)
entity graph            1 queries (15 books)
DTO projection          1 queries (5 rows)

Same data, 6× fewer round trips. With 500 authors: 501 vs 1.

Fix 1: JOIN FETCH

select a from Author a join fetch a.books

Loads authors and books in one SQL join. Hibernate 6 removes duplicate authors automatically (older versions needed select distinct a).

Fix 2: Entity graphs

Keep the query, declare what to fetch separately. In Spring Data JPA:

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "books")
List<Author> findAll();

Fix 3: Batch fetching (@BatchSize)

When you can't change the query (e.g. it's generated), make lazy loading smarter: load the books for many authors at once using IN (...):

@OneToMany(mappedBy = "author")
@BatchSize(size = 25)
private List<Book> books;

Or globally: hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=25. N+1 becomes 1 + ⌈N/25⌉ queries: 500 authors → 21 queries. Many teams turn this on globally as a safety net.

Fix 4: DTO projections

If the screen only needs names and counts, don't load entities at all. One aggregate query returns exactly what's needed, with no tracking overhead.

Which fix when?

Two traps: fetching two collections with JOIN FETCH at once (join fetch a.books join fetch a.awards) creates a Cartesian product (or a MultipleBagFetchException for Lists). Fetch one collection per query. And JOIN FETCH a collection + setMaxResults makes Hibernate paginate in memory.

Detecting N+1 early

  • Watch the SQL log in development (show_sql), or use a tool like p6spy to log SQL with parameters.
  • Assert statement counts in tests with Statistics.getPrepareStatementCount(), or libraries like Hypersistence Utils / datasource-proxy.
  • Disable open-session-in-view so lazy loads in the web layer fail loudly instead of quietly running hundreds of queries.

Exercise

  1. Run the demo with 50 authors. How many queries does lazy loading run?
  2. Add @BatchSize(size = 10) on books and re-run the lazy version. Predict the count first.
  3. Add Book → Publisher (@ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY)) and print each book's publisher. Fix the new N+1 with a fetch join join fetch a.books b join fetch b.publisher.
Hint for 2

1 query for authors + ⌈50 / 10⌉ = 5 batch queries for books = 6 queries.

Interview corner

  • What is the N+1 problem? One query loads N parents, then N extra queries load each parent's lazy association.
  • How do you fix it? JOIN FETCH, entity graphs, batch fetching (@BatchSize), or DTO projections.
  • Does EAGER fix N+1? No. EAGER on a collection or ToOne relationship is often loaded with separate queries per row, still N+1, and now on every query.
  • How do you detect it? SQL logging, Hibernate statistics, query-count assertions in tests.

Summary

  • N+1 = 1 query for the list + 1 per item for a lazy relationship.
  • Fix with JOIN FETCH, entity graphs, @BatchSize or DTO projections.
  • Measure with statistics; fetch one collection per query; don't paginate fetch-joined collections.

Next: the second-level cache.

items.title: Hibernate Caching - First-Level, Second-Level and Query Cache
items.excerpt: Understand Hibernate's three caches, enable the second-level cache with JCache, choose cache concurrency strategies, cache queries and collections, and learn when caching helps or hurts.
items.content:
Reading the same data from the database again and again is wasteful. Hibernate has three caching layers. One is always on; the other two are opt-in and powerful when used for the right data.

The three caches

em.find(Course, 1)
   │
   ├─▶ 1st-level (this session)?   hit → return the same object
   ├─▶ 2nd-level (shared)?         hit → build the object, no SQL
   └─▶ database                    SELECT → store in both caches

You met the first-level cache in the JPA course. Let's look at the second-level cache.

Enabling the second-level cache

Hibernate needs a cache provider. JCache (JSR-107) with Ehcache or Caffeine is the common choice:

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
  <artifactId>hibernate-jcache</artifactId>
  <version>6.5.2.Final</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>com.github.ben-manes.caffeine</groupId>
  <artifactId>jcache</artifactId>
  <version>3.1.8</version>
</dependency>

Properties:

<property name="hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache" value="true"/>
<property name="hibernate.cache.region.factory_class" value="jcache"/>
<property name="jakarta.persistence.sharedCache.mode" value="ENABLE_SELECTIVE"/>
<!-- create cache regions automatically (otherwise Hibernate logs a warning per region) -->
<property name="hibernate.javax.cache.missing_cache_strategy" value="create"/>

ENABLE_SELECTIVE means only entities marked @Cacheable are cached. Then mark the entity:

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.annotations.Cache;
import org.hibernate.annotations.CacheConcurrencyStrategy;

@Entity
@Cacheable
@Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_WRITE)
public class Country {
    @Id
    private String code;
    private String name;

    protected Country() { }
    public Country(String code, String name) { this.code = code; this.name = name; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
}

Proof: no SQL on the second session

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.stat.Statistics;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        Statistics stats = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
        stats.setStatisticsEnabled(true);

        EntityManager setup = emf.createEntityManager();
        setup.getTransaction().begin();
        setup.persist(new Country("IN", "India"));
        setup.getTransaction().commit();
        setup.close();
        emf.getCache().evictAll();                     // start with an empty L2 cache
        stats.clear();

        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
            EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();   // a NEW session each time
            System.out.println("session " + i + ": " + em.find(Country.class, "IN").getName());
            em.close();
        }
        System.out.println("SQL statements: " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
        System.out.println("L2 hits: " + stats.getSecondLevelCacheHitCount()
                + ", misses: " + stats.getSecondLevelCacheMissCount());
        emf.close();
    }
}
select c1_0.code,c1_0.name from Country c1_0 where c1_0.code=?
session 1: India
session 2: India
session 3: India
SQL statements: 1
L2 hits: 2, misses: 1

Three different sessions, one query.

Concurrency strategies

Caching collections

Collections are cached separately; mark them too:

@OneToMany(mappedBy = "course")
@Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_WRITE)
private List<Lesson> lessons;

The collection cache stores the ids of the lessons; the lessons themselves must also be @Cacheable, or each one is loaded with a query (an N+1 in disguise!).

The query cache

find by id uses the L2 cache, but queries don't, unless you enable the query cache and mark the query:

<property name="hibernate.cache.use_query_cache" value="true"/>
List<Country> all = em.createQuery("select c from Country c order by c.name", Country.class)
        .setHint("org.hibernate.cacheable", true)
        .getResultList();

The query cache stores the list of ids for that query and parameters. Hibernate invalidates it whenever any row in the tables involved changes, so it only pays off for queries on tables that rarely change.

When NOT to cache

  • Frequently updated data (orders, stock, balances): constant invalidation, little benefit, stale-data risk.
  • Huge tables accessed randomly: the cache just fills memory.
  • Data changed by other applications or direct SQL: Hibernate won't know, so cached data goes stale.
  • Multiple app servers with a local (in-memory) cache: each server has its own copy. Use a distributed cache (Hazelcast, Infinispan, Redis-based) or short expiry times.

Good candidates: reference data (countries, categories, plans, settings), read-mostly product catalogues, user roles.

Measure before and after. Many apps get bigger wins from fixing N+1 problems and adding indexes than from caching. In Spring Boot, @Cacheable from Spring's cache abstraction (caching method results) is often simpler than Hibernate's L2 cache for API responses.

Exercise

  1. Enable the L2 cache for a Category entity and confirm with statistics that the second find in a new session runs no SQL.
  2. Update the category in one session, then load it in another. Is the new value returned? Why?
  3. Cache the query select c from Category c order by c.name and check getQueryCacheHitCount().
Hint for 2

Yes: with READ_WRITE, Hibernate updates (or invalidates) the cache entry when the transaction commits, so other sessions see the new value.

Interview corner

  • First-level vs second-level cache? First-level is per Session and always on; second-level is shared across sessions, optional, and needs a provider.
  • What is the query cache? A cache of query results (entity ids) keyed by query and parameters, invalidated when related tables change.
  • Cache concurrency strategies? READ_ONLY, NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE, READ_WRITE, TRANSACTIONAL.
  • What data should you cache? Read-mostly, small to medium reference data that's accessed often.

Summary

  • First-level cache: per session, automatic.
  • Second-level cache: shared, opt-in with @Cacheable + a provider like JCache/Caffeine/Ehcache.
  • Query cache: caches result ids, invalidated on any change to the tables.
  • Cache reference data; don't cache volatile data.

Next: batch processing and performance tuning.

items.title: Hibernate Batch Processing and Performance Tuning
items.excerpt: Make Hibernate fast. JDBC batching, sequence allocation, flush and clear in loops, StatelessSession, bulk updates, read-only queries, @DynamicUpdate, connection pools and a performance checklist.
items.content:
Hibernate is fast when used well and painfully slow when used carelessly. Most slowness comes from a handful of causes: too many round trips, too much tracked data, and loading more than needed. This lesson covers the fixes senior developers apply.

1. JDBC batching

By default every INSERT/UPDATE is a separate round trip to the database. With batching, Hibernate sends many statements in one go:

<property name="hibernate.jdbc.batch_size" value="50"/>
<property name="hibernate.order_inserts" value="true"/>   <!-- group inserts by table -->
<property name="hibernate.order_updates" value="true"/>

In Spring Boot: spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50.

Batching inserts does not work with GenerationType.IDENTITY, because Hibernate must run each INSERT immediately to get the generated id. Use SEQUENCE with an allocationSize (PostgreSQL, Oracle, H2, MariaDB) to batch inserts. On MySQL, which has no sequences, use UUIDs or accept unbatched inserts.

2. Insert many rows: flush and clear

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Product {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "product_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "product_seq", allocationSize = 50)
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private int price;

    protected Product() { }
    public Product(String name, int price) { this.name = name; this.price = price; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.stat.Statistics;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        Statistics stats = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
        stats.setStatisticsEnabled(true);

        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        for (int i = 1; i <= 10_000; i++) {
            em.persist(new Product("Product " + i, 100 + i % 900));
            if (i % 50 == 0) {         // same as batch_size
                em.flush();            // send this batch
                em.clear();            // forget the managed objects: memory stays flat
            }
        }
        em.getTransaction().commit();
        em.close();
        System.out.println("10,000 rows in " + (System.currentTimeMillis() - start) + " ms");
        System.out.println("SQL statements prepared: " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
        emf.close();
    }
}

Output with hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50 (H2 in memory, times vary):

10,000 rows in 561 ms
SQL statements prepared: 401

Without the batch setting the same loop prepares 10,201 statements: one per row plus the sequence calls. Against a real database over the network, every statement is a round trip, so batching often makes inserts 5-10× faster. (H2 runs in memory, so the time difference is small here.)

Without clear(), all 10,000 products and their snapshots stay in the persistence context, and every flush dirty-checks all of them: the loop gets slower and slower. With a sequence allocationSize of 50, Hibernate fetches ids once per 50 rows instead of once per row.

3. StatelessSession for big jobs

A StatelessSession has no persistence context: no first-level cache, no dirty checking, no cascades, no lazy loading. Perfect for imports and exports:

SessionFactory sf = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class);
try (StatelessSession ss = sf.openStatelessSession()) {
    Transaction tx = ss.beginTransaction();
    for (ProductRow row : rowsFromCsv) {
        ss.insert(new Product(row.name(), row.price()));   // immediate INSERT (batched if configured)
    }
    tx.commit();
}

4. Bulk updates and deletes

Don't load 50,000 entities to change one column:

// ❌ loads everything into memory, 50,000 UPDATEs
for (Product p : em.createQuery("select p from Product p", Product.class).getResultList()) p.raisePrice(10);

// ✅ one statement
em.createQuery("update Product p set p.price = p.price + 10 where p.category = :cat")
  .setParameter("cat", "BOOKS")
  .executeUpdate();

Remember: bulk statements skip the persistence context, callbacks and @Version increments (unless you include versioned/version updates yourself).

5. Read-only queries

When you load entities only to display them, tell Hibernate not to keep snapshots:

List<Product> list = em.createQuery("select p from Product p", Product.class)
        .setHint("org.hibernate.readOnly", true)
        .getResultList();

In Spring: @Transactional(readOnly = true) on the service method does this for the whole transaction. Even better for screens: DTO projections (only the needed columns, nothing tracked).

6. Fetch only what you need

  • Lazy everywhere; JOIN FETCH or entity graphs per use case (lessons 2-3).
  • Projections for lists and reports.
  • Paginate. Never load "all orders" for a list page.

7. @DynamicUpdate

By default Hibernate's UPDATE sets all columns (one cached statement per entity). For wide tables where only one column changes, @DynamicUpdate generates SQL with only the changed columns:

@Entity
@DynamicUpdate
public class UserProfile { /* 40 columns */ }

Trade-off: less data sent, but a statement per combination of changed columns. Use it for wide tables or to reduce lock conflicts on specific columns.

8. The database still matters

  • Indexes on columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY (foreign keys especially). Hibernate doesn't create them for you unless you declare @Index in @Table(indexes = ...).
  • Check slow queries with EXPLAIN.
  • A properly sized connection pool (HikariCP): more connections isn't always faster; start around 10.

A performance checklist

Exercise

  1. Run the insert demo with and without hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50 and compare times.
  2. Remove em.clear() and insert 50,000 rows. What happens to the time per batch?
  3. Rewrite a "deactivate users inactive for 1 year" loop as one bulk JPQL update.
  4. Add @Table(indexes = @Index(columnList = "category")) to Product and check the generated DDL.
Hint for 2

Each flush dirty-checks every managed entity, so time per batch keeps growing (and memory too). With clear() it stays constant.

Interview corner

  • How do you insert a million rows with Hibernate? JDBC batching, SEQUENCE ids with allocationSize, flush/clear every batch, or StatelessSession (or plain JDBC/COPY for extreme cases).
  • Why doesn't batching work with IDENTITY? The id is only known after each INSERT executes, so Hibernate can't delay and group them.
  • What is a StatelessSession? A session without persistence context, caching or dirty checking, for bulk operations.
  • How do you make reads cheaper? Read-only transactions/hints, DTO projections, pagination, proper fetching and indexes.

Summary

  • Batch writes (jdbc.batch_size + SEQUENCE ids) and flush/clear in loops.
  • Use StatelessSession or bulk JPQL for large jobs.
  • Read-only hints and DTO projections make reads lighter.
  • Indexes and query counts matter more than clever tricks.

Next: handy Hibernate-specific annotations.

items.title: Useful Hibernate Annotations - Soft Delete, Timestamps, Formula and More
items.excerpt: Hibernate-only annotations that save real work - @CreationTimestamp, @UpdateTimestamp, soft delete with @SoftDelete and @SQLRestriction, @Formula, @Immutable, @NaturalId, @ColumnDefault, @Check and Envers auditing.
items.content:
Beyond standard JPA, Hibernate ships annotations that solve common problems in one line. You'll find these all over real Spring Boot codebases.

Automatic timestamps

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.annotations.*;
import java.time.Instant;

@Entity
@SoftDelete                                            // DELETE becomes "mark as deleted"
public class Post {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private int likes;

    @CreationTimestamp                                  // set once on INSERT
    private Instant createdAt;

    @UpdateTimestamp                                    // refreshed on every UPDATE
    private Instant updatedAt;

    @Formula("likes * 2 + length(title)")               // computed by SQL, read-only
    private int score;

    protected Post() { }
    public Post(String title, int likes) { this.title = title; this.likes = likes; }
    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public int getScore() { return score; }
    public Instant getCreatedAt() { return createdAt; }
}

No @PrePersist code needed for createdAt/updatedAt.

Soft delete

Many apps never truly delete data (for audits, undo, analytics). Hibernate 6.4+ has @SoftDelete: em.remove() runs an UPDATE that sets a deleted flag, and every query automatically skips deleted rows.

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        Post hello = new Post("Hello", 10);
        em.persist(hello);
        em.persist(new Post("Learn Hibernate", 25));
        em.getTransaction().commit();
        System.out.println("created at set? " + (hello.getCreatedAt() != null));

        em.getTransaction().begin();
        em.remove(hello);                                   // soft delete
        em.getTransaction().commit();
        em.clear();

        em.createQuery("select p from Post p", Post.class).getResultList()
          .forEach(p -> System.out.println(p.getTitle() + " (score " + p.getScore() + ")"));
        Object rows = em.createNativeQuery("select count(*) from Post").getSingleResult();
        System.out.println("rows really in the table: " + rows);
        em.close();
        emf.close();
    }
}
created at set? true
update Post set deleted=true where id=? and deleted=false
Learn Hibernate (score 65)
rows really in the table: 2

The JPQL query returned only the non-deleted post, while the table still has both rows. For older Hibernate versions the same idea is done with @SQLDelete(sql = "UPDATE post SET deleted = true WHERE id = ?") plus @SQLRestriction("deleted = false") (formerly @Where).

Soft-deleted rows still count for unique constraints. If users can re-register with an email after deleting their account, include the deleted flag in the unique index or anonymise the old row.

@Formula: computed columns

@Formula maps a field to an SQL expression evaluated in the SELECT: totals, scores, counts from other tables:

@Formula("(select count(*) from comment c where c.post_id = id)")
private int commentCount;

It's read-only and computed at load time. Keep formulas cheap: they run for every load.

@Immutable

@Entity
@Immutable                 // never updated: Hibernate skips dirty checking
public class ExchangeRate { ... }

Great for audit logs, history tables and database views mapped as entities.

@NaturalId

A unique business key (email, ISBN, slug) that Hibernate can look up by and cache:

@NaturalId
@Column(unique = true)
private String slug;

Post p = session.bySimpleNaturalId(Post.class).load("learn-hibernate");

Schema helpers

@ColumnDefault("0")                              // DEFAULT 0 in the DDL
private int likes;

@Check(constraints = "price >= 0")               // CHECK constraint
private int price;

@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON)                     // store a Map or record as JSON (PostgreSQL jsonb etc.)
private Map<String, Object> settings;

Envers: full change history

Add hibernate-envers and annotate an entity with @Audited. Hibernate keeps an _AUD table with every version of every row, plus who/when via a revision entity:

@Entity
@Audited
public class Course { ... }

AuditReader reader = AuditReaderFactory.get(em);
List<Number> revisions = reader.getRevisions(Course.class, courseId);
Course old = reader.find(Course.class, courseId, revisions.get(0));   // the course as it was

Perfect for "who changed the price and when?" requirements in banking, HR and admin panels.

Quick reference

Exercise

  1. Add @CreationTimestamp and @UpdateTimestamp to an entity and update it twice. Check the values.
  2. Implement soft delete on a Comment entity and prove that queries skip deleted comments.
  3. Add a @Formula that counts the lessons of a course.
  4. Map a read-only @Immutable entity to a database view course_stats.
Hint for 3

@Formula("(select count(*) from Lesson l where l.course_id = id)"). Inside a formula, id refers to the current row's column.

Interview corner

  • How do you implement soft delete in Hibernate? @SoftDelete in 6.4+, or @SQLDelete to turn DELETE into UPDATE plus @SQLRestriction to filter queries.
  • What does @Formula do? Maps a read-only property to an SQL expression evaluated when the entity is loaded.
  • What is Hibernate Envers? An auditing module that records entity versions in audit tables.
  • @CreationTimestamp vs @PrePersist? Both set values at insert; the annotation needs no code and is Hibernate-specific.

Summary

  • Timestamps, soft delete, formulas, immutability and natural ids are one annotation each.
  • Envers adds full history with @Audited.
  • These are Hibernate-specific: fine for most apps, which use Hibernate anyway.

Next: best practices and a review of the whole course.

items.title: Hibernate Best Practices and Common Mistakes
items.excerpt: A practical checklist from real projects - mapping, fetching, transactions, equals/hashCode for entities, DTOs, schema migrations, logging and testing - plus a slow-page case study you can fix step by step.
items.content:
You now know how Hibernate works. This final lesson turns that into habits. These are the rules experienced teams follow, and the mistakes code reviewers look for.

Mapping

  • ✅ FetchType.LAZY on every @ManyToOne and @OneToOne.
  • ✅ @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) for enums.
  • ✅ SEQUENCE ids with an allocationSize (or UUIDs) where the database supports it; IDENTITY on MySQL is fine but disables insert batching.
  • ✅ Bidirectional relationships only when you navigate both ways; keep both sides in sync with helper methods.
  • ✅ Set for @ManyToMany; turn link tables with extra data into entities.
  • ❌ CascadeType.ALL or REMOVE on @ManyToOne or many-to-many.
  • ❌ Relationships in toString(), equals() or hashCode().

equals and hashCode for entities

Entities are tricky: the id is null before persisting, and proxies are subclasses. A safe pattern compares by id when it exists and keeps hashCode constant:

@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (!(o instanceof Course other)) return false;
    return id != null && id.equals(other.getId());     // getter: works through proxies
}

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return getClass().hashCode();                        // constant: safe across persist
}

Or base equality on an immutable natural id (email, ISBN, slug). Never use mutable fields.

Fetching

  • ✅ Decide what to load per use case: JOIN FETCH, entity graphs or DTO projections.
  • ✅ Turn on hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size (e.g. 16-50) as a safety net.
  • ✅ spring.jpa.open-in-view=false.
  • ❌ EAGER "to fix" LazyInitializationException.
  • ❌ JOIN FETCH of two collections at once, or JOIN FETCH + pagination on a collection.

Transactions and units of work

  • ✅ Transactions at the service layer (@Transactional), short and focused.
  • ✅ Read-only transactions for queries.
  • ✅ @Version on entities edited by users.
  • ❌ HTTP calls, emails or file processing inside transactions.
  • ❌ Catching exceptions inside a transaction and continuing as if nothing happened (the Session may be in an inconsistent state; roll back).

API boundaries

  • ✅ Return DTOs/records from controllers, not entities. It avoids lazy-loading errors, infinite JSON recursion, leaking internal fields (password hashes!) and accidental updates.
  • ✅ Validate input with Bean Validation before it reaches entities.

Schema

  • ✅ Manage the schema with Flyway or Liquibase migrations; set hbm2ddl.auto=validate (or none) in production.
  • ✅ Add indexes for foreign keys and frequent filters.
  • ❌ hbm2ddl.auto=update in production: it never drops or renames safely and can't migrate data.

Observability and testing

  • ✅ Log SQL in development; use p6spy or datasource-proxy to see parameters.
  • ✅ Assert query counts in integration tests for critical endpoints.
  • ✅ Test against the same database engine as production with Testcontainers (H2 hides dialect differences).
  • ✅ Enable hibernate.generate_statistics temporarily when investigating.

Case study: a slow course page

The course page takes 3 seconds. The log shows:

select ... from course where id=?
select ... from teacher where id=?
select ... from lesson where course_id=?
select ... from quiz where lesson_id=?      ← ×40 (one per lesson)
select ... from review where course_id=?    ← loads 2,000 reviews
select ... from student where id=?          ← ×2,000 (one per review author)

What's wrong and how do we fix it?

  1. Quizzes N+1 (40 queries): fetch lessons with quizzes in one query (join fetch l.quiz), or set default_batch_fetch_size.
  2. 2,000 reviews loaded to show 5 on the page and an average: use a paginated DTO query for the latest 5 reviews and an aggregate query select avg(r.rating), count(r) for the summary.
  3. Students N+1 (2,000 queries): the DTO query joins the student name directly: select new ReviewView(r.rating, r.text, s.name) from Review r join r.student s where r.course.id = :id order by r.createdAt desc.
  4. Teacher: a lazy @ManyToOne fetched in the course query: join fetch c.teacher.

Result: 4,042 queries → 4 queries, 3 s → 40 ms. No caching, no new hardware: just correct fetching.

When a page is slow, count the queries before anything else. In most Hibernate apps, the fix is fetching less and in fewer round trips.

Interview quick-fire

  • Hibernate vs JPA? Implementation vs specification.
  • Entity states? Transient, managed, detached, removed.
  • What is dirty checking? Automatic UPDATEs for changed managed entities at flush.
  • N+1 and fixes? JOIN FETCH, entity graphs, batch fetching, DTOs.
  • LazyInitializationException? Lazy access after the session closed; fetch what you need inside the transaction.
  • First vs second-level cache? Per session vs shared, opt-in.
  • get vs load / find vs getReference? Immediate SELECT (null if missing) vs proxy (exception when used).
  • Optimistic locking? @Version column checked in UPDATE's WHERE.
  • How to batch inserts? jdbc.batch_size, sequences, flush/clear, StatelessSession.

Exercise

  1. Review an entity class you've written against the mapping checklist. What would you change?
  2. Write the DTO query for the case study's "latest 5 reviews with student names".
  3. Write a Flyway migration V2__add_course_level.sql that adds a level column with a default.
Hint for 2

Use setMaxResults(5) with order by r.createdAt desc and a constructor expression into a ReviewView record.

Summary

  • Lazy by default, fetch per use case, DTOs at the edges.
  • Short service-layer transactions, @Version for user edits.
  • Migrations for schema, indexes for speed, query counts in tests.

Congratulations, you've finished the Hibernate course! Next, learn Spring and Spring Boot, where all of this runs with @Transactional, Spring Data repositories and almost no boilerplate.

items.title: Spring Framework Introduction
items.excerpt: What the Spring Framework is, the problems it solves (tight coupling, boilerplate, plumbing), its main modules, how Spring differs from Spring Boot, and why it dominates Java back-end jobs.
items.content:
Spring is the most popular framework for building Java applications. Banks, e-commerce sites, Netflix, and most Java back-end jobs in India use it. Spring Boot (next course) is built on top of it, so understanding Spring's core ideas makes everything in Spring Boot click.

The problem Spring solves

Imagine an OrderService that needs a repository, a payment gateway and an email sender:

public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo = new MySqlOrderRepository(new HikariDataSource(config));
    private final PaymentGateway payments = new RazorpayGateway("key", "secret");
    private final EmailSender email = new SmtpEmailSender("smtp.gmail.com", 587);

    public void placeOrder(Order order) { ... }
}

Problems:

  • Tight coupling: OrderService decides which database, which payment provider and which email server. Changing any of them means editing this class.
  • Hard to test: you can't test placeOrder without a real database, a real payment account and a real mail server.
  • Duplicated setup: every class that needs a database creates its own connection pool.
  • Plumbing everywhere: transactions, security checks and logging get copied into every method.

Spring's answer

  1. Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection (DI): your classes declare what they need; Spring creates and connects them.
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    private final PaymentGateway payments;
    private final EmailSender email;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repo, PaymentGateway payments, EmailSender email) {
        this.repo = repo;            // Spring passes these in
        this.payments = payments;
        this.email = email;
    }
}

Now OrderService depends only on interfaces. Swap Razorpay for Paytm, or pass fakes in tests, without touching it.

  1. AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming): add transactions, security and logging around methods with annotations like @Transactional, instead of copying code.
  1. Ready-made integrations: database access, web MVC, REST, security, messaging, caching, scheduling, testing.

The Spring ecosystem

Spring vs Spring Boot

Spring Boot is Spring: same annotations, same container, same concepts. Boot just removes the setup work.

Key vocabulary

  • Bean: an object created and managed by Spring.
  • ApplicationContext: the Spring container that creates, wires and manages beans.
  • Dependency injection: Spring supplies a bean's dependencies (usually through the constructor).
  • Component scanning: Spring finds classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller.
  • Configuration class: a class with @Configuration and @Bean methods that define beans.
  • Proxy: a wrapper Spring puts around a bean to add behaviour (transactions, security).

You'll learn faster if you remember one sentence: *Spring creates your objects, connects them, and wraps them with extra behaviour.* Every lesson in this course is one part of that sentence.

Exercise

  1. List the dependencies of a CourseService that saves courses, sends a welcome email and charges a fee.
  2. Rewrite its constructor so it receives those dependencies instead of creating them.
  3. Explain why the rewritten class is easier to test.
Hint for 3

In a test you can pass a fake EmailSender that just records the messages, and a fake payment gateway that always succeeds or always fails, with no network calls.

Interview corner

  • What is Spring? A comprehensive Java framework providing an IoC container, DI, AOP and integrations for building enterprise applications.
  • What is IoC? Inversion of Control: the framework, not your code, creates and wires objects.
  • Spring vs Spring Boot? Boot is Spring with auto-configuration, starters and an embedded server.
  • What is a bean? An object instantiated, assembled and managed by the Spring container.

Summary

  • Spring removes tight coupling and plumbing with IoC/DI and AOP.
  • The ecosystem covers web, data, security, cloud and batch.
  • Spring Boot is the fast way to use Spring; the core concepts are the same.

Next: IoC and dependency injection, animated.

items.title: Spring IoC Container and Dependency Injection
items.excerpt: Watch the Spring container scan, build and wire beans in an animation, then run a real ApplicationContext with @Component, @Service, @Repository and constructor injection. Learn why constructor injection beats field injection.
items.content:
The heart of Spring is the IoC container (the ApplicationContext). You mark your classes, and the container finds them, creates them in the right order, and passes each one the objects it needs. That's dependency injection (DI).

Watch the container work

  1. Scan: find classes annotated with @Component (and its specialisations).
  2. Analyse: read constructors to build a dependency graph.
  3. Create: build beans with no dependencies first.
  4. Inject: pass finished beans into the constructors of beans that need them.
  5. Ready: every bean is a singleton by default: one shared instance.

A runnable example

Add spring-context (Spring Boot projects already have it):

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
  <version>6.1.13</version>
</dependency>
package com.vitalstack.shop;

public interface Notifier {
    void send(String to, String message);
}
package com.vitalstack.shop;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class EmailNotifier implements Notifier {
    @Override
    public void send(String to, String message) {
        System.out.println("EMAIL to " + to + ": " + message);
    }
}
package com.vitalstack.shop;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

@Repository
public class OrderRepository {
    private final List<String> orders = new ArrayList<>();
    public int save(String item) { orders.add(item); return orders.size(); }
}
package com.vitalstack.shop;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    private final Notifier notifier;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repo, Notifier notifier) {   // constructor injection
        this.repo = repo;
        this.notifier = notifier;
    }

    public void placeOrder(String customer, String item) {
        int id = repo.save(item);
        notifier.send(customer, "Order #" + id + " for " + item + " confirmed");
    }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import com.vitalstack.shop.OrderService;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.AnnotationConfigApplicationContext;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.ComponentScan;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import java.util.Arrays;

@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.vitalstack.shop")            // where to look for components
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Main.class)) {
            OrderService service = context.getBean(OrderService.class);
            service.placeOrder("asha@example.com", "Java course");
            service.placeOrder("asha@example.com", "Spring course");

            System.out.println("Same instance? " + (service == context.getBean(OrderService.class)));
            Arrays.stream(context.getBeanDefinitionNames())
                  .filter(n -> !n.startsWith("org.springframework"))
                  .sorted()
                  .forEach(n -> System.out.println("bean: " + n));
        }
    }
}

Output:

EMAIL to asha@example.com: Order #1 for Java course confirmed
EMAIL to asha@example.com: Order #2 for Spring course confirmed
Same instance? true
bean: emailNotifier
bean: main
bean: orderRepository
bean: orderService

You never wrote new OrderService(...). Spring saw that OrderService needs an OrderRepository and a Notifier, found one bean of each type (EmailNotifier implements Notifier), and wired them. Bean names default to the class name with a lowercase first letter.

The stereotype annotations

Three ways to inject

// 1. Constructor injection ✅ recommended
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository repo;
    public OrderService(OrderRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }   // @Autowired optional with one constructor
}

// 2. Setter injection: for optional dependencies
@Autowired
public void setAuditLog(AuditLog log) { this.log = log; }

// 3. Field injection ❌ avoid
@Autowired
private OrderRepository repo;

Why constructor injection wins:

  • Dependencies can be final: the object is always complete and immutable.
  • Required dependencies are obvious from the constructor.
  • Easy to test: new OrderService(fakeRepo, fakeNotifier) with no Spring needed.
  • Circular dependencies fail fast at startup instead of hiding.
  • Too many constructor parameters is a visible warning that the class does too much.

With Lombok, @RequiredArgsConstructor generates the constructor for all final fields. That's why so many Spring Boot classes look like @Service @RequiredArgsConstructor public class X { private final Y y; }.

Testing without Spring

Because OrderService just takes interfaces in its constructor, a unit test needs no container:

List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>();
Notifier fake = (to, msg) -> sent.add(msg);
OrderService service = new OrderService(new OrderRepository(), fake);
service.placeOrder("x@y.com", "Book");
assert sent.get(0).contains("Order #1");

That's the real payoff of DI.

Common errors

  • **NoSuchBeanDefinitionException**: no bean of the required type. Is the class annotated? Is it inside the scanned package?
  • **NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException**: two beans implement the interface; Spring doesn't know which to inject (next lesson: @Primary, @Qualifier).
  • Circular dependency: A needs B and B needs A. Redesign (extract a third class) instead of forcing it.

Exercise

  1. Run the example. Then add an SmsNotifier implements Notifier with @Component. What error do you get?
  2. Add a DiscountService bean and inject it into OrderService to apply 10% off.
  3. Write a unit test for OrderService with a fake notifier, without starting Spring.
Hint for 1

NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: expected single matching bean but found 2: emailNotifier,smsNotifier. You'll fix it in the next lesson.

Interview corner

  • What is dependency injection? A design where an object's dependencies are supplied from outside (by the container) instead of created inside.
  • IoC vs DI? IoC is the principle (the framework controls object creation); DI is the technique that implements it.
  • Constructor vs field injection? Constructor injection supports final fields, explicit required dependencies and easy testing; field injection hides dependencies and needs reflection.
  • @Component vs @Service vs @Repository? All register beans; @Service marks business logic, @Repository adds persistence exception translation.

Summary

  • The ApplicationContext scans, creates and wires beans.
  • Mark classes with @Component/@Service/@Repository; prefer constructor injection.
  • DI makes classes loosely coupled and easy to test.

Next: @Configuration, @Bean, and choosing between multiple beans.

items.title: Spring @Configuration, @Bean, @Primary and @Qualifier
items.excerpt: Define beans with @Configuration and @Bean for classes you don't own, resolve multiple implementations with @Primary and @Qualifier, inject all beans of a type as a List or Map, and use conditional beans.
items.content:
Component scanning works for your classes. But how do you make a bean from a library class (a RestClient, an ObjectMapper, a payment SDK) that you can't annotate? And what if two beans implement the same interface? This lesson answers both.

@Configuration and @Bean

A @Configuration class contains @Bean methods. Each method's return value becomes a bean:

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public Clock clock() {
        return Clock.systemDefaultZone();          // a JDK class: can't put @Component on it
    }

    @Bean
    public PriceCalculator priceCalculator(Clock clock) {   // parameters are injected too
        return new PriceCalculator(clock, new BigDecimal("0.18"));
    }
}
  • The bean name is the method name (clock, priceCalculator).
  • Method parameters are resolved from the container, just like constructor injection.
  • Use @Bean for third-party classes and for objects that need custom setup.

Multiple implementations: the ambiguity problem

package com.vitalstack.pay;

public interface PaymentGateway {
    String name();
    int feeFor(int amount);
}
package com.vitalstack.pay;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Primary;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
@Primary                                          // the default when someone asks for "a PaymentGateway"
public class UpiGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public String name() { return "UPI"; }
    public int feeFor(int amount) { return 0; }
}
package com.vitalstack.pay;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component("card")                                // explicit bean name
public class CardGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public String name() { return "Card"; }
    public int feeFor(int amount) { return amount * 2 / 100; }
}
package com.vitalstack.pay;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class WalletGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public String name() { return "Wallet"; }
    public int feeFor(int amount) { return amount / 100; }
}

@Primary, @Qualifier, and injecting them all

package com.vitalstack.pay;

import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Qualifier;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

@Service
public class Checkout {
    private final PaymentGateway defaultGateway;
    private final PaymentGateway cardGateway;
    private final List<PaymentGateway> all;
    private final Map<String, PaymentGateway> byName;

    public Checkout(PaymentGateway defaultGateway,                     // @Primary wins
                    @Qualifier("card") PaymentGateway cardGateway,    // pick by name
                    List<PaymentGateway> all,                         // every implementation
                    Map<String, PaymentGateway> byName) {             // bean name → bean
        this.defaultGateway = defaultGateway;
        this.cardGateway = cardGateway;
        this.all = all;
        this.byName = byName;
    }

    public void report(int amount) {
        System.out.println("default: " + defaultGateway.name());
        System.out.println("qualified: " + cardGateway.name());
        all.forEach(g -> System.out.println(g.name() + " fee on ₹" + amount + " = ₹" + g.feeFor(amount)));
        System.out.println("names: " + byName.keySet());
    }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import com.vitalstack.pay.Checkout;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.*;

@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.vitalstack.pay")
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var ctx = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Main.class)) {
            ctx.getBean(Checkout.class).report(1000);
        }
    }
}

Output:

default: UPI
qualified: Card
Card fee on ₹1000 = ₹20
UPI fee on ₹1000 = ₹0
Wallet fee on ₹1000 = ₹10
names: [card, upiGateway, walletGateway]

Conditional beans

Create a bean only when something is true. This is exactly how Spring Boot's auto-configuration works:

@Bean
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "payments.mock", havingValue = "true")   // Spring Boot annotation
public PaymentGateway mockGateway() { return new MockGateway(); }

@Bean
@Profile("dev")                                                       // only in the dev profile
public DataSeeder dataSeeder() { return new DataSeeder(); }

Lite mode vs full @Configuration

Inside a @Configuration class, calling another @Bean method returns the same singleton, because Spring proxies the class:

@Bean public Clock clock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); }
@Bean public Scheduler scheduler() { return new Scheduler(clock()); }   // the same Clock bean, not a new one

In a plain @Component class, @Bean methods are not proxied ("lite mode"), and that call would create a new object. Prefer method parameters for dependencies to avoid the question entirely.

Keep configuration classes small and grouped by topic (SecurityConfig, WebConfig, PaymentConfig). In Spring Boot you'll need far fewer of them, because auto-configuration creates most infrastructure beans for you.

Exercise

  1. Run the example, then remove @Primary. What happens at startup?
  2. Add a @Bean method that creates a java.util.Random with a fixed seed and inject it into a DiceService.
  3. Use the Map<String, PaymentGateway> to implement pay(String method, int amount), throwing an error for unknown methods.
  4. Annotate the gateways with @Order(1), @Order(2), @Order(3) and check the List order.
Hint for 1

Injecting a single PaymentGateway fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, because there are three candidates and no default.

Interview corner

  • @Component vs @Bean? @Component goes on your own class (found by scanning); @Bean is a method in a @Configuration class, used for third-party classes or custom creation.
  • @Primary vs @Qualifier? @Primary sets a default; @Qualifier selects a specific bean at the injection point (and wins over @Primary).
  • How do you inject all implementations? Inject List<Interface> or Map<String, Interface>.
  • Why are @Configuration classes proxied? So inter-bean method calls return container singletons.

Summary

  • @Configuration + @Bean create beans from any class.
  • Resolve ambiguity with @Primary or @Qualifier; inject List/Map for all implementations.
  • Conditional beans (@Profile, @ConditionalOn...) power Spring Boot's auto-configuration.

Next: bean scopes and the bean lifecycle.

items.title: Spring Bean Scopes and Lifecycle
items.excerpt: Compare singleton and prototype scopes in an animation, learn request and session scopes, hook into the lifecycle with @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy, lazy beans, and the prototype-in-singleton trap.
items.content:
Spring decides how many instances of a bean exist and when they are created and destroyed. Getting this wrong causes some of the nastiest bugs: one user seeing another user's data.

Singleton vs prototype, animated

Switch the scope and watch whether a and b point to the same cart:

The golden rule of singletons

Singletons are shared by every request and every user, on many threads at once. So:

  • ✅ Keep them stateless: only final dependencies, no per-user fields.
  • ❌ Never store "current user", "current order" or counters in a singleton's fields.
@Service
public class CartService {
    private List<String> items = new ArrayList<>();   // ❌ every user shares ONE cart!
}

Store per-user state in the database, the session, or pass it as method parameters.

Lifecycle callbacks

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct;
import jakarta.annotation.PreDestroy;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
public class Main {

    @Component
    static class PriceCache {
        PriceCache() { System.out.println("1. constructor"); }

        @PostConstruct                      // after dependencies are injected
        void load() { System.out.println("2. @PostConstruct: warm up the cache"); }

        @PreDestroy                         // before the container shuts down
        void close() { System.out.println("4. @PreDestroy: release resources"); }
    }

    @Component
    @Scope("prototype")
    static class Ticket {
        private static int counter = 0;
        final int number = ++counter;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (var ctx = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Main.class)) {
            System.out.println("3. container ready");
            Ticket t1 = ctx.getBean(Ticket.class);
            Ticket t2 = ctx.getBean(Ticket.class);
            System.out.println("tickets: " + t1.number + ", " + t2.number + " (same object? " + (t1 == t2) + ")");
            PriceCache c1 = ctx.getBean(PriceCache.class), c2 = ctx.getBean(PriceCache.class);
            System.out.println("cache singleton? " + (c1 == c2));
        }
    }
}

Output:

1. constructor
2. @PostConstruct: warm up the cache
3. container ready
tickets: 1, 2 (same object? false)
cache singleton? true
4. @PreDestroy: release resources

The full lifecycle of a singleton:

  1. Instantiate (constructor) → 2. Inject dependencies → 3. Aware callbacks → 4. BeanPostProcessor before-init → 5. @PostConstruct / afterPropertiesSet() / initMethod → 6. BeanPostProcessor after-init (proxies for @Transactional etc. are created here) → 7. Ready → 8. @PreDestroy / destroy() on shutdown.

Spring does not call @PreDestroy on prototype beans: once handed out, they're yours to clean up.

Eager vs lazy

Singletons are created at startup (eager). Good: configuration errors show up immediately, not on the first user request. Mark rarely used, expensive beans @Lazy to create them on first use.

The prototype-in-singleton trap

If a singleton gets a prototype injected through its constructor, it receives one prototype instance, once, at startup, and keeps it forever. The prototype effectively becomes a singleton.

Fix: ask for a new instance each time with ObjectProvider:

@Service
public class TicketService {
    private final ObjectProvider<Ticket> tickets;

    public TicketService(ObjectProvider<Ticket> tickets) { this.tickets = tickets; }

    public Ticket issue() {
        return tickets.getObject();     // a fresh prototype every call
    }
}

Request and session scopes

In web apps you can scope beans to a request or session. Because they're injected into singletons, Spring injects a proxy that finds the right instance for the current request:

@Component
@SessionScope                       // = @Scope(value = "session", proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS)
public class RecentlyViewed {
    private final Deque<String> courses = new ArrayDeque<>();
    public void add(String slug) { courses.addFirst(slug); if (courses.size() > 5) courses.removeLast(); }
    public List<String> list() { return List.copyOf(courses); }
}

Exercise

  1. Run the example and add a second @PostConstruct bean that depends on PriceCache. Which @PostConstruct runs first?
  2. Inject the prototype Ticket into a singleton's constructor, call getBean on the singleton twice and print the ticket number. Then fix it with ObjectProvider.
  3. Find the bug: a @Service with a field private int requestCount; incremented in every call. What goes wrong under load, and how would you fix it?
Hint for 3

Many threads update the same field at once, so counts get lost (race condition). Use an AtomicInteger, or better, a metrics library like Micrometer.

Interview corner

  • Default scope? Singleton: one instance per ApplicationContext.
  • Are singleton beans thread-safe? Not automatically. They're safe only if stateless or properly synchronised.
  • Singleton vs prototype? One shared instance vs a new instance per request to the container; Spring doesn't manage prototype destruction.
  • How do you inject a prototype into a singleton? ObjectProvider/Provider, lookup method injection (@Lookup), or a scoped proxy.
  • Bean lifecycle? Instantiate → populate → aware callbacks → BeanPostProcessors → init (@PostConstruct) → ready → destroy (@PreDestroy).

Summary

  • Singleton (default) beans are shared: keep them stateless.
  • Prototype gives a new instance per lookup; use ObjectProvider inside singletons.
  • @PostConstruct for setup after injection, @PreDestroy for cleanup.

Next: externalised configuration with properties and profiles.

items.title: Spring Properties, @Value, @ConfigurationProperties and Profiles
items.excerpt: Keep settings out of code. Read values with @Value and Environment, bind typed config with @ConfigurationProperties records, switch environments with profiles, and keep secrets out of Git.
items.content:
Database URLs, API keys, feature flags and limits change between your laptop, testing and production. Hard-coding them means rebuilding the app for every environment. Spring reads them from properties, so the same build runs everywhere.

application.properties

# application.properties
app.name=VitalStack
app.max-cart-items=20
app.support-email=help@example.com
app.payment.provider=razorpay
app.payment.timeout=5s
app.payment.retries=2

Or the same in YAML (application.yml):

app:
  name: VitalStack
  max-cart-items: 20
  payment:
    provider: razorpay
    timeout: 5s
    retries: 2

@Value: one value at a time

@Service
public class CartService {
    private final int maxItems;

    public CartService(@Value("${app.max-cart-items:10}") int maxItems) {   // ":10" = default
        this.maxItems = maxItems;
    }
}

Fine for one or two values. For groups of settings, use typed properties.

@ConfigurationProperties: typed, validated groups

package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import java.time.Duration;

@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.payment")
public record PaymentProperties(String provider, Duration timeout, int retries) { }
package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.EnableConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.core.env.Environment;

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProperties.class)
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Main.class);
        app.setWebApplicationType(org.springframework.boot.WebApplicationType.NONE);
        app.run(args).close();
    }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner show(PaymentProperties pay, Environment env) {
        return args -> {
            System.out.println("provider=" + pay.provider() + ", timeout=" + pay.timeout().toMillis()
                    + "ms, retries=" + pay.retries());
            System.out.println("app.name=" + env.getProperty("app.name"));
            System.out.println("profiles=" + String.join(",", env.getActiveProfiles()));
        };
    }
}
# application.properties
spring.main.banner-mode=off
logging.level.root=warn
app.name=VitalStack
app.payment.provider=razorpay
app.payment.timeout=5s
app.payment.retries=2

Output:

provider=razorpay, timeout=5000ms, retries=2
app.name=VitalStack
profiles=

Benefits over @Value: type conversion (5s → Duration), one place for related settings, IDE autocompletion, and validation with @Validated + @NotBlank, @Min.

Profiles: different settings per environment

Create files per profile:

application.properties          ← shared defaults
application-dev.properties      ← used when profile "dev" is active
application-prod.properties     ← used when profile "prod" is active
# application-dev.properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:devdb
app.payment.provider=mock
logging.level.com.vitalstack=debug

Activate a profile:

java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
# or an environment variable
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod java -jar app.jar

Profile-specific values override the defaults. Beans can be profile-specific too:

@Bean
@Profile("dev")
CommandLineRunner seedDemoData(CourseRepository repo) { ... }

Where values can come from (highest priority first)

  1. Command-line arguments (--app.payment.retries=5)
  2. Environment variables (APP_PAYMENT_RETRIES=5: dots become underscores, upper case)
  3. Profile-specific files (application-prod.properties)
  4. application.properties / application.yml
  5. Defaults in code (@Value("${x:default}"))

So the same jar can be configured by your hosting platform or Docker through environment variables, without editing files.

Never commit secrets (database passwords, API keys, JWT secrets) to Git. Reference them as ${DB_PASSWORD} in properties and supply them through environment variables or a secrets manager. If a secret ever lands in Git, rotate it: deleting the commit isn't enough.

spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
app.jwt.secret=${JWT_SECRET}

Exercise

  1. Create @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail") with from, host and port, and print them at startup.
  2. Add application-dev.properties and application-prod.properties with different app.name values and switch between them with --spring.profiles.active.
  3. Override a property with an environment variable and confirm it wins over the file.
  4. Add @Validated and @Min(1) to retries, set it to 0, and read the startup error.
Hint for 3

APP_NAME=FromEnv java -jar app.jar overrides app.name thanks to relaxed binding.

Interview corner

  • @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties? @Value injects single values; @ConfigurationProperties binds a typed, validated group with relaxed binding.
  • What are profiles? Named sets of configuration and beans activated per environment (dev, test, prod).
  • Property precedence? Command line > environment variables > profile files > application.properties > code defaults (simplified).
  • How do you handle secrets? Environment variables or a vault/secret manager, never in source control.

Summary

  • Externalise settings in application.properties/.yml.
  • @Value for single values; @ConfigurationProperties records for typed groups.
  • Profiles switch config and beans per environment; environment variables override files.
  • Keep secrets out of Git.

Next: AOP, adding behaviour around methods.

items.title: Spring AOP - Aspects, Advice and Proxies
items.excerpt: Add logging, timing, security and auditing around methods without touching them. Learn aspects, pointcuts and @Around/@Before/@AfterReturning advice, how Spring proxies work, and the self-invocation trap.
items.content:
Some code belongs everywhere: "log how long this took", "check the user is an admin", "record who changed this". Copying it into every method buries your business logic. Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) lets you write it once and apply it around many methods.

Cross-cutting concerns

public Order placeOrder(Order o) {
    long start = System.nanoTime();                 // timing
    log.info("placeOrder called by {}", user());    // logging
    if (!security.canOrder(user())) throw ...;      // security
    try {
        tx.begin();                                 // transactions
        // ↓ the only line that is actually about orders
        Order saved = repo.save(o);
        tx.commit();
        return saved;
    } catch (Exception e) { tx.rollback(); throw e; }
    finally { metrics.record(System.nanoTime() - start); }
}

With AOP, the method shrinks to its real job, and the rest is applied by annotations or rules.

Vocabulary

A timing aspect

package com.vitalstack;

import java.lang.annotation.*;

@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Timed { }
package com.vitalstack;

import org.aspectj.lang.ProceedingJoinPoint;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Aspect
@Component
public class TimingAspect {

    @Around("@annotation(com.vitalstack.Timed)")              // pointcut: methods annotated @Timed
    public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint jp) throws Throwable {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return jp.proceed();                                // call the real method
        } finally {
            long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
            System.out.println("[timed] " + jp.getSignature().toShortString() + " took ~" + (ms / 100 * 100) + " ms");
        }
    }

    @AfterThrowing(pointcut = "execution(* com.vitalstack.ReportService.*(..))", throwing = "ex")
    public void logError(Exception ex) {
        System.out.println("[error] " + ex.getMessage());
    }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class ReportService {
    @Timed
    public String monthly() throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(300);                                      // pretend to work
        return "report ready";
    }

    public void broken() {
        throw new IllegalStateException("no data for this month");
    }

    public String selfCall() throws InterruptedException {
        return monthly();                                       // calls itself: NOT through the proxy
    }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.*;

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
@EnableAspectJAutoProxy                                         // Spring Boot enables this automatically
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (var ctx = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Main.class)) {
            ReportService reports = ctx.getBean(ReportService.class);
            System.out.println("bean class: " + reports.getClass().getSimpleName());
            System.out.println(reports.monthly());
            try { reports.broken(); } catch (IllegalStateException ignored) { }
            System.out.println("self call: " + reports.selfCall());
        }
    }
}

Output:

bean class: ReportService$$SpringCGLIB$$0
[timed] ReportService.monthly() took ~300 ms
report ready
[error] no data for this month
self call: report ready

ReportService itself never mentions timing or error logging.

How it works: proxies

The bean you receive isn't your ReportService. It's a generated proxy subclass (ReportService$$SpringCGLIB$$0). Calls go through the proxy, which runs the advice and then calls the real method:

caller ──▶ [proxy: advice before] ──▶ real ReportService.monthly() ──▶ [proxy: advice after] ──▶ caller

Spring uses JDK dynamic proxies for interfaces and CGLIB subclasses for classes. This is how @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @PreAuthorize and @Retryable all work.

The self-invocation trap

Look at the last output line: selfCall() called monthly(), but no timing was printed. Inside the object, this.monthly() calls the real method directly, bypassing the proxy. The same trap breaks @Transactional on internal calls (next lesson).

Fixes: move the method to another bean (cleanest), or inject the bean into itself lazily.

Other proxy limits: advice doesn't apply to private or final methods, or to objects you create with new.

Pointcut expressions

Which advice?

Use AOP for truly cross-cutting concerns. For regular business logic, plain method calls are easier to read and debug. Too much "magic" makes code hard to follow.

Exercise

  1. Write an @AuditLog annotation and an aspect that prints the method name and arguments before each annotated method.
  2. Write an @Around retry aspect that retries a method up to 3 times when it throws IOException.
  3. Fix the self-invocation in ReportService by moving monthly() into a separate MonthlyReport bean.
Hint for 1

@Before("@annotation(com.vitalstack.AuditLog)") public void log(JoinPoint jp) { System.out.println(jp.getSignature().getName() + " " + Arrays.toString(jp.getArgs())); }

Interview corner

  • What is AOP? A way to modularise cross-cutting concerns (logging, security, transactions) into aspects applied around methods.
  • How does Spring implement AOP? With runtime proxies (JDK dynamic proxies or CGLIB subclasses) around beans.
  • Advice types? Before, AfterReturning, AfterThrowing, After (finally), Around.
  • Why doesn't advice run on internal method calls? Self-invocation calls the target directly, bypassing the proxy.

Summary

  • Aspects hold cross-cutting code; pointcuts choose methods; advice says when it runs.
  • Spring wraps beans in proxies; calls through the proxy get the advice.
  • Self-invocation, private and final methods bypass proxies.

Next: @Transactional, the most important aspect of all.

items.title: Spring @Transactional - Transactions Made Simple
items.excerpt: See @Transactional commit or roll back a money transfer in an animation, then learn rollback rules for checked exceptions, propagation (REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW), readOnly, isolation and the common pitfalls.
items.content:
In the JPA course you wrote begin(), commit() and rollback() by hand. In Spring, you write one annotation: **@Transactional**. Spring's AOP proxy opens a transaction before your method and commits or rolls back after it.

All or nothing, animated

Try a transfer that fits the balance (like 300) and one that doesn't (1500):

A real example

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Account {
    @Id private String owner;
    private int balance;

    protected Account() { }
    public Account(String owner, int balance) { this.owner = owner; this.balance = balance; }

    public void withdraw(int amount) { balance -= amount; }
    public void deposit(int amount) { balance += amount; }
    public int getBalance() { return balance; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, String> { }
package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class BankService {
    private final AccountRepository accounts;

    public BankService(AccountRepository accounts) { this.accounts = accounts; }

    @Transactional
    public void transfer(String from, String to, int amount) {
        Account a = accounts.findById(from).orElseThrow();
        Account b = accounts.findById(to).orElseThrow();
        a.withdraw(amount);                                    // UPDATE pending (dirty checking)
        if (a.getBalance() < 0) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds");   // → ROLLBACK: the withdraw is undone
        }
        b.deposit(amount);
    }                                                          // no exception → COMMIT

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)                            // a read-only transaction for queries
    public int totalMoney() {
        return accounts.findAll().stream().mapToInt(Account::getBalance).sum();
    }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.boot.*;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;

@SpringBootApplication
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Main.class);
        app.setWebApplicationType(WebApplicationType.NONE);
        app.run(args).close();
    }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner demo(AccountRepository repo, BankService bank) {
        return args -> {
            repo.save(new Account("A", 1000));
            repo.save(new Account("B", 500));

            bank.transfer("A", "B", 300);
            System.out.println("after 300: A=" + repo.findById("A").get().getBalance()
                    + ", B=" + repo.findById("B").get().getBalance());

            try {
                bank.transfer("A", "B", 1500);
            } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
                System.out.println("failed: " + e.getMessage());
            }
            System.out.println("after 1500: A=" + repo.findById("A").get().getBalance()
                    + ", B=" + repo.findById("B").get().getBalance());
        };
    }
}
# application.properties
spring.main.banner-mode=off
logging.level.root=warn
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

Output:

after 300: A=700, B=800
failed: Insufficient funds
after 1500: A=700, B=800

The failed transfer changed nothing: atomic, as promised.

Rollback rules: the checked-exception surprise

By default Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error), but commits on checked exceptions (Exception, IOException)!

@Transactional
public void importCourses(Path file) throws IOException {
    repo.save(new Course("A"));
    throw new IOException("file broken");     // ⚠️ the save is COMMITTED by default
}

@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) // ✅ roll back on any exception
public void importCoursesSafely(Path file) throws IOException { ... }

Many teams use rollbackFor = Exception.class everywhere, or only throw unchecked exceptions from services.

Propagation: what if a transaction is already running?

Classic REQUIRES_NEW use: an audit log that must be saved even when the main operation fails:

@Service
public class AuditService {
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void record(String event) { auditRepo.save(new AuditEntry(event)); }   // commits on its own
}

readOnly and isolation

@Transactional(readOnly = true)                          // no dirty checking/flush; may route to read replicas
public List<CourseView> listCourses() { ... }

@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.SERIALIZABLE, timeout = 5)
public void bookSeat(...) { ... }

The pitfalls (very common in interviews)

  1. Self-invocation: calling a @Transactional method from another method in the same class bypasses the proxy, so no transaction starts. Move it to another bean.
  2. Private methods: @Transactional on a private method does nothing.
  3. Catching the exception inside: if you catch it within the transactional method, Spring never sees it and commits. Re-throw, or call TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly().
  4. Checked exceptions commit by default (see above).
  5. Long transactions: don't call slow external APIs or send emails inside a transaction: it holds database connections and locks.
  6. **Putting @Transactional on controllers:** keep it on the service layer, where business operations live.

"UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only" means an inner REQUIRED method threw an exception (marking the shared transaction for rollback) and an outer method caught it and tried to commit. Let the exception propagate, or use REQUIRES_NEW for truly independent work.

Exercise

  1. Run the example, then remove @Transactional from transfer. What are the balances after the failed transfer now?
  2. Make transfer throw a checked Exception instead and observe that the withdrawal is committed. Fix it with rollbackFor.
  3. Add an AuditService with REQUIRES_NEW that records every transfer attempt, including failed ones.
  4. Move transfer into a private helper called from a public non-transactional method in the same class. Does rollback still work?
Hint for 1

Surprise: even the successful transfer isn't saved (A=1000, B=500). Without a transaction, findById returns detached objects, so dirty checking never runs. If you add accounts.save(a) and accounts.save(b), each save commits on its own, and a failure between them makes money disappear. That's exactly what a transaction prevents.

Interview corner

  • How does @Transactional work? A proxy (AOP) begins a transaction before the method and commits/rolls back after it, using a PlatformTransactionManager.
  • Default rollback behaviour? Roll back on RuntimeException and Error; commit on checked exceptions unless rollbackFor is set.
  • REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW? Join the current transaction vs suspend it and run an independent one.
  • Why doesn't @Transactional work on internal calls? Self-invocation bypasses the proxy.

Summary

  • @Transactional on service methods gives all-or-nothing behaviour.
  • Roll back on checked exceptions with rollbackFor.
  • Propagation controls joining vs new transactions; readOnly for queries.
  • Beware self-invocation, private methods, swallowed exceptions and long transactions.
