items.title: Relationships, Pagination and Performance in a Spring Boot API
items.excerpt: Expose one-to-many data in a REST API without N+1 queries or JSON loops - nested resources, @EntityGraph, DTO mapping, Pageable endpoints with sorting, and counting queries to prove it's fast.
items.content:
Real APIs return related data: a course with its lessons, a student with enrollments. This is where most Spring Boot apps get slow or crash with JSON recursion. Let's do it properly.

The model

package com.vitalstack.school;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private int price;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "course", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    @OrderBy("position")
    private List<Lesson> lessons = new ArrayList<>();

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title, int price) { this.title = title; this.price = price; }

    public Lesson addLesson(String title) {
        Lesson l = new Lesson(this, title, lessons.size() + 1);
        lessons.add(l);
        return l;
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public int getPrice() { return price; }
    public List<Lesson> getLessons() { return lessons; }
}
package com.vitalstack.school;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Lesson {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private int position;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    private Course course;

    protected Lesson() { }
    Lesson(Course course, String title, int position) { this.course = course; this.title = title; this.position = position; }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public int getPosition() { return position; }
}

DTOs shaped for each endpoint

Never serialise the entities: Course → lessons → course → lessons… loops forever, and lazy collections explode outside transactions.

package com.vitalstack.school;

import java.util.List;

public final class Dtos {
    private Dtos() { }

    public record CourseSummary(Long id, String title, int price, int lessonCount) { }
    public record LessonView(Long id, int position, String title) { }
    public record CourseDetail(Long id, String title, int price, List<LessonView> lessons) {
        static CourseDetail from(Course c) {
            return new CourseDetail(c.getId(), c.getTitle(), c.getPrice(),
                    c.getLessons().stream().map(l -> new LessonView(l.getId(), l.getPosition(), l.getTitle())).toList());
        }
    }
    public record PageResponse<T>(List<T> items, int page, int size, long total, int totalPages) { }
    public record NewLesson(String title) { }
}

Repository: fetch what each endpoint needs

package com.vitalstack.school;

import com.vitalstack.school.Dtos.CourseSummary;
import org.springframework.data.domain.*;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.*;
import java.util.Optional;

public interface CourseRepository extends JpaRepository<Course, Long> {

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lessons")                 // course + lessons in ONE query
    Optional<Course> findWithLessonsById(Long id);

    // list page: a DTO projection with a count, no lessons loaded at all
    @Query(value = """
            select new com.vitalstack.school.Dtos$CourseSummary(c.id, c.title, c.price, cast(size(c.lessons) as int))
            from Course c""",
           countQuery = "select count(c) from Course c")
    Page<CourseSummary> summaries(Pageable pageable);
}

Service and controller

package com.vitalstack.school;

import com.vitalstack.school.Dtos.*;
import org.springframework.data.domain.*;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

@Service
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public class CourseService {
    private final CourseRepository repo;

    public CourseService(CourseRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    public PageResponse<CourseSummary> list(Pageable pageable) {
        Page<CourseSummary> p = repo.summaries(pageable);
        return new PageResponse<>(p.getContent(), p.getNumber(), p.getSize(), p.getTotalElements(), p.getTotalPages());
    }

    public CourseDetail detail(long id) {
        return repo.findWithLessonsById(id).map(CourseDetail::from)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new NoSuchElementException("Course " + id + " not found"));
    }

    @Transactional
    public LessonView addLesson(long courseId, String title) {
        Course c = repo.findById(courseId).orElseThrow(() -> new NoSuchElementException("Course " + courseId + " not found"));
        Lesson l = c.addLesson(title);
        repo.flush();                                                      // get the generated id now
        return new LessonView(l.getId(), l.getPosition(), l.getTitle());
    }
}
package com.vitalstack.school;

import com.vitalstack.school.Dtos.*;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Pageable;
import org.springframework.data.web.PageableDefault;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/courses")
public class CourseController {
    private final CourseService service;

    public CourseController(CourseService service) { this.service = service; }

    @GetMapping                                   // ?page=0&size=2&sort=price,desc
    public PageResponse<CourseSummary> list(@PageableDefault(size = 10, sort = "id") Pageable pageable) {
        return service.list(pageable);
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public CourseDetail detail(@PathVariable long id) { return service.detail(id); }

    @PostMapping("/{id}/lessons")                 // nested resource: lessons belong to a course
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    public LessonView addLesson(@PathVariable long id, @RequestBody NewLesson body) {
        return service.addLesson(id, body.title());
    }
}

Missing courses become a clean 404, as in the DTO and validation lesson:

package com.vitalstack.school;

import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiErrors {
    @ExceptionHandler(NoSuchElementException.class)
    public ProblemDetail notFound(NoSuchElementException e) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage());
    }
}
package com.vitalstack.school;

import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;

@SpringBootApplication
public class SchoolApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(SchoolApplication.class, args); }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner seed(CourseRepository repo) {
        return args -> {
            String[][] data = { {"Java Basics", "499", "Variables", "Loops", "Methods"},
                                {"Spring Boot", "799", "REST", "Data JPA"},
                                {"React", "599", "JSX", "State", "Hooks", "Router"} };
            for (String[] d : data) {
                Course c = new Course(d[0], Integer.parseInt(d[1]));
                for (int i = 2; i < d.length; i++) c.addLesson(d[i]);
                repo.save(c);
            }
        };
    }
}
# application.properties
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=25
spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size=50

The responses

GET /api/courses?page=0&size=2&sort=price,desc
← {"items":[{"id":2,"title":"Spring Boot","price":799,"lessonCount":2},
            {"id":3,"title":"React","price":599,"lessonCount":4}],
   "page":0,"size":2,"total":3,"totalPages":2}

GET /api/courses/1
← {"id":1,"title":"Java Basics","price":499,"lessons":[{"id":1,"position":1,"title":"Variables"},
   {"id":2,"position":2,"title":"Loops"},{"id":3,"position":3,"title":"Methods"}]}

POST /api/courses/1/lessons {"title":"Arrays"}
← 201 {"id":10,"position":4,"title":"Arrays"}

GET /api/courses/99
← 404 {"type":"about:blank","title":"Not Found","status":404,"detail":"Course 99 not found","instance":"/api/courses/99"}

Proving it's efficient

With spring.jpa.show-sql=true you'll see:

  • GET /api/courses: 2 queries (the page of summaries with a count subquery for lessons, and the total count), however many courses are on the page.
  • GET /api/courses/1: 1 query (course left join lessons, from @EntityGraph).

A naive version (findAll(pageable) returning entities, mapped with c.getLessons().size()) runs 1 + N queries, and with open-in-view disabled it throws LazyInitializationException instead.

Pagination best practices

  • Always paginate list endpoints, and cap the size (spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size).
  • Use a stable sort (include id) so items don't jump between pages.
  • Return your own PageResponse DTO rather than Spring's Page (whose JSON format isn't a stable contract).
  • For infinite scroll over huge tables, consider keyset pagination (where id > :lastSeenId order by id limit 20): it stays fast deep into the list, unlike large OFFSETs.

spring.jpa.open-in-view=false is the single most useful line in this lesson. It turns hidden N+1 queries in the web layer into loud errors during development, so you fix fetching where it belongs: in the repository.

Exercise

  1. Add GET /api/courses/{id}/lessons?page=0&size=2 returning paginated lessons of a course.
  2. Add DELETE /api/courses/{courseId}/lessons/{lessonId} (orphanRemoval deletes it).
  3. Add a level to Course and a ?level= filter to the list endpoint using a derived query Page<...> findByLevel(Level level, Pageable p).
  4. Turn on show-sql and count the queries for each endpoint.
Hint for 1

Add a LessonRepository with Page<Lesson> findByCourseId(Long courseId, Pageable pageable) and map to LessonView.

Interview corner

  • How do you avoid N+1 in Spring Data JPA? @EntityGraph, JOIN FETCH queries, DTO projections, batch fetching.
  • How do you return entities with bidirectional relationships as JSON? Don't: map to DTOs (or use @JsonIgnore/@JsonManagedReference as a last resort).
  • Offset vs keyset pagination? Offset is simple but slows down for large offsets; keyset uses the last seen key and stays fast.
  • What does open-in-view do? Keeps the persistence context open during view rendering/serialisation, hiding lazy loading in the web layer.

Summary

  • Shape DTOs per endpoint; never serialise entities with relationships.
  • @EntityGraph for details, DTO projections for lists, batch fetching as a safety net.
  • Paginate everything, cap page sizes, disable open-in-view.

items.title: Spring Boot Actuator, Docker and Deployment
items.excerpt: Get your API production-ready - health checks and metrics with Actuator, building an executable jar, a small Docker image, configuration with environment variables, database migrations with Flyway, and deploying to a VPS or cloud platform.
items.content:
Your API works on your laptop. Production needs more: health checks for load balancers, metrics to spot problems, safe database migrations, and a repeatable way to ship. Spring Boot covers all of it.

Actuator: health and metrics

Add spring-boot-starter-actuator, then choose what to expose:

# application.yml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,metrics,prometheus
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized
      probes:
        enabled: true          # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness for Kubernetes
info:
  app:
    name: course-api
    version: 1.0.0
curl localhost:8080/actuator/health
{"status":"UP"}
curl localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/http.server.requests

Load balancers and Kubernetes call /actuator/health to decide whether to send traffic to an instance.

Never expose all endpoints publicly (include: "*"): /env, /heapdump and /loggers reveal secrets and internals. Expose only what you need, and protect the rest with Spring Security or a separate management port (management.server.port=8081, not open to the internet).

Database migrations with Flyway

ddl-auto=update is fine while learning, but production needs versioned, reviewed schema changes. Add flyway-core (plus flyway-mysql or flyway-database-postgresql), then write SQL files:

src/main/resources/db/migration/
├── V1__create_course.sql
├── V2__create_lesson.sql
└── V3__add_course_level.sql
-- V3__add_course_level.sql
ALTER TABLE course ADD COLUMN level VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'BEGINNER';
CREATE INDEX idx_course_level ON course(level);

On startup, Flyway runs the new scripts in order and records them in flyway_schema_history. Set spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate so Hibernate only checks that entities match the schema.

Build an executable jar

./mvnw clean package          # runs the tests too
java -jar target/course-api-1.0.0.jar

The jar contains your code, all libraries and Tomcat. That single file is your deployable.

Docker

A multi-stage Dockerfile builds the jar and then copies it into a small runtime image:

# Dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY .mvn .mvn
COPY mvnw pom.xml ./
RUN ./mvnw -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src src
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
USER app
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75", "-jar", "app.jar"]
docker build -t course-api .
docker run -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/courses \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=courses \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=secret \
  -e JWT_SECRET=a-very-long-random-secret-value \
  course-api

Or skip the Dockerfile: ./mvnw spring-boot:build-image creates an optimised image with Cloud Native Buildpacks.

Run the app and a database together

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: courses
      POSTGRES_USER: courses
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes: [dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/courses
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: courses
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: secret
    depends_on: [db]
volumes:
  dbdata:

docker compose up --build starts both.

Where to deploy

Note: regular shared web hosting (the kind used for WordPress and PHP) can't run Java apps. You need a VPS or a platform that runs containers or jars.

Production checklist

  • ✅ prod profile; secrets only from environment variables.
  • ✅ Flyway migrations; ddl-auto=validate.
  • ✅ HTTPS (Nginx/Caddy or the platform's TLS).
  • ✅ Health checks and basic metrics; log to stdout (the platform collects logs).
  • ✅ Enough memory: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 makes the JVM respect container limits.
  • ✅ Graceful shutdown: server.shutdown=graceful finishes in-flight requests before stopping.
  • ✅ CORS restricted to your front-end domain.
  • ✅ Backups of the database.

Exercise

  1. Add Actuator and open /actuator/health and /actuator/metrics/jvm.memory.used.
  2. Add a custom health indicator that reports DOWN when a payment provider is unreachable (implements HealthIndicator).
  3. Convert your schema to Flyway migrations V1__init.sql and V2__seed.sql.
  4. Build the Docker image and run it with docker compose up.
Hint for 2

@Component class PaymentHealth implements HealthIndicator { public Health health() { return reachable() ? Health.up().build() : Health.down().withDetail("provider", "razorpay").build(); } }

Interview corner

  • What is Spring Boot Actuator? Production-ready endpoints for health, metrics, info, environment and more.
  • How do you manage schema changes? Versioned migrations with Flyway or Liquibase, never ddl-auto=update in production.
  • How do you containerise a Spring Boot app? A multi-stage Dockerfile with a JRE base image, or spring-boot:build-image (Buildpacks).
  • How do you pass configuration to a container? Environment variables (relaxed binding), mounted config files, or a config server/secret manager.

Summary

  • Actuator gives health checks and metrics; expose only what's needed.
  • Flyway versions your schema; Hibernate just validates.
  • Ship a jar or a Docker image configured by environment variables, behind HTTPS.

Next: the capstone project that puts the whole course together.

items.title: Spring Boot Project: Course Enrollment API
items.excerpt: Build a complete, layered REST API - students, courses and enrollments with progress tracking, validation, business rules, ProblemDetail errors, an efficient leaderboard query and tests. Portfolio-ready.
items.content:
Let's build a real back-end like the one behind an e-learning site: students enroll in courses, complete lessons, and see a leaderboard. It brings together everything from this course: entities and relationships, Spring Data JPA, DTOs, validation, transactions, error handling and efficient queries.

Features

  • POST /api/students: register a student (unique email).
  • GET /api/courses: list courses.
  • POST /api/enrollments: enroll a student in a course (no duplicates, max 3 active courses).
  • POST /api/enrollments/{id}/progress: complete lessons (progress can't exceed 100%).
  • GET /api/students/{id}/enrollments: a student's courses with progress.
  • GET /api/leaderboard: top students by completed lessons.

Package structure

com.vitalstack.enroll
├── EnrollApplication.java      (main + seed data)
├── domain/                     (entities + repositories)
├── service/                    (business rules, transactions)
└── web/                        (controllers, DTOs, error handling)

Domain

package com.vitalstack.enroll.domain;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Student {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String name;
    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;

    protected Student() { }
    public Student(String name, String email) { this.name = name; this.email = email; }
    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public String getEmail() { return email; }
}
package com.vitalstack.enroll.domain;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private int totalLessons;

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title, int totalLessons) { this.title = title; this.totalLessons = totalLessons; }
    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public int getTotalLessons() { return totalLessons; }
}
package com.vitalstack.enroll.domain;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.LocalDate;

@Entity
@Table(uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(columnNames = { "student_id", "course_id" }))
public class Enrollment {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    private Student student;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    private Course course;

    private int completedLessons;
    private LocalDate enrolledOn;

    @Version
    private int version;                               // safe concurrent progress updates

    protected Enrollment() { }
    public Enrollment(Student student, Course course) {
        this.student = student; this.course = course; this.enrolledOn = LocalDate.now();
    }

    /** Business rule lives with the data. */
    public void completeLessons(int count) {
        if (count <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Count must be positive");
        completedLessons = Math.min(course.getTotalLessons(), completedLessons + count);
    }

    public boolean isFinished() { return completedLessons >= course.getTotalLessons(); }
    public int percent() { return completedLessons * 100 / course.getTotalLessons(); }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public Student getStudent() { return student; }
    public Course getCourse() { return course; }
    public int getCompletedLessons() { return completedLessons; }
}
package com.vitalstack.enroll.domain;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface StudentRepository extends JpaRepository<Student, Long> {
    boolean existsByEmailIgnoreCase(String email);
}
package com.vitalstack.enroll.domain;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface CourseRepository extends JpaRepository<Course, Long> { }
package com.vitalstack.enroll.domain;

import org.springframework.data.domain.Pageable;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.*;
import java.util.List;

public interface EnrollmentRepository extends JpaRepository<Enrollment, Long> {
    boolean existsByStudentIdAndCourseId(Long studentId, Long courseId);

    @Query("select count(e) from Enrollment e where e.student.id = :sid and e.completedLessons < e.course.totalLessons")
    long countActive(Long sid);

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "course")                       // no N+1 when listing
    List<Enrollment> findByStudentIdOrderByEnrolledOnDesc(Long studentId);

    @Query("""
           select new com.vitalstack.enroll.domain.LeaderboardRow(s.name, sum(e.completedLessons), count(e))
           from Enrollment e join e.student s
           group by s.id, s.name
           order by sum(e.completedLessons) desc, s.name""")
    List<LeaderboardRow> leaderboard(Pageable top);
}
package com.vitalstack.enroll.domain;

public record LeaderboardRow(String student, long lessonsCompleted, long courses) { }

Service: business rules and transactions

package com.vitalstack.enroll.service;

import com.vitalstack.enroll.domain.*;
import org.springframework.data.domain.PageRequest;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

@Service
@Transactional
public class EnrollmentService {
    public static final int MAX_ACTIVE = 3;

    private final StudentRepository students;
    private final CourseRepository courses;
    private final EnrollmentRepository enrollments;

    public EnrollmentService(StudentRepository s, CourseRepository c, EnrollmentRepository e) {
        this.students = s; this.courses = c; this.enrollments = e;
    }

    public Student register(String name, String email) {
        String normalised = email.trim().toLowerCase();
        if (students.existsByEmailIgnoreCase(normalised)) throw new BusinessRuleException("Email already registered");
        return students.save(new Student(name.trim(), normalised));
    }

    public Enrollment enroll(long studentId, long courseId) {
        Student s = students.findById(studentId).orElseThrow(() -> new NoSuchElementException("Student " + studentId + " not found"));
        Course c = courses.findById(courseId).orElseThrow(() -> new NoSuchElementException("Course " + courseId + " not found"));
        if (enrollments.existsByStudentIdAndCourseId(studentId, courseId)) throw new BusinessRuleException("Already enrolled in " + c.getTitle());
        if (enrollments.countActive(studentId) >= MAX_ACTIVE) throw new BusinessRuleException("Finish a course first: max " + MAX_ACTIVE + " active courses");
        return enrollments.save(new Enrollment(s, c));
    }

    public Enrollment progress(long enrollmentId, int lessons) {
        Enrollment e = enrollments.findById(enrollmentId).orElseThrow(() -> new NoSuchElementException("Enrollment " + enrollmentId + " not found"));
        e.completeLessons(lessons);                      // dirty checking + @Version
        return e;
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<Enrollment> enrollmentsOf(long studentId) { return enrollments.findByStudentIdOrderByEnrolledOnDesc(studentId); }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<LeaderboardRow> leaderboard(int top) { return enrollments.leaderboard(PageRequest.of(0, top)); }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<Course> courses() { return courses.findAll(); }
}
package com.vitalstack.enroll.service;

public class BusinessRuleException extends RuntimeException {
    public BusinessRuleException(String message) { super(message); }
}

Web layer: DTOs, controller, errors

package com.vitalstack.enroll.web;

import com.vitalstack.enroll.domain.Enrollment;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;

public final class Api {
    private Api() { }

    public record RegisterRequest(@NotBlank @Size(max = 60) String name, @NotBlank @Email String email) { }
    public record EnrollRequest(@NotNull Long studentId, @NotNull Long courseId) { }
    public record ProgressRequest(@Min(1) @Max(50) int lessons) { }

    public record StudentView(Long id, String name, String email) { }
    public record CourseView(Long id, String title, int totalLessons) { }
    public record EnrollmentView(Long id, String course, int completed, int percent, boolean finished) {
        static EnrollmentView of(Enrollment e) {
            return new EnrollmentView(e.getId(), e.getCourse().getTitle(), e.getCompletedLessons(), e.percent(), e.isFinished());
        }
    }
}
package com.vitalstack.enroll.web;

import com.vitalstack.enroll.domain.LeaderboardRow;
import com.vitalstack.enroll.service.EnrollmentService;
import com.vitalstack.enroll.web.Api.*;
import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.List;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
public class EnrollmentController {
    private final EnrollmentService service;

    public EnrollmentController(EnrollmentService service) { this.service = service; }

    @PostMapping("/students")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    public StudentView register(@Valid @RequestBody RegisterRequest r) {
        var s = service.register(r.name(), r.email());
        return new StudentView(s.getId(), s.getName(), s.getEmail());
    }

    @GetMapping("/courses")
    public List<CourseView> courses() {
        return service.courses().stream().map(c -> new CourseView(c.getId(), c.getTitle(), c.getTotalLessons())).toList();
    }

    @PostMapping("/enrollments")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    public EnrollmentView enroll(@Valid @RequestBody EnrollRequest r) {
        return EnrollmentView.of(service.enroll(r.studentId(), r.courseId()));
    }

    @PostMapping("/enrollments/{id}/progress")
    public EnrollmentView progress(@PathVariable long id, @Valid @RequestBody ProgressRequest r) {
        return EnrollmentView.of(service.progress(id, r.lessons()));
    }

    @GetMapping("/students/{id}/enrollments")
    public List<EnrollmentView> mine(@PathVariable long id) {
        return service.enrollmentsOf(id).stream().map(EnrollmentView::of).toList();
    }

    @GetMapping("/leaderboard")
    public List<LeaderboardRow> leaderboard(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "10") int top) {
        return service.leaderboard(Math.min(top, 50));
    }
}
package com.vitalstack.enroll.web;

import com.vitalstack.enroll.service.BusinessRuleException;
import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.*;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiErrors {
    @ExceptionHandler(NoSuchElementException.class)
    public ProblemDetail notFound(NoSuchElementException e) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(BusinessRuleException.class)
    public ProblemDetail rule(BusinessRuleException e) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, e.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ProblemDetail invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) {
        Map<String, String> fields = new TreeMap<>();
        e.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().forEach(f -> fields.put(f.getField(), f.getDefaultMessage()));
        ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Invalid request");
        p.setProperty("errors", fields);
        return p;
    }
}

Application and seed data

package com.vitalstack.enroll;

import com.vitalstack.enroll.domain.*;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import java.util.List;

@SpringBootApplication
public class EnrollApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(EnrollApplication.class, args); }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner seed(CourseRepository courses) {
        return args -> courses.saveAll(List.of(
                new Course("Java Basics", 16), new Course("Java OOP", 12), new Course("Spring Boot", 10),
                new Course("React", 12), new Course("SQL", 15)));
    }
}
# application.properties
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

A session with the API

POST /api/students {"name":"Asha","email":"Asha@Example.com"}       → 201 {"id":1,"name":"Asha","email":"asha@example.com"}
POST /api/students {"name":"Ravi","email":"ravi@example.com"}       → 201 {"id":2,"name":"Ravi","email":"ravi@example.com"}
POST /api/students {"name":"Copy","email":"asha@example.com"}       → 409 "Email already registered"
POST /api/students {"name":"","email":"not-an-email"}               → 400 errors: email, name
POST /api/enrollments {"studentId":1,"courseId":1}                   → 201 {"id":1,"course":"Java Basics","completed":0,"percent":0,"finished":false}
POST /api/enrollments {"studentId":1,"courseId":1}                   → 409 "Already enrolled in Java Basics"
POST /api/enrollments {"studentId":1,"courseId":2}                   → 201
POST /api/enrollments {"studentId":1,"courseId":3}                   → 201
POST /api/enrollments {"studentId":1,"courseId":4}                   → 409 "Finish a course first: max 3 active courses"
POST /api/enrollments/3/progress {"lessons":10}                     → 200 {"id":3,"course":"Spring Boot","completed":10,"percent":100,"finished":true}
POST /api/enrollments {"studentId":1,"courseId":4}                   → 201 (a slot is free again)
POST /api/enrollments/1/progress {"lessons":8}                      → 200 {"id":1,"course":"Java Basics","completed":8,"percent":50,"finished":false}
POST /api/enrollments {"studentId":2,"courseId":1}                   → 201
POST /api/enrollments/5/progress {"lessons":5}                      → 200
GET  /api/leaderboard?top=5    → [{"student":"Asha","lessonsCompleted":18,"courses":4},{"student":"Ravi","lessonsCompleted":5,"courses":1}]
GET  /api/students/99/enrollments → 200 []
POST /api/enrollments {"studentId":99,"courseId":1}                  → 404 "Student 99 not found"

What makes this production-style

  • Layers: web (DTOs, validation, HTTP), service (rules, transactions), domain (entities, repositories).
  • Business rules in the service and the entity (completeLessons caps progress), not in controllers.
  • Database constraints back up the rules (unique email, unique student+course).
  • Optimistic locking on progress updates.
  • Efficient reads: @EntityGraph for a student's courses, one aggregate query for the leaderboard.
  • Consistent errors: 400 / 404 / 409 ProblemDetails.

Make it your portfolio project

  1. Add JWT security (lesson 6): students can only see and update their own enrollments; admins manage courses.
  2. Add tests (lesson 7): unit tests for the enrollment rules, @WebMvcTest for the controller, @DataJpaTest for the leaderboard query.
  3. Switch to PostgreSQL + Flyway and add a Dockerfile (lesson 9).
  4. Build a React or Angular front end for it (next courses on VitalStack).
  5. Write a README with the endpoints, how to run it, and screenshots. Deploy it and put the link on your CV and LinkedIn.
Hint for 1

In the controller, read the user from @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt and check that the enrollment's student email equals jwt.getSubject(), or use @PreAuthorize with a custom bean method.

Interviewers love "walk me through a project you built". With this API you can explain layering, transactions, validation, N+1 avoidance, optimistic locking and error design, which covers most Spring Boot interview questions.

Summary

You built a complete Spring Boot API with relationships, rules, validation, transactions, efficient queries and clean errors. Congratulations on finishing the Spring Boot course!

items.title: Jmix Introduction - Full-Stack Business Apps in Java
items.excerpt: What Jmix is, how it builds on Spring Boot, JPA and Vaadin to create complete business applications in Java only, what you get out of the box, and when Jmix is (and isn't) the right tool.
items.content:
Companies run on internal business apps: CRMs, inventory systems, HR portals, loan processing, admin panels. Building them with Spring Boot plus React or Angular means two codebases, two teams and weeks of CRUD screens. Jmix lets one Java developer build the whole application, back end and UI, in Java.

What is Jmix?

Jmix is an open-source (Apache 2.0) full-stack framework for data-centric business applications. It's built on technologies you already know:

          ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  UI      │ Vaadin Flow: web UI written in Java + XML    │
          ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  Jmix    │ data access, security, views, add-ons        │
          ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  Base    │ Spring Boot · Spring Security · JPA/EclipseLink│
          └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                         Database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle…)
  • Spring Boot underneath: everything from the Spring courses applies (beans, DI, transactions, configuration).
  • JPA entities for the data model (Jmix uses EclipseLink as the JPA provider).
  • Vaadin Flow for the UI: you write views in XML + Java, and the browser UI is generated. No JavaScript framework to learn.
  • Jmix Studio, an IntelliJ IDEA plugin, generates entities, views, roles and database migrations visually.

What you get out of the box

A taste: an entity becomes a working screen

@JmixEntity
@Table(name = "CUSTOMER")
@Entity
public class Customer {
    @JmixGeneratedValue
    @Id
    @Column(name = "ID", nullable = false)
    private UUID id;

    @InstanceName
    @NotNull
    @Column(name = "NAME", nullable = false)
    private String name;

    @Email
    @Column(name = "EMAIL")
    private String email;

    @Version
    @Column(name = "VERSION", nullable = false)
    private Integer version;

    // getters and setters
}

From this entity, Studio generates a list view (a searchable, sortable, paginated table with filters and Create/Edit/Remove buttons) and a detail view (a validated form). Add a security role, and users only see what they're allowed to. Watch the request flow:

Jmix vs Spring Boot + React/Angular

Jmix is a strong fit for enterprise and internal applications with many entities and forms. For a public marketing site or a pixel-perfect consumer app, a SPA framework (React, Angular) is usually better. Many companies use both: Jmix for back-office, React for the customer-facing site.

Versions

  • Jmix 2.x (current): Spring Boot 3, Java 17+, Vaadin Flow; UI units are called views.
  • Jmix 1.x (older): Vaadin 8; UI units were called screens. Tutorials mentioning "screens" are for 1.x.

Licensing in short

The Jmix framework and its core add-ons are open source. Jmix Studio has a free plan for learning and smaller projects, and paid subscriptions that unlock all visual designers for larger projects and some commercial add-ons. Check jmix.io for current terms.

If you already know Spring Boot and JPA from this site's courses, you're 70% of the way to Jmix. The new parts are the view XML, data containers and loaders, fetch plans, DataManager and the role-based security model, which is exactly what the next lessons cover.

Exercise

  1. List three internal apps at a company you know (or your college) that would suit Jmix.
  2. For one of them, write down five entities and their main attributes.
  3. Decide which users need which permissions (who can read, create, edit, delete each entity).
Hint for 1

Library management, hostel room allocation, placement-cell company tracker, leave management, asset inventory, fee collection.

Interview corner

  • What is Jmix? A full-stack Java framework for business apps built on Spring Boot, JPA and Vaadin, with data access, security and UI generation.
  • What's a view in Jmix 2? A UI unit defined by an XML descriptor and a Java controller (list views, detail views, custom views).
  • Which ORM does Jmix use? JPA with EclipseLink.
  • When would you not choose Jmix? Public consumer-facing apps with highly custom UI or mobile-first design.

Summary

  • Jmix = Spring Boot + JPA + Vaadin + ready-made data, UI and security features.
  • Write the data model, get working list/detail views, add roles.
  • Best for data-heavy business and back-office applications.

Next: install Jmix Studio and create your first project.

items.title: Installing Jmix Studio and Creating Your First Project
items.excerpt: Install IntelliJ IDEA and the Jmix Studio plugin, create a project from a template, understand the generated structure, run the app, log in as admin and explore the Jmix tool window.
items.content:
Let's set up a Jmix development environment and run your first application.

Requirements

  • JDK 17 or 21.
  • IntelliJ IDEA (Community or Ultimate).
  • Jmix Studio plugin: in IntelliJ, open *Settings → Plugins → Marketplace*, search Jmix, install, and restart.
  • Internet access the first time (Gradle downloads dependencies).

Create a project

  1. *File → New → Project*, choose Jmix Project on the left.
  2. Pick the Full-Stack Application (Java) template.
  3. Project name: course-admin, base package: com.vitalstack.courseadmin.
  4. JDK 17+, keep the default HSQLDB in-memory database for now (switch to PostgreSQL or MySQL later in *Data Stores*).
  5. Click Create and wait for Gradle to sync. The first time takes a few minutes.

The generated structure

course-admin/
├── build.gradle                      ← dependencies (Jmix BOM, add-ons)
├── src/main/java/com/vitalstack/courseadmin/
│   ├── CourseAdminApplication.java   ← @SpringBootApplication main class
│   ├── entity/User.java              ← the user entity (login, password, names)
│   ├── security/                     ← FullAccessRole, UiMinimalRole, DatabaseUserRepository
│   └── view/
│       ├── main/MainView.java        ← the app shell: menu + header
│       ├── login/LoginView.java
│       └── user/                     ← user list and detail views
├── src/main/resources/com/vitalstack/courseadmin/
│   ├── view/**/*.xml                 ← view layouts (descriptors)
│   ├── menu.xml                      ← main menu
│   ├── messages_en.properties        ← UI text (i18n)
│   └── liquibase/                    ← database changelogs
├── src/main/resources/application.properties
└── frontend/themes/course-admin/     ← CSS theme

It's a normal Spring Boot application with extra Jmix modules.

Run it

In the Jmix tool window (left side), or the run configurations dropdown, choose Course Admin Jmix Application and click Run. When the log says the app started, open:

http://localhost:8080

Log in with admin / admin. You'll see the main view with a menu containing Users. Open it: a fully working list view with search, paging, and Create/Edit/Remove. You haven't written any code yet.

The Jmix tool window

The tool window shows your project the Jmix way:

  • Data Model: entities and enums. Right-click → New → JPA Entity.
  • User Interface: views, menu, themes.
  • Security: resource and row-level roles.
  • Data Stores: database connections and Liquibase changelogs.
  • Add-ons: install reports, BPM, email, REST, etc. with one click.

Studio's visual designers (entity designer, view designer with a component palette and preview) write the Java and XML for you; you can always edit the code directly.

application.properties

main.datasource.url=jdbc:hsqldb:file:.jmix/hsqldb/courseadmin
main.datasource.username=sa
main.datasource.password=

jmix.ui.login-view-id=LoginView
jmix.ui.main-view-id=MainView
jmix.ui.menu-config=com/vitalstack/courseadmin/menu.xml

# show SQL while learning
logging.level.eclipselink.logging.sql=debug

Note the main.datasource prefix: Jmix supports multiple data stores, and main is the default one.

Switching to PostgreSQL

In *Data Stores → Main Data Store*, choose PostgreSQL and enter the URL, user and password. Studio updates build.gradle (driver) and application.properties. Use environment variables for the password in shared or production setups:

main.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost/courseadmin
main.datasource.username=courseadmin
main.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}

Useful Gradle tasks

./gradlew bootRun                                   # run from the terminal
./gradlew -Pvaadin.productionMode=true bootJar      # build a production jar (lesson 7)
./gradlew test

On the first run, Vaadin builds the front-end bundle (with Node.js, downloaded automatically), which takes a while. Later runs are much faster. If the UI looks unstyled after a dependency change, run the Clean Vaadin frontend action or delete node_modules and restart.

Common problems

  • Port 8080 already in use: stop the other app, or set server.port=8081.
  • Gradle sync fails behind a proxy: configure the proxy in gradle.properties.
  • Wrong JDK: check *Project Structure → SDK* and Gradle JVM in settings both point to JDK 17+.

Exercise

  1. Create and run the project, log in as admin, and create a new user.
  2. Log in as the new user. What happens? (Hint: roles.)
  3. Change the app title shown in the browser tab in messages_en.properties.
  4. Find the generated Liquibase changelog for the User table.
Hint for 2

A new user has no roles, so login is refused or they see an empty app. Assign the UiMinimalRole and a role with permissions (lesson 6) to let them in.

Interview corner

  • What is Jmix Studio? An IntelliJ IDEA plugin with project templates, visual designers and code generation for Jmix apps.
  • Where is the database schema managed? Liquibase changelogs that Studio generates from entity changes.
  • What's the default admin login? admin/admin in a new project; change it before deploying!

Summary

  • Install IntelliJ + the Jmix plugin; create a Full-Stack Application project.
  • A Jmix app is a Spring Boot app with views (XML + Java), entities, roles and Liquibase changelogs.
  • Run it and log in as admin/admin to see a working user management UI.

Next: design the data model with Jmix entities.

items.title: Jmix Entities and the Data Model
items.excerpt: Design a Jmix data model with the entity designer - @JmixEntity, UUID ids, @InstanceName, enums, references and compositions, audit and soft-delete traits, validation, and Liquibase changelogs generated for you.
items.content:
Everything in a Jmix app starts from the data model. Define your entities well, and Studio can generate views, roles and database changes from them. Our example: a course admin app with Courses, Lessons, Instructors and Categories.

Creating an entity

In the Jmix tool window: *Data Model → right-click → New → JPA Entity*. Name it Course, keep the defaults (UUID id, versioned), and tick the traits you want (audit of creation/modification, soft delete). Studio opens the entity designer where you add attributes with types, mandatory flags and validation.

The generated (and slightly trimmed) code:

@JmixEntity
@Table(name = "COURSE", indexes = {
        @Index(name = "IDX_COURSE_CATEGORY", columnList = "CATEGORY_ID")})
@Entity
public class Course {

    @JmixGeneratedValue
    @Id
    @Column(name = "ID", nullable = false)
    private UUID id;

    @Version
    @Column(name = "VERSION", nullable = false)
    private Integer version;

    @InstanceName
    @NotBlank
    @Size(max = 120)
    @Column(name = "TITLE", nullable = false, length = 120)
    private String title;

    @Column(name = "LEVEL_")
    private String level;                        // stores the enum id (see below)

    @PositiveOrZero
    @Column(name = "PRICE", precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal price;

    @JoinColumn(name = "CATEGORY_ID")
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    private Category category;

    @JoinColumn(name = "INSTRUCTOR_ID")
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    private Instructor instructor;

    @Composition
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "course")
    @OrderBy("position")
    private List<Lesson> lessons;

    @CreatedBy
    @Column(name = "CREATED_BY")
    private String createdBy;

    @CreatedDate
    @Column(name = "CREATED_DATE")
    private OffsetDateTime createdDate;

    @LastModifiedDate
    @Column(name = "LAST_MODIFIED_DATE")
    private OffsetDateTime lastModifiedDate;

    @DeletedDate
    @Column(name = "DELETED_DATE")
    private OffsetDateTime deletedDate;

    public CourseLevel getLevel() { return level == null ? null : CourseLevel.fromId(level); }
    public void setLevel(CourseLevel level) { this.level = level == null ? null : level.getId(); }

    // other getters and setters generated by Studio
}

What the Jmix annotations mean

Validation annotations (@NotBlank, @Size, @PositiveOrZero, @Email) are standard Bean Validation, so forms validate automatically and show messages next to fields.

Enums

Jmix enums implement EnumClass and store a stable id, not the ordinal or name, so renaming a constant in code is safe:

public enum CourseLevel implements EnumClass<String> {
    BEGINNER("B"), INTERMEDIATE("I"), ADVANCED("A");

    private final String id;
    CourseLevel(String id) { this.id = id; }
    public String getId() { return id; }

    @Nullable
    public static CourseLevel fromId(String id) {
        for (CourseLevel l : values()) if (l.getId().equals(id)) return l;
        return null;
    }
}

Captions for each value live in messages_en.properties, so the UI can show "Beginner" (or a Hindi translation) instead of BEGINNER.

References vs compositions

  • Reference (@ManyToOne Category): an independent entity. In the course form you pick a category from a dropdown; deleting a course doesn't delete the category.
  • Composition (@Composition @OneToMany lessons): child entities that only exist inside the parent. The course detail view shows a lessons table with create/edit inside it, and everything is saved in one transaction when the course is saved.

Delete policies control what happens to related rows:

@OnDelete(DeletePolicy.CASCADE)        // on Course.lessons: deleting a course deletes its lessons
@OnDeleteInverse(DeletePolicy.DENY)    // on Course.category: a category can't be deleted while courses use it

Liquibase changelogs

When you add or change entities, Studio compares them with the database and generates a Liquibase changelog (in src/main/resources/.../liquibase/changelog/). Review it, and it runs automatically on the next start. These changelogs are your versioned database history, the same idea as Flyway in the Spring Boot course.

Model first, screens later. Spend time on names, mandatory fields, relationships and instance names. Changing a data model after users have entered thousands of records is much harder than changing a view.

The full model for our app

Category (name)            1 ──< Course >── 1  Instructor (name, email, user)
                                  │
                                  └──< Lesson (title, position, durationMinutes, videoUrl)   [composition]

Exercise

  1. Create Category (name, unique) and Instructor (name, email) entities.
  2. Create Course with the attributes above, a reference to both, and the CourseLevel enum.
  3. Create Lesson as a composition of Course, with position and durationMinutes.
  4. Run the app and check the generated Liquibase changelog and tables.
Hint for 3

In the entity designer, add an attribute lessons of type Lesson with cardinality ONE_TO_MANY and the Composition checkbox ticked; Studio adds the inverse course attribute to Lesson.

Interview corner

  • Why UUID ids in Jmix? Entities get ids at creation time (before saving), which simplifies UI work and distributed systems.
  • Reference vs composition? References link independent entities; compositions own child entities that are edited and saved with the parent.
  • What is @InstanceName? The attribute(s) used as the entity's display name in the UI.
  • How is the schema updated? Studio generates Liquibase changelogs from entity changes.

Summary

  • Entities are JPA classes with Jmix annotations for ids, display names, compositions, audit and soft delete.
  • Enums store stable ids; validation annotations drive form validation.
  • Studio generates Liquibase changelogs for every model change.

Next: generate list and detail views for the courses.
items.subject: jmix

items.title: Jmix Views - List and Detail Screens
items.excerpt: Generate list and detail views, understand view XML descriptors and Java controllers, data containers and loaders, data grids with filters and pagination, forms, actions and event handlers.
items.content:
A Jmix view is one screen of your application: a list of courses, a course form, a dashboard. Each view has an XML descriptor (layout and data) and a Java controller (behaviour).

Watch a request flow through a Jmix app

Switch between opening the list and saving a new record:

Generate views

Right-click the Course entity → *Views → Create View* → Entity list and detail views. Studio asks for the fetch plan (which attributes and references to load) and creates four files:

view/course/CourseListView.java        view/course/course-list-view.xml
view/course/CourseDetailView.java      view/course/course-detail-view.xml

It also adds a menu item. Restart, and Courses appears in the menu with a working table and form.

The list view

<view xmlns="http://jmix.io/schema/flowui/view"
      title="msg://courseListView.title"
      focusComponent="coursesDataGrid">
    <data>
        <collection id="coursesDc" class="com.vitalstack.courseadmin.entity.Course">
            <fetchPlan extends="_base">
                <property name="category" fetchPlan="_base"/>
                <property name="instructor" fetchPlan="_base"/>
            </fetchPlan>
            <loader id="coursesDl" readOnly="true">
                <query>
                    <![CDATA[select e from Course e order by e.title]]>
                </query>
            </loader>
        </collection>
    </data>
    <facets>
        <dataLoadCoordinator auto="true"/>
        <urlQueryParameters>
            <genericFilter component="genericFilter"/>
            <pagination component="pagination"/>
        </urlQueryParameters>
    </facets>
    <layout>
        <genericFilter id="genericFilter" dataLoader="coursesDl"/>
        <hbox id="buttonsPanel" classNames="buttons-panel">
            <button id="createButton" action="coursesDataGrid.create"/>
            <button id="editButton" action="coursesDataGrid.edit"/>
            <button id="removeButton" action="coursesDataGrid.remove"/>
            <simplePagination id="pagination" dataLoader="coursesDl"/>
        </hbox>
        <dataGrid id="coursesDataGrid" width="100%" minHeight="20em" dataContainer="coursesDc">
            <actions>
                <action id="create" type="list_create"/>
                <action id="edit" type="list_edit"/>
                <action id="remove" type="list_remove"/>
            </actions>
            <columns>
                <column property="title"/>
                <column property="level"/>
                <column property="category"/>
                <column property="instructor"/>
                <column property="price"/>
            </columns>
        </dataGrid>
    </layout>
</view>
@Route(value = "courses", layout = MainView.class)
@ViewController("Course.list")
@ViewDescriptor("course-list-view.xml")
@LookupComponent("coursesDataGrid")
@DialogMode(width = "64em")
public class CourseListView extends StandardListView<Course> {
}

The key ideas:

  • Data container (coursesDc): holds the loaded entities; UI components bind to it.
  • Data loader (coursesDl): runs the JPQL query and fills the container, with paging and the filter's conditions added automatically.
  • Fetch plan: which attributes and references to load in one go. Loading category and instructor here avoids N+1 queries when the grid shows them (the problem you studied in the Hibernate course).
  • Facets: dataLoadCoordinator loads data when the view opens; urlQueryParameters puts filter and page into the URL so users can bookmark and share them.
  • Actions: standard list_create, list_edit, list_remove open the detail view, ask for confirmation, check security and refresh the grid.

The detail view

<view xmlns="http://jmix.io/schema/flowui/view"
      title="msg://courseDetailView.title"
      focusComponent="form">
    <data>
        <instance id="courseDc" class="com.vitalstack.courseadmin.entity.Course">
            <fetchPlan extends="_base">
                <property name="category" fetchPlan="_base"/>
                <property name="instructor" fetchPlan="_base"/>
                <property name="lessons" fetchPlan="_base"/>
            </fetchPlan>
            <loader id="courseDl"/>
            <collection id="lessonsDc" property="lessons"/>
        </instance>
    </data>
    <facets>
        <dataLoadCoordinator auto="true"/>
    </facets>
    <actions>
        <action id="saveAction" type="detail_saveClose"/>
        <action id="closeAction" type="detail_close"/>
    </actions>
    <layout>
        <formLayout id="form" dataContainer="courseDc">
            <textField id="titleField" property="title"/>
            <select id="levelField" property="level"/>
            <entityComboBox id="categoryField" property="category" itemsQuery="select c from Category c order by c.name"/>
            <entityPicker id="instructorField" property="instructor">
                <actions>
                    <action id="entityLookup" type="entity_lookup"/>
                    <action id="entityClear" type="entity_clear"/>
                </actions>
            </entityPicker>
            <bigDecimalField id="priceField" property="price"/>
        </formLayout>
        <h4 text="msg://lessons"/>
        <dataGrid id="lessonsDataGrid" dataContainer="lessonsDc" width="100%" height="15em">
            <actions>
                <action id="create" type="list_create"/>
                <action id="edit" type="list_edit"/>
                <action id="remove" type="list_remove"/>
            </actions>
            <columns>
                <column property="position"/>
                <column property="title"/>
                <column property="durationMinutes"/>
            </columns>
        </dataGrid>
        <hbox id="detailActions">
            <button id="saveAndCloseButton" action="saveAction"/>
            <button id="closeButton" action="closeAction"/>
        </hbox>
    </layout>
</view>
@Route(value = "courses/:id", layout = MainView.class)
@ViewController("Course.detail")
@ViewDescriptor("course-detail-view.xml")
@EditedEntityContainer("courseDc")
public class CourseDetailView extends StandardDetailView<Course> {

    @ViewComponent
    private JmixBigDecimalField priceField;

    @Subscribe
    public void onInitEntity(final InitEntityEvent<Course> event) {
        event.getEntity().setLevel(CourseLevel.BEGINNER);          // defaults for NEW courses
    }

    @Subscribe("levelField")
    public void onLevelFieldValueChange(final ComponentValueChangeEvent<JmixSelect<CourseLevel>, CourseLevel> event) {
        if (event.getValue() == CourseLevel.ADVANCED && getEditedEntity().getPrice() == null) {
            priceField.setValue(new BigDecimal("999"));            // suggest a price
        }
    }
}
  • Form fields bind to entity attributes with property="..."; validation annotations on the entity are enforced, and the save button stays safe.
  • @Subscribe methods handle view lifecycle events (InitEntityEvent, BeforeShowEvent, BeforeSaveEvent) and component events.
  • @ViewComponent injects components declared in the XML by id.
  • On save, the DataContext collects every changed entity (the course and its lessons) and commits them in one transaction.

Customising the UI

  • Studio's view designer: drag components from the palette (text fields, combo boxes, tabs, charts) and edit properties with a live preview.
  • Navigation: ViewNavigators / DialogWindows beans open views from code, e.g. a detail view in a dialog.
  • Notifications: inject Notifications and call notifications.create("Course published").show().
  • Themes: edit CSS in frontend/themes/<app>/.

Prefer XML + standard actions for what they do well (CRUD, filters, paging). Write Java only for real behaviour. Generated views take minutes; your time goes into business logic and good UX.

Exercise

  1. Generate list and detail views for Course, Category and Instructor.
  2. Add a level column filter to the course list using the generic filter's "Add condition".
  3. In the course detail view, show a notification after saving (@Subscribe AfterSaveEvent).
  4. Add a custom button "Duplicate" on the list that copies the selected course with " (copy)" in the title.
Hint for 4

Add <button id="duplicateButton" text="Duplicate"/>, then in the controller @Subscribe(id = "duplicateButton", subject = "clickListener") to create a copy with dataManager.create(Course.class), set its fields, dataManager.save(copy) and reload the loader coursesDl.load().

Interview corner

  • What makes up a Jmix view? An XML descriptor (data components, layout, actions, facets) and a Java controller.
  • Data container vs data loader? Containers hold entities for binding; loaders fetch them with JPQL into containers.
  • What is a fetch plan? A description of which attributes and references to load, preventing lazy-loading problems and N+1 queries.
  • How are changes saved? The view's DataContext tracks modified entities and commits them together.

Summary

  • Studio generates list and detail views from entities.
  • XML defines data (containers, loaders, fetch plans), facets and layout; Java controllers add behaviour with @Subscribe.
  • Standard actions give CRUD with security checks; the DataContext saves everything in one transaction.

Next: data access in Java with DataManager.

items.title: Jmix Data Access with DataManager and Fetch Plans
items.excerpt: Load and save entities from Java code with DataManager's fluent API, control loading with fetch plans, understand security-aware vs unconstrained access, write services, and react to entity events.
items.content:
Views load data declaratively. In services, scheduled jobs and event handlers you work with data in Java through DataManager, Jmix's main data access API. It's similar to Spring Data repositories, but security-aware and fetch-plan-aware.

DataManager basics

@Component
public class CourseService {
    private final DataManager dataManager;

    public CourseService(DataManager dataManager) { this.dataManager = dataManager; }

    public List<Course> beginnerCourses() {
        return dataManager.load(Course.class)
                .query("select c from Course c where c.level = :level order by c.title")
                .parameter("level", CourseLevel.BEGINNER)
                .list();
    }

    public Optional<Course> byTitle(String title) {
        return dataManager.load(Course.class)
                .query("select c from Course c where lower(c.title) = lower(:t)")
                .parameter("t", title)
                .optional();
    }

    public Course byId(UUID id) {
        return dataManager.load(Course.class).id(id).one();      // throws if not found
    }

    public Course createCourse(String title, Category category) {
        Course c = dataManager.create(Course.class);              // new instance with UUID assigned
        c.setTitle(title);
        c.setCategory(category);
        c.setLevel(CourseLevel.BEGINNER);
        return dataManager.save(c);                                // INSERT, returns the saved instance
    }

    public void raisePrice(Course course, BigDecimal percent) {
        course.setPrice(course.getPrice().multiply(BigDecimal.ONE.add(percent.movePointLeft(2))));
        dataManager.save(course);                                  // UPDATE
    }

    public void delete(Course course) {
        dataManager.remove(course);                                // soft delete if the entity has the trait
    }
}

Key points:

  • load(...).query(...) with named parameters (:level) only, never string concatenation.
  • list(), one() (exactly one, else exception), optional().
  • .firstResult(n).maxResults(m) for paging.
  • save(...) accepts several entities and saves them in one transaction: dataManager.save(course, lesson1, lesson2).
  • Use SaveContext for complex saves with removals.

Fetch plans: loading related data correctly

Entities loaded by DataManager are detached. If a reference wasn't loaded, accessing it later fails. A fetch plan says what to load:

List<Course> courses = dataManager.load(Course.class)
        .query("select c from Course c")
        .fetchPlan(fp -> fp.addFetchPlan(FetchPlan.BASE)          // all local attributes
                           .add("category", FetchPlan.BASE)         // + the category
                           .add("lessons", FetchPlan.BASE))         // + the lessons
        .list();
  • FetchPlan.BASE (_base): all local (non-reference) attributes.
  • FetchPlan.INSTANCE_NAME (_instance_name): only what's needed for the display name.
  • Named fetch plans can also be declared once in a fetch-plans.xml file and reused by name.

Jmix builds efficient queries from the plan (joins or batch loading), avoiding the N+1 problem automatically.

Security: DataManager vs UnconstrainedDataManager

DataManager applies the current user's permissions: entity operations (read/create/update/delete) and row-level policies. A user without permission to read salaries simply doesn't get those rows or attributes.

For system code that must see everything (a nightly job, a migration), use the unconstrained variant explicitly:

@Component
public class NightlyReport {
    private final UnconstrainedDataManager system;

    public NightlyReport(UnconstrainedDataManager system) { this.system = system; }

    public long countAllCourses() {
        return system.load(Course.class).all().list().size();
    }
}

(dataManager.unconstrained() returns the same thing.) Be deliberate about it: unconstrained access in user-facing code is a security hole.

Services and transactions

Put business logic in Spring beans. DataManager operations each run in their own transaction; for several operations that must succeed together, save them in one call or use Spring's @Transactional with a TransactionalDataManager.

@Component
public class EnrollmentService {
    private final DataManager dataManager;

    public EnrollmentService(DataManager dataManager) { this.dataManager = dataManager; }

    public Enrollment enroll(Student student, Course course) {
        long active = dataManager.loadValue(
                        "select count(e) from Enrollment e where e.student = :s and e.completed = false", Long.class)
                .parameter("s", student)
                .one();
        if (active >= 3) throw new IllegalStateException("Finish a course first");
        Enrollment e = dataManager.create(Enrollment.class);
        e.setStudent(student);
        e.setCourse(course);
        return dataManager.save(e);
    }
}

loadValue / loadValues return scalar values and aggregates (counts, sums) instead of entities.

Entity events

React to data changes in one place, whatever saved the data (a view, a service, the REST API):

@Component
public class CourseEventListener {

    @EventListener
    public void onCourseSaving(final EntitySavingEvent<Course> event) {
        Course c = event.getEntity();
        c.setTitle(c.getTitle().trim());                          // normalise before saving
    }

    @TransactionalEventListener
    public void onCourseChanged(final EntityChangedEvent<Course> event) {
        if (event.getType() == EntityChangedEvent.Type.CREATED) {
            // after commit: send a notification, update a search index…
        }
    }
}
  • EntitySavingEvent / EntityLoadingEvent: change the entity before it's saved or after it's loaded.
  • EntityChangedEvent: what changed (old values available); with @TransactionalEventListener it runs after the commit, the right place for emails and integrations.

Same rule as Spring Boot: views stay thin, services hold business rules, events handle side effects. Your Jmix code then stays testable with normal Spring Boot tests (@SpringBootTest + DataManager).

Exercise

  1. Write CourseService.totalPriceByCategory() using loadValues with group by.
  2. Load courses with their lessons using a fetch plan and print the lesson count of each.
  3. Add an EntitySavingEvent listener that rejects lessons with durationMinutes > 180.
  4. Call your service from a button in the course list view and show the result in a notification.
Hint for 1

dataManager.loadValues("select c.category.name, sum(c.price) from Course c group by c.category.name").properties("category", "total").list() returns KeyValueEntity objects; read them with kv.getValue("total").

Interview corner

  • What is DataManager? Jmix's main API to load, save and remove entities, applying security and fetch plans.
  • DataManager vs UnconstrainedDataManager? The first enforces the current user's permissions; the second bypasses them for system operations.
  • What problem do fetch plans solve? They define the object graph to load, avoiding lazy-loading errors and N+1 queries.
  • When does EntityChangedEvent fire? On entity changes; with @TransactionalEventListener it's handled after the transaction commits.

Summary

  • DataManager.load(...).query(...).parameter(...).list()/one()/optional(), plus create, save, remove.
  • Fetch plans load exactly the graph you need.
  • DataManager is security-aware; use UnconstrainedDataManager deliberately.
  • Entity events centralise normalisation and side effects.

Next: securing the app with roles.

items.title: Jmix Security - Resource Roles and Row-Level Roles
items.excerpt: Control who can do what in a Jmix app - users, resource roles with entity, attribute, view and menu policies, row-level roles with JPQL conditions, assigning roles, and testing permissions.
items.content:
Business apps hold sensitive data: salaries, fees, student records. Jmix security answers two questions for every user: which operations can they perform (resource roles), and which rows can they see (row-level roles).

The model

User ──has──▶ Resource roles   (what: entities, attributes, views, menu items, specific actions)
     └─has──▶ Row-level roles  (which rows: JPQL/predicate conditions)

Permissions are additive: a user gets the union of all their roles. With no roles, a user can do nothing. Every new project includes:

  • FullAccessRole (system-full-access): everything. Only for administrators.
  • UiMinimalRole (ui-minimal): the minimum to log in and see the main view.

A resource role in code

Roles are interfaces with annotated methods (or designed visually in Studio, or created at runtime in the admin UI):

@ResourceRole(name = "Course manager", code = CourseManagerRole.CODE, scope = SecurityScope.UI)
public interface CourseManagerRole {
    String CODE = "course-manager";

    @EntityPolicy(entityClass = Course.class, actions = EntityPolicyAction.ALL)
    @EntityAttributePolicy(entityClass = Course.class, attributes = "*", action = EntityAttributePolicyAction.MODIFY)
    void course();

    @EntityPolicy(entityClass = Lesson.class, actions = EntityPolicyAction.ALL)
    @EntityAttributePolicy(entityClass = Lesson.class, attributes = "*", action = EntityAttributePolicyAction.MODIFY)
    void lesson();

    @EntityPolicy(entityClass = Category.class, actions = EntityPolicyAction.READ)
    @EntityAttributePolicy(entityClass = Category.class, attributes = "*", action = EntityAttributePolicyAction.VIEW)
    void category();

    @ViewPolicy(viewIds = {"Course.list", "Course.detail", "Lesson.detail"})
    @MenuPolicy(menuIds = {"Course.list"})
    void screens();
}

A read-only auditor role would grant READ on entities and VIEW on attributes. To hide salaries, simply don't grant the salary attribute: Jmix hides the column in grids and the field in forms automatically, and DataManager doesn't return the value.

Row-level roles

An instructor should see only their own courses:

@RowLevelRole(name = "Own courses only", code = OwnCoursesRole.CODE)
public interface OwnCoursesRole {
    String CODE = "own-courses";

    @JpqlRowLevelPolicy(entityClass = Course.class,
                        where = "{E}.instructor.user.username = :current_user_username")
    void course();
}
  • {E} is replaced by the entity alias in every query on Course.
  • :current_user_username (and other current_user_... parameters) are filled with the logged-in user's values.
  • The condition is added to every DataManager query, including list views, dropdowns and the REST API, so there's no way around it from the UI.

Predicate-based policies (@PredicateRowLevelPolicy) can check rows in Java for in-memory checks, for example to block updates to published courses.

Assigning roles

  • Admin UI: *Users → select a user → Role assignments*. Assign ui-minimal, course-manager and own-courses to an instructor.
  • Programmatically: assign roles when creating users through code, or map roles from an external identity provider (LDAP, Keycloak/OIDC) via add-ons.

Checking permissions in code

Code can check permissions with the AccessManager bean. The most common check is a specific policy:

SpecificOperationAccessContext ctx = new SpecificOperationAccessContext("course.publish");
accessManager.applyRegisteredConstraints(ctx);
if (!ctx.isPermitted()) throw new AccessDeniedException("specific", "course.publish");

and the standard UI actions already respect entity policies (a user without DELETE doesn't see an enabled Remove button).

Design roles around jobs, not people: "course manager", "finance viewer", "instructor". Combine small roles per user. And test with a non-admin user before every release: most security bugs are "it worked for admin".

Common mistakes

  • Giving everyone system-full-access "for now".
  • Forgetting ui-minimal, so users can't log in.
  • Using UnconstrainedDataManager in user-facing services, bypassing row-level rules.
  • Not changing the default admin/admin password before deployment.

Exercise

  1. Create CourseManagerRole and CourseViewerRole (read-only) and assign them to two test users.
  2. Hide the price attribute from viewers and confirm the column disappears.
  3. Create the own-courses row-level role and check an instructor sees only their courses in the list and in dropdowns.
  4. Add a specific policy course.publish and enable a Publish button only for users who have it.
Hint for 4

Declare @SpecificPolicy(resources = "course.publish") in a role, then in the view check it with AccessManager and SpecificOperationAccessContext in onBeforeShow and call publishButton.setEnabled(ctx.isPermitted()).

Interview corner

  • Resource vs row-level roles? Resource roles control operations on entities, attributes, views and menus; row-level roles restrict which records are visible.
  • How do roles combine? Additively: a user's permissions are the union of their roles.
  • Where are row-level conditions applied? To every query executed through DataManager for that entity.
  • How do you hide one field? Don't grant that attribute in an entity attribute policy.

Summary

  • Resource roles: entity, attribute, view, menu and specific policies.
  • Row-level roles: JPQL conditions with current-user parameters, applied to every query.
  • Assign small job-based roles; always test as a non-admin user.

Next: finish the app and deploy it.
