items.title: Angular Project: Course Hub Front End
items.excerpt: Build the Course Hub front end in Angular for the Spring Boot enrollment API - a typed API service, a signal-based store, routed pages, enrollment with server error messages, progress tracking, a leaderboard and deployment.
items.content:
Let's build the same Course Hub app as the React course, the Angular way, against the Course Enrollment API from the Spring Boot course. Comparing the two versions is a great way to understand both frameworks.

What we'll build

Project setup

ng new course-hub --style=css --ssr=false
cd course-hub
ng serve --proxy-config proxy.conf.json      # proxy /api to Spring Boot (lesson 10)

1. Models and the API service

// src/app/models.ts
export interface Course { id: number; title: string; totalLessons: number; }
export interface Enrollment { id: number; course: string; completed: number; percent: number; finished: boolean; }
export interface LeaderRow { student: string; lessonsCompleted: number; courses: number; }
// src/app/hub-api.service.ts
import { HttpClient, HttpErrorResponse } from '@angular/common/http';
import { Injectable, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { Observable, catchError, throwError } from 'rxjs';
import { Course, Enrollment, LeaderRow } from './models';

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class HubApi {
  private http = inject(HttpClient);

  private friendly<T>(source: Observable<T>): Observable<T> {
    return source.pipe(
      catchError((e: HttpErrorResponse) =>
        throwError(() => new Error(e.error?.detail ?? `Request failed (${e.status})`)))   // ProblemDetail → message
    );
  }

  courses() { return this.friendly(this.http.get<Course[]>('/api/courses')); }
  enrollments(studentId: number) { return this.friendly(this.http.get<Enrollment[]>(`/api/students/${studentId}/enrollments`)); }
  enroll(studentId: number, courseId: number) { return this.friendly(this.http.post<Enrollment>('/api/enrollments', { studentId, courseId })); }
  progress(id: number, lessons: number) { return this.friendly(this.http.post<Enrollment>(`/api/enrollments/${id}/progress`, { lessons })); }
  leaderboard() { return this.friendly(this.http.get<LeaderRow[]>('/api/leaderboard?top=10')); }
}

2. A signal store for "my enrollments"

// src/app/enrollment.store.ts
import { Injectable, computed, inject, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { HubApi } from './hub-api.service';
import { Enrollment } from './models';

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class EnrollmentStore {
  private api = inject(HubApi);
  readonly studentId = signal(1);                    // after adding login: from the JWT
  readonly enrollments = signal<Enrollment[]>([]);
  readonly error = signal<string | null>(null);
  readonly active = computed(() => this.enrollments().filter(e => !e.finished).length);

  load() {
    this.api.enrollments(this.studentId()).subscribe({
      next: list => { this.enrollments.set(list); this.error.set(null); },
      error: (e: Error) => this.error.set(e.message),
    });
  }

  completeLesson(id: number) {
    this.api.progress(id, 1).subscribe({
      next: updated => this.enrollments.update(list => list.map(e => (e.id === id ? updated : e))),
      error: (e: Error) => this.error.set(e.message),
    });
  }
}

3. Pages

// src/app/pages/courses-page.component.ts
import { ChangeDetectionStrategy, Component, inject, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { toSignal } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';
import { HubApi } from '../hub-api.service';
import { EnrollmentStore } from '../enrollment.store';
import { Course } from '../models';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-courses-page',
  standalone: true,
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  template: `
    <h1>Courses</h1>
    @if (message(); as m) {
      <p [attr.role]="m.ok ? 'status' : 'alert'" [class.error]="!m.ok">{{ m.text }}</p>
    }
    <ul class="grid">
      @for (c of courses(); track c.id) {
        <li class="card">
          <h3>{{ c.title }}</h3>
          <p>{{ c.totalLessons }} lessons</p>
          <button [disabled]="busy() === c.id" (click)="enroll(c)">{{ busy() === c.id ? 'Enrolling…' : 'Enroll' }}</button>
        </li>
      } @empty {
        <li>Loading courses…</li>
      }
    </ul>
  `,
})
export class CoursesPageComponent {
  private api = inject(HubApi);
  private store = inject(EnrollmentStore);
  courses = toSignal(this.api.courses(), { initialValue: [] as Course[] });
  busy = signal<number | null>(null);
  message = signal<{ ok: boolean; text: string } | null>(null);

  enroll(course: Course) {
    this.busy.set(course.id);
    this.api.enroll(this.store.studentId(), course.id).subscribe({
      next: () => { this.message.set({ ok: true, text: `Enrolled in ${course.title}. Happy learning!` }); this.busy.set(null); },
      error: (e: Error) => { this.message.set({ ok: false, text: e.message }); this.busy.set(null); },
    });
  }
}
// src/app/pages/my-courses-page.component.ts
import { ChangeDetectionStrategy, Component, OnInit, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { EnrollmentStore } from '../enrollment.store';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-my-courses-page',
  standalone: true,
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  template: `
    <h1>My courses <small>({{ store.active() }} active)</small></h1>
    @if (store.error()) { <p role="alert">{{ store.error() }}</p> }
    @for (e of store.enrollments(); track e.id) {
      <article class="card">
        <h3>{{ e.course }} @if (e.finished) { 🎉 }</h3>
        <div class="bar" role="progressbar" [attr.aria-valuenow]="e.percent"><div [style.width.%]="e.percent"></div></div>
        <p class="stats">{{ e.completed }} lessons · {{ e.percent }}%</p>
        @if (!e.finished) { <button (click)="store.completeLesson(e.id)">+1 lesson</button> }
      </article>
    } @empty {
      <p>You haven't enrolled in any course yet.</p>
    }
  `,
})
export class MyCoursesPageComponent implements OnInit {
  store = inject(EnrollmentStore);
  ngOnInit() { this.store.load(); }
}
// src/app/pages/leaderboard-page.component.ts
import { ChangeDetectionStrategy, Component, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { toSignal } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';
import { HubApi } from '../hub-api.service';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-leaderboard-page',
  standalone: true,
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  template: `
    <h1>Leaderboard</h1>
    <ol>
      @for (row of rows(); track row.student; let i = $index) {
        <li>{{ medals[i] ?? '#' + (i + 1) }} {{ row.student }}: {{ row.lessonsCompleted }} lessons</li>
      }
    </ol>
  `,
})
export class LeaderboardPageComponent {
  medals = ['🥇', '🥈', '🥉'];
  rows = toSignal(inject(HubApi).leaderboard(), { initialValue: [] });
}

4. Routes and shell

// src/app/app.routes.ts
import { Routes } from '@angular/router';

export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: '', loadComponent: () => import('./pages/courses-page.component').then(m => m.CoursesPageComponent), title: 'Courses' },
  { path: 'my-courses', loadComponent: () => import('./pages/my-courses-page.component').then(m => m.MyCoursesPageComponent), title: 'My courses' },
  { path: 'leaderboard', loadComponent: () => import('./pages/leaderboard-page.component').then(m => m.LeaderboardPageComponent), title: 'Leaderboard' },
  { path: '**', redirectTo: '' },
];
// src/app/app.component.ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { RouterLink, RouterLinkActive, RouterOutlet } from '@angular/router';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [RouterOutlet, RouterLink, RouterLinkActive],
  template: `
    <nav>
      <a routerLink="/" routerLinkActive="active" [routerLinkActiveOptions]="{ exact: true }">Courses</a>
      <a routerLink="/my-courses" routerLinkActive="active">My courses</a>
      <a routerLink="/leaderboard" routerLinkActive="active">Leaderboard</a>
    </nav>
    <main><router-outlet /></main>
  `,
})
export class AppComponent {}
// src/app/app.config.ts
import { ApplicationConfig, provideZoneChangeDetection } from '@angular/core';
import { provideRouter, withComponentInputBinding } from '@angular/router';
import { provideHttpClient } from '@angular/common/http';
import { routes } from './app.routes';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideZoneChangeDetection({ eventCoalescing: true }),
    provideRouter(routes, withComponentInputBinding()),
    provideHttpClient(),
  ],
};

5. Try it end to end

  1. Start the Spring Boot API and register student 1.
  2. ng serve --proxy-config proxy.conf.json and open http://localhost:4200.
  3. Enroll in four courses: the fourth shows "Finish a course first: max 3 active courses" from the server.
  4. On My courses, click "+1 lesson" and watch the progress bar move; finished courses get 🎉.

6. Deploy

ng build                 # dist/course-hub/browser

Host the static files anywhere with an SPA fallback, or serve them from Spring Boot's static folder. In production, put the API URL in an InjectionToken or environment file, and enable CORS for your domain in Spring.

Angular vs React: what you noticed

Extend it

  1. Login with JWT + an interceptor + a route guard (lessons 8 and 10).
  2. An enroll confirmation dialog with Angular Material (ng add @angular/material).
  3. Unit tests with TestBed and HttpTestingController.
  4. Optimistic progress updates with rollback on error.
Hint for 3

TestBed.configureTestingModule({ providers: [provideHttpClient(), provideHttpClientTesting()] }), then const ctrl = TestBed.inject(HttpTestingController); ctrl.expectOne('/api/courses').flush([{ id: 1, title: 'Java', totalLessons: 16 }]);

Put both front ends (React and Angular) and the Spring Boot API on GitHub with live links. It shows you can work in any Java full-stack team, which is exactly what Indian IT companies hire for.

Summary

  • A typed API service turns ProblemDetail errors into friendly messages.
  • A signal store holds enrollment state; pages use toSignal, OnPush and @for/@if.
  • Lazy routes and a simple shell complete a production-style Angular app.

Congratulations on finishing the Angular course!

items.title: DSA Introduction
items.excerpt: What data structures and algorithms really are, why every big tech interview tests them, the 15 patterns that solve most problems, and the 6-step method you will use in every lesson.
items.content:
DSA stands for Data Structures and Algorithms. It sounds scary, but you already use both every day. A to-do list is a data structure. "Look through my bag until I find my keys" is an algorithm. This course turns those everyday ideas into tools that make programs fast, and that get you through coding interviews at companies like Google, Amazon and Microsoft.

Two simple definitions

  • A data structure is a way to store and organise data so it is easy to use. Examples: a list, a stack of plates, a phone book, a family tree, a map of cities and roads.
  • An algorithm is a step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. Examples: "check every item", "always look in the middle", "follow the roads from city to city".

The right data structure makes the algorithm easy. Finding a word in a dictionary is fast because the words are sorted: you open the middle, see if your word comes before or after, and throw away half the book. That trick has a name, binary search, and you can watch it work right now:

Press Play, then change the numbers and the target and press Visualize. Every pattern in this course has a live animation like this one.

Why DSA matters

Speed that users can feel

Searching 1,000,000 sorted items one by one can take up to 1,000,000 checks. Binary search needs 20. The same computer, the same data, a 50,000× difference, just from choosing a better algorithm.

Interviews at almost every tech company

Big tech companies (Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, Adobe, Flipkart, Uber and many startups) use DSA problems in interviews because they show how you think: can you break a problem down, choose the right tool, and explain the trade-offs?

Better everyday code

Knowing that a set checks membership in O(1) while a list needs O(n) changes how you write ordinary programs, not just interview answers.

The secret: patterns, not problems

There are thousands of practice problems online. Nobody memorises them all, and you don't need to. Most interview problems are variations of about 15 patterns:

Learn the pattern once, and you can solve dozens of problems with it.

The 6-step method (use it every time)

Good problem solvers follow the same steps. Interviewers love to see them out loud.

  1. Understand. Repeat the problem in your own words. What is the input? What must you return?
  2. Examples. Work through a small example by hand. Add tricky ones: empty input, one item, duplicates, negatives.
  3. Brute force. What is the simplest correct solution, even if it is slow? Say its complexity.
  4. Optimise. Which pattern removes the wasted work? (This course teaches you to spot it.)
  5. Code. Write clean code with good names.
  6. Test. Walk through your examples with the code, line by line. Fix bugs. State the final time and space complexity.

A tiny example of the method

Problem: return True if a list contains any duplicate number.

  • Understand: input a list of numbers; output True/False.
  • Examples: [1, 2, 3, 1] → True. [1, 2, 3] → False. [] → False.
  • Brute force: compare every pair: two loops, O(n²).
  • Optimise: "Have I seen this before?" → that's the hash set pattern: O(n).
def contains_duplicate(nums):
    seen = set()
    for x in nums:
        if x in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False

print(contains_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 1]))  # True
print(contains_duplicate([1, 2, 3]))     # False
print(contains_duplicate([]))            # False

That is the whole journey of this course in miniature: spot the pattern, write a few clean lines.

How this course works

Every lesson has:

  • A real-life analogy so the idea sticks.
  • A live visualizer: play it, step through it, and try your own input.
  • Python code that you can copy and run. (Python reads almost like English, which keeps the focus on the idea. The same patterns work in Java, C++ or JavaScript.)
  • Solved problems, from easy to interview-level.
  • An interview corner: where the pattern shows up and what interviewers look for.
  • An exercise and a short summary.

Learn in order, one lesson a day. When you are tired, play a two-minute brain game and come back fresh.

What you need first

  • Basic Python: variables, lists, loops, functions and dictionaries. If you are new, do the first 13 lessons of our Python course.
  • Patience. Everyone finds DSA hard at first. Every expert was once confused by recursion.

Common mistakes when learning DSA

  • Memorising solutions instead of understanding the pattern. A small twist then breaks everything.
  • Jumping straight to code without examples. Most bugs come from skipping steps 1–3.
  • Grinding hundreds of random problems. 3–5 problems per pattern, understood deeply, beat 300 rushed ones.
  • Ignoring complexity. "It works" is only half an answer in interviews.

Exercise

  1. Write down two data structures and two algorithms you use in daily life.
  2. Play the binary search visualizer above with target 21, then with a number that is not in the list. How many steps did each take?
  3. Use the 6-step method to write count_evens(nums), returning how many numbers are even. State its complexity.

Summary

  • Data structures store data; algorithms are step-by-step recipes.
  • The right choice can make code thousands of times faster.
  • About 15 patterns cover most interview problems.
  • Use the 6 steps every time: understand, examples, brute force, optimise, code, test.

Next, you'll learn Big O notation, the language for describing how fast an algorithm is.

items.title: Big O Notation
items.excerpt: Measure how an algorithm's work grows with input size. Learn O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²) and O(2ⁿ) with a live chart, how to read complexity from code, and space complexity.
items.content:
How fast is your code? "0.2 seconds on my laptop" isn't a useful answer: a different computer, different data, and the number changes. Big O notation answers a better question: how does the amount of work grow as the input gets bigger?

The chai stall analogy

Imagine three ways to serve chai to a queue of n people:

  • O(1): you hand out pre-made cups from a table. 1 person or 1,000, it takes the same few seconds to pick up a cup.
  • O(n): you make each cup when the person arrives. Twice the people, twice the time.
  • O(n²): before serving each person, you ask every other person in the queue if they want sugar. 10 people means 100 questions; 1,000 people means 1,000,000. The stall collapses.

Big O describes this growth, ignoring small details like "each cup takes 30 seconds".

Watch the growth

Press Play and watch what happens to each complexity as n doubles:

At n = 64, O(n²) needs 4,096 steps while O(log n) needs only 6. That gap is the whole point of learning DSA.

The common complexities, from fast to slow

A computer does very roughly 10⁸ simple steps per second. So for a million items, O(n log n) finishes in a fraction of a second, while O(n²) would take hours.

Reading Big O from code

O(1): no loop over the input

def first_item(items):
    return items[0]          # one step, whatever the size

print(first_item([7, 8, 9]))  # 7

O(n): one loop

def total(items):
    s = 0
    for x in items:          # runs n times
        s += x
    return s

print(total([1, 2, 3, 4]))  # 10

O(n²): a loop inside a loop

def count_pairs(items):
    count = 0
    for i in range(len(items)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(items)):   # nested: about n²/2 pairs
            count += 1
    return count

print(count_pairs([1, 2, 3, 4]))  # 6

O(log n): halving

def halvings(n):
    steps = 0
    while n > 1:
        n //= 2              # the problem halves each time
        steps += 1
    return steps

print(halvings(1000000))  # 19

Whenever the remaining work is cut in half each step, think O(log n).

The rules of simplification

Big O keeps only what matters for huge inputs:

  1. Drop constants. 3n steps is O(n). n/2 is O(n).
  2. Keep the biggest term. n² + n + 100 is O(n²): for large n, the n² part dwarfs the rest.
  3. Different inputs, different letters. Looping over list a then list b is O(a + b), not O(n). A loop over a inside a loop over b is O(a × b).
  4. Sequential steps add, nested steps multiply. Two separate loops: O(n + n) = O(n). Nested loops: O(n × n) = O(n²).
def example(nums):
    for x in nums:            # O(n)
        print(x)
    for x in nums:            # + O(n)
        for y in nums:        # × O(n)
            pass
    # total: O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²)

Hidden costs in Python

Some single lines hide loops:

The classic trap: if x in my_list inside a loop is secretly O(n²). Switching the list to a set makes it O(n).

Space complexity

Big O also measures memory. How much extra space does the algorithm use as n grows?

def reversed_copy(items):
    return items[::-1]          # makes a new list: O(n) extra space

def reverse_in_place(items):
    i, j = 0, len(items) - 1
    while i < j:                # only two variables: O(1) extra space
        items[i], items[j] = items[j], items[i]
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return items

print(reversed_copy([1, 2, 3]))     # [3, 2, 1]
print(reverse_in_place([1, 2, 3]))  # [3, 2, 1]

Recursion uses space too: each call waiting on the call stack takes memory, so a recursion that goes n levels deep uses O(n) space.

Best, average and worst case

Linear search finds the target immediately if it's first (best case), or checks everything if it's last or missing (worst case). Interviews usually ask for the worst case, unless stated otherwise. Some structures are quoted with their average case, like hash maps (O(1) average).

Interview corner

At Google, Amazon, Microsoft and nearly every other company, you are expected to state the time and space complexity of every solution you write, without being asked. A typical exchange:

> "My brute force compares every pair, so it's O(n²) time and O(1) space. With a hash set I can get O(n) time at the cost of O(n) space."

Practise saying that sentence for every problem in this course.

Quick check

Code that loops over n items and does a dictionary lookup inside the loop is O(n), not O(n²), because each lookup is O(1).

Common mistakes

  • Counting lines instead of growth. Ten lines with no loops are still O(1).
  • Forgetting hidden loops like in on a list, insert(0, …) or slicing.
  • Calling two separate loops O(n²). They add (O(n)), they don't multiply.
  • Forgetting the recursion call stack in space complexity.

Exercise

Give the time complexity of each:

  1. A loop from 1 to n that prints i * i.
  2. Two nested loops, both from 1 to n, followed by one more loop from 1 to n.
  3. A while loop that starts at n and does n = n // 3 until n reaches 0.
  4. Checking if word in banned_list for every word in a document of m words, with k banned words. How can you make it O(m)?

Then play Big-O Snap in Brain Games to test your speed.

Summary

  • Big O describes how work grows with input size, not exact seconds.
  • From fast to slow: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ).
  • Drop constants, keep the biggest term; sequential adds, nested multiplies.
  • Watch for hidden loops, and always state time and space complexity.

Next, you'll explore the most basic data structure of all: arrays and strings.

items.title: Arrays and Strings
items.excerpt: How arrays live in memory, why indexing is O(1) but inserting is O(n), linear search, in-place techniques, and classic string problems like palindromes and reversing words.
items.content:
Arrays are the foundation of almost every other data structure. Strings are just arrays of characters. Most interview problems start with "given an array…" or "given a string…", so let's understand exactly how they work and what each operation costs.

The train analogy

An array is like a train: coaches in a row, numbered 0, 1, 2, 3… Because every coach is the same size and they are joined in order, the conductor can walk straight to coach 7 without checking coaches 0 to 6. That is why **reading arr[i] is O(1)**.

But adding a coach in the middle of the train means uncoupling and shifting every coach behind it. That is why inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n).

index:   0    1    2    3    4
       [ 12 | 7  | 31 | 4  | 19 ]

Costs at a glance (Python lists)

Linear search: the simplest algorithm

When the array is not sorted, the only way to find a value is to check items one by one:

def linear_search(arr, target):
    for i in range(len(arr)):
        if arr[i] == target:
            return i
    return -1

print(linear_search([12, 7, 31, 4, 19], 19))  # 4
print(linear_search([12, 7, 31, 4, 19], 5))   # -1

O(n) time, O(1) space. If you search the same array many times, it is worth sorting it once and using binary search, or putting the values in a set.

Pattern: do it in one pass

Many array problems can be solved by walking through the array once while remembering a few things. Finding the maximum is the simplest example:

def find_max(arr):
    best = arr[0]
    for x in arr[1:]:
        if x > best:
            best = x
    return best

print(find_max([3, 9, 2, 14, 6]))  # 14

Ask yourself: "As I walk through, what do I need to remember?" For the maximum, just one number.

Second largest in one pass

def second_largest(arr):
    first = second = float("-inf")
    for x in arr:
        if x > first:
            first, second = x, first
        elif first > x > second:
            second = x
    return second if second != float("-inf") else None

print(second_largest([3, 9, 2, 14, 6]))  # 9
print(second_largest([5, 5, 5]))         # None

Pattern: work in place

"In place" means changing the array itself instead of building a new one: O(1) extra space. Interviewers often ask for it.

Reverse an array in place

def reverse_in_place(arr):
    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while left < right:
        arr[left], arr[right] = arr[right], arr[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return arr

print(reverse_in_place([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))  # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

Two indexes walk towards each other, swapping as they go. This is your first taste of the two pointers pattern (lesson 5).

Rotate an array by k

Rotating [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] right by 3 gives [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]. A neat in-place trick: reverse everything, then reverse the two parts.

def rotate(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n

    def rev(i, j):
        while i < j:
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
            i += 1
            j -= 1

    rev(0, n - 1)   # [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
    rev(0, k - 1)   # [5, 6, 7, 4, 3, 2, 1]
    rev(k, n - 1)   # [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]
    return nums

print(rotate([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], 3))  # [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4]

Strings are arrays of characters

In Python, strings are immutable: you can't change one character in place. Building a string with += in a loop can cost O(n²) because each step copies the whole string. Collect pieces in a list and "".join() them once instead.

Is it a palindrome?

A palindrome reads the same both ways: "racecar", "madam".

def is_palindrome(s):
    left, right = 0, len(s) - 1
    while left < right:
        if s[left] != s[right]:
            return False
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return True

print(is_palindrome("racecar"))  # True
print(is_palindrome("chai"))     # False

Reverse the words in a sentence

def reverse_words(sentence):
    return " ".join(reversed(sentence.split()))

print(reverse_words("learn  DSA   the easy way"))  # way easy the DSA learn

split() with no argument also handles extra spaces.

Count characters

def char_counts(s):
    counts = {}
    for ch in s:
        counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1
    return counts

print(char_counts("banana"))  # {'b': 1, 'a': 3, 'n': 2}

Counting with a dictionary is the bridge to the next lesson: hashing.

2D arrays (matrices)

A grid is a list of lists. grid[r][c] reads row r, column c.

grid = [
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
]
transposed = [[grid[r][c] for r in range(len(grid))] for c in range(len(grid[0]))]
print(transposed)  # [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]

Visiting every cell of an r × c grid is O(r × c).

Interview corner

Array and string problems are the most common warm-up questions at Amazon, Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, TCS, Accenture and nearly every company. Interviewers check:

  • Do you handle edge cases: empty array, one item, all items equal, negative numbers?
  • Can you do it in place with O(1) extra space when asked?
  • Do you avoid hidden O(n²) costs like insert(0, …) in a loop or string +=?

Before coding, always ask: "Can the array be empty? Can it contain negatives or duplicates?" It shows care, and often changes the solution.

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one errors: the last index is len(arr) - 1.
  • Changing a list while looping over it, which skips items.
  • **String += in a loop** on long strings.
  • **Forgetting k %= n** in rotation problems when k is larger than the array.

Exercise

  1. Write move_zeros(nums) that moves all zeros to the end, keeping the order of other numbers, in place. ([0, 1, 0, 3, 12] → [1, 3, 12, 0, 0])
  2. Write is_anagram(a, b) that checks whether two words use the same letters ("listen", "silent" → True).
  3. Write max_profit(prices): buy one day, sell a later day, maximum profit. Hint: in one pass, remember the cheapest price so far.

Summary

  • Arrays give O(1) access by index but O(n) insert/delete in the middle.
  • Unsorted search is linear: O(n).
  • Many problems are solved in one pass by remembering the right few values.
  • In-place techniques use O(1) extra space; strings are immutable in Python, so join pieces.

Next, you'll learn the most useful tool in all of DSA: hash maps and sets.

items.title: Hashing: Hash Maps and Sets
items.excerpt: The most useful tool in DSA. How hash maps and sets give O(1) lookups, and the patterns they unlock: seen-before checks, counting, Two Sum, anagram groups and more.
items.content:
If you learn only one data structure for interviews, make it the hash map (a Python dict) and its sibling the hash set (set). They answer "have I seen this before?" and "how many times?" in O(1) on average, which turns many slow O(n²) solutions into fast O(n) ones.

The cloakroom analogy

At a wedding hall cloakroom, you hand over your bag and get token number 47. Later, the attendant doesn't search every shelf: they go straight to shelf 47. That's hashing:

  1. A hash function turns a key (like "apple") into a number.
  2. That number picks a bucket (a shelf) in an internal array.
  3. Looking up the key repeats the same calculation and jumps straight to the right bucket.

No searching, so lookup, insert and delete are all O(1) on average.

"apple"  --hash-->  3  --> bucket 3: ("apple", 120)
"banana" --hash-->  7  --> bucket 7: ("banana", 40)

Sometimes two keys land in the same bucket (a collision). Good implementations handle this so well that, on average, operations stay O(1). In the rare worst case they degrade to O(n), which is why we say "average".

Set vs map

Keys must be immutable (numbers, strings, tuples). Lists can't be keys.

Pattern 1: "Have I seen this before?"

Contains duplicate

def contains_duplicate(nums):
    seen = set()
    for x in nums:
        if x in seen:        # O(1) check
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False

print(contains_duplicate([4, 1, 7, 1]))  # True
print(contains_duplicate([4, 1, 7]))     # False

Brute force compares every pair: O(n²). With a set: O(n) time, O(n) space. This trade (more memory for much more speed) is the heart of hashing.

Pattern 2: Store what you need, look up what you're missing

Two Sum (the most famous interview problem)

Given a list and a target, return the indexes of two numbers that add up to the target.

Brute force tries every pair: O(n²). The hashing insight: for each number x, the partner we need is target - x. Remember every number we have seen (with its index) and look up the missing partner.

def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                      # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        need = target - x
        if need in seen:
            return [seen[need], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []

print(two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9))   # [0, 1]
print(two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6))        # [1, 2]
print(two_sum([1, 2], 7))           # []

Why check before storing? So a number can't pair with itself: in [3, 2, 4] with target 6, the first 3 must not match itself.

Pattern 3: Counting

Valid anagram

Two words are anagrams if they use the same letters the same number of times.

from collections import Counter

def is_anagram(a, b):
    return Counter(a) == Counter(b)

print(is_anagram("listen", "silent"))  # True
print(is_anagram("chai", "chat"))      # False

Counter is a dictionary that counts things. By hand it looks like this:

def count_letters(word):
    counts = {}
    for ch in word:
        counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1
    return counts

print(count_letters("letter"))  # {'l': 1, 'e': 2, 't': 2, 'r': 1}

First unique character

from collections import Counter

def first_unique(s):
    counts = Counter(s)
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if counts[ch] == 1:
            return i
    return -1

print(first_unique("leetcode"))      # 0
print(first_unique("loveleetcode"))  # 2
print(first_unique("aabb"))          # -1

Two passes, both O(n): count first, then find.

Top k frequent elements

from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    return [x for x, _ in Counter(nums).most_common(k)]

print(top_k_frequent([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2))  # [1, 2]

Pattern 4: Grouping by a key

Group anagrams

All anagrams share the same sorted letters. Use that as the dictionary key:

from collections import defaultdict

def group_anagrams(words):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words:
        groups["".join(sorted(w))].append(w)
    return list(groups.values())

print(group_anagrams(["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]))
# [['eat', 'tea', 'ate'], ['tan', 'nat'], ['bat']]

Choosing the right key is the creative part of grouping problems.

Pattern 5: Longest consecutive sequence

Find the length of the longest run of consecutive numbers (in any order) in O(n): [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2] → 4 (1, 2, 3, 4).

def longest_consecutive(nums):
    s = set(nums)
    best = 0
    for x in s:
        if x - 1 not in s:          # x starts a run
            length = 1
            while x + length in s:
                length += 1
            best = max(best, length)
    return best

print(longest_consecutive([100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]))  # 4

The trick "only start counting at the beginning of a run" means each number is visited a constant number of times: O(n).

When to reach for a hash map

  • "Have I seen…?", "Is there a pair…?", "How many times…?"
  • You need to find something by value, not by position.
  • A brute-force solution has an inner loop that searches for something.

Whenever you write a nested loop where the inner loop searches for something, ask: "Could a set or dictionary find it in O(1) instead?"

Interview corner

Two Sum is famously one of the most reported interview questions anywhere; Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Apple and Adobe all use hashing problems like Group Anagrams, Top K Frequent and Longest Consecutive Sequence. Interviewers want to hear you say the trade-off: "This uses O(n) extra space to get O(n) time."

Common mistakes

  • Pairing a number with itself in Two Sum (store after checking).
  • Using a list for membership (x in list is O(n)).
  • Using mutable keys like lists: convert to a tuple or string.
  • Forgetting the O(n) space cost when stating complexity.

Exercise

  1. Write intersection(a, b) returning the unique numbers in both lists.
  2. Write is_isomorphic(s, t): can letters in s be replaced to get t, consistently? ("egg", "add" → True; "foo", "bar" → False.)
  3. Write subarray_count(nums, k) that counts pairs i < j with nums[i] + nums[j] == k in O(n). Hint: count how many times you've seen each value.

Summary

  • Hash maps and sets give O(1) average lookup, insert and delete.
  • Patterns: seen-before, store-and-look-up (Two Sum), counting, grouping by a key.
  • They trade O(n) memory for big speed gains.
  • Reach for them whenever an inner loop is searching.

Next, you'll learn two pointers, the pattern for sorted arrays and pairs that needs no extra memory at all.
items.subject: dsa

items.title: Two Pointers
items.excerpt: Solve sorted-array and pair problems in one pass with O(1) memory. Opposite-end pointers, slow and fast writer pointers, palindromes, removing duplicates and Container With Most Water.
items.content:
The two pointers pattern uses two indexes that move through an array in a coordinated way. It turns many O(n²) "check every pair" solutions into O(n), without any extra memory.

The dance partners analogy

Picture students lined up by height, shortest on the left. A teacher wants a pair whose heights add up to exactly 300 cm. Instead of trying every pair, she stands one student at each end:

  • Too short together? The left student steps aside and the next taller one comes in.
  • Too tall together? The right student steps aside for a shorter one.

Each step rules out one student forever. In at most n steps she either finds the pair or knows none exists.

Style 1: Opposite ends (converging)

Start one pointer at each end and move them towards each other. Works when the array is sorted, or when you compare the two ends (palindromes).

Pair with a target sum (sorted input)

def pair_sum(arr, target):
    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while left < right:
        total = arr[left] + arr[right]
        if total == target:
            return [left, right]
        elif total < target:
            left += 1        # need a bigger sum
        else:
            right -= 1       # need a smaller sum
    return []

print(pair_sum([1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 15], 14))  # [1, 5]
print(pair_sum([1, 2, 3], 10))                # []

Why is it safe to move a pointer? If arr[left] + arr[right] is too small, then arr[left] plus anything to the left of right is even smaller, so arr[left] can never be part of the answer. We can drop it.

O(n) time, O(1) space. (For an unsorted array, the hash map version from the previous lesson is better.)

Valid palindrome (ignoring spaces and punctuation)

def is_palindrome(s):
    left, right = 0, len(s) - 1
    while left < right:
        if not s[left].isalnum():
            left += 1
        elif not s[right].isalnum():
            right -= 1
        elif s[left].lower() != s[right].lower():
            return False
        else:
            left += 1
            right -= 1
    return True

print(is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"))  # True
print(is_palindrome("race a car"))                      # False

Container with most water

Each number is the height of a vertical line. Pick two lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water.

def max_area(height):
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    best = 0
    while left < right:
        width = right - left
        best = max(best, width * min(height[left], height[right]))
        if height[left] < height[right]:
            left += 1        # the shorter line limits us: move it
        else:
            right -= 1
    return best

print(max_area([1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]))  # 49

The insight: the water level is set by the shorter line. Moving the taller line can only make the width smaller without raising the level, so we always move the shorter one.

Style 2: Same direction (reader and writer)

One pointer reads every item; the other writes the items we keep. Perfect for "remove in place" problems.

Remove duplicates from a sorted array

def remove_duplicates(nums):
    if not nums:
        return 0
    write = 1
    for read in range(1, len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != nums[read - 1]:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return write            # length of the unique part

nums = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]
k = remove_duplicates(nums)
print(k, nums[:k])  # 4 [1, 2, 3, 4]

Move zeroes to the end

def move_zeroes(nums):
    write = 0
    for read in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != 0:
            nums[write], nums[read] = nums[read], nums[write]
            write += 1
    return nums

print(move_zeroes([0, 1, 0, 3, 12]))  # [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]

The writer always points at the next position for a non-zero number; swapping pushes zeros backwards while keeping the order of everything else.

Style 3: Two arrays at once

Merge two sorted lists

def merge_sorted(a, b):
    i = j = 0
    out = []
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        if a[i] <= b[j]:
            out.append(a[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            out.append(b[j])
            j += 1
    return out + a[i:] + b[j:]

print(merge_sorted([1, 4, 7], [2, 3, 8, 9]))  # [1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9]

This merge step is the core of merge sort (lesson 11).

Interview level: 3Sum

Find all unique triplets that sum to zero. Sort, fix one number, then run the pair-sum two pointers on the rest:

def three_sum(nums):
    nums.sort()
    res = []
    for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
            continue                      # skip duplicate first numbers
        left, right = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while left < right:
            s = nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right]
            if s < 0:
                left += 1
            elif s > 0:
                right -= 1
            else:
                res.append([nums[i], nums[left], nums[right]])
                left += 1
                while left < right and nums[left] == nums[left - 1]:
                    left += 1             # skip duplicate second numbers
    return res

print(three_sum([-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]))  # [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]

O(n²) instead of the brute-force O(n³).

How to recognise the pattern

  • The input is sorted (or you can sort it).
  • You're looking for a pair (or triplet) meeting a condition.
  • You must work in place with O(1) extra space.
  • You compare elements from both ends (palindromes, mirror problems).

If a problem says "sorted array" and "pair", your first thought should be two pointers.

Interview corner

Two Sum II (sorted input), Valid Palindrome, Container With Most Water, 3Sum, Remove Duplicates and Move Zeroes are commonly reported at Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Google, Bloomberg and Adobe. Interviewers often ask *why* moving a pointer can't skip the answer, so practise explaining it.

Common mistakes

  • **Using <= instead of <** in while left < right, letting a pointer pair with itself.
  • Forgetting to move a pointer in some branch, causing an infinite loop.
  • Not skipping duplicates in 3Sum, producing repeated triplets.
  • Using converging pointers on unsorted data where the logic doesn't hold.

Exercise

  1. Try the visualizer with [2, 4, 5, 9, 12] and target 16, then 100.
  2. Write squares_sorted(nums) for a sorted array with negatives: return the squares in sorted order in O(n). ([-4, -1, 0, 3, 10] → [0, 1, 9, 16, 100].) Hint: the biggest square is at one of the two ends.
  3. Write is_subsequence(s, t): are the letters of s found in t in order? ("abc" in "ahbgdc" → True.)

Summary

  • Two pointers move through data in a coordinated way, usually in one pass: O(n) time, O(1) space.
  • Converging pointers: sorted pairs, palindromes, container problems.
  • Reader/writer pointers: in-place removal and partitioning.
  • Explain *why* each move is safe: that's what interviewers listen for.

Next, you'll learn the sliding window, a two-pointer cousin for contiguous subarrays and substrings.

items.title: Sliding Window
items.excerpt: Solve "best contiguous subarray or substring" problems in O(n). Fixed-size windows, growing and shrinking windows, and the template behind longest substring, minimum window and more.
items.content:
Many problems ask about a contiguous part of an array or string: "the best 3 days in a row", "the longest substring without repeats", "the shortest subarray with sum ≥ 7". Checking every possible part is O(n²) or worse. The sliding window pattern does it in O(n).

The train window analogy

You are on a train looking through a window that shows exactly 3 houses at a time. When the train moves forward, one new house appears on the right and one house disappears on the left. You don't re-look at the middle houses; you only notice what changed.

That's the whole idea: when the window slides, update your answer using only the item that entered and the item that left.

Type 1: Fixed-size window

Maximum sum of k consecutive numbers

Brute force recalculates each window from scratch: O(n·k). Sliding window adds the new item and subtracts the old one: O(n).

def max_sum_k(arr, k):
    window = sum(arr[:k])
    best = window
    for right in range(k, len(arr)):
        window += arr[right] - arr[right - k]   # one in, one out
        best = max(best, window)
    return best

print(max_sum_k([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2, 7, 1], 3))  # 12

Average of every window of size k

def window_averages(arr, k):
    out, window = [], 0
    for i, x in enumerate(arr):
        window += x
        if i >= k:
            window -= arr[i - k]
        if i >= k - 1:
            out.append(window / k)
    return out

print(window_averages([1, 3, 2, 6, 4], 2))  # [2.0, 2.5, 4.0, 5.0]

Type 2: Variable-size window (grow and shrink)

Here the window size changes. The template:

  1. Move right forward one step at a time, adding the new item to the window.
  2. While the window breaks a rule, move left forward, removing items, until the rule holds again.
  3. Update the answer.

Each item enters once and leaves at most once, so the total work is O(n) even with the inner while.

Longest substring without repeating characters

def longest_unique(s):
    seen = set()
    left = best = 0
    for right in range(len(s)):
        while s[right] in seen:        # rule broken: a repeat
            seen.remove(s[left])
            left += 1
        seen.add(s[right])
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

print(longest_unique("abcabcbb"))  # 3
print(longest_unique("bbbbb"))     # 1
print(longest_unique("pwwkew"))    # 3
print(longest_unique(""))          # 0

Shortest subarray with sum at least target

Positive numbers only. Find the length of the shortest contiguous subarray with sum ≥ target.

def min_subarray_len(target, nums):
    left = total = 0
    best = float("inf")
    for right, x in enumerate(nums):
        total += x
        while total >= target:         # valid: try to shrink
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            total -= nums[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best

print(min_subarray_len(7, [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3]))  # 2
print(min_subarray_len(100, [1, 2, 3]))         # 0

Notice the difference: for "longest" problems we shrink while the window is invalid; for "shortest" problems we shrink while the window is valid, recording the answer as we go.

Longest substring with at most k distinct characters

from collections import defaultdict

def longest_k_distinct(s, k):
    counts = defaultdict(int)
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        counts[ch] += 1
        while len(counts) > k:
            counts[s[left]] -= 1
            if counts[s[left]] == 0:
                del counts[s[left]]
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

print(longest_k_distinct("eceba", 2))   # 3
print(longest_k_distinct("aabbcc", 1))  # 2

A dictionary of counts is the window's "memory" in most string window problems.

Interview level: permutation in a string

Does s2 contain any rearrangement of s1 as a substring? Use a fixed window of size len(s1) and compare letter counts.

from collections import Counter

def check_inclusion(s1, s2):
    k = len(s1)
    need = Counter(s1)
    window = Counter(s2[:k])
    if window == need:
        return True
    for right in range(k, len(s2)):
        window[s2[right]] += 1
        window[s2[right - k]] -= 1
        if window[s2[right - k]] == 0:
            del window[s2[right - k]]
        if window == need:
            return True
    return False

print(check_inclusion("ab", "eidbaooo"))  # True
print(check_inclusion("ab", "eidboaoo"))  # False

Comparing two counters costs at most 26 steps for lowercase letters, so the total is still O(n).

How to recognise the pattern

  • The words contiguous, subarray, substring, consecutive or window.
  • "Longest", "shortest", "maximum sum", "at most k", "contains all of…".
  • Brute force would check every start and end position.

Sliding window needs a rule you can maintain incrementally. If adding and removing one item can update your "window memory" (a sum, a count, a set), the pattern fits.

When it does NOT work

With negative numbers, "shrink while the sum is too big" breaks, because removing an item could make the sum bigger. Then use prefix sums with a hash map (next lesson).

Interview corner

Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, Minimum Size Subarray Sum, Permutation in String, Maximum Average Subarray and Minimum Window Substring are frequently reported at Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Uber and Flipkart. Interviewers expect you to explain why the solution is O(n) despite the nested while.

Common mistakes

  • Recomputing the whole window each step (that's brute force in disguise).
  • Off-by-one in window length: it's right - left + 1.
  • Forgetting to remove zero counts from the dictionary, so len(counts) is wrong.
  • Using a shrinking window with negative numbers.

Exercise

  1. In the visualizer, try k = 1 and k = 8. What happens?
  2. Write max_vowels(s, k): the maximum number of vowels in any substring of length k.
  3. Write longest_ones(nums, k): the longest run of 1s if you may flip at most k zeros. ([1,1,0,0,1,1,1,0,1], k = 1 → 5.)

Summary

  • Sliding window solves contiguous subarray/substring problems in O(n).
  • Fixed windows add the new item and remove the old one.
  • Variable windows grow with right and shrink with left while a rule is broken (longest) or kept (shortest).
  • A sum, set or count dictionary is the window's memory.

Next, you'll learn prefix sums, which answer any range-sum question in O(1).
items.subject: dsa

items.title: Prefix Sums
items.excerpt: Precompute running totals once and answer any range sum in O(1). Then combine prefix sums with a hash map to count subarrays that sum to k, even with negative numbers.
items.content:
"What is the total of items 3 to 7?" Answering that once is easy: add them up. Answering it a million times for different ranges is slow if each answer needs a loop. Prefix sums do the work once up front, then every range question costs a single subtraction.

The cricket scoreboard analogy

A scoreboard shows the total runs after each over: 6, 14, 20, 31, 45… To know how many runs were scored in overs 3 to 5, you don't replay the overs. You take the total after over 5 and subtract the total after over 2. Done.

That running total is a prefix sum.

Building prefix sums

prefix[i] = sum of the first i items. We add a 0 at the start so the formula works for ranges starting at index 0.

def build_prefix(arr):
    prefix = [0]
    for x in arr:
        prefix.append(prefix[-1] + x)
    return prefix

def range_sum(prefix, l, r):          # sum of arr[l..r], inclusive
    return prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]

arr = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
p = build_prefix(arr)
print(p)                   # [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25, 31]
print(range_sum(p, 2, 5))  # 19
print(range_sum(p, 0, 0))  # 3

Building: O(n) once. Each query: O(1). For q queries that's O(n + q) instead of O(n·q).

Python's itertools.accumulate(arr) builds the running totals too (without the leading 0).

Problem: find the pivot index

The pivot is where the sum on the left equals the sum on the right.

def pivot_index(nums):
    total = sum(nums)
    left = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if left == total - left - x:
            return i
        left += x
    return -1

print(pivot_index([1, 7, 3, 6, 5, 6]))  # 3
print(pivot_index([1, 2, 3]))           # -1

We only need the running left sum; the right sum is total - left - x.

Problem: product of array except self

Return an array where each item is the product of all the other items, without division. Use a prefix product from the left and a suffix product from the right:

def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return out

print(product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4]))  # [24, 12, 8, 6]

O(n) time, O(1) extra space besides the output. A favourite at Amazon, Meta and Microsoft.

Prefix sums + hash map: count subarrays with sum k

This is where prefix sums become a superpower. Count how many contiguous subarrays add up to k. Numbers may be negative, so a sliding window won't work.

The key idea: a subarray from i+1 to j sums to k when

prefix[j] - prefix[i] = k   →   prefix[i] = prefix[j] - k

So as we walk through, we ask: **"How many earlier prefix sums equal current - k?"** A hash map counts how often each prefix sum has appeared.

def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count = 0
    current = 0
    seen = {0: 1}              # the empty prefix
    for x in nums:
        current += x
        count += seen.get(current - k, 0)
        seen[current] = seen.get(current, 0) + 1
    return count

print(subarray_sum([1, 1, 1], 2))         # 2
print(subarray_sum([1, 2, 3], 3))         # 2
print(subarray_sum([3, -1, 2, -2, 4], 2)) # 4

seen = {0: 1} handles subarrays that start at index 0. This one pattern solves a whole family: subarrays divisible by k, equal numbers of 0s and 1s, and more.

Longest subarray with equal 0s and 1s

Treat 0 as −1. Then "equal 0s and 1s" means "sum is 0". Remember the first index where each prefix sum appeared:

def find_max_length(nums):
    first = {0: -1}
    current = best = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        current += 1 if x == 1 else -1
        if current in first:
            best = max(best, i - first[current])
        else:
            first[current] = i
    return best

print(find_max_length([0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0]))  # 6

2D prefix sums (a peek)

For grids, P[r][c] stores the sum of the rectangle from (0,0) to (r−1,c−1). Any rectangle sum is then four lookups. It's the same idea in two dimensions and powers "range sum query 2D" problems.

How to recognise the pattern

  • Many questions about sums of ranges.
  • "Count subarrays with sum / property X", especially with negative numbers.
  • "Left part vs right part" comparisons (pivot, product except self).

When you see "subarray sum equals k", think: prefix sum + hash map counting current - k.

Interview corner

Subarray Sum Equals K, Product of Array Except Self, Find Pivot Index, Range Sum Query and Contiguous Array are commonly reported at Meta, Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Goldman Sachs. The hash map version is a classic "do you really understand it?" question: be ready to explain why seen starts with {0: 1}.

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one in the formula: it's prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l] with the leading 0.
  • **Forgetting {0: 1}** and missing subarrays that start at index 0.
  • **Updating seen before counting**, which can count an empty subarray when k = 0.
  • Trying sliding window with negative numbers.

Exercise

  1. In the visualizer, query the whole array (l = 0, r = 7). What is prefix[8] - prefix[0]?
  2. Write running_sum(nums) that returns the running totals ([1, 2, 3] → [1, 3, 6]).
  3. Write count_divisible(nums, k): count subarrays whose sum is divisible by k. Hint: use current % k as the hash map key.

Summary

  • prefix[i] stores the sum of the first i items; any range sum is one subtraction.
  • Prefix and suffix products solve "everything except me" problems.
  • Prefix sums + a hash map count subarrays with sum k in O(n), even with negatives.
  • Remember the leading 0 and the {0: 1} starting entry.

Next, you'll learn Kadane's algorithm for the maximum subarray: a beautiful one-pass idea.

items.title: Kadane's Algorithm: Maximum Subarray
items.excerpt: Find the contiguous subarray with the biggest sum in one pass. The "extend or restart" idea behind Kadane's algorithm, the stock-trading variant, and maximum product.
items.content:
Problem: given numbers (some negative), find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum. For [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4] the answer is [4, -1, 2, 1] with sum 6.

Checking every subarray is O(n²) (or O(n³) if you re-add each one). Kadane's algorithm does it in one pass, O(n), with O(1) memory. It is short, elegant, and one of the most frequently asked interview questions.

The road trip analogy

You're on a road trip collecting money from friends along the way (positive numbers) and paying tolls (negative numbers). At each town you ask yourself one question:

> "Is the trip so far helping me, or dragging me down?"

If your running total has gone negative, carrying it forward can only hurt. You'd be better off starting a fresh trip from this town. Meanwhile, you remember the best total you have ever had.

That's Kadane: at each number, either extend the current run or restart from here.

The code

def max_subarray(nums):
    cur = best = nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)     # extend, or restart at x
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

print(max_subarray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]))  # 6
print(max_subarray([5, 4, -1, 7, 8]))                 # 23
print(max_subarray([-3, -1, -2]))                     # -1
  • cur = the best sum of a subarray that ends exactly here.
  • best = the best sum seen anywhere so far.

Starting with nums[0] (not 0) makes the all-negative case correct: the answer is the largest single number, −1.

Why does it work?

Any subarray ending at position i either:

  1. is just [nums[i]] on its own, or
  2. is a subarray ending at i−1, plus nums[i].

The best of option 2 is cur + nums[i] (because cur is already the best ending at i−1). So the best ending at i is max(nums[i], cur + nums[i]). That's dynamic programming in disguise (lesson 26): each answer builds on the previous one.

Also return the subarray itself

def max_subarray_with_range(nums):
    cur = best = nums[0]
    start = best_start = best_end = 0
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):
        if nums[i] > cur + nums[i]:
            cur = nums[i]
            start = i                 # restart here
        else:
            cur += nums[i]
        if cur > best:
            best, best_start, best_end = cur, start, i
    return best, nums[best_start:best_end + 1]

print(max_subarray_with_range([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]))  # (6, [4, -1, 2, 1])

Variant: best time to buy and sell a stock

Given daily prices, buy once and sell later for the maximum profit. Same spirit: walk once, remembering the cheapest price so far.

def max_profit(prices):
    cheapest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        cheapest = min(cheapest, p)
        best = max(best, p - cheapest)
    return best

print(max_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]))  # 5
print(max_profit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1]))     # 0

Buy at 1, sell at 6: profit 5. If prices only fall, don't trade: 0.

Variant: maximum product subarray

With products, a negative × negative becomes positive, so the smallest (most negative) product can suddenly become the largest. Track both:

def max_product(nums):
    hi = lo = best = nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        candidates = (x, hi * x, lo * x)
        hi, lo = max(candidates), min(candidates)
        best = max(best, hi)
    return best

print(max_product([2, 3, -2, 4]))     # 6
print(max_product([-2, 3, -4]))       # 24
print(max_product([-2, 0, -1]))       # 0

Variant: maximum circular subarray

If the array wraps around, the best subarray is either a normal one (Kadane), or it wraps, which means it's the total minus the minimum subarray:

def max_circular(nums):
    def kadane(arr):
        cur = best = arr[0]
        for x in arr[1:]:
            cur = max(x, cur + x)
            best = max(best, cur)
        return best

    best_normal = kadane(nums)
    if best_normal < 0:
        return best_normal                     # all negative
    min_sub = -kadane([-x for x in nums])      # minimum subarray
    return max(best_normal, sum(nums) - min_sub)

print(max_circular([5, -3, 5]))     # 10
print(max_circular([-3, -2, -3]))   # -2

How to recognise the pattern

  • "Maximum (or minimum) sum of a contiguous subarray."
  • "Best profit from one buy and one sell."
  • Any running decision of the form "keep going or start over".

Kadane is a sliding window that never needs a left pointer: the "restart" decision replaces the shrinking.

Interview corner

Maximum Subarray and Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock are among the most reported interview problems at Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Apple, LinkedIn and Bloomberg; Maximum Product Subarray is a common follow-up. Expect to be asked: "What if all numbers are negative?" and "Can you return the subarray, not just the sum?"

Common mistakes

  • **Starting best at 0**, which returns 0 for an all-negative array.
  • **Resetting cur to 0** instead of to the current number.
  • Forgetting the negative × negative case in the product variant.
  • Selling before buying in the stock problem (update cheapest first, then profit is ≥ 0).

Exercise

  1. Play the visualizer with [1, -2, 3, 10, -4, 7, 2, -5]. What is the best subarray?
  2. Write min_subarray(nums) that returns the smallest contiguous sum.
  3. Write max_profit_many(prices) where you may buy and sell many times (but hold one share at a time). Hint: add up every upward step.

Summary

  • Kadane: at each number, extend the current run or restart; remember the best.
  • O(n) time, O(1) space; start from nums[0] to handle all-negative input.
  • Stock profit: remember the cheapest price so far.
  • Products need both the max and the min because of negatives.

Next, you'll master binary search, the O(log n) workhorse of sorted data.

items.title: Binary Search
items.excerpt: Halve the search space every step for O(log n). The bug-free template, first and last positions, search insert position, rotated arrays, and "binary search on the answer".
items.content:
Binary search finds an item in sorted data by checking the middle and throwing away the half that can't contain the answer. For a million items it needs about 20 checks instead of a million. It's simple to describe and famously easy to get subtly wrong, so this lesson gives you a template you can trust.

The guessing game analogy

"I'm thinking of a number from 1 to 100." The smart first guess is 50. "Higher!" Now only 51–100 is possible, so guess 75, and so on. Each guess halves the range: 100 → 50 → 25 → 13 → 7 → 4 → 2 → 1. Never more than 7 guesses. (Play Binary Hunt in Brain Games to feel it.)

The classic template

def binary_search(arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if arr[mid] == target:
            return mid
        elif arr[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1          # answer is to the right
        else:
            hi = mid - 1          # answer is to the left
    return -1

print(binary_search([2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38], 23))  # 5
print(binary_search([2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38], 7))   # -1

Three details that prevent most bugs:

  1. while lo <= hi (with <=): a range of one item is still worth checking.
  2. lo = mid + 1 and hi = mid - 1: mid has already been checked, so exclude it. Otherwise the loop can run forever.
  3. The range [lo, hi] always contains the answer if it exists. Ask yourself after every line: "Is that still true?"

O(log n) time, O(1) space. (In languages with fixed-size integers, mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2 avoids overflow; Python doesn't need it, but interviewers like seeing you know.)

The "boundary" template: first position where a condition becomes true

Many problems aren't "find x" but "find the first index where something becomes true". Example: the first index with a value ≥ target. The condition looks like False False False True True across the array, and we want the first True.

def lower_bound(arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr)          # note: hi = len(arr)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if arr[mid] >= target:
            hi = mid              # mid might be the answer: keep it
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo                     # first index with arr[i] >= target

print(lower_bound([1, 3, 5, 5, 5, 8], 5))  # 2
print(lower_bound([1, 3, 5, 5, 5, 8], 6))  # 5
print(lower_bound([1, 3, 5, 5, 5, 8], 9))  # 6

Here the loop is while lo < hi, and hi = mid (not mid - 1) because mid could be the answer. When the loop ends, lo == hi is the boundary.

Python's bisect module does exactly this:

from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

arr = [1, 3, 5, 5, 5, 8]
print(bisect_left(arr, 5))   # 2
print(bisect_right(arr, 5))  # 5

bisect_left gives the index of the first 5; bisect_right gives the index just after the last 5.

First and last position of a value

from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

def search_range(nums, target):
    first = bisect_left(nums, target)
    if first == len(nums) or nums[first] != target:
        return [-1, -1]
    return [first, bisect_right(nums, target) - 1]

print(search_range([5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], 8))  # [3, 4]
print(search_range([5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], 6))  # [-1, -1]

Search insert position

Where would the target go to keep the list sorted? That is lower_bound:

from bisect import bisect_left

print(bisect_left([1, 3, 5, 6], 5))  # 2
print(bisect_left([1, 3, 5, 6], 2))  # 1
print(bisect_left([1, 3, 5, 6], 7))  # 4

Search in a rotated sorted array

[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] was sorted, then rotated. At any mid, one half is still sorted. Check whether the target lies in that sorted half; if not, it's in the other.

def search_rotated(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[lo] <= nums[mid]:                 # left half is sorted
            if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]:
                hi = mid - 1
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        else:                                     # right half is sorted
            if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]:
                lo = mid + 1
            else:
                hi = mid - 1
    return -1

print(search_rotated([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], 0))  # 4
print(search_rotated([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], 3))  # -1

Binary search on the answer

Sometimes there's no array to search, but the answer itself has a range, and you can test "does this answer work?". If the test goes False False True True as the answer grows, binary search the answer.

Integer square root

def int_sqrt(x):
    lo, hi = 0, x
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2      # round up so the loop always shrinks
        if mid * mid <= x:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return lo

print(int_sqrt(8))   # 2
print(int_sqrt(16))  # 4

Koko eating bananas

Koko eats piles of bananas at speed k per hour (one pile per hour at most). What's the slowest speed that finishes within h hours? Faster always works if slower works, so binary search k:

def min_eating_speed(piles, h):
    def hours(k):
        return sum((p + k - 1) // k for p in piles)   # ceil(p / k)

    lo, hi = 1, max(piles)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if hours(mid) <= h:
            hi = mid          # fast enough: try slower
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

print(min_eating_speed([3, 6, 7, 11], 8))  # 4

This "minimise the maximum" / "find the smallest value that works" trick appears in many hard-sounding problems (shipping packages in D days, splitting arrays…).

How to recognise the pattern

  • The data is sorted (or partly sorted, like rotated).
  • The problem asks for O(log n).
  • "Find the minimum / maximum value such that a condition holds," where the condition flips only once.

Write the condition as a function that returns True/False, check it flips only once (False…False True…True), then binary search for the first True.

Interview corner

Binary Search, Search in Rotated Sorted Array, Find First and Last Position, Find Minimum in Rotated Array and Koko Eating Bananas are commonly reported at Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, LinkedIn and Uber. Interviewers watch closely for off-by-one errors: walk through a 2-element example out loud before saying you're done.

Common mistakes

  • Infinite loops from lo = mid with mid = (lo + hi) // 2 (round up in that case).
  • Mixing templates: while lo <= hi goes with hi = mid - 1; while lo < hi goes with hi = mid.
  • Using binary search on unsorted data.
  • Not checking that the found index is really the target (as in search_range).

Exercise

  1. In the visualizer, search for 91 and then for 2. Count the steps.
  2. Write find_min_rotated(nums) returning the smallest value in a rotated sorted array in O(log n).
  3. Write ship_within_days(weights, days): the minimum ship capacity to ship all packages in order within the given days.

Summary

  • Binary search halves the search space each step: O(log n).
  • Template 1 (lo <= hi) finds an exact value; template 2 (lo < hi) finds a boundary.
  • bisect_left / bisect_right give first and after-last positions.
  • "Binary search on the answer" solves optimisation problems with a once-flipping condition.

Next, you'll learn how sorting works, and why O(n log n) is the magic number.

items.title: Sorting Basics
items.excerpt: Bubble, selection and insertion sort animated step by step, what stable sorting means, Python's built-in sort with custom keys, and when sorting first makes a problem easy.
items.content:
Sorting puts data in order, and a surprising number of problems become easy once the data is sorted: duplicates sit next to each other, binary search works, and two pointers become possible. In this lesson you'll see the simple sorting algorithms move, then learn to use Python's fast built-in sort like a pro.

The playing cards analogy

When you pick up cards one at a time and slide each new card into the right place in your hand, you're doing insertion sort. When you repeatedly compare neighbours and swap them until nothing moves, you're doing bubble sort. Everyone already knows these algorithms; we're just giving them names.

Bubble sort

Compare each pair of neighbours and swap if they're in the wrong order. After one full pass, the largest value has "bubbled" to the end.

def bubble_sort(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
        swapped = False
        for i in range(end):
            if arr[i] > arr[i + 1]:
                arr[i], arr[i + 1] = arr[i + 1], arr[i]
                swapped = True
        if not swapped:          # already sorted: stop early
            break
    return arr

print(bubble_sort([5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 3]))  # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8]

O(n²) in the worst case; O(n) if the data is already sorted (thanks to the swapped check).

Selection sort

Find the smallest remaining item and put it next in line.

def selection_sort(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n):
        smallest = i
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if arr[j] < arr[smallest]:
                smallest = j
        arr[i], arr[smallest] = arr[smallest], arr[i]
    return arr

print(selection_sort([29, 10, 14, 37, 13]))  # [10, 13, 14, 29, 37]

Always O(n²), but it makes at most n swaps, which matters when writing data is expensive.

Insertion sort

Keep the left part sorted; take the next item and shift bigger items right until it fits.

def insertion_sort(arr):
    for i in range(1, len(arr)):
        key = arr[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and arr[j] > key:
            arr[j + 1] = arr[j]
            j -= 1
        arr[j + 1] = key
    return arr

print(insertion_sort([7, 3, 9, 1, 5, 2]))  # [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9]

O(n²) worst case, but very fast on nearly sorted data (close to O(n)). That's why real-world sorts like Python's Timsort use insertion sort on small chunks.

Comparing the simple sorts

What does "stable" mean?

A stable sort keeps items with equal keys in their original order. If you sort students by marks and two students both have 90, a stable sort keeps them in the order they were before (for example, alphabetical). This lets you sort by several keys in steps.

Python's built-in sorting (use this in real code)

nums = [5, 2, 9, 1]
print(sorted(nums))                 # [1, 2, 5, 9]
nums.sort(reverse=True)             # in place
print(nums)                         # [9, 5, 2, 1]

Sorting with a key

words = ["banana", "kiwi", "apple", "fig"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))                    # ['fig', 'kiwi', 'apple', 'banana']
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: (len(w), w)))  # ['fig', 'kiwi', 'apple', 'banana']

students = [("Asha", 92), ("Rohan", 85), ("Meera", 92)]
print(sorted(students, key=lambda s: (-s[1], s[0])))  # [('Asha', 92), ('Meera', 92), ('Rohan', 85)]

A tuple key sorts by the first part, then breaks ties with the next. A minus sign sorts numbers descending.

Sorting first makes problems easy

Are any two meetings overlapping?

def can_attend_all(meetings):
    meetings.sort()                          # by start time
    for i in range(1, len(meetings)):
        if meetings[i][0] < meetings[i - 1][1]:
            return False
    return True

print(can_attend_all([[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]]))  # False
print(can_attend_all([[7, 10], [2, 4]]))             # True

After sorting, only neighbours can overlap. O(n log n).

Largest number from digits

from functools import cmp_to_key

def largest_number(nums):
    strs = [str(n) for n in nums]
    strs.sort(key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: -1 if a + b > b + a else 1))
    result = "".join(strs)
    return "0" if result[0] == "0" else result

print(largest_number([3, 30, 34, 5, 9]))  # 9534330

A custom comparison: put a before b if a + b makes a bigger number than b + a.

Counting sort: faster than n log n (sometimes)

When values are small integers in a known range, count them instead of comparing:

def counting_sort(arr, max_value):
    counts = [0] * (max_value + 1)
    for x in arr:
        counts[x] += 1
    out = []
    for value, c in enumerate(counts):
        out.extend([value] * c)
    return out

print(counting_sort([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 2], 5))  # [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

O(n + k) for values 0..k. Great for ages, marks out of 100, or letters.

Interview corner

You'll rarely be asked to code bubble sort, but Sort Colors (Dutch national flag), Meeting Rooms, Largest Number, Merge Intervals and "sort then two pointers" problems are common at Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Bloomberg and Goldman Sachs. Know that comparison sorting can't beat O(n log n) in general, and when counting sort can.

Stuck on a problem? Ask: "Would this be easy if the data were sorted?" Sorting costs O(n log n), which is often acceptable.

Common mistakes

  • **Using nums = nums.sort()**: .sort() returns None.
  • Forgetting that sorting changes the original positions: copy indexes first if you need them.
  • Sorting inside a loop, turning O(n log n) into O(n² log n).
  • Assuming an unstable sort keeps tie order.

Exercise

  1. Play Sort Sprint in Brain Games. How does your swap count compare with bubble sort?
  2. Write sort_colors(nums) that sorts a list of 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass. Hint: three pointers.
  3. Sort a list of (name, city, age) tuples by city, then by age descending.

Summary

  • Bubble, selection and insertion sort are simple O(n²) algorithms; insertion sort shines on nearly sorted data.
  • Stable sorts keep the order of equal items.
  • In real code use sorted() / .sort() with key=; tuples sort by several keys.
  • Sorting first often unlocks two pointers, binary search or greedy solutions.

Next, you'll learn the fast sorts that power the real world: merge sort and quick sort.
