items.title: Strong Passwords and Two-Step Verification
items.excerpt: Why "Rahul@123" is cracked in seconds, how long passphrases beat complex passwords, why every account needs a different password, how password managers help, and how to turn on two-step verification for email, WhatsApp and banking apps.
items.content:
Your email account is the master key to your digital life: every "forgot password" link goes there. If someone gets into your email, they can reset almost everything else. A strong, unique password plus two-step verification (2FA) makes your accounts dramatically harder to take over.

🎬 The master key

  1. Asha uses "Asha@1998" for email, Instagram and a shopping site.
  2. The shopping site gets hacked. Her email and password are leaked online.
  3. Criminals try that pair on Gmail, Instagram and banks automatically.
  4. A unique passphrase for each site and 2FA on email stop the attack cold.

Why simple passwords fail

Attackers don't guess one password at a time. They use software that tries billions of combinations and lists of the most common passwords, names, dates and patterns like Name@123.

Length beats complexity. A passphrase of 4–5 random words is stronger than a short password full of symbols.

The rule that matters most: one password, one account

When any website is hacked, its passwords leak. Criminals then try the same email and password on every popular site, which is called credential stuffing. If each account has its own password, one leak stays one leak.

Password managers

Nobody can remember 50 different passphrases. A password manager remembers them for you:

  • It creates a long random password for each site and fills it in automatically.
  • You remember only one strong master passphrase.
  • Many phones and browsers include one (Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain), and there are dedicated apps.

It also protects you from phishing: the manager won't fill your password on a fake lookalike site.

Two-step verification (2FA)

With 2FA, logging in needs your password and something you have, usually your phone. Even if your password leaks, the attacker is stuck.

Turn it on first for: email, WhatsApp (Settings → Account → Two-step verification), banking apps, Instagram/Facebook and your Google or Apple account.

Passkeys: the future without passwords

Many sites now offer passkeys: you log in with your phone's fingerprint or face unlock. There is nothing to type, nothing to leak and nothing to phish. If a site offers passkeys, use them.

Check whether your email has appeared in a known data leak at haveibeenpwned.com. If it has, change that password everywhere you reused it, starting with your email account.

Summary

  • Long passphrases of random words beat short "complex" passwords.
  • Use a different password for every account; a password manager makes this easy.
  • Turn on two-step verification for email, WhatsApp, banking and social media.
  • Prefer passkeys and authenticator apps over SMS when available.
items.subject: cyber-safety

items.title: Spotting Phishing: Fake Emails, SMS and Links
items.excerpt: Phishing tricks you into clicking a fake link or opening a bad file. Learn the 7 red flags, how to read a link before tapping it, lookalike domains, fake delivery and KYC messages, and what to do if you already clicked.
items.content:
Phishing is when someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to make you click a link, open a file or share information. The name comes from "fishing": they throw out bait and wait for a bite. It arrives by email, SMS ("smishing"), WhatsApp, social media and even QR codes.

🎬 The parcel that never was

  1. "Your parcel is on hold. Pay ₹25 redelivery fee: dhl-in-track.co"
  2. The link isn't the courier's real website, and Dev never ordered anything.
  3. Urgent, small payment, strange link, no order number.
  4. Dev deletes it and reports it. The real courier app shows no parcel.

The 7 red flags

  1. Urgency or threat: "within 24 hours", "account suspended", "legal action".
  2. Too good to be true: lottery wins, free iPhones, huge refunds, easy money jobs.
  3. A link you didn't expect, especially shortened links (bit.ly, tinyurl) or odd domains.
  4. Asks for secrets: OTP, PIN, password, card number, Aadhaar or PAN photos.
  5. Generic greeting: "Dear customer" instead of your name.
  6. Small mistakes: spelling errors, odd logos, strange sender addresses like support@sbi-kyc-update.online.
  7. Unusual request from a known person: your "boss" asks for gift cards, a "friend" needs money urgently on a new number.

One red flag is enough to stop and verify.

How to read a link before you tap it

On a computer, hover over the link to see where it really goes. On a phone, press and hold the link to preview it. Then read the domain: the part just before the first single /.

The trick in the second row is common: scammers put a famous name at the start of their own domain. Always read from the right side of the domain.

Common phishing stories in India

  • KYC update: "Your account will be blocked, update PAN/KYC here."
  • Electricity bill: "Power will be cut tonight, call this officer."
  • Courier/customs: "Parcel on hold", "illegal items found in your parcel".
  • Income tax refund: "Claim your refund now" with a fake portal.
  • Job offers: "Earn ₹5,000 a day liking videos" (task scams).
  • Fake shopping sites with huge discounts that take payment and never deliver.

If you already clicked

  1. Don't enter anything on the page. Close it.
  2. If you entered a password, change it immediately from the real app or website, and turn on 2FA.
  3. If you entered card or bank details, call your bank and block the card.
  4. If you lost money, call 1930 (India's cyber crime helpline) right away and report at cybercrime.gov.in.
  5. Report fraud SMS and calls on the government's Sancharsaathi portal (Chakshu).

Make it a habit to open apps and websites yourself instead of using links in messages. If your bank or courier really needs something, you'll see it when you log in normally.

Summary

  • Phishing uses fake messages to make you click, pay or share secrets.
  • Watch for urgency, rewards, odd links, requests for secrets and small mistakes.
  • Read a link's real domain from the right; famous names at the start mean nothing.
  • Already clicked? Change passwords, call your bank, and report on 1930.

items.title: UPI and OTP Scams: Keep Your Money Safe
items.excerpt: The golden rule of UPI (you never need a PIN to receive money), collect-request and QR code scams, fake payment screenshots, screen-sharing app tricks, OTP fraud and the settings that protect your bank account.
items.content:
UPI made payments instant and easy, and scammers love instant and easy too. The good news: almost every UPI scam breaks one simple rule. Learn the rule and a few tricks, and you are safer than most people.

🎬 The buyer who sends money

  1. Meera lists an old sofa online. A "buyer" agrees instantly and wants to pay ₹8,000.
  2. A UPI request pops up. "Just enter your PIN to receive the money."
  3. Meera remembers: entering a PIN always means money LEAVES your account.
  4. She declines and blocks the number. The "buyer" disappears.

The golden rule

> You never need to enter your UPI PIN or scan a QR code to RECEIVE money.

If anyone asks you to enter a PIN, approve a request or scan a code "to receive" a payment, it's a scam. A PIN is only for sending money out.

The common UPI tricks

OTP fraud

An OTP (one-time password) is the final lock on a transaction. That's why scammers want it so badly. They'll pretend to be your bank ("to stop a suspicious transaction"), a delivery agent ("to confirm your parcel"), or a friend ("I sent my OTP to your number by mistake").

No genuine person needs your OTP. Read the full OTP message: it usually says what it's for, like "OTP for payment of ₹19,999 to XYZ". That line alone exposes most scams.

Settings that protect you

  • Set a daily UPI limit in your app that matches your real needs.
  • Turn on transaction alerts by SMS and app notifications, and actually read them.
  • Lock your UPI apps with a phone lock and app lock.
  • Use a separate account with a small balance for daily UPI if you can, and keep savings elsewhere.
  • Never save your UPI PIN in notes or messages.

If money is taken

Time matters. Act in the first hour:

  1. Call 1930 (National Cyber Crime Helpline) and report at cybercrime.gov.in.
  2. Call your bank's official number and ask them to block the account or card and raise a dispute.
  3. Keep screenshots of messages, the scammer's UPI ID and number, and the transaction ID.

Under RBI rules, the faster you report an unauthorised transaction, the less you may have to bear, especially if you report within three working days.

Teach this one line to every family member: "PIN means paying, never receiving." It stops the most common UPI scam in India.

Summary

  • You never need a PIN or QR scan to receive money.
  • Decline unexpected collect requests; verify payments in your own bank app.
  • Never share OTPs or install screen-sharing apps for callers.
  • Set limits and alerts, and report fraud on 1930 within the first hour.
items.subject: cyber-safety

items.title: Fake Calls, Digital Arrest and Social Engineering
items.excerpt: How scammers use fear and authority on the phone: fake police and "digital arrest" video calls, courier and customs scams, fake relatives in trouble, job and task scams, and the simple script to end any suspicious call safely.
items.content:
Social engineering means manipulating people instead of hacking machines. The most powerful tool is the phone: a confident voice, a uniform on a video call, a threat of arrest. The scam works only while you stay on the call and stay scared. Your best defence is to hang up and verify.

🎬 The video call from "police"

  1. "A parcel in your name has drugs and fake passports. Stay on this call."
  2. A video call shows a "police station" and a man in uniform. "You are under digital arrest."
  3. "Transfer your savings to a verification account to clear your name."
  4. Kabir hangs up and calls 1930. There is no such thing as a digital arrest.

"Digital arrest" is not real

Police, CBI, customs, the RBI or courts never arrest anyone on a video call, never keep you on a call for hours, and never ask you to transfer money to "verify" or "clear" your name. If someone says you are under "digital arrest", it is a scam, every time.

The common call scams

The psychology they use

  • Authority: uniforms, official logos, legal words.
  • Fear: arrest, account blocked, family in danger.
  • Urgency: "right now", "don't hang up", "don't tell anyone".
  • Isolation: they tell you to stay on the call and not talk to family. That alone is a huge red flag.

Your 4-line safety script

  1. "I'll call you back on the official number." (Then hang up.)
  2. Look up the official number yourself, never the one they give you.
  3. Talk to a family member or friend before doing anything with money.
  4. Report the number on Sancharsaathi (Chakshu) and, if money is involved, call 1930.

Real officials don't mind you calling back. Scammers do.

Protecting older family members

  • Agree on a family code word for real emergencies.
  • Tell them: "No real officer asks for money on the phone. Call me first."
  • Turn on spam call filtering on their phone, and save important numbers (bank, family) with clear names.

If a call makes you scared or rushed, that feeling itself is your signal. Hang up first, think second. You lose nothing by calling back on an official number.

Summary

  • Social engineering uses authority, fear, urgency and isolation.
  • "Digital arrest" does not exist; real agencies never take money on calls.
  • Hang up, verify on official numbers, and talk to someone you trust.
  • Report scam numbers on Sancharsaathi and money fraud on 1930.
items.subject: cyber-safety

items.title: Safe Browsing and Public Wi-Fi
items.excerpt: What the padlock really means, how to spot fake shopping and government sites, safe downloads, risky browser extensions, and how to use public Wi-Fi at cafes, airports and railway stations without exposing your accounts.
items.content:
The browser is your window to the internet, and some windows open onto fake shops, fake government portals and booby-trapped downloads. A few habits make everyday browsing much safer, at home or on free airport Wi-Fi.

🎬 The too-good sale

  1. An Instagram ad: branded shoes at 80% off, today only.
  2. The site has a padlock, so Zoya thinks it's safe.
  3. The domain is new and odd, there's no return policy, and payment is UPI only.
  4. Zoya buys from the brand's official app instead. Same shoes, real delivery.

What the padlock really means

The padlock (HTTPS) means the connection between you and the website is encrypted: nobody in between can read it. It does not mean the website is honest. Scam sites get padlocks for free too. Always check who you are talking to (the domain), not just how (the padlock).

Spotting fake websites

For government services, use the official .gov.in sites and typing the address yourself. Search ads can lead to lookalike portals that charge "fees" for free services.

Safe downloads

  • Download apps and software only from official stores or the maker's website.
  • Be very careful with files named like invoice.pdf.exe or .apk files sent on WhatsApp: they can install malware.
  • Cracked or "free premium" apps and games are a favourite way to spread malware.

Browser extensions

Extensions can read everything you do in your browser. Keep only those you really use, from known developers, and remove the rest. An extension that suddenly asks for new permissions after an update deserves suspicion.

Public Wi-Fi

Free Wi-Fi at cafes, stations and airports is convenient but shared with strangers.

  • Prefer your mobile data for banking and payments.
  • Check the exact network name with staff; attackers create lookalikes such as "Airport_Free_WiFi".
  • Make sure sites show HTTPS, and don't ignore browser certificate warnings.
  • Turn off auto-connect to open networks, and forget the network when you leave.
  • A trusted VPN adds protection on public Wi-Fi, but avoid unknown free VPN apps that may sell your data.

Bookmark the sites you use for money: your bank, your UPI app's site, government portals. Opening a bookmark is safer than searching every time, because scam ads often appear at the top of search results.

Summary

  • The padlock means "encrypted", not "trustworthy": always read the domain.
  • Fake shops show unreal prices, odd domains, no policies and UPI-only payments.
  • Download only from official sources; prune browser extensions.
  • On public Wi-Fi, prefer mobile data for money and avoid lookalike networks.
items.subject: cyber-safety

items.title: Securing Your Phone: Apps, Permissions and SIM Swap
items.excerpt: Your phone holds your bank, email, photos and OTPs. Learn to lock it properly, review app permissions, avoid fake apps and APK files, keep it updated, protect against SIM swap, and what to do if it's lost or stolen.
items.content:
Your phone receives your OTPs, runs your UPI and banking apps, and stores your photos, chats and documents. For most people it is the single most important device to protect. The steps below take about 15 minutes and protect you for years.

🎬 The APK on WhatsApp

  1. "Download the new bank rewards app to claim ₹5,000" with an .apk file attached.
  2. Rahul installs it. It asks to read SMS and show over other apps.
  3. That app could read every OTP that arrives. Chip shouts "Stop!"
  4. Rahul uninstalls it, changes passwords and calls his bank. No money lost.

Lock it properly

  • Use a 6-digit PIN or longer plus fingerprint or face unlock. Avoid patterns: people can see them over your shoulder.
  • Set the screen to lock after 30 seconds to 1 minute.
  • Hide OTP and message previews on the lock screen (notification settings), so a stranger can't read them.

Apps and permissions

  • Install apps only from the Play Store or App Store. Never install .apk files sent on WhatsApp, Telegram or SMS.
  • Before installing, check the developer name, downloads and reviews. Fake apps copy famous names and logos.
  • Review permissions regularly (Settings → Privacy / Permission manager). Be suspicious of apps that ask for: - SMS access (can read OTPs), - Accessibility (can see and tap things on your screen), - Display over other apps and device admin.
  • Remove apps you no longer use.

Updates

Updates fix security holes that attackers already know about. Turn on automatic updates for your phone and apps, and restart when asked. An old phone that no longer gets security updates should not be your main banking phone.

SIM swap

In a SIM swap, a criminal gets a new SIM for your number (using fake documents or a lie to the shop) and receives your OTPs. Warning signs: your phone suddenly shows "No service" for a long time while others around you have signal.

  • Act fast: contact your mobile operator and bank immediately if this happens.
  • Use authenticator apps or passkeys instead of SMS codes where possible.
  • Check which mobile numbers are registered on your ID using the government's Sancharsaathi portal, and report ones you don't recognise.

If your phone is lost or stolen

  1. Use Find My Device (Android) or Find My (iPhone) to lock or erase it remotely.
  2. Call your mobile operator to block the SIM.
  3. Inform your bank and block UPI from another device or by calling the bank.
  4. Report the device on Sancharsaathi (CEIR) so it can be blocked.
  5. Change your email password from another device.

Set this up today, before you need it: Find My Device turned on, a recovery email and phone number on your accounts, and automatic photo backup. Recovery is ten times easier when it's prepared in advance.

Summary

  • Use a strong PIN plus biometrics and hide OTP previews on the lock screen.
  • Install only from official stores; never install APKs from messages; review permissions.
  • Keep the phone updated; watch for sudden "No service" (possible SIM swap).
  • Prepare Find My Device and backups before your phone is ever lost.
items.subject: cyber-safety

items.title: Privacy on Social Media: Share Without Oversharing
items.excerpt: How scammers use what you post, the privacy settings to change today, location and photo risks, fake profiles and romance scams, deepfakes and sextortion, and keeping children safe online.
items.content:
Every post tells the world something about you: where you live, where you are right now, who your family is, when you're on holiday. Most of the time that's harmless. But scammers and stalkers collect these pieces to make convincing scams. Privacy isn't about hiding; it's about choosing who sees what.

🎬 The holiday post

  1. "Off to Goa for a week! 🏖️" with the family photo and a check-in.
  2. A stranger now knows the house is empty, and the pet's name used in passwords.
  3. Zoya switches to "friends only" and posts holiday photos after returning.
  4. Same memories shared, much less risk.

What scammers can learn from your profile

  • Your answers to security questions: pet names, school, birthday, mother's name.
  • When your home is empty: live travel posts and check-ins.
  • Your family and friends: useful for "your son is in trouble" calls and impersonation.
  • Your workplace and role: used for fake HR mails and boss-impersonation scams.

Privacy settings to change today

Photos and location

Photos can contain location data (GPS) in the file. Most social apps remove it, but files sent as documents may keep it. Post travel photos after you're back, and avoid showing your house number, vehicle number, school uniforms and ID cards.

Fake profiles and romance scams

Be careful with friendly strangers who move fast: compliments, a sad story, then a need for money, a "crypto opportunity", or a private video call. Check by reverse image search on their photos, and never send money or intimate photos to someone you haven't met in real life.

Deepfakes and sextortion

AI can now create fake videos and voices. Criminals use this for fake celebrity endorsements, fake "relative in trouble" voice calls, and blackmail.

  • If someone threatens to share intimate or fake images: don't pay, don't delete the evidence, block the account, and report on cybercrime.gov.in (there's a category for women and children) or call 1930.
  • Use a family code word to verify urgent voice calls.

Children and teenagers

  • Use parental controls and child accounts where available.
  • Keep devices in shared spaces for younger children.
  • Talk openly: tell them they can always come to you, even if they made a mistake. Shame keeps children silent, and silence helps criminals.

Once a year, search your own name and phone number online and check what a stranger can see. Then tighten what you don't like.

Summary

  • Scammers build convincing stories from small details you post.
  • Set profiles to private, hide phone numbers and turn off location tags.
  • Post travel photos after returning; watch for fast-moving strangers.
  • For blackmail or deepfake threats: don't pay, keep evidence, report on 1930.
items.subject: cyber-safety

items.title: Malware, Ransomware and Backups
items.excerpt: What viruses, spyware and ransomware are, how they get onto computers and phones, the warning signs, how to clean up, and the 3-2-1 backup rule that makes even ransomware survivable.
items.content:
Malware means "malicious software": any program designed to harm you, spy on you or steal from you. Ransomware is the scariest kind: it locks all your files and demands money to unlock them. The best protection isn't fear; it's good habits and a backup you can restore from.

🎬 The locked laptop

  1. Kabir downloads a "free full version" of an editing app from a random site.
  2. Next morning every file shows a strange extension and a ransom note.
  3. But his photos and projects were backed up to cloud and an external drive.
  4. He resets the laptop and restores everything. He pays nothing.

Types of malware

How it gets in

  • Cracked software, "free premium" apps and pirated games.
  • Email attachments and files sent on chat apps (.exe, .apk, macros in Office files).
  • Fake update pop-ups ("Your Flash/Chrome is out of date, click here").
  • Unpatched, outdated systems.
  • Infected USB drives.

Warning signs

  • The device is suddenly slow, hot, or the battery drains fast.
  • Pop-ups and ads everywhere, or a new browser homepage you didn't set.
  • Unknown apps, or apps with admin/accessibility access you didn't give.
  • Friends receive messages from you that you didn't send.

Cleaning up

  1. Disconnect from the internet if you suspect something serious.
  2. On computers, run the built-in security scanner (for example Windows Security) and a full scan.
  3. On phones, uninstall unknown apps (start Android in safe mode if an app won't uninstall) and remove device-admin rights.
  4. From a clean device, change important passwords and check your bank activity.
  5. If in doubt, back up your personal files and reset the device to factory settings.

The 3-2-1 backup rule

Keep 3 copies of important files, on 2 different kinds of storage, with 1 copy somewhere else (cloud or offline).

  • Turn on automatic photo and document backup on your phone.
  • Use an external drive for your laptop and unplug it after backing up, so ransomware can't reach it.
  • Test that you can actually restore a file.

Paying a ransom is risky: there is no guarantee you get your files back, and it funds more attacks. Report ransomware to CERT-In and cybercrime.gov.in.

Set a monthly reminder: "Backup check". Five minutes a month is the difference between losing everything and a mild inconvenience.

Summary

  • Malware arrives mostly through cracked software, attachments and fake updates.
  • Watch for slowness, pop-ups, unknown apps and messages you didn't send.
  • Clean up with official scanners, remove unknown apps, change passwords from a clean device.
  • The 3-2-1 backup rule makes ransomware survivable.
items.subject: cyber-safety

items.title: If You Are Scammed: The First Hour Checklist
items.excerpt: Exactly what to do if you lose money or an account: call 1930, report on cybercrime.gov.in, block cards and UPI, secure your email, collect evidence, report scam numbers, and look after yourself and your family afterwards.
items.content:
Anyone can be scammed, including careful, educated and technical people. Scammers are professionals who do this all day. If it happens, don't waste time on embarrassment: fast action can freeze stolen money before it disappears. Keep this checklist somewhere your family can find it.

🎬 The first hour

  1. ₹40,000 left Asha's account after a fake "refund" call.
  2. She calls the cyber crime helpline within 20 minutes and gives the transaction details.
  3. She blocks UPI with her bank and files a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in.
  4. The money is frozen in the scammer's account while police investigate.

If you lost money

  1. Call 1930 immediately. This is India's National Cyber Crime Helpline. The sooner you call, the better the chance the money can be frozen.
  2. Report on cybercrime.gov.in ("Report other cyber crime" → financial fraud). Note your complaint number.
  3. Call your bank on its official number: block cards and UPI, and raise a fraud dispute. Ask for a reference number.
  4. Write down everything while you remember: time, amount, transaction IDs, UPI IDs, phone numbers, website links.

If an account was taken over

  1. Use the platform's official "Hacked account" or recovery page (Google, Meta, WhatsApp, etc.).
  2. Change the password and turn on two-step verification.
  3. Log out of all other devices (security settings).
  4. Check the recovery email and phone number: attackers often change them.
  5. Warn friends and family that messages from the account may be fake.

Evidence to keep

  • Screenshots of chats, messages, call logs and payment screens.
  • The scammer's phone numbers, UPI IDs, bank account numbers, websites and social profiles.
  • Emails with full headers, if relevant.

Don't delete chats or block numbers before taking screenshots.

Other places to report

Beware of "recovery" scams

After a fraud, you may get calls offering to "recover your money" for a fee, sometimes pretending to be police or lawyers. Real police don't charge recovery fees. Work only through 1930, the portal, your bank and your local police station.

Look after yourself

Losing money to a scam is stressful and embarrassing, but it is a crime done to you, not a failure by you. Talk to family, share your story to warn others, and use what you learned in this course to protect them.

Save "1930 Cyber Crime Helpline" in every family member's phone contacts today. In a panic, nobody remembers numbers.

Summary

  • Lost money? Call 1930 immediately, report on cybercrime.gov.in, and call your bank.
  • Account hacked? Recover it officially, change the password, enable 2FA, sign out other devices.
  • Keep evidence before blocking or deleting anything.
  • Avoid "recovery" scams; real help never charges a fee.

🎉 You've finished Cyber Safety for Everyone. Share it with your family: it's free, and it could save someone's savings.

items.title: Data Visualization Introduction
items.excerpt: Why charts matter, how to pick the right chart for your question, and the parts of every Matplotlib chart.
items.content:
A table of 1,000 numbers hides its story. A chart shows it in two seconds: the trend going up, the one month that crashed, the outlier nobody noticed. Data visualization is the skill of turning numbers into pictures that answer a question.

In Python, the two libraries you'll use are:

  • Matplotlib: the original plotting library. Full control over every line and label.
  • Seaborn: built on Matplotlib. Beautiful statistical charts from a DataFrame in one line.
pip install matplotlib seaborn

Pick the chart from the question

The most common mistake is choosing a chart because it looks nice. Start from your question instead:

If you can't say what question your chart answers in one sentence, it's not ready. Write the question as the chart's title.

Your first chart

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun"]
visitors = [1200, 1350, 1100, 1800, 2400, 2900]

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.plot(months, visitors, marker="o")
plt.title("Website visitors are growing fast since April")
plt.xlabel("Month")
plt.ylabel("Visitors")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="dataviz-first-line.svg" alt="Line chart of website visitors from January to June, rising sharply from April"]

plt.show() displays the chart. In Jupyter or Colab, charts appear right under the cell.

The parts of a Matplotlib chart

Every chart has the same anatomy, and knowing the names helps when you search for "how do I change…":

  • Figure: the whole picture, like the paper. figsize=(7, 4) is its width and height in inches.
  • Axes: one chart area inside the figure, with its own x-axis and y-axis. A figure can hold several axes (subplots).
  • Title, labels, ticks, legend: the text that tells readers what they're looking at.

There are two ways to write Matplotlib code. The quick plt. style above, and the object style, which is clearer when you have more than one chart:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"], [10, 14, 9], marker="o")
ax.set_title("Orders per month")
ax.set_ylabel("Orders")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="dataviz-object-style.svg" alt="A small line chart of orders per month drawn with fig and ax"]

fig is the figure, ax is the axes. Methods on ax start with set_ for labels and titles.

Saving charts

plt.savefig("visitors.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

Call savefig before plt.show(). bbox_inches="tight" trims empty margins, and dpi=150 gives a sharp image for reports and slides.

Quick check

You want to show how a student's marks changed across 5 exams. Which chart? A line chart, because the x-axis is time (exam 1, 2, 3…).

Summary

  • Choose the chart from the question: time → line, categories → bar, spread → histogram, relationship → scatter.
  • A Matplotlib figure holds one or more axes (charts).
  • Always add a title and axis labels; save with plt.savefig.
items.subject: data-visualization

items.title: Line and Bar Charts with Matplotlib
items.excerpt: Compare trends with line charts and categories with bar charts, and add colours, legends and value labels.
items.content:
Line and bar charts answer most everyday questions. This lesson shows how to make them clear: several lines with a legend, sorted bars, and labels on the bars so readers don't have to guess.

Several lines with a legend

Give each line a label, then call legend():

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun"]
pune = [120, 135, 150, 145, 170, 190]
delhi = [140, 130, 125, 160, 165, 175]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(months, pune, marker="o", label="Pune")
ax.plot(months, delhi, marker="s", linestyle="--", label="Delhi")
ax.set_title("Monthly orders: Pune overtook Delhi in May")
ax.set_ylabel("Orders")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="matplotlib-two-lines.svg" alt="Two line charts, Pune and Delhi monthly orders, with Pune overtaking Delhi in May"]

Useful styling options:

Bar charts for categories

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

languages = ["Python", "JavaScript", "Java", "SQL", "C++"]
students = [420, 310, 280, 190, 120]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
bars = ax.bar(languages, students, color="#0a7d4f")
ax.bar_label(bars)
ax.set_title("Most popular course among our students: Python")
ax.set_ylabel("Students enrolled")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="matplotlib-bar.svg" alt="Bar chart of students per language, Python highest with 420"]

ax.bar_label(bars) writes each value on top of its bar, so nobody has to read the y-axis.

Sort bars from biggest to smallest (unless the categories have a natural order like months or age groups). Sorted bars are much faster to read.

Horizontal bars for long names

When category names are long, turn the chart sideways with barh:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

topics = ["Data cleaning", "Exploratory analysis", "Feature engineering", "Model training", "Reporting"]
hours = [12, 8, 6, 4, 3]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.barh(topics[::-1], hours[::-1], color="tab:orange")
ax.set_title("Where a data project's time really goes")
ax.set_xlabel("Hours")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="matplotlib-barh.svg" alt="Horizontal bar chart showing data cleaning takes the most hours in a project"]

We reversed the lists with [::-1] so the biggest bar appears at the top.

Grouped bars

To compare two series per category, shift each set of bars left and right by half a bar width:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

subjects = ["Maths", "Science", "English"]
class_a = [72, 81, 77]
class_b = [78, 74, 83]
x = np.arange(len(subjects))
w = 0.38

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.bar(x - w / 2, class_a, w, label="Class A")
ax.bar(x + w / 2, class_b, w, label="Class B")
ax.set_xticks(x, subjects)
ax.set_ylabel("Average marks")
ax.set_title("Class B leads in Maths and English")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="matplotlib-grouped-bars.svg" alt="Grouped bar chart comparing Class A and Class B averages in three subjects"]
Quick check

Your y-axis starts at 70 instead of 0 and a small difference looks huge. For bar charts, always start the y-axis at zero, otherwise the bar heights lie.

Summary

  • ax.plot() for trends; give each line a label and call ax.legend().
  • ax.bar() for categories, ax.barh() for long names; ax.bar_label() adds values.
  • Sort bars, start bar axes at zero, and write the conclusion in the title.

items.title: Histograms, Scatter Plots and Subplots
items.excerpt: See how values are spread with histograms, find relationships with scatter plots, and put several charts in one figure.
items.content:
Line and bar charts summarise. Histograms and scatter plots show every data point, which is how you discover what the averages hide: two groups of students, an outlier, a relationship between two numbers.

Histograms: how are values spread?

A histogram splits numbers into ranges (bins) and counts how many fall in each:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
marks = np.clip(rng.normal(68, 12, 300), 0, 100)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.hist(marks, bins=15, color="#0a7d4f", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(marks.mean(), color="tab:red", linestyle="--", label=f"mean = {marks.mean():.1f}")
ax.set_title("Most students scored between 55 and 80")
ax.set_xlabel("Marks")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of students")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="matplotlib-histogram.svg" alt="Histogram of 300 students' marks, bell-shaped around a mean of about 68"]

rng.normal(68, 12, 300) generates 300 realistic marks around 68. axvline draws a vertical line at the mean.

Try different bins values. Too few bins hide the shape; too many make it noisy. Between 10 and 30 is a good start.

Scatter plots: are two numbers related?

Each dot is one row: x is one column, y is another.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
hours = rng.uniform(0, 10, 60)
score = 35 + 5.5 * hours + rng.normal(0, 7, 60)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.scatter(hours, score, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_title("More study hours, higher scores")
ax.set_xlabel("Hours studied per week")
ax.set_ylabel("Test score")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="matplotlib-scatter.svg" alt="Scatter plot showing test scores rising with weekly study hours"]

The dots go up from left to right: a positive relationship. alpha=0.7 makes dots slightly see-through, so overlapping points are visible. In the Machine Learning course you'll fit a line through exactly this kind of data.

Careful

A relationship isn't proof that one thing causes the other. Ice-cream sales and drowning both rise in summer; neither causes the other.

Subplots: several charts in one figure

plt.subplots(rows, cols) returns a grid of axes. Draw each chart on its own ax:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun"]
revenue = [42, 45, 39, 51, 58, 63]
orders = [310, 330, 290, 360, 400, 455]

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
ax1.plot(months, revenue, marker="o", color="tab:green")
ax1.set_title("Revenue (₹ lakh)")
ax2.bar(months, orders, color="tab:blue")
ax2.set_title("Orders")
fig.suptitle("First half of the year", fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="matplotlib-subplots.svg" alt="Two charts side by side: revenue line chart and orders bar chart for six months"]
  • plt.subplots(1, 2): 1 row, 2 columns.
  • fig.suptitle(): one title over the whole figure.
  • fig.tight_layout(): stops labels from overlapping.

Summary

  • ax.hist(values, bins=...) shows the spread of one column.
  • ax.scatter(x, y) shows whether two columns move together.
  • plt.subplots(r, c) gives a grid of axes for side-by-side comparisons.
items.subject: data-visualization

items.title: Seaborn Basics
items.excerpt: Make clean statistical charts straight from a DataFrame with Seaborn's countplot, barplot, histplot and boxplot.
items.content:
Seaborn sits on top of Matplotlib and speaks Pandas. You hand it a DataFrame and column names, and it does the grouping, averaging and colouring for you. Charts that take ten lines in Matplotlib take one.

pip install seaborn

We'll use this small dataset of students:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 120
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "course": rng.choice(["Python", "Java", "Web"], n, p=[0.45, 0.3, 0.25]),
    "gender": rng.choice(["Female", "Male"], n),
    "hours": rng.uniform(1, 12, n).round(1),
})
df["score"] = (40 + 4.5 * df["hours"] + rng.normal(0, 8, n)).clip(0, 100).round()
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
print(df.head())

Output:

   course  gender  hours  score
0  Python  Female    6.7   66.0
1  Python    Male    2.8   67.0
2     Web  Female    5.9   59.0
3    Java    Male   10.6  100.0
4  Python    Male    7.2   72.0

sns.set_theme() switches on Seaborn's clean default look for every chart after it.

countplot: how many in each category?

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.countplot(data=df, x="course", order=df["course"].value_counts().index, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Python is our most chosen course")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="seaborn-countplot.svg" alt="Count plot of students per course, Python highest"]

No value_counts, no loop: Seaborn counted the rows itself.

barplot: average per category

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.barplot(data=df, x="course", y="score", hue="gender", ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Average score by course and gender")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="seaborn-barplot.svg" alt="Bar plot of average score per course, split by gender, with error bars"]

barplot shows the mean of y for each x, and hue splits each bar by a second category. The small black lines are error bars: how sure we are about each average. Long lines mean few students or very mixed scores.

histplot: distribution, optionally by group

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.histplot(data=df, x="score", hue="course", kde=True, element="step", ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Score distribution per course")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="seaborn-histplot.svg" alt="Overlapping histograms of scores for Python, Java and Web courses with smooth curves"]

kde=True adds a smooth curve that estimates the shape, which is easier to compare than bars.

boxplot: spread and outliers at a glance

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="course", y="hours", ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Weekly study hours per course")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="seaborn-boxplot.svg" alt="Box plots of weekly study hours for each course"]

How to read a box:

  • The line in the middle is the median.
  • The box covers the middle 50% of students (from the 25th to the 75th percentile).
  • The whiskers reach the rest of the normal range; dots beyond them are outliers.

Box plots are perfect for comparing groups when you have many values: you see the typical value, the spread and the unusual cases in one picture.

Quick check

Seaborn functions take data=df and column names as strings: x="course", not x=df["course"]. Both work, but the first gives automatic axis labels.

Summary

items.title: Relationships and Heatmaps with Seaborn
items.excerpt: Show relationships with scatterplot and regplot, find which columns move together with a correlation heatmap, and build a mini dashboard.
items.content:
Before building a machine learning model, data scientists look for relationships: which columns rise and fall together? Seaborn makes that exploration fast. This lesson covers scatter plots with a trend line and the correlation heatmap, a chart you'll see in almost every data science notebook.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n = 150
area = rng.uniform(500, 2500, n)
rooms = np.clip((area / 550 + rng.normal(0, 0.7, n)).round(), 1, 6)
age = rng.uniform(0, 30, n).round()
price = (2500000 + area * 5200 + rooms * 150000 - age * 150000 + rng.normal(0, 600000, n)) / 100000
homes = pd.DataFrame({"area_sqft": area.round(), "rooms": rooms, "age_years": age, "price_lakh": price.round(1)})
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
print(homes.describe().round(1).loc[["mean", "min", "max"]])

Output:

      area_sqft  rooms  age_years  price_lakh
mean     1409.0    2.6       14.8        79.9
min       534.0    1.0        0.0        16.6
max      2498.0    6.0       29.0       167.3

A made-up but realistic table of 150 homes: area, rooms, age and price.

scatterplot with hue

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=homes, x="area_sqft", y="price_lakh", hue="rooms", palette="viridis", ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Bigger homes cost more")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="seaborn-scatter-hue.svg" alt="Scatter plot of home price against area, coloured by number of rooms"]

Colour (hue) adds a third column to a 2-D chart: you can see bigger homes also tend to have more rooms.

regplot: add the trend line

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.regplot(data=homes, x="age_years", y="price_lakh", scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.5}, line_kws={"color": "tab:red"}, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Older homes are a little cheaper")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="seaborn-regplot.svg" alt="Scatter of price against home age with a slightly downward red trend line"]

regplot fits a straight line through the points (a linear regression, which you'll build yourself in the Machine Learning course). The shaded band shows the uncertainty.

Correlation heatmap

Correlation is a number from -1 to 1 that measures how strongly two columns move together:

  • close to 1: when one rises, the other rises;
  • close to -1: when one rises, the other falls;
  • close to 0: no straight-line relationship.
corr = homes.corr().round(2)
print(corr["price_lakh"])

Output:

area_sqft     0.92
rooms         0.81
age_years    -0.26
price_lakh    1.00
Name: price_lakh, dtype: float64

A heatmap shows the whole table as colours:

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=-1, vmax=1, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Which columns move together?")
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="seaborn-heatmap.svg" alt="Correlation heatmap: area and rooms strongly linked to price, age weakly negative"]

Area has the strongest link to price (0.92), and age a weak negative one (-0.26), so it would be the most useful input for a model predicting prices.

annot=True prints the numbers in each cell, and vmin=-1, vmax=1 keeps the colours honest so that 0.3 doesn't look as strong as 0.9.

Mini dashboard

Combine what you've learned into one figure you could put in a report:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.8))
sns.histplot(homes["price_lakh"], bins=20, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Price distribution")
sns.boxplot(data=homes, x="rooms", y="price_lakh", ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("Price by rooms")
sns.regplot(data=homes, x="area_sqft", y="price_lakh", scatter_kws={"s": 12}, ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title("Price vs area")
fig.suptitle("Home prices at a glance", fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
[vs_figure file="seaborn-dashboard.svg" alt="Three-chart dashboard: price histogram, price by rooms box plot and price versus area trend"]
Next step

You've explored the data and found that area predicts price well. In the Machine Learning course, you'll train a model that actually makes that prediction.

Summary

  • sns.scatterplot(..., hue=...) shows a relationship plus a category.
  • sns.regplot adds a trend line.
  • df.corr() + sns.heatmap(annot=True) shows which columns move together.
  • Combine charts with plt.subplots for a simple dashboard.

items.title: Neurons, Layers and How a Neural Network Learns
items.excerpt: Build a neural network from scratch in NumPy: neurons, weights, activation functions, forward pass, loss, and backpropagation, and watch it learn XOR, a problem a straight line can't solve.
items.content:
Deep learning powers face unlock, Google Translate, voice assistants and every large language model. Underneath, it's a simple idea stacked many times: a neuron multiplies inputs by weights, adds them up, and squashes the result. Stack neurons in layers and you can learn almost any pattern.

🎬 Inside the network

  1. Inputs come in, each multiplied by a weight. Add them up with a bias.
  2. A squashing function (ReLU, sigmoid) decides how strongly the neuron fires.
  3. Neurons are stacked in layers; each layer builds on the last: edges, shapes, faces.
  4. The error flows backwards, telling every weight which way to move.
  5. After thousands of nudges, the network solves a problem no straight line could.

One neuron

import numpy as np

def relu(z):
    return np.maximum(0, z)

inputs = np.array([0.5, 0.8, 0.2])       # e.g. three features
weights = np.array([0.4, -0.6, 0.9])
bias = 0.3
z = inputs @ weights + bias              # weighted sum
print("weighted sum:", round(z, 3), "| after ReLU:", round(relu(z), 3))

Output:

weighted sum: 0.2 | after ReLU: 0.2

That's a neuron. A layer is many neurons side by side (a matrix of weights); a network is layers in a row.

Activation functions

Without a non-linear activation, stacking layers would still only draw straight lines.

Learn XOR from scratch

XOR is "true if exactly one input is true". No single straight line separates it; one hidden layer does.

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([[0], [1], [1], [0]], dtype=float)

W1, b1 = rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 4)), np.zeros((1, 4))
W2, b2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (4, 1)), np.zeros((1, 1))
sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
lr = 1.0

for epoch in range(3001):
    h = np.tanh(X @ W1 + b1)                 # forward: hidden layer
    out = sigmoid(h @ W2 + b2)               # forward: output
    loss = np.mean((out - y) ** 2)
    d_out = (out - y) * out * (1 - out)      # backward: output error
    d_h = (d_out @ W2.T) * (1 - h ** 2)      # backward: hidden error
    W2 -= lr * h.T @ d_out;  b2 -= lr * d_out.sum(0, keepdims=True)
    W1 -= lr * X.T @ d_h;    b1 -= lr * d_h.sum(0, keepdims=True)
    if epoch in (0, 500, 3000):
        print(f"epoch {epoch:>4}: loss {loss:.4f}")

print("predictions:", out.round(2).ravel())

Output:

epoch    0: loss 0.2400
epoch  500: loss 0.0008
epoch 3000: loss 0.0001
predictions: [0.   0.99 0.99 0.01]

The network learned XOR: near 0 for (0,0) and (1,1), near 1 for the others. Every deep-learning framework automates exactly these steps.

Backpropagation in one step

x, w, target = 2.0, 0.5, 3.0
pred = w * x
loss = (pred - target) ** 2
grad = 2 * (pred - target) * x
w = w - 0.1 * grad
print(pred, loss, grad, w)
  1. Line 1: One input, one weight, and the value we want.
  2. Line 2: Forward pass: the prediction 0.5 × 2 = 1.
  3. Line 3: The loss: how far off, squared.
  4. Line 4: Backward pass: the chain rule gives d(loss)/dw = 2 × (pred − target) × x.
  5. Line 5: Gradient descent: move w against the gradient. The new prediction would be 1.8 × 2 = 3.6, much closer to 3.
  6. Line 6: One step of learning. Networks do millions of these.

Words you'll hear

  • Epoch: one pass over all the training data.
  • Batch: the small group of examples used for one update.
  • Learning rate: step size; too big diverges, too small crawls.
  • Overfitting: memorising training data; fight it with more data, dropout, early stopping.
  • Optimiser: Adam is the usual default; it adapts the step size per weight.

A network is only "deep" because it has many layers. More layers can learn richer patterns but need more data and compute. For small tabular datasets, gradient boosting usually beats neural networks.

Summary

  • Neuron = weighted sum + bias + activation; layers stack neurons.
  • Non-linear activations (ReLU, sigmoid, softmax) let networks learn curves.
  • Training = forward pass, loss, backpropagation (chain rule), gradient descent.
  • You trained a network on XOR from scratch in NumPy.

items.title: Your First Neural Network with Keras (TensorFlow)
items.excerpt: Build, train and evaluate a neural network with Keras: Sequential models, Dense layers, compile, fit with validation, callbacks like EarlyStopping, and a runnable scikit-learn MLP version.
items.content:
Writing backpropagation by hand teaches the idea; real projects use a framework. Keras, part of TensorFlow, lets you define a network in a few lines and handles the gradients, batching and GPU for you.

🎬 Five lines to a neural network

  1. Stack layers: 64 neurons, then 32, then one output neuron.
  2. Pick the optimiser (Adam), the loss and the metrics.
  3. Train for a few epochs, watching validation accuracy.
  4. When validation stops improving, training stops itself and keeps the best weights.

The Keras recipe

Install with pip install tensorflow. A binary classifier for tabular data:

import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input(shape=(20,)),
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    keras.layers.Dropout(0.2),
    keras.layers.Dense(32, activation="relu"),
    keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"),
])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="binary_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
model.summary()

early = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=5, restore_best_weights=True)
history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_split=0.2, epochs=100, batch_size=32, callbacks=[early])
print(model.evaluate(X_test, y_test))
model.save("churn_model.keras")

The same network, runnable with scikit-learn

scikit-learn's MLPClassifier is a small neural network: perfect for trying the ideas without TensorFlow.

from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=2000, n_features=20, n_informative=8, random_state=0)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)

mlp = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64, 32), early_stopping=True, validation_fraction=0.2,
                    max_iter=300, random_state=0)
mlp.fit(scaler.transform(X_train), y_train)
print("epochs run:", mlp.n_iter_, "| test accuracy:", round(mlp.score(scaler.transform(X_test), y_test), 3))

Output:

epochs run: 37 | test accuracy: 0.882

Counting parameters

layers = [20, 64, 32, 1]
params = 0
for a, b in zip(layers, layers[1:]):
    params += a * b + b
print(params)
  1. Line 1: Input size 20, then layers of 64, 32 and 1 neurons.
  2. Line 2: Start counting.
  3. Line 3: Between each pair of layers…
  4. Line 4: …there are a × b weights plus b biases: 20×64+64 = 1,344, then 64×32+32 = 2,080, then 32×1+1 = 33.
  5. Line 5: 3,457 trainable numbers.

Reading the training curves

Plot history.history["loss"] and ["val_loss"]:

  • Both falling → still learning; train longer.
  • Training falls, validation rises → overfitting; add dropout, regularisation or data, or stop earlier.
  • Both high and flat → underfitting; bigger model, more epochs, better features, or a higher learning rate.

Always scale inputs (StandardScaler or Normalization layer) for neural networks. Unscaled features make training slow and unstable: the most common beginner bug.

Summary

  • Keras: Sequential → compile → fit → evaluate → save.
  • Dense layers + ReLU inside, sigmoid/softmax/linear at the output, Adam optimiser.
  • Use a validation split, EarlyStopping and Dropout against overfitting.
  • Parameters = weights + biases; read the loss curves to diagnose training.

items.title: CNNs for Images: Convolution, Pooling and Transfer Learning
items.excerpt: How convolutional neural networks see images: filters that detect edges, pooling, feature maps, a Keras CNN, and transfer learning with pretrained models like ResNet. Convolution runs in NumPy.
items.content:
To a computer, an image is a grid of numbers. A normal dense network would treat every pixel separately and need millions of weights. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) instead slide small filters across the image, spotting edges, then shapes, then whole objects, using the same few weights everywhere.

🎬 How a CNN sees a cat

  1. A 224×224 photo is just 150,528 numbers.
  2. A 3×3 filter slides across the image, lighting up wherever it finds a vertical edge.
  3. Deeper layers combine edges into ears, eyes and whiskers.
  4. The final layer says: 97% cat.

Convolution by hand

A filter (kernel) is a tiny grid of weights. At each position, multiply it with the pixels under it and add up.

import numpy as np

image = np.array([[0, 0, 9, 9],
                  [0, 0, 9, 9],
                  [0, 0, 9, 9],
                  [0, 0, 9, 9]], dtype=float)          # dark left, bright right
edge = np.array([[-1, 0, 1],
                 [-1, 0, 1],
                 [-1, 0, 1]], dtype=float)              # vertical-edge detector

out = np.zeros((2, 2))
for r in range(2):
    for c in range(2):
        out[r, c] = np.sum(image[r:r + 3, c:c + 3] * edge)
print(out)

Output:

[[27. 27.]
 [27. 27.]]

Big numbers mean "edge found here". In a CNN, the network learns its filter values during training instead of you writing them.

patch = [[0, 0, 9], [0, 0, 9], [0, 0, 9]]
kernel = [[-1, 0, 1], [-1, 0, 1], [-1, 0, 1]]
products = [patch[r][c] * kernel[r][c] for r in range(3) for c in range(3)]
value = sum(products)
print(value)
  1. Line 1: The 3×3 patch of pixels under the filter: dark, dark, bright.
  2. Line 2: The vertical-edge filter: negative on the left, positive on the right.
  3. Line 3: Multiply each pixel by the matching weight.
  4. Line 4: Add them up. Dark-to-bright left-to-right gives a big positive number.
  5. Line 5: One cell of the feature map. Slide and repeat over the whole image.

Pooling: shrink and keep the strongest signal

Max pooling keeps the largest value in each 2×2 block, halving width and height:

fmap = np.array([[1, 3, 2, 0], [4, 6, 1, 1], [0, 2, 9, 5], [1, 1, 3, 7]])
pooled = fmap.reshape(2, 2, 2, 2).max(axis=(1, 3))
print(pooled)

Output:

[[6 2]
 [2 9]]

A CNN in Keras

from tensorflow import keras

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3)),
    keras.layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu", padding="same"),
    keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),
    keras.layers.Conv2D(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same"),
    keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),
    keras.layers.Flatten(),
    keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
    keras.layers.Dropout(0.3),
    keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),         # 10 classes, e.g. CIFAR-10
])
model.compile("adam", "sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])

Transfer learning: stand on giants' shoulders

Training a big CNN from scratch needs millions of images. Instead, take a model pretrained on ImageNet (ResNet, EfficientNet, MobileNet), freeze its layers, and train only a small new head on your images: often a few hundred per class is enough.

from tensorflow import keras

base = keras.applications.MobileNetV2(input_shape=(224, 224, 3), include_top=False, weights="imagenet")
base.trainable = False
model = keras.Sequential([base, keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D(), keras.layers.Dense(3, activation="softmax")])

Try it now: a classifier on real digit images

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

digits = load_digits()                                     # 8×8 grayscale digits
a, b, ya, yb = train_test_split(digits.data / 16, digits.target, random_state=0)
clf = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64,), max_iter=500, random_state=0).fit(a, ya)
print("digit accuracy:", round(clf.score(b, yb), 3))

Output:

digit accuracy: 0.973

Use data augmentation (random flips, rotations, crops, brightness) so the model sees varied versions of each photo. It's one of the cheapest ways to improve image models.

Summary

  • Convolution slides learned filters over images to make feature maps.
  • Pooling shrinks maps and keeps strong signals; deeper layers see bigger shapes.
  • Keras: Conv2D → MaxPooling2D → … → Dense softmax.
  • Transfer learning with pretrained models needs far less data.

items.title: RNNs and LSTMs for Sequences
items.excerpt: Networks with memory: how recurrent neural networks read sequences step by step, why plain RNNs forget, how LSTM and GRU gates fix it, and an LSTM forecaster in Keras.
items.content:
Sentences, stock prices, sensor readings and music are sequences: order matters. A Recurrent Neural Network reads them one step at a time and keeps a memory (the hidden state) of what came before.

🎬 A network with a notebook

  1. The network reads "the movie was not good" one word at a time.
  2. After each word it updates a small notebook: its hidden state.
  3. Plain RNNs smudge old notes: by the end they've forgotten "not".
  4. LSTMs add gates that decide what to keep, what to forget and what to output. "not" survives.

An RNN step by step

At each step: h_new = tanh(W_x × input + W_h × h_old + b). The same weights are reused at every step.

import math
w_x, w_h = 0.8, 0.5
h = 0.0
for x in [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]:
    h = math.tanh(w_x * x + w_h * h)
print(round(h, 3))
  1. Line 1: tanh keeps the memory between −1 and 1.
  2. Line 2: Two weights: how much the new input matters, and how much the old memory matters.
  3. Line 3: The memory starts empty.
  4. Line 4: Read a sequence: a signal, then two zeros.
  5. Line 5: Step 1: h = tanh(0.8). Steps 2 and 3 only carry memory: 0.5 × h each time, so it fades.
  6. Line 6: After just two steps of silence, the memory of the signal is down to a quarter.

LSTM and GRU: memory with gates

An LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) keeps a separate cell state and uses three gates (each a small sigmoid layer giving 0–1):

A GRU is a lighter variant with two gates; it often performs similarly with fewer parameters.

import numpy as np

sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
cell = 1.0                                    # important memory, e.g. "not"
for step in range(5):
    forget = sig(4.0)                         # a learned gate near 1: keep it
    cell = forget * cell
print("LSTM-style memory after 5 steps:", round(cell, 3))
print("plain RNN-style memory after 5 steps:", round(0.5 ** 5, 3))

Output:

LSTM-style memory after 5 steps: 0.913
plain RNN-style memory after 5 steps: 0.031

Because the forget gate can learn to stay close to 1, important information survives many steps.

An LSTM forecaster in Keras

import numpy as np
from tensorflow import keras

def windows(series, size=12):
    X = np.array([series[i:i + size] for i in range(len(series) - size)])
    y = series[size:]
    return X[..., np.newaxis], y              # shape: (samples, timesteps, features)

X, y = windows(scaled_sales)                  # scale the series to roughly 0-1 first
model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input(shape=(12, 1)),
    keras.layers.LSTM(32),
    keras.layers.Dense(1),
])
model.compile("adam", "mse")
model.fit(X, y, epochs=50, validation_split=0.2, verbose=0)

The key idea is the sliding window: use the last 12 values to predict the next one:

series = np.arange(1, 17)
X = np.array([series[i:i + 12] for i in range(len(series) - 12)])
print(X.shape, "first window ends at", X[0, -1], "-> target", series[12])

Output:

(4, 12) first window ends at 12 -> target 13

Where sequence models are used today

  • Time series: demand, energy load, sensor anomaly detection.
  • Text: before 2018 LSTMs dominated translation and sentiment; now transformers (attention) have largely replaced them for language, because they process all words in parallel and handle long range better.
  • Speech and handwriting: combined with CNNs.

For forecasting, compare an LSTM against ARIMA and gradient boosting on lag features. On small or medium datasets the simpler models often win, and they're much cheaper to train and explain.

Summary

  • RNNs read sequences step by step with a hidden-state memory and shared weights.
  • Plain RNNs forget (vanishing gradients); LSTM/GRU gates keep important information.
  • Keras: LSTM layers on windows shaped (samples, timesteps, features).
  • Transformers now lead for text; LSTMs remain useful for many time series.

items.title: The Same Models in PyTorch
items.excerpt: Learn PyTorch, the framework behind most AI research and LLMs: tensors, autograd, nn.Module, the training loop, DataLoaders and moving to a GPU, compared side by side with Keras.
items.content:
Keras is great for getting started. PyTorch is what most AI research, Hugging Face models and large language models are written in. It feels like writing normal Python: you write the training loop yourself, which makes it flexible and easy to debug.

🎬 PyTorch's training loop

  1. Data lives in tensors: NumPy arrays that can run on a GPU.
  2. Every operation is recorded, so loss.backward() computes all gradients automatically.
  3. zero_grad, forward, loss, backward, step. Five lines, repeated every batch.
  4. .to("cuda") moves the model and data to the GPU, often many times faster.

Tensors and autograd

import torch

x = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
w = torch.tensor(0.5, requires_grad=True)
loss = (w * x - 3.0) ** 2
loss.backward()                      # autograd computes d(loss)/dw and d(loss)/dx
print(loss.item(), w.grad.item())    # 4.0  -8.0  (same as our hand-made backprop)

A model and the training loop

import torch
from torch import nn

class ChurnNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_features):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(n_features, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.2),
                                 nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 1))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)           # raw scores (logits)

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model = ChurnNet(20).to(device)
loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()     # sigmoid + binary cross-entropy, numerically stable
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(X_train, y_train), batch_size=32, shuffle=True)

for epoch in range(20):
    model.train()
    for xb, yb in loader:
        xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
        opt.zero_grad()              # 1. clear old gradients
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb).squeeze(1), yb)   # 2-3. forward + loss
        loss.backward()              # 4. backpropagate
        opt.step()                   # 5. update weights

The loop, simulated in plain Python

The five steps are the same everywhere. Here they are training our one-weight model until it fits:

w, lr = 0.5, 0.05
for step in range(30):
    grad = 0.0
    pred = w * 2.0
    loss = (pred - 3.0) ** 2
    grad = 2 * (pred - 3.0) * 2.0
    w -= lr * grad
print(round(w, 3), round(loss, 6))
  1. Line 1: Start with a bad weight and a learning rate.
  2. Line 2: Thirty training steps.
  3. Line 3: zero_grad: forget the previous step's gradient.
  4. Line 4: forward: make a prediction.
  5. Line 5: loss: measure the error.
  6. Line 6: backward: compute the gradient (PyTorch: loss.backward()).
  7. Line 7: step: update the weight (PyTorch: opt.step()).
  8. Line 8: The weight converges to 1.5, because 1.5 × 2 = 3, and the loss is practically 0.

Keras vs PyTorch

Both are excellent. Learn the concepts once and switching is easy.

Evaluating in PyTorch

import torch

model.eval()                         # switches off dropout
with torch.no_grad():                # no gradient tracking: faster, less memory
    probs = torch.sigmoid(model(X_test.to(device))).squeeze(1)
    accuracy = ((probs > 0.5).float() == y_test.to(device)).float().mean().item()

Always call model.train() before training and model.eval() before evaluating. Dropout and batch-norm layers behave differently in each mode, and mixing them up silently gives wrong results.

Summary

  • Tensors are GPU-ready arrays; autograd computes gradients with loss.backward().
  • Models subclass nn.Module; the loop is zero_grad → forward → loss → backward → step.
  • DataLoader batches and shuffles; .to(device) moves work to the GPU.
  • Use model.eval() + torch.no_grad() for evaluation.

🎉 You've finished Deep Learning Foundations.

items.title: A Chat UI with Streamlit
items.excerpt: Build a ChatGPT-style chat page in about 30 lines of Python with Streamlit: chat bubbles, session memory, streaming replies, keeping history short, a per-user limit, secrets, and free deployment on Streamlit Community Cloud.
items.content:
You have a prompt that works. Now people need a page to use it. Streamlit turns a Python script into a web app, and it has ready-made chat parts: message bubbles, an input box at the bottom and streaming text. No HTML, CSS or JavaScript needed.

🎬 From script to shareable app

  1. Dev has a tutor prompt that works in the terminal. Nobody else can use it.
  2. Chip adds st.chat_message and st.chat_input: it looks like a real chat app.
  3. Byte keeps the conversation in st.session_state, so follow-up questions make sense.
  4. Bugsy deploys it for free and sends the link to the whole class.

The whole app

Save as app.py, put your key in .streamlit/secrets.toml, then run streamlit run app.py:

import streamlit as st
import anthropic

st.set_page_config(page_title="Study Chat", page_icon="💬")
st.title("💬 Study Chat")
client = anthropic.Anthropic(api_key=st.secrets["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"])

if "messages" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.messages = []

for m in st.session_state.messages:                    # redraw the chat so far
    with st.chat_message(m["role"]):
        st.markdown(m["content"])

if prompt := st.chat_input("Ask about any lesson…"):
    st.session_state.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": prompt})
    with st.chat_message("user"):
        st.markdown(prompt)

    def stream():
        with client.messages.stream(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                    system="You are a friendly tutor for beginners. Keep answers short, with one example.",
                                    messages=st.session_state.messages[-19:]) as s:   # odd number: starts with a user turn
            yield from s.text_stream

    with st.chat_message("assistant"):
        reply = st.write_stream(stream())              # types the answer out live
    st.session_state.messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

How it works:

  • Streamlit reruns the whole script on every click or message. st.session_state is the box that survives reruns, so the chat history lives there.
  • st.chat_input returns the text when the user presses Enter (and None otherwise).
  • st.write_stream shows text as it arrives and returns the full reply.

Keep the history short

Long chats get slow and costly, because the whole history is sent every time. Keep only the most recent messages that fit a budget:

history = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is a list in Python?"},
           {"role": "assistant", "content": "A list is an ordered collection, like [1, 2, 3]."},
           {"role": "user", "content": "And a tuple?"},
           {"role": "assistant", "content": "A tuple is like a list you cannot change, like (1, 2, 3)."},
           {"role": "user", "content": "When should I use which?"}]

def trim(history, max_words=30):
    kept, words = [], 0
    for m in reversed(history):
        w = len(m["content"].split())
        if words + w > max_words:
            break
        kept.insert(0, m)
        words += w
    while kept and kept[0]["role"] != "user":         # the conversation must start with the user
        kept.pop(0)
    return kept

print([m["content"][:20] for m in trim(history)])

Output:

['And a tuple?', 'A tuple is like a li', 'When should I use wh']

Real apps count tokens instead of words, and often replace the old part with a short summary.

A limit per user

A public AI page without limits can run up a big bill overnight. Count messages per user:

from collections import defaultdict
used = defaultdict(int)
LIMIT = 3
def allow(user):
    used[user] += 1
    return used[user] <= LIMIT
print([allow("asha") for _ in range(4)])
  1. Line 1: defaultdict gives every new user a starting count of 0.
  2. Line 2: Messages used per user.
  3. Line 3: Three free messages (per day, in a real app).
  4. Line 4: Called before every model request.
  5. Line 5: Count this message.
  6. Line 6: Allowed while the count is within the limit.
  7. Line 7: Asha's fourth message is refused. Show "Daily limit reached: come back tomorrow, or upgrade."

Deploying for free

  1. Push app.py and a requirements.txt (streamlit, anthropic) to a GitHub repository. Never commit secrets.toml.
  2. On Streamlit Community Cloud, create an app from that repository.
  3. Paste your key into the app's Secrets settings.
  4. Share the link. Every push to GitHub redeploys the app.

Hugging Face Spaces is another free option for demos.

Nice extras

Add a small line under the input: "AI can make mistakes. Check important answers." It sets honest expectations and builds trust with users.

Summary

  • st.chat_message, st.chat_input and st.write_stream build a chat UI in a few lines.
  • st.session_state keeps the history across Streamlit's reruns.
  • Trim history to control cost, and store per-user limits on the server.
  • Deploy free from GitHub, with keys in the platform's secrets settings.

items.title: An AI API with FastAPI
items.excerpt: Wrap your AI feature in a real web API with FastAPI: request and response models, validation errors, an API key header, error handling, a health check, caching repeated questions, and streaming.
items.content:
A Streamlit page is great for one app. But when a mobile app, a website and a WhatsApp bot all need the same AI feature, you build it once as an API: a URL other programs call with JSON. FastAPI is the most popular Python framework for this: fast, typed and with automatic interactive docs.

🎬 One brain, many apps

  1. Dev puts the tutor prompt behind POST /ask.
  2. The website, the Android app and a bot all call the same URL.
  3. Bugsy sends an empty question. The API answers 422 with a clear message, without calling the model.
  4. Byte notices 30% of questions repeat. Cached answers return instantly and cost nothing.

The API

import os
import secrets
from typing import Literal

import anthropic
from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI(title="Study Buddy API")
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

class Ask(BaseModel):
    question: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=2000)
    level: Literal["beginner", "intermediate"] = "beginner"

class Answer(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    input_tokens: int
    output_tokens: int

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

@app.post("/ask", response_model=Answer)
def ask(body: Ask, x_api_key: str = Header()):
    if not secrets.compare_digest(x_api_key, os.environ["APP_KEY"]):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid API key")
    try:
        r = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=800,
                                   system=f"Explain clearly for a {body.level} learner, with one example.",
                                   messages=[{"role": "user", "content": body.question}])
    except anthropic.APIError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail="AI service unavailable, please retry")
    return Answer(answer=r.content[0].text, input_tokens=r.usage.input_tokens,
                  output_tokens=r.usage.output_tokens)

Run it with uvicorn main:app --reload and open http://localhost:8000/docs: FastAPI builds a page where you can try every endpoint. Callers send the key in an x-api-key header.

What validation does for you

Pydantic checks every request before your code runs. Here's the same idea by hand, so you can see the logic:

body = {"question": "  ", "level": "expert"}
q = body.get("question", "").strip()
errors = []
if not q: errors.append("question is empty")
if body.get("level") not in ("beginner", "intermediate"): errors.append("level must be beginner or intermediate")
print(422 if errors else 200, errors)
  1. Line 1: A bad request: a blank question and a level we don't support.
  2. Line 2: Strip spaces so " " counts as empty.
  3. Line 3: Collect every problem, not just the first, so the caller can fix them all at once.
  4. Line 4: Problem 1.
  5. Line 5: Problem 2.
  6. Line 6: 422 means "I understood the request, but the data is invalid".

Status codes your API should use

Cache repeated questions

Many users ask the same things. Normalise the question and cache the answer:

import hashlib

cache = {}
calls = 0

def fake_llm(question):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    return f"Answer to: {question}"

def ask_cached(question):
    key = hashlib.sha256(question.strip().lower().encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
    if key in cache:
        return cache[key], "cache"
    cache[key] = fake_llm(question)
    return cache[key], "model"

for q in ["What is RAG?", "  what is rag?", "What is MCP?"]:
    answer, source = ask_cached(q)
    print(f"{source:<5} | {answer}")
print("model calls:", calls)

Output:

model | Answer to: What is RAG?
cache | Answer to: What is RAG?
model | Answer to: What is MCP?
model calls: 2

Three questions, two paid calls. In production, use Redis with an expiry time, and don't cache personal or time-sensitive answers. Providers also offer prompt caching for long, repeated system prompts, which cuts cost on every call.

Streaming from an API

For long answers, return text as it's generated with StreamingResponse:

from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

@app.post("/ask/stream")
def ask_stream(body: Ask):
    def gen():
        with client.messages.stream(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=800,
                                    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": body.question}]) as s:
            yield from s.text_stream
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/plain")

Return token counts (like input_tokens above) in every response and log them. When your bill grows, you'll know exactly which endpoint and which customer caused it.

Summary

  • FastAPI + Pydantic give you typed requests, automatic validation and docs at /docs.
  • Protect the endpoint with an API key, and return clear status codes.
  • Catch provider errors and return 502 instead of crashing.
  • Cache repeated questions, and stream long answers.
