items.title: Docker and Cloud Deployment
items.excerpt: Package your AI app in a Docker container and run it in the cloud: a Dockerfile line by line, keeping secrets out of the image, environment variables, choosing a host, a monthly cost estimate and a launch checklist.
items.content:
"It works on my laptop" isn't a deployment. Docker packs your app, its Python version and its libraries into one image that runs the same everywhere. Cloud platforms then run that image for you, restart it when it crashes, and give it a public HTTPS address.

🎬 The lunchbox

  1. Dev packs the app, Python and every library into one container image: a sealed lunchbox.
  2. The same box runs on Chip's laptop, a test server and the cloud. No "missing library" surprises.
  3. Byte checks the box: the API key isn't packed in. The cloud adds it at start-up.
  4. Bugsy opens the public link and sees the health check say "ok".

The Dockerfile

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"]

And a .dockerignore so secrets and junk never enter the image:

.env
.git
__pycache__/
*.ipynb
.streamlit/secrets.toml

Build and run locally:

docker build -t study-buddy .
docker run -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env study-buddy

Configuration from the environment

The image has no secrets; the platform passes them in as environment variables at start-up:

env = {"ANTHROPIC_API_KEY": "set", "PORT": "8080"}
port = int(env.get("PORT", "8000"))
missing = [k for k in ("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", "APP_KEY") if k not in env]
print(port, missing)
  1. Line 1: What the platform provided (in real code this is os.environ).
  2. Line 2: Many platforms tell you which port to listen on through PORT; fall back to 8000 locally.
  3. Line 3: List every required secret that's missing.
  4. Line 4: APP_KEY wasn't set, so the app should refuse to start and tell you exactly why.

Pre-flight check

files = {"Dockerfile", "requirements.txt", "main.py", ".env"}
gitignore = {".env", "__pycache__/"}
checks = {
    "Dockerfile present": "Dockerfile" in files,
    "requirements.txt present": "requirements.txt" in files,
    ".env kept out of git": ".env" in gitignore,
    ".dockerignore present": ".dockerignore" in files,
}
for name, ok in checks.items():
    print("✅" if ok else "❌", name)

Output:

✅ Dockerfile present
✅ requirements.txt present
✅ .env kept out of git
❌ .dockerignore present

The missing .dockerignore matters: without it, COPY . . would copy .env, and your API key would be inside the image for anyone who gets it.

Where to run it

All of them can build from your GitHub repository or a container registry, set environment variables in a dashboard and give you HTTPS.

What will it cost?

users_per_day, questions_per_user = 300, 5
tokens_in, tokens_out = 1200, 400
price_in, price_out = 3.00, 15.00          # example $ per million tokens
api = users_per_day * questions_per_user * 30 * (tokens_in * price_in + tokens_out * price_out) / 1e6
hosting = 7                                 # example small container, $ per month
print(f"API ${api:,.2f} + hosting ${hosting} = ${api + hosting:,.2f} per month")

Output:

API $432.00 + hosting $7 = $439.00 per month

For AI apps, the model bill is usually far bigger than hosting. Caching, shorter prompts and a smaller model for easy questions cut it fastest. (Prices are illustrative; check your provider's current pricing.)

Launch checklist

  • [ ] Secrets only in the platform's environment settings, never in Git or the image.
  • [ ] A /health endpoint the platform can check.
  • [ ] Rate limits per user and a spending limit set in your AI provider's console.
  • [ ] Logs with request ids and token counts (no personal data).
  • [ ] An alert when errors or costs jump.
  • [ ] A rollback plan: redeploy the previous image tag.

Set a monthly spending limit (or budget alert) in your AI provider's dashboard before you share the link. It's the cheapest insurance in all of AI engineering.

Summary

  • Docker packages your app and its dependencies into one image that runs anywhere.
  • Keep secrets out with .dockerignore, and pass them in as environment variables.
  • Pick a host from free demo platforms to serverless containers.
  • Estimate monthly cost (the model is usually the biggest part) and follow a launch checklist.

🎉 You've finished Deploying AI Apps.

items.title: Project 1: Sales Performance Analysis and Dashboard
items.excerpt: A complete portfolio project: analyse a year of retail sales with pandas, find the top products, regions and trends, build KPI charts, and write the insights a manager can act on.
items.content:
Every company asks the same questions about sales: what's growing, what's falling, where, and why. In this project you answer them end to end, the most common task in data analyst interviews and jobs.

🎬 The Monday-morning sales review

  1. "How did we do this year, and where should we focus next quarter?" asks the sales head.
  2. 12 months of orders, cleaned and joined with product and region tables.
  3. Revenue by month, region and category; growth rates; top and bottom products.
  4. One page: four KPIs, two charts and three clear recommendations.

The data

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 3000
dates = pd.to_datetime("2025-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.integers(0, 365, n), unit="D")
category = rng.choice(["Tea", "Snacks", "Kitchen", "Gifts"], n, p=[0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1])
region = rng.choice(["North", "South", "East", "West"], n)
base = {"Tea": 300, "Snacks": 180, "Kitchen": 650, "Gifts": 900}
festive = np.isin(dates.month, [10, 11]) * (category == "Gifts") * 1.8 + 1
qty = rng.integers(1, 5, n)
sales = pd.DataFrame({"date": dates, "category": category, "region": region, "qty": qty,
                      "revenue": (np.array([base[c] for c in category]) * qty * festive).round()})
print(sales.shape, "| total revenue: Rs", f"{sales['revenue'].sum():,.0f}")

Output:

(3000, 5) | total revenue: Rs 3,115,400

KPIs

kpi = {
    "revenue": sales["revenue"].sum(),
    "orders": len(sales),
    "avg_order": sales["revenue"].mean(),
    "units": sales["qty"].sum(),
}
print({k: round(float(v)) for k, v in kpi.items()})

Output:

{'revenue': 3115400, 'orders': 3000, 'avg_order': 1038, 'units': 7426}

Trends and breakdowns

monthly = sales.groupby(sales["date"].dt.to_period("M"))["revenue"].sum()
print("best month:", monthly.idxmax(), "| worst month:", monthly.idxmin())

by_cat = sales.groupby("category")["revenue"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
print((by_cat / by_cat.sum()).round(3).to_dict())

h1 = sales[sales["date"].dt.month <= 6].groupby("region")["revenue"].sum()
h2 = sales[sales["date"].dt.month > 6].groupby("region")["revenue"].sum()
print("H2 vs H1 growth:", ((h2 / h1 - 1) * 100).round(1).to_dict())

Output:

best month: 2025-10 | worst month: 2025-09
{'Kitchen': 0.3, 'Tea': 0.29, 'Gifts': 0.281, 'Snacks': 0.129}
H2 vs H1 growth: {'East': 13.1, 'North': 17.7, 'South': 17.5, 'West': 9.9}
gifts_share = 0.10
gifts_revenue_share = 0.281
multiplier = gifts_revenue_share / gifts_share
insight = f"Gifts are {gifts_share:.0%} of orders but {gifts_revenue_share:.0%} of revenue"
print(insight, round(multiplier, 1))
  1. Line 1: Gifts are about 10% of orders (from how we generated the data).
  2. Line 2: But they bring 28.1% of revenue (from the category breakdown).
  3. Line 3: Each gift order is worth about 2.8× its share: high-value orders.
  4. Line 4: Write the finding in plain words.
  5. Line 5: This sentence is worth more to a manager than any chart.

Charts for the dashboard

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.5))
monthly.plot(ax=axes[0], marker="o", title="Monthly revenue (Rs)")
by_cat.plot.barh(ax=axes[1], title="Revenue by category (Rs)")
plt.tight_layout()

Build the same in Power BI or Tableau for the final version: KPI cards on top, the trend line, the category bars and a region slicer.

Recommendations (the part that gets you hired)

  1. Gifts: high value and highly seasonal → run gifting campaigns for Rakhi and weddings, not only Diwali.
  2. West region grew slowest in H2 → investigate delivery times and local pricing there.
  3. September dip just before the festive season → plan a promotion or new-product launch for the slow month.

Put it in your portfolio

  • GitHub repo: README.md (problem, data, approach, 3 insights, screenshot), notebook, dashboard file.
  • Use a real public dataset next (for example the Superstore sample data or a Kaggle retail dataset).
  • CV line: *"Analysed 3,000 orders across 4 regions; identified gifts as 28% of revenue from 10% of orders; dashboard in Power BI."*

Summary

  • Clean → KPIs → trends → breakdowns → growth → insights → recommendations.
  • Every insight needs a number, a comparison and a "so what".
  • Present on one page; publish the repo with a clear README.

items.title: Project 2: Customer Churn Prediction
items.excerpt: Predict which telecom customers will leave: EDA, feature engineering, a scikit-learn pipeline, model comparison, threshold choice by business cost, and an explainable result.
items.content:
Keeping a customer is far cheaper than winning a new one. A telecom or subscription company that knows who is likely to leave can call them with an offer first. Churn prediction is a classic interview project because it uses every ML skill.

🎬 Saving customers before they leave

  1. A telecom loses thousands of subscribers every month. Each costs Rs 2,000 to replace.
  2. Predict, for every customer, the chance they'll leave next month.
  3. Call the riskiest customers with an offer. But calls cost money too: where to draw the line?
  4. The model-driven campaign saves far more than it costs.

Data and features

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 4000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "tenure_months": rng.integers(1, 72, n),
    "monthly_bill": rng.normal(550, 180, n).clip(150, 1500).round(),
    "contract": rng.choice(["monthly", "yearly"], n, p=[0.6, 0.4]),
    "complaints": rng.poisson(0.6, n),
    "data_gb": rng.gamma(2, 6, n).round(1),
})
logit = (-1.0 - 0.05 * df["tenure_months"] + 0.002 * df["monthly_bill"]
         + 1.2 * (df["contract"] == "monthly") + 0.7 * df["complaints"])
df["churned"] = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
df["bill_per_gb"] = (df["monthly_bill"] / (df["data_gb"] + 1)).round(1)     # engineered feature
print("churn rate:", round(df["churned"].mean(), 3))
print(df.groupby("contract")["churned"].mean().round(3).to_dict())

Output:

churn rate: 0.379
{'monthly': 0.467, 'yearly': 0.252}

EDA already shows the story: monthly-contract customers churn almost twice as often as yearly ones.

Model comparison

from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

X, y = df.drop(columns="churned"), df["churned"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)
prep = ColumnTransformer([("cat", OneHotEncoder(), ["contract"]),
                          ("num", StandardScaler(), ["tenure_months", "monthly_bill", "complaints", "data_gb", "bill_per_gb"])])
models = {"logistic": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced"),
          "boosting": GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0)}
for name, m in models.items():
    auc = cross_val_score(Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("m", m)]), X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
    print(f"{name}: CV ROC-AUC {auc:.3f}")

Output:

logistic: CV ROC-AUC 0.799
boosting: CV ROC-AUC 0.781

The simple logistic model wins here, and it's explainable: a good result to report honestly.

Choosing the threshold by money

p_churn = 0.40
save_rate = 0.30
customer_value = 2000
call_cost = 100
profit = p_churn * save_rate * customer_value - call_cost
print(profit, profit > 0)
  1. Line 1: The model says this customer has a 40% chance of leaving.
  2. Line 2: Our retention offer convinces 30% of would-be leavers to stay (from past campaigns).
  3. Line 3: Keeping a customer is worth Rs 2,000.
  4. Line 4: Each call plus offer costs Rs 100.
  5. Line 5: Expected profit = 0.40 × 0.30 × 2000 − 100 = Rs 140.
  6. Line 6: Positive: worth calling.
pipe = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("m", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced"))]).fit(X_train, y_train)
p = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
for t in (0.5, 0.17):
    called = p >= t
    saved_value = (y_test[called] * 0.3 * 2000).sum()
    cost = called.sum() * 100
    print(f"threshold {t}: call {called.sum()} customers, expected net Rs {saved_value - cost:,.0f}")

Output:

threshold 0.5: call 453 customers, expected net Rs 122,700
threshold 0.17: call 828 customers, expected net Rs 133,800

Calling more customers at the break-even threshold earns more here, because each saved customer is worth far more than a call. But note that class_weight="balanced" shifts probabilities upwards, so the break-even maths is only a starting point: always check thresholds on held-out data with real costs.

Explain the drivers

coefs = pd.Series(pipe.named_steps["m"].coef_[0], index=pipe.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out())
print(coefs.round(2).sort_values().to_dict())

Output:

{'num__tenure_months': -0.97, 'cat__contract_yearly': -0.79, 'num__bill_per_gb': -0.05, 'num__data_gb': -0.04, 'num__monthly_bill': 0.33, 'num__complaints': 0.58, 'cat__contract_monthly': 0.6}

Short tenure, monthly contracts and complaints drive churn: recommend yearly-plan offers to new monthly customers and fast complaint resolution.

Portfolio checklist

  • [ ] EDA with churn rate by segment
  • [ ] Pipeline with no leakage; cross-validated comparison
  • [ ] Threshold chosen with business costs on a test set
  • [ ] Drivers explained in plain language
  • [ ] README: "the campaign at threshold X saves an estimated Rs Y per month"

Summary

  • Churn = imbalanced classification; use ROC-AUC and business-cost thresholds.
  • Simple, explainable models can win; report honestly.
  • Turn coefficients into actions the business can take.

items.title: Project 3: House Price Prediction
items.excerpt: Predict flat prices from size, location and amenities: log-transformed targets, one-hot locations, linear vs random forest vs boosting, MAE in lakhs, and error analysis.
items.content:
What should a 2BHK in Pune's Baner cost? Property sites, banks and buyers all want that number. House-price prediction is the classic regression project: predict a number, measure how far off you are, and explain what drives the price.

🎬 The pricing desk

  1. 980 sq ft, 2BHK, Baner, 3 years old, with parking. Price?
  2. Location dominates: the same flat costs very different amounts in different localities.
  3. The model learns price per square foot by locality, then adjusts for age and amenities.
  4. Off by a few lakh on average: good enough to flag overpriced listings.

Data

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n = 2500
locality = rng.choice(["Baner", "Hinjewadi", "Kothrud", "Wakad", "Hadapsar"], n)
rate = {"Baner": 11500, "Hinjewadi": 7800, "Kothrud": 13000, "Wakad": 8500, "Hadapsar": 7200}
sqft = rng.normal(1000, 280, n).clip(400, 2200).round()
age = rng.integers(0, 25, n)
parking = rng.random(n) < 0.6
price = (np.array([rate[l] for l in locality]) * sqft * (1 - 0.008 * age) * np.where(parking, 1.04, 1.0)
         * rng.lognormal(0, 0.08, n)) / 1e5                       # price in lakhs
df = pd.DataFrame({"locality": locality, "sqft": sqft, "age": age, "parking": parking.astype(int), "price_lakh": price.round(1)})
print(df.groupby("locality")["price_lakh"].median().round(1).sort_values().to_dict())

Output:

{'Hadapsar': 66.8, 'Hinjewadi': 70.1, 'Wakad': 78.8, 'Baner': 107.6, 'Kothrud': 117.4}

Model comparison

from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

X, y = df.drop(columns="price_lakh"), df["price_lakh"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)
prep = ColumnTransformer([("loc", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["locality"])], remainder="passthrough")

candidates = {
    "linear": LinearRegression(),
    "linear on log(price)": TransformedTargetRegressor(LinearRegression(), func=np.log, inverse_func=np.exp),
    "random forest": RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=0),
    "boosting": HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0),
}
for name, model in candidates.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("m", model)]).fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(f"{name:>21}: MAE {mean_absolute_error(y_test, pipe.predict(X_test)):.2f} lakh")

Output:

               linear: MAE 7.11 lakh
 linear on log(price): MAE 7.38 lakh
        random forest: MAE 6.64 lakh
             boosting: MAE 6.20 lakh

Boosting captures the "locality × size" interaction (price per sq ft differs by area) best.

prices = [45, 60, 90, 250]
logs = [round(__import__("math").log(p), 2) for p in prices]
ratio_small = round(60 / 45, 2)
ratio_big = round(250 / 90, 2)
print(logs, ratio_small, ratio_big)
  1. Line 1: Flat prices in lakhs: a few very expensive flats stretch the scale.
  2. Line 2: The log turns multiplicative differences into additive ones and squashes the long tail.
  3. Line 3: 60 vs 45 is +33%.
  4. Line 4: 250 vs 90 is +178%. In logs both are simple differences.
  5. Line 5: Price effects are usually percentages ("parking adds 4%"), which logs model naturally.

Error analysis

best = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("m", HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0))]).fit(X_train, y_train)
errors = X_test.assign(actual=y_test, predicted=best.predict(X_test).round(1))
errors["abs_err"] = (errors["actual"] - errors["predicted"]).abs()
print(errors.groupby("locality")["abs_err"].mean().round(2).sort_values().to_dict())

Output:

{'Hinjewadi': 4.28, 'Hadapsar': 4.67, 'Wakad': 5.83, 'Baner': 7.16, 'Kothrud': 9.15}

Errors are larger in the costliest localities in absolute lakhs: report percentage error (MAPE) too, and consider separate models or more features (floor, view, society amenities) for premium areas.

Portfolio checklist

  • [ ] Real data next: a public housing dataset (Kaggle has Indian city listings) with honest cleaning notes
  • [ ] Baseline (median price per locality) vs models, in lakhs
  • [ ] Error analysis by segment
  • [ ] A tiny Streamlit "price estimator" app as a demo (see the Gen AI project for Streamlit basics)

Summary

  • Regression project: clean → encode locations → compare models → MAE in business units.
  • Boosting handles interactions like locality × size well; test log targets.
  • Error analysis by segment shows where the model needs more features.

items.title: Project 4: Movie Recommendation System
items.excerpt: Build "Because you watched…" recommendations three ways: popularity, content-based similarity on genres, and collaborative filtering with user-item ratings and cosine similarity.
items.content:
Netflix, Hotstar, Spotify, Amazon and Flipkart all run on recommendations. A good recommender keeps users watching and buying, so it's one of the most valuable models a company has, and a great portfolio project.

🎬 Because you watched…

  1. Riya watched three thrillers and a comedy this week. What next?
  2. Option 1: show what everyone watches. Safe, but not personal.
  3. Option 2: find movies with similar genres to what she liked.
  4. Option 3: find users with similar taste and recommend what they loved.

The data: a rating matrix

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

movies = ["Dhamaka Run", "Silent Signal", "Laugh Riot", "Family Feast", "Night Chase", "Cricket Dreams"]
genres = pd.DataFrame({"thriller": [1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0], "comedy": [0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0],
                       "drama": [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1], "sports": [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1]}, index=movies)
ratings = pd.DataFrame([[5, 4, 0, 0, 5, 0],
                        [4, 5, 0, 1, 4, 0],
                        [0, 0, 5, 4, 0, 3],
                        [1, 0, 4, 5, 0, 4],
                        [5, 0, 0, 0, 4, 1]],
                       index=["Riya", "Arjun", "Meera", "Kabir", "Sana"], columns=movies)   # 0 = not watched
print(ratings.loc["Sana"].to_dict())

Output:

{'Dhamaka Run': 5, 'Silent Signal': 0, 'Laugh Riot': 0, 'Family Feast': 0, 'Night Chase': 4, 'Cricket Dreams': 1}

1. Popularity baseline

watched = ratings.replace(0, np.nan)
popular = watched.mean().where(watched.count() >= 2).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(popular.round(2).dropna().to_dict())

Output:

{'Silent Signal': 4.5, 'Laugh Riot': 4.5, 'Night Chase': 4.33, 'Dhamaka Run': 3.75, 'Family Feast': 3.33, 'Cricket Dreams': 2.67}

2. Content-based: similar genres

from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

sim = pd.DataFrame(cosine_similarity(genres), index=movies, columns=movies)
print("like 'Silent Signal':", sim["Silent Signal"].drop("Silent Signal").sort_values(ascending=False).head(2).round(2).to_dict())

Output:

like 'Silent Signal': {'Dhamaka Run': 0.71, 'Night Chase': 0.71}

3. Collaborative filtering: similar users

sana = [5, 0, 0, 0, 4, 1]
riya = [5, 4, 0, 0, 5, 0]
dot = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(sana, riya))
norms = (sum(a * a for a in sana) ** 0.5) * (sum(b * b for b in riya) ** 0.5)
print(round(dot / norms, 2))
  1. Line 1: Sana's ratings for the six movies (0 = not watched).
  2. Line 2: Riya's ratings.
  3. Line 3: Dot product: 25 + 20 = 45. Movies both liked add a lot.
  4. Line 4: Divide by the vector lengths to remove "how much they rate overall".
  5. Line 5: 0.85: very similar taste. Riya loved "Silent Signal", which Sana hasn't seen: recommend it.
user_sim = pd.DataFrame(cosine_similarity(ratings), index=ratings.index, columns=ratings.index)

def recommend(user, k=2):
    neighbours = user_sim[user].drop(user)
    scores = ratings.drop(user).T.dot(neighbours) / neighbours.sum()
    unseen = ratings.loc[user] == 0
    return scores[unseen].sort_values(ascending=False).head(k).round(2).to_dict()

print("for Sana:", recommend("Sana"))
print("for Meera:", recommend("Meera"))

Output:

for Sana: {'Silent Signal': 3.86, 'Family Feast': 1.04}
for Meera: {'Dhamaka Run': 1.44, 'Night Chase': 0.51}

Sana gets the thriller her taste-twin Riya loved. (Meera's list shows a weakness of simple collaborative filtering with so little data: with only five users, weak neighbours still add noise. Real systems have millions of users and use better methods.)

Evaluating recommenders

  • Offline: hide some known ratings, recommend, measure precision@k / recall@k or ranking metrics like NDCG.
  • Online: A/B test: do users click, watch or buy more? That's the real test.
  • Cold start: new users or movies have no ratings: fall back to popularity and content-based methods.

Mention trade-offs in interviews: diversity (not ten identical thrillers), freshness (new releases), and fairness (not only blockbusters). Recommenders shape what people see.

Summary

  • Popularity is a baseline; content-based uses item features; collaborative filtering uses similar users or items.
  • Cosine similarity on rating vectors finds taste twins.
  • Evaluate offline with precision@k, online with A/B tests; handle cold start.

items.title: Project 5: Retail Sales Forecasting
items.excerpt: Forecast daily store sales for the next four weeks: calendar and lag features, festival effects, a gradient-boosting forecaster, a backtest against baselines, and a stock-planning recommendation.
items.content:
A store that orders too little runs out of stock and loses sales; too much, and money sits on shelves or food spoils. Forecasting demand is one of the most practical, high-value data science jobs in retail and FMCG.

🎬 Stocking up for Diwali

  1. A Kirana chain with 40 stores must order stock four weeks ahead.
  2. Weekends are busier, salaries arrive on the 1st, Diwali triples sweets sales.
  3. A boosting model learns from calendar features, recent sales and festival flags.
  4. The forecast plus a safety buffer becomes the order quantity. Fewer stock-outs, less waste.

Daily sales with real-world patterns

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
days = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2025-12-31", freq="D")
weekday_boost = np.where(days.dayofweek >= 5, 1.35, 1.0)
payday_boost = np.where(days.day <= 3, 1.2, 1.0)
festive = np.where(((days.month == 10) & (days.day >= 20)) | ((days.month == 11) & (days.day <= 5)), 1.8, 1.0)
trend = np.linspace(200, 260, len(days))
sales = pd.Series((trend * weekday_boost * payday_boost * festive * rng.lognormal(0, 0.08, len(days))).round(), index=days)
print(sales.resample("ME").sum().loc["2025-09":"2025-11"].astype(int).to_dict())

Output:

{Timestamp('2025-09-30 00:00:00'): 8532, Timestamp('2025-10-31 00:00:00'): 11233, Timestamp('2025-11-30 00:00:00'): 10305}

Features

def make_features(s):
    f = pd.DataFrame({"y": s})
    f["dow"] = s.index.dayofweek
    f["day"] = s.index.day
    f["month"] = s.index.month
    f["festive"] = (((s.index.month == 10) & (s.index.day >= 20)) | ((s.index.month == 11) & (s.index.day <= 5))).astype(int)
    f["lag_28"] = s.shift(28)                      # known 4 weeks ahead
    f["roll_28_mean"] = s.shift(28).rolling(28).mean()
    return f.dropna()

data = make_features(sales)
print(data.columns.tolist(), len(data))

Output:

['y', 'dow', 'day', 'month', 'festive', 'lag_28', 'roll_28_mean'] 676
horizon = 28
lag = 7
usable = lag >= horizon
safe_lag = max(lag, horizon)
print(usable, safe_lag)
  1. Line 1: We order stock 28 days ahead, so we forecast 28 days out.
  2. Line 2: A tempting feature: sales 7 days ago.
  3. Line 3: But for a day 28 days in the future, "7 days before it" is still in the future: we don't know it yet. Using it would be leakage.
  4. Line 4: So we use lag 28 (or longer) and rolling means that end 28 days back.
  5. Line 5: Only information known at ordering time.

Backtest: train on the past, test on the last 8 weeks

from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

train, test = data[:"2025-11-05"], data["2025-11-06":]
X_cols = ["dow", "day", "month", "festive", "lag_28", "roll_28_mean"]
model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(train[X_cols], train["y"])
pred = model.predict(test[X_cols])

def mape(actual, forecast):
    return float(np.mean(np.abs(actual - forecast) / actual) * 100)

seasonal_naive = test["lag_28"]
print(f"model MAPE {mape(test['y'], pred):.1f}%  vs  seasonal-naive MAPE {mape(test['y'], seasonal_naive):.1f}%")

Output:

model MAPE 12.2%  vs  seasonal-naive MAPE 33.9%

The model beats the naive "same day 4 weeks ago" baseline by a wide margin, mostly because it knows weekdays and paydays.

From forecast to order

next_4_weeks = pred[-28:].sum()
error_spread = np.std(test["y"] - pred)
safety = 1.65 * error_spread * np.sqrt(28)          # about 95% service level
print(f"forecast {next_4_weeks:,.0f} units + safety stock {safety:,.0f} = order {next_4_weeks + safety:,.0f}")

Output:

forecast 7,091 units + safety stock 241 = order 7,331

Safety stock covers forecast error so the store rarely runs out. The 1.65 multiplier corresponds to roughly a 95% chance of not stocking out.

Portfolio checklist

  • [ ] Real data: a public retail dataset (for example the Kaggle store sales datasets), with holiday calendars
  • [ ] Baselines (naive, seasonal naive) vs model, MAPE per week
  • [ ] No leakage: lags ≥ horizon, time-based split
  • [ ] Turn the forecast into a business decision (order quantity, staffing)

Summary

  • Retail demand has weekly, payday, festival and trend patterns: encode them as features.
  • Use lags at least as long as the forecast horizon to avoid leakage.
  • Backtest on the latest period against seasonal-naive.
  • Forecast + safety stock = an order the business can use.

items.title: Project 6: Image Classifier with Transfer Learning
items.excerpt: Classify crop-leaf photos as healthy or diseased: dataset layout, augmentation, transfer learning with MobileNetV2 in Keras, evaluation with a confusion matrix, and a runnable small-scale version.
items.content:
A farmer photographs a tomato leaf with a cheap phone; an app says "early blight, 92% sure, here's what to do". Image classification with transfer learning makes projects like this possible with a few thousand photos and an ordinary laptop or free GPU notebook.

🎬 A plant doctor in your pocket

  1. Leaf diseases spread fast. Experts can't visit every farm.
  2. Thousands of labelled leaf photos: healthy, early blight, leaf mould.
  3. A model pretrained on millions of images already knows edges, textures and shapes. We teach it only the last step.
  4. The trained model, shrunk for phones, gives an answer in a second, even offline.

Dataset layout

Keras (and most tools) can read images straight from class folders:

leaves/
  train/
    healthy/      img001.jpg ...
    early_blight/ img201.jpg ...
    leaf_mould/   img401.jpg ...
  val/
    healthy/ ...  early_blight/ ...  leaf_mould/ ...

Public datasets like PlantVillage have tens of thousands of labelled leaf images. Check the licence, and note that lab photos look cleaner than real field photos: collect some real ones for testing.

The transfer-learning model (Keras)

from tensorflow import keras

train = keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory("leaves/train", image_size=(224, 224), batch_size=32)
val = keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory("leaves/val", image_size=(224, 224), batch_size=32)

augment = keras.Sequential([keras.layers.RandomFlip("horizontal"), keras.layers.RandomRotation(0.1),
                            keras.layers.RandomZoom(0.1), keras.layers.RandomContrast(0.2)])
base = keras.applications.MobileNetV2(input_shape=(224, 224, 3), include_top=False, weights="imagenet")
base.trainable = False                                   # stage 1: train only the new head

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(224, 224, 3))
x = augment(inputs)
x = keras.applications.mobilenet_v2.preprocess_input(x)
x = base(x, training=False)
x = keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
x = keras.layers.Dropout(0.3)(x)
outputs = keras.layers.Dense(3, activation="softmax")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
model.compile(keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3), "sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
model.fit(train, validation_data=val, epochs=10,
          callbacks=[keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=3, restore_best_weights=True)])

base.trainable = True                                    # stage 2: fine-tune gently
model.compile(keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-5), "sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
model.fit(train, validation_data=val, epochs=5)

A small runnable version of the same workflow

No GPU here, so we use scikit-learn's 8×8 digit images to practise the full workflow: split, augment, train, evaluate.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report

digits = load_digits()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(digits.images, digits.target, test_size=0.25,
                                                    stratify=digits.target, random_state=0)
shifted = np.roll(X_train, 1, axis=2)                            # augmentation: shift right by 1 pixel
X_aug = np.concatenate([X_train, shifted]).reshape(-1, 64) / 16
y_aug = np.concatenate([y_train, y_train])

clf = SVC(gamma="scale", C=5).fit(X_aug, y_aug)
pred = clf.predict(X_test.reshape(-1, 64) / 16)
print("accuracy:", round((pred == y_test).mean(), 3))
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, pred)
off = cm - np.diag(np.diag(cm))
i, j = np.unravel_index(off.argmax(), off.shape)
print(f"most common mistake: true {i} predicted as {j} ({off[i, j]} times)")

Output:

accuracy: 0.991
most common mistake: true 8 predicted as 1 (2 times)
row_true_blight = {"healthy": 6, "early_blight": 88, "leaf_mould": 6}
total = sum(row_true_blight.values())
recall = row_true_blight["early_blight"] / total
worst = max((k for k in row_true_blight if k != "early_blight"), key=row_true_blight.get)
print(total, recall, worst)
  1. Line 1: One row of a leaf-disease confusion matrix: 100 leaves that truly had early blight, and what the model said.
  2. Line 2: 100 truly diseased leaves.
  3. Line 3: Recall for early blight: 88%.
  4. Line 4: The most common confusion (healthy and leaf mould tie at 6; max picks the first).
  5. Line 5: Errors are where you collect more data next.

Deploying to a phone

  • Convert with TensorFlow Lite (tf.lite.TFLiteConverter), optionally with 8-bit quantisation to shrink the model about 4×.
  • Show the top prediction and the confidence; below a threshold, say "not sure, retake the photo in daylight".
  • Collect (with permission) photos users submit, label the hard ones, and retrain.

Portfolio checklist

  • [ ] Data card: source, licence, class counts, train/val/test split by source (no near-duplicates across splits)
  • [ ] Baseline (frozen base) vs fine-tuned, accuracy and per-class recall
  • [ ] Confusion matrix with the dangerous mistakes discussed
  • [ ] A demo: Streamlit or Hugging Face Spaces app where people upload a photo

Summary

  • Organise images in class folders; augment to simulate real-world variety.
  • Transfer learning: freeze a pretrained base, train a new head, then fine-tune gently.
  • Evaluate with per-class recall and the confusion matrix; focus on costly mistakes.
  • Shrink with TFLite for phones and keep improving with real user photos.

🎉 You've finished the Data Scientist portfolio projects, and the whole Data Scientist track.

items.title: Signature Project 1: UPI Fraud Radar
items.excerpt: Build a fraud alert system for Indian digital payments on a real-looking dataset of 3,000 transactions where only 1.4% are fraud. Find the signals, score every payment, and pick the alert threshold by rupees saved, not by accuracy.
items.content:
Every bank and payment app in India runs a fraud radar. The hard part is not the model. It is that fraud is rare (here 42 of 3,000 payments), every missed fraud costs real money, and every false alarm annoys a genuine customer. This project teaches the thinking a fraud analyst uses on day one, on a dataset you will not find anywhere else: the VitalStack bank transactions set from the Datasets Hub.

🎬 Catching the 1.4%

  1. 3,000 payments. Only 42 are fraud. A model that says "never fraud" is 98.6% accurate and completely useless.
  2. New device, odd hours, gaming and electronics, big amounts: fraud leaves fingerprints.
  3. Every alert costs about ₹30 in support time and annoyed customers. Every miss costs the full amount.
  4. From ₹1.75 lakh lost to about ₹16,000 total cost. That is the number your manager wants.

Load the data

The dataset is free on the Datasets Hub. You can download the CSV or read it straight from its address:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

DATA = "https://vitalstack.co.in/wp-content/themes/vitalstack/data/datasets/"
df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "bank-transactions.csv", parse_dates=["timestamp"])
print(df.shape)
print(df["is_fraud"].value_counts().to_dict())
print("fraud rate:", round(df["is_fraud"].mean() * 100, 2), "%")

Output:

(3000, 9)
{0: 2958, 1: 42}
fraud rate: 1.4 %

This is the first lesson of fraud work: accuracy lies. Predicting "not fraud" for everyone scores 98.6% accuracy and catches nothing. We will judge models by how much fraud they catch and what they cost.

Find the fingerprints

Fraud analysts start with simple group-by questions: *where* is fraud more common than normal?

df["hour"] = df["timestamp"].dt.hour
df["night"] = (df["hour"] < 6).astype(int)            # midnight to 6 am
for col in ["new_device", "night", "merchant_category"]:
    rate = df.groupby(col)["is_fraud"].mean().mul(100).round(1)
    print(col, rate.sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).to_dict())
print(df.groupby("is_fraud")["amount_inr"].median().to_dict())

Output:

new_device {'Yes': 15.4, 'No': 0.6}
night {1: 2.6, 0: 1.0}
merchant_category {'Gaming': 4.3, 'Electronics': 2.5, 'Travel': 1.7}
{0: 474.77, 1: 2246.87}

Four clear signals:

  1. A payment from a new device is 25 times more likely to be fraud (15.4% vs 0.6%). This is why your bank sends an OTP when you log in on a new phone.
  2. Night-time payments are 2.6 times riskier.
  3. Gaming and electronics lead: easy to resell, popular with scammers.
  4. The median fraud is ₹2,247, almost five times a normal payment (₹475).

Score every payment

We turn the signals into features and train a logistic regression. With only 42 frauds, a single train/test split is noisy, so we use 5-fold cross-validation: every payment gets a risk score from a model that never saw it.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score

df["new_dev"] = (df["new_device"] == "Yes").astype(int)
df["log_amt"] = np.log10(df["amount_inr"])            # ₹100 → 2, ₹10,000 → 4
df["risky_cat"] = df["merchant_category"].isin(["Gaming", "Electronics"]).astype(int)
df["current_ac"] = (df["account_type"] == "Current").astype(int)
X = df[["log_amt", "new_dev", "night", "risky_cat", "current_ac"]]
y = df["is_fraud"]

model = LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=1000)
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
df["risk"] = cross_val_predict(model, X, y, cv=cv, method="predict_proba")[:, 1]
print("ROC-AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(y, df["risk"]), 3))
print("PR-AUC :", round(average_precision_score(y, df["risk"]), 3))

Output:

ROC-AUC: 0.943
PR-AUC : 0.428
  • ROC-AUC 0.943: pick one fraud and one genuine payment at random, and 94% of the time the fraud gets the higher risk score.
  • PR-AUC 0.428: on rare events this is the honest number. Random guessing would score about 0.014, the fraud rate, so the model is about 30 times better than chance.

class_weight="balanced" tells the model that each fraud matters as much as 70 genuine payments. Without it, the model learns to say "not fraud" almost always.

Compare with a hand-written rule

Banks often start with rules. Ours: "new device and more than ₹2,000".

rule = (df["new_dev"] == 1) & (df["amount_inr"] > 2000)
print("rule flags", int(rule.sum()), "payments and catches", int((rule & (y == 1)).sum()), "of", int(y.sum()))

Output:

rule flags 21 payments and catches 11 of 42

The rule is precise (11 of 21 flags are fraud) but misses 31 frauds. Models shine where many weak signals add up.

Pick the threshold by money

Every alert costs about ₹30: an OTP call, a blocked payment, a customer who might switch apps. Every missed fraud costs its full amount. So the best threshold is the one with the lowest total cost, not 0.5.

ALERT_COST = 30
flagged = 333
missed_amount = 5709
total = missed_amount + ALERT_COST * flagged
print(total)
  1. Line 1: Each alert costs about ₹30 in support time and friction.
  2. Line 2: At this threshold the radar flags 333 of 3,000 payments.
  3. Line 3: The frauds it still misses add up to ₹5,709.
  4. Line 4: Total cost = missed money + cost of all alerts.
  5. Line 5: ₹15,699, compared with ₹1,74,522 lost with no radar at all.
ALERT_COST = 30

def total_cost(threshold):
    flagged = df["risk"] >= threshold
    missed = df.loc[~flagged & (y == 1), "amount_inr"].sum()
    return missed + ALERT_COST * flagged.sum(), int((flagged & (y == 1)).sum()), int(flagged.sum())

print("no radar:", round(df.loc[y == 1, "amount_inr"].sum()))
for t in [0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]:
    cost, caught, flagged = total_cost(t)
    print(f"threshold {t}: catch {caught}/42, alerts {flagged}, total cost ₹{cost:,.0f}")
best = min(np.arange(0.05, 0.99, 0.01), key=lambda t: total_cost(t)[0])
print("best threshold:", round(best, 2), "cost ₹{:,.0f}".format(total_cost(best)[0]))

Output:

no radar: 174522
threshold 0.3: catch 39/42, alerts 560, total cost ₹18,639
threshold 0.5: catch 37/42, alerts 358, total cost ₹16,449
threshold 0.7: catch 31/42, alerts 232, total cost ₹29,030
threshold 0.9: catch 23/42, alerts 86, total cost ₹42,843
best threshold: 0.54 cost ₹15,699

At threshold 0.54 the radar catches 37 of 42 frauds with 333 alerts, cutting the total cost by 91%. Notice how a "safe-looking" high threshold (0.9) costs almost three times more: the frauds it lets through are expensive.

Explain it to the risk team

model.fit(X, y)
weights = pd.Series(model.coef_[0], index=X.columns).round(2).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(weights.to_dict())

Output:

{'new_dev': 4.22, 'log_amt': 3.57, 'risky_cat': 2.26, 'night': 1.03, 'current_ac': 0.66}

In plain words for the risk team: *"A new device is the strongest warning sign. Each tenfold increase in amount adds strong risk. Gaming and electronics come next, then night-time."* That sentence, plus the cost table, is what gets a model approved.

Real fraud systems also look at things this dataset does not have: how fast payments arrive (velocity), whether the payee is new, and the device's location. Add one such feature in your own version (for example, payments per account per hour) and show how much it saves.

Make it yours

  • Velocity feature: simulate several payments from one account within 10 minutes and add a "payments in the last hour" column.
  • Two-stage radar: auto-block above 0.9, send an in-app confirmation from 0.54 to 0.9 (cost ₹5 instead of ₹30), and recompute the total cost.
  • Dashboard: in Power BI or Streamlit, show alerts per hour, top risky categories, and money saved this week.

Portfolio checklist

  • [ ] Shows why accuracy is the wrong metric for rare events
  • [ ] Fraud rate by device, hour and category, with a short business reading
  • [ ] Cross-validated risk scores, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC explained in plain words
  • [ ] A rule baseline next to the model
  • [ ] Threshold chosen by total rupee cost, with the cost table in the README
  • [ ] One feature or idea of your own that the lesson did not include

items.title: Signature Project 2: The 30-Minute Promise (Food Delivery ETA)
items.excerpt: Predict how long a food order will take across eight Indian cities, clean impossible delivery times, explain the effect of rain and peak hours in minutes, and choose an ETA promise that keeps customers happy.
items.content:
Open any food app and you see a promise: "Arriving in 32 min". Promise too little time and the order is late, the rating drops and support gets angry calls. Promise too much and the customer orders from a competitor. In this project you build the ETA engine behind that promise on the VitalStack food delivery dataset (2,500 orders, 8 cities) from the Datasets Hub.

🎬 Behind "Arriving in 32 min"

  1. A biryani, 8 km away, at 8 pm, in the rain. How long will it really take?
  2. A few orders say 250 to 350 minutes. Real, or a cancelled order that was never closed?
  3. Each extra kilometre, rain and peak hour adds a number of minutes you can explain.
  4. Add a smart buffer so 9 out of 10 orders arrive on time.

Load and look

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

DATA = "https://vitalstack.co.in/wp-content/themes/vitalstack/data/datasets/"
df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "food-delivery.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df["delivery_time_min"].describe().round(1)[["mean", "50%", "max"]].to_dict())

Output:

(2500, 10)
{'mean': 46.1, '50%': 46.0, 'max': 350.0}

A maximum of 350 minutes (almost six hours) for a food order is a red flag. Before any model, we deal with outliers.

Clean the impossible orders

q1, q3 = df["delivery_time_min"].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
fence = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
print("IQR fence:", fence, "minutes; orders above it:", int((df["delivery_time_min"] > fence).sum()))
print(df.nlargest(5, "delivery_time_min")[["distance_km", "prep_time_min", "weather", "delivery_time_min"]].to_string(index=False))

Output:

IQR fence: 87.5 minutes; orders above it: 10
 distance_km  prep_time_min weather  delivery_time_min
        8.72             27   Rainy                350
        3.83             11   Clear                311
        4.11             33  Cloudy                288
        8.08             34   Clear                268
        5.47             10  Cloudy                253

A 3.8 km order on a clear day cannot take 311 minutes. These are almost certainly orders that were cancelled or never closed in the system. The statistical fence (87.5 minutes) also flags two slow but believable orders, so we use a business rule instead: drop anything over 2 hours, and report how many.

clean = df[df["delivery_time_min"] <= 120].copy()
print("removed:", len(df) - len(clean), "orders")
print("mean before:", round(df["delivery_time_min"].mean(), 1), "after:", round(clean["delivery_time_min"].mean(), 1))

Output:

removed: 8 orders
mean before: 46.1 after: 45.4

Eight bad rows out of 2,500 moved the average by almost a minute. On a squared-error model, their effect would be much bigger.

What makes an order late?

We call an order late if it takes more than 45 minutes.

clean["late"] = (clean["delivery_time_min"] > 45).astype(int)
print("late overall:", round(clean["late"].mean() * 100, 1), "%")
for col in ["weather", "peak_hour"]:
    print(col, clean.groupby(col)["late"].mean().mul(100).round(1).to_dict())
bands = pd.cut(clean["delivery_time_min"], [0, 30, 45, 60, 120], labels=["0-30", "31-45", "46-60", "61-120"])
print("rating by minutes:", clean.groupby(bands, observed=True)["rating"].mean().round(2).to_dict())

Output:

late overall: 49.9 %
weather {'Clear': 46.4, 'Cloudy': 42.1, 'Rainy': 68.4}
peak_hour {'No': 42.6, 'Yes': 63.7}
rating by minutes: {'0-30': 4.83, '31-45': 4.48, '46-60': 3.2, '61-120': 1.88}

The rating line is the business case in one row: orders under 30 minutes average 4.83 stars, and orders over an hour average 1.88. Rain pushes the late rate from about 46% to 68%, and peak hours to 64%.

Build an explainable ETA model

A linear regression is perfect here because every coefficient is "minutes per something", which operations teams understand.

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

clean["peak"] = (clean["peak_hour"] == "Yes").astype(int)
clean["rain"] = (clean["weather"] == "Rainy").astype(int)
X = clean[["distance_km", "prep_time_min", "peak", "rain"]]
y = clean["delivery_time_min"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)

eta = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
print({k: round(float(v), 2) for k, v in zip(X.columns, eta.coef_)})
pred = eta.predict(X_test)
print("model MAE:", round(mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred), 1), "min")
print("guess-the-average MAE:", round(mean_absolute_error(y_test, np.full(len(y_test), y_train.mean())), 1), "min")

Output:

{'distance_km': 3.19, 'prep_time_min': 1.02, 'peak': 7.71, 'rain': 9.91}
model MAE: 3.1 min
guess-the-average MAE: 12.0 min

Read it like an operations manager: every kilometre adds 3.2 minutes, rain adds about 10, peak hour adds about 8, and each minute of kitchen time adds one minute to delivery. The model is wrong by about 3 minutes on average, four times better than guessing the average.

Turn the prediction into a promise

If we show the raw prediction, half the orders arrive a bit late, because the prediction is a middle estimate. So we add a buffer, chosen from the model's past errors.

predicted = 58
buffer = 5
promise = predicted + buffer
print("Arriving in", promise, "min")
  1. Line 1: The model predicts 58 minutes for this order.
  2. Line 2: Past errors show that adding about 5 minutes covers 9 out of 10 orders.
  3. Line 3: The promise shown in the app is the prediction plus the buffer.
  4. Line 4: The customer sees one honest number.
errors = y_train - eta.predict(X_train)
buffer = np.percentile(errors, 90)
print("90th percentile buffer:", round(buffer, 1), "min")
for b in [0, 5, 8, 10]:
    on_time = (y_test <= pred + b).mean() * 100
    print(f"buffer {b:>2} min: {on_time:.1f}% on time")

Output:

90th percentile buffer: 5.1 min
buffer  0 min: 49.9% on time
buffer  5 min: 88.1% on time
buffer  8 min: 96.3% on time
buffer 10 min: 98.6% on time

Without a buffer, the app breaks its promise half the time. A 5-minute buffer keeps 88% of promises, and 8 minutes keeps 96%. Which to choose is a product decision: a longer promise costs some orders, and a broken promise costs ratings.

Try three real orders

orders = pd.DataFrame({"distance_km": [3, 8, 8], "prep_time_min": [15, 25, 25],
                       "peak": [0, 1, 1], "rain": [0, 0, 1]},
                      index=["3 km, quiet, clear", "8 km, peak, clear", "8 km, peak, rain"])
orders["promise_min"] = (eta.predict(orders) + buffer).round()
print(orders["promise_min"].to_dict())

Output:

{'3 km, quiet, clear': 29.0, '8 km, peak, clear': 63.0, '8 km, peak, rain': 73.0}

Same restaurant, same distance: rain adds 10 minutes to the promise. That is exactly the kind of number a city manager uses to plan extra riders on monsoon evenings.

The dataset's ratings drop sharply after 45 minutes. A strong extra step is to predict the chance of being late (a classifier) and send a ₹20 coupon automatically when it is above 70%, then estimate how many 1-star ratings that saves.

Make it yours

  • City effects: add one-hot city columns. Is Hyderabad slower even after distance and rain?
  • Quantile model: train GradientBoostingRegressor(loss="quantile", alpha=0.9) to predict the 90% promise directly, and compare it with the buffer approach.
  • Rider planning: for rainy peak hours, estimate how many extra riders keep the late rate under 30%.

Portfolio checklist

  • [ ] Outliers found, explained and removed with a clear business rule
  • [ ] Late rate by weather and peak hour, and ratings by delivery time
  • [ ] Linear ETA model with coefficients explained in minutes
  • [ ] MAE compared with a naive baseline
  • [ ] Buffer chosen from errors, with an on-time table
  • [ ] One recommendation for operations, backed by a number

items.title: Signature Project 3: Clean-Air Alert for Indian Cities
items.excerpt: Turn a year of weather and AQI readings from eight Indian cities into a health alert. Fill missing readings the right way, map AQI to the official categories, find the seasonal pattern, and design an early warning that is tested against an honest baseline.
items.content:
Every winter, news channels show Delhi's sky turning grey. Parents of children with asthma want one simple thing: a warning before a bad-air day, so they can keep inhalers ready and plan indoor play. In this project you build that alert on the VitalStack city weather and AQI dataset (8 cities, one reading every 3 days in 2025) from the Datasets Hub, and you learn the most important rule of forecasting: always beat the simple baseline, or admit you didn't.

🎬 A warning before the smog

  1. Delhi's air turns "Severe" in winter. Families want a heads-up, not a surprise.
  2. Some days have no AQI reading. Drop them or fill them?
  3. AQI follows the seasons: clean monsoons, dirty winters.
  4. Missing a bad day is worse than one extra warning. So we warn a little early.

Load and find the gaps

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

DATA = "https://vitalstack.co.in/wp-content/themes/vitalstack/data/datasets/"
df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "city-weather-aqi.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).sort_values(["city", "date"])
print(df.shape)
print("missing AQI readings:", int(df["aqi"].isna().sum()))
print(df[df["aqi"].isna()]["city"].value_counts().to_dict())

Output:

(976, 7)
missing AQI readings: 20
{'Lucknow': 5, 'Pune': 4, 'Bengaluru': 4, 'Mumbai': 3, 'Ahmedabad': 2, 'Chennai': 1, 'Delhi': 1}

Sensors fail and stations go offline, so real air data always has holes. Air quality changes slowly, so the best estimate for a missing reading is between its neighbours in the same city. That is linear interpolation, done city by city so Delhi's values never leak into Bengaluru's.

df["aqi_filled"] = (df.groupby("city")["aqi"]
                      .transform(lambda s: s.interpolate(limit_direction="both"))
                      .round())
print("still missing:", int(df["aqi_filled"].isna().sum()))
lko = df[df["city"] == "Lucknow"]
print("Lucknow mean, dropping gaps:", round(lko["aqi"].mean(), 1), "| filling gaps:", round(lko["aqi_filled"].mean(), 1))

Output:

still missing: 0
Lucknow mean, dropping gaps: 204.8 | filling gaps: 207.0

Filling changed Lucknow's average by about two points. Small here, but if the gaps had all been on bad winter days, simply dropping them would have made the city look cleaner than it is.

Speak the official language: AQI categories

People don't act on "AQI 287". They act on "Poor". India's national AQI uses six bands, so we map every reading to its band.

bands = [0, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500]
names = ["Good", "Satisfactory", "Moderate", "Poor", "Very Poor", "Severe"]
df["band"] = pd.cut(df["aqi_filled"], bands, labels=names, include_lowest=True)
table = pd.crosstab(df["city"], df["band"])
print(table.loc[["Delhi", "Lucknow", "Kolkata", "Bengaluru"]].to_string())

Output:

band       Good  Satisfactory  Moderate  Poor  Very Poor  Severe
city
Delhi         0             1        57    33         17      14
Lucknow       0            13        61    18         29       1
Kolkata       4            24        63    28          3       0
Bengaluru    34            53        35     0          0       0

Delhi has 14 Severe readings in the year and Bengaluru has none. The cities live in different worlds, which is why a national alert must be set city by city.

The seasonal story

delhi = df[df["city"] == "Delhi"]
monthly = delhi.groupby(delhi["date"].dt.month)["aqi_filled"].mean().round()
print(monthly.to_dict())
print("winter-ness vs AQI (correlation of min temperature):", round(delhi["temp_min_c"].corr(delhi["aqi_filled"]), 2))

Output:

{1: 402.0, 2: 209.0, 3: 206.0, 4: 218.0, 5: 208.0, 6: 134.0, 7: 120.0, 8: 126.0, 9: 134.0, 10: 197.0, 11: 403.0, 12: 399.0}
winter-ness vs AQI (correlation of min temperature): -0.74

Delhi's average AQI doubles from about 200 in October to 400 in November, and stays there till January. Cold nights trap pollution near the ground, which shows up as a strong negative correlation (−0.74) with the minimum temperature. Monsoon rain (June to September) washes the air clean.

The baseline you must beat

Our question: will the next reading be Poor or worse (above 200)? The simplest forecast is *persistence*: "it will be like today". Any model must beat it.

today_aqi = 236
alert = today_aqi > 200
print("Alert for next reading:", alert)
  1. Line 1: Today's AQI reading is 236 (Poor).
  2. Line 2: Persistence says tomorrow looks like today, so alert if today is above 200.
  3. Line 3: The family gets a warning.
df["next_aqi"] = df.groupby("city")["aqi_filled"].shift(-1)
data = df.dropna(subset=["next_aqi"])
test = data[data["date"] >= "2025-09-01"]           # judge on the last four months only
bad_next = test["next_aqi"] > 200

def score(alert):
    return {"caught": int((alert & bad_next).sum()), "of": int(bad_next.sum()),
            "missed": int((~alert & bad_next).sum()), "false_alarms": int((alert & ~bad_next).sum())}

print("persistence:", score(test["aqi_filled"] > 200))

Output:

persistence: {'caught': 85, 'of': 103, 'missed': 18, 'false_alarms': 13}

Persistence catches 85 of 103 bad readings. Now the honest test: can a model do better?

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

g = data.groupby("city")["aqi_filled"]
data = data.assign(trend=g.diff().fillna(0))           # is the air getting worse or better?
train = data[data["date"] < "2025-09-01"]
test = data[data["date"] >= "2025-09-01"]
features = ["aqi_filled", "trend"]
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(train[features], train["next_aqi"] > 200)
print("model:", score(pd.Series(model.predict(test[features]), index=test.index)))

Output:

model: {'caught': 78, 'of': 103, 'missed': 25, 'false_alarms': 10}

The model misses more bad days (25 versus 18). In this dataset the next reading is mostly "today plus noise", so the model has nothing extra to learn. Saying so in your report is a strength, not a weakness: many beginner projects hide a model that loses to the baseline.

Design the early warning

For a child with asthma, a missed bad day is far worse than an extra warning. So instead of a fancier model, we move the alert line: warn when today's AQI is above a lower number.

for line in [200, 180, 160, 140]:
    print(f"alert when AQI > {line}:", score(test["aqi_filled"] > line))

Output:

alert when AQI > 200: {'caught': 85, 'of': 103, 'missed': 18, 'false_alarms': 13}
alert when AQI > 180: {'caught': 93, 'of': 103, 'missed': 10, 'false_alarms': 25}
alert when AQI > 160: {'caught': 98, 'of': 103, 'missed': 5, 'false_alarms': 45}
alert when AQI > 140: {'caught': 101, 'of': 103, 'missed': 2, 'false_alarms': 73}

At 160, the alert misses only 5 of 103 bad readings, at the cost of 45 extra warnings over four months across 8 cities: less than one extra warning per city per fortnight. That is a trade-off families will happily accept, and you can explain it in one sentence.

Health messages make the alert useful. For example: Poor, sensitive groups should limit long outdoor activity. Very Poor, everyone should reduce outdoor exertion and asthma patients should keep medicines ready. Severe, avoid outdoor activity. Always point people to official sources such as the national AQI bulletin for decisions.

Make it yours

  • Daily data: this set has a reading every 3 days. Explain how a 1-day forecast would change the baseline, and why persistence gets even stronger.
  • City-specific lines: choose a different alert line per city so each one misses at most 5% of bad days.
  • A WhatsApp-style message: write a function that turns a city, date and band into a short Hindi and English alert text.

Portfolio checklist

  • [ ] Missing readings filled per city, with the effect of filling vs dropping
  • [ ] Every reading mapped to the six national AQI bands, compared across cities
  • [ ] Seasonal pattern shown and explained (winter inversion, monsoon wash-out)
  • [ ] Persistence baseline measured on a time-based test period
  • [ ] A model honestly compared with the baseline
  • [ ] Alert line chosen by the cost of missed days, with the trade-off table

items.title: Signature Project 4: Fair Pay and Attrition Audit
items.excerpt: Act as the data analyst for an HR head with 1,200 employees across eight cities. Fill missing salaries correctly, test whether remote workers are paid fairly once experience and department are taken into account, find who is about to leave, and put a rupee figure on keeping them.
items.content:
An HR head asks two questions every appraisal season: "Are we paying people fairly?" and "Who is about to leave?" Answering them with raw averages leads to wrong and sometimes unfair decisions. In this project you answer both properly, with the VitalStack HR employees dataset (1,200 people, 6 departments, 8 cities) from the Datasets Hub.

🎬 The appraisal-season brief

  1. "Are remote workers underpaid? And why are good people leaving?"
  2. 30 salaries are missing. The average would put a senior engineer on a fresher's pay.
  3. Compare like with like: same department, same experience.
  4. Retaining a few high performers costs far less than replacing them.

Load and inspect

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

DATA = "https://vitalstack.co.in/wp-content/themes/vitalstack/data/datasets/"
df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "hr-employees.csv")
print(df.shape)
print("missing salaries:", int(df["salary_lpa"].isna().sum()))
print("left the company:", round((df["left_company"] == "Yes").mean() * 100, 1), "%")

Output:

(1200, 10)
missing salaries: 30
left the company: 11.8 %

Fill missing salaries like an analyst

Filling with the overall average (₹8 lakh) would give a 13-year engineer the same pay as a support fresher. Salary depends on department and experience, so we fill each gap with the median of people like them.

df["exp_band"] = pd.cut(df["experience_years"], [-1, 2, 5, 10, 40], labels=["0-2", "3-5", "6-10", "10+"])
peers = df.groupby(["department", "exp_band"], observed=True)["salary_lpa"].transform("median")
df["salary"] = df["salary_lpa"].fillna(peers).round(2)
print("overall average:", round(df["salary_lpa"].mean(), 2), "lakh")
print(df.loc[df["salary_lpa"].isna(), ["department", "experience_years", "salary"]].head(3).to_string(index=False))

Output:

overall average: 8.04 lakh
 department  experience_years  salary
  Marketing                 7    8.76
    Support                13    6.47
Engineering                13   24.08

The senior engineer gets ₹24 lakh instead of 8. Group-wise filling keeps the analysis honest.

Is remote work paid fairly?

The raw medians suggest remote workers earn a little less. But raw medians mix departments and experience levels together.

print(df.groupby("work_mode")["salary"].median().to_dict())

Output:

{'Hybrid': 6.81, 'Office': 6.99, 'Remote': 6.7}

To compare like with like we use a regression on the log of salary, so each coefficient becomes a percentage difference, holding the other columns fixed.

coef = 0.072
pct = (2.718281828 ** coef - 1) * 100
print(round(pct, 1), "% more salary per year of experience")
  1. Line 1: The regression gives 0.072 for experience_years on log(salary).
  2. Line 2: exp(coef) − 1 converts it into a percentage change.
  3. Line 3: About 7.5% more pay for each extra year.
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = pd.get_dummies(df[["department", "work_mode"]], drop_first=True).astype(int)
X["experience_years"] = df["experience_years"]
X["performance_rating"] = df["performance_rating"]
reg = LinearRegression().fit(X, np.log(df["salary"]))
effect = pd.Series((np.exp(reg.coef_) - 1) * 100, index=X.columns).round(1)
print(effect[["work_mode_Office", "work_mode_Remote", "experience_years", "performance_rating"]].to_dict())
print("R²:", round(reg.score(X, np.log(df["salary"])), 2))

Output:

{'work_mode_Office': -0.2, 'work_mode_Remote': 0.1, 'experience_years': 7.5, 'performance_rating': -0.7}
R²: 0.85

Once department and experience are held fixed, office and remote staff are paid the same (differences of −0.2% and +0.1%). The raw gap came from *who* works remotely, not from unfair pay. The model explains 85% of the variation in pay (R² 0.85), so this conclusion rests on solid ground.

But one line should worry the HR head: performance rating has no effect on pay (−0.7% per rating point, basically zero). Top performers are paid like everyone else in their band.

Who is leaving?

df["left"] = (df["left_company"] == "Yes").astype(int)
df["top_performer"] = df["performance_rating"] >= 4
rates = df.pivot_table(index="overtime", columns="top_performer", values="left", aggfunc="mean").mul(100).round(1)
print(rates.to_string())
print(df.groupby("overtime")["left"].mean().mul(100).round(1).to_dict())

Output:

top_performer  False  True
overtime
No               8.1    5.9
Yes             22.5   22.2
{'No': 7.2, 'Yes': 22.4}

Overtime is the loudest signal: people on regular overtime leave about three times as often (22% against 7%). Among top performers on overtime, more than one in five leaves within the year, and they are exactly the people the company can least afford to lose.

Put a rupee figure on keeping them

We find top performers who do overtime and are paid at or below the median of their peers (same department and experience band), then compare two options:

  • Do nothing: expect their observed leave rate to continue. Replacing an employee commonly costs about half a year's salary (hiring, notice period, ramp-up time). Treat that 50% as an assumption your HR team can change.
  • Act: give them a 10% raise and cut their overtime, and assume (another assumption to test) that this halves their attrition.
df["vs_peers"] = df["salary"] / df.groupby(["department", "exp_band"], observed=True)["salary"].transform("median")
at_risk = df[df["top_performer"] & (df["overtime"] == "Yes") & (df["vs_peers"] <= 1)]
total_pay = at_risk["salary"].sum() * 100000              # lakh → rupees
leave_rate = at_risk["left"].mean()
REPLACE = 0.5                                            # replacement cost = 50% of salary (assumption)
do_nothing = leave_rate * total_pay * REPLACE
act = 0.10 * total_pay + (leave_rate / 2) * total_pay * 1.10 * REPLACE
print("people at risk:", len(at_risk), "| their yearly pay: ₹{:.1f} crore".format(total_pay / 1e7))
print("observed leave rate:", round(leave_rate * 100, 1), "%")
print("cost of doing nothing: ₹{:.1f} lakh".format(do_nothing / 1e5))
print("cost of 10% raise + less overtime: ₹{:.1f} lakh".format(act / 1e5))

Output:

people at risk: 78 | their yearly pay: ₹5.3 crore
observed leave rate: 24.4 %
cost of doing nothing: ₹65.0 lakh
cost of 10% raise + less overtime: ₹89.1 lakh

Read this result carefully. With these assumptions, a blanket 10% raise costs more than the attrition it prevents. That is a valuable finding: the cheaper lever is the one that drives the risk, overtime, not salary. A good audit recommends fixing workload first and saving raises for people whose pay is clearly below their peers. The raise only pays for itself if replacing someone costs more than about 90% of a year's salary (try REPLACE = 1.0, a figure often used for senior roles).

Fair pay analysis touches real people. Never publish individual salaries, aggregate small groups (fewer than 5 people) before sharing, and check results for gender or other protected groups only with proper consent and legal guidance. This dataset has no gender column on purpose.

Make it yours

  • Break-even: find the replacement cost (as a share of salary) at which the raise becomes worth it.
  • Attrition model: train a classifier on overtime, pay vs peers, experience and city, and list the top 20 people by risk for HR (anonymised by employee ID).
  • City view: Delhi and Pune show higher attrition than Ahmedabad. Is that overtime, pay or something else?

Portfolio checklist

  • [ ] Missing salaries filled by department and experience, with the reason
  • [ ] Raw pay gap vs adjusted gap from a log-salary regression, explained as percentages
  • [ ] Finding on pay vs performance, stated plainly
  • [ ] Attrition by overtime and performance
  • [ ] A rupee comparison of two actions, with every assumption written down
  • [ ] A clear recommendation (and what data would make it stronger)

items.title: An EDA Checklist for Any New Dataset
items.excerpt: Exploratory Data Analysis in seven steps: shape, types, missing values, duplicates, distributions, relationships and surprises. A repeatable pandas checklist for every new dataset.
items.content:
A new dataset is like a new city. Before you plan a route, you walk around: which roads exist, which are broken, where the traffic is. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is that walk. Skip it and your model will learn from typos, duplicates and missing values without you ever knowing.

🎬 The data detective

  1. A CSV of 10,000 food delivery orders lands on your desk. Your manager wants a model by Friday.
  2. Before any model, you open the file and ask: what is in here, really?
  3. Missing ratings, a delivery time of minus five minutes, the same order twice.
  4. Rainy days are slower. Weekend orders are bigger. Now you know what matters.
  5. Clean data, clear questions. Now the model has a fair chance.

The seven-step checklist

Let's build a small delivery dataset with realistic problems and walk through it.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 12
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110, 110, 111],
    "city": ["Pune", "Mumbai", "pune", "Delhi", "Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune", "Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune", "Pune", "Mumbai"],
    "minutes": [32, 41, 28, -5, 55, 38, 30, 47, 120, 35, 35, 44],
    "amount": [250, 480, 199, 320, None, 610, 275, 390, 450, 300, 300, None],
    "rating": [5, 4, None, 3, 2, 4, 5, 4, 1, 5, 5, 4],
})
print(df.shape)

Output:

(12, 5)

Step 1: shape and types. How many rows and columns, and is every column the type you expect?

print(df.dtypes)

Output:

order_id      int64
city         object
minutes       int64
amount      float64
rating      float64
dtype: object

rating became float64 because one value is missing: pandas stores missing numbers as NaN, which is a float.

Step 2: missing values.

print(df.isna().sum())

Output:

order_id    0
city        0
minutes     0
amount      2
rating      1
dtype: int64

Step 3: duplicates. Order 110 appears twice:

print(df.duplicated().sum(), "exact duplicate row(s)")
print(df["order_id"].duplicated().sum(), "repeated order_id(s)")

Output:

1 exact duplicate row(s)
1 repeated order_id(s)

Step 4: inconsistent categories. "pune" and "Pune" should be one city:

print(df["city"].value_counts().to_dict())
print(df["city"].str.title().value_counts().to_dict())

Output:

{'Pune': 4, 'Mumbai': 4, 'Delhi': 3, 'pune': 1}
{'Pune': 5, 'Mumbai': 4, 'Delhi': 3}

Step 5: impossible and extreme values. describe() shows them at a glance:

print(df["minutes"].describe()[["min", "50%", "max"]])

Output:

min     -5.0
50%     36.5
max    120.0
Name: minutes, dtype: float64

A delivery can't take −5 minutes: that's a data error. 120 minutes is possible (heavy rain?) but unusual: lesson 2 decides what to do with it.

Step 6: relationships. Are slow deliveries rated lower?

print(round(df["minutes"].corr(df["rating"]), 2))

Output:

-0.63

A clear negative correlation: the longer the wait, the worse the rating. That's the kind of finding a business cares about.

Step 7: write down what you found. EDA is only useful if it turns into decisions.

Watch step 5 catch the impossible value

minutes = [32, 41, -5, 55, 120]
bad = [m for m in minutes if m <= 0]
long = [m for m in minutes if m > 90]
print("impossible:", bad, "| check:", long)
  1. Line 1: Five delivery times, in minutes.
  2. Line 2: A delivery time of zero or less is impossible: those are errors to fix or remove.
  3. Line 3: Over 90 minutes is possible but unusual: a value to check, not delete automatically.
  4. Line 4: Two different lists, two different decisions.

The checklist as a reusable function

def eda_report(frame):
    return {
        "rows": len(frame),
        "missing": int(frame.isna().sum().sum()),
        "duplicate_rows": int(frame.duplicated().sum()),
        "numeric_cols": list(frame.select_dtypes("number").columns),
    }

print(eda_report(df))

Output:

{'rows': 12, 'missing': 3, 'duplicate_rows': 1, 'numeric_cols': ['order_id', 'minutes', 'amount', 'rating']}

Note that order_id is numeric but meaningless as a number: averaging IDs makes no sense. Part of EDA is deciding which columns are identifiers, which are categories and which are real measurements.

Your EDA notes for this dataset

Summary

  • EDA = walk around the data before modelling.
  • Seven steps: shape and types, missing values, duplicates, categories, impossible/extreme values, relationships, written decisions.
  • isna, duplicated, value_counts, describe and corr do most of the work.
  • Every finding should lead to a decision.

items.title: Missing Values and Outliers: Find, Decide, Fix
items.excerpt: Why data goes missing (MCAR, MAR, MNAR), when to drop or fill, and how to find outliers with the IQR and z-score methods, with pandas code you can reuse.
items.content:
Missing values and outliers are where most real-world data science time goes. There is no single right answer, only good decisions you can explain. This lesson gives you the decision rules.

🎬 The case of the missing ratings

  1. 15% of customer ratings are blank. Do you delete those rows? Fill them in?
  2. If ratings are missing at random, filling with the median is fine.
  3. But what if unhappy customers skip the rating? Then the blanks ARE the signal.
  4. You fill the blanks and add a column "rating_missing", so the model can learn from it.

Why data goes missing

Options for missing values

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi", "Delhi", "Delhi", "Mumbai"],
    "amount": [250, np.nan, 600, 640, np.nan, 480],
    "rating": [5, 4, np.nan, 2, 3, np.nan],
})

dropped = df.dropna()
print("drop rows with any gap:", len(df), "->", len(dropped))

filled = df.copy()
filled["amount"] = filled["amount"].fillna(filled.groupby("city")["amount"].transform("median"))
filled["rating_missing"] = filled["rating"].isna().astype(int)
filled["rating"] = filled["rating"].fillna(filled["rating"].median())
print(filled)

Output:

drop rows with any gap: 6 -> 2
     city  amount  rating  rating_missing
0    Pune   250.0     5.0               0
1    Pune   250.0     4.0               0
2   Delhi   600.0     3.5               1
3   Delhi   640.0     2.0               0
4   Delhi   620.0     3.0               0
5  Mumbai   480.0     3.5               1

Dropping threw away two thirds of the data. Filling kept every row: amount was filled with the median of the same city (MAR thinking), and rating got a median fill plus a flag in case the gaps mean something (MNAR thinking).

Rule of thumb: drop rows only when very few are missing (a few percent) and they look random. Otherwise fill, and add a "was missing" flag for anything that might not be random.

Finding outliers: the IQR method

The interquartile range (IQR) is the middle 50% of the data. Values more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles are flagged.

import numpy as np
x = np.array([28, 30, 32, 35, 35, 38, 41, 44, 47, 120])
q1, q3 = np.percentile(x, [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
low, high = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
print(x[(x < low) | (x > high)])
  1. Line 1: NumPy for percentiles.
  2. Line 2: Ten delivery times in minutes. One looks suspicious.
  3. Line 3: The 25th and 75th percentiles: a quarter of values are below q1, a quarter above q3.
  4. Line 4: The IQR: how wide the middle half is.
  5. Line 5: The fences: 1.5 × IQR beyond each quartile.
  6. Line 6: Anything outside the fences is flagged. Only 120.

The z-score method

A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. Values beyond about ±3 are rare in roughly bell-shaped data.

x = pd.Series([28, 30, 32, 35, 35, 38, 41, 44, 47, 120])
z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
print(z.round(2).tolist())

Output:

[-0.63, -0.55, -0.48, -0.37, -0.37, -0.26, -0.15, -0.04, 0.07, 2.77]

Notice 120 gets z ≈ 2.8, just under 3. One big outlier inflates the standard deviation and partly hides itself. That's why the IQR method is often preferred for small or skewed data.

What to do with an outlier

  1. Error? (−5 minutes, age 250) → fix it or set it to missing.
  2. Real but rare? (120 minutes in a storm) → keep it; consider capping (winsorising) or a model that's robust to outliers.
  3. The thing you're looking for? (fraud, machine failure) → never delete it: that's your signal.
capped = x.clip(upper=x.quantile(0.95))
print(round(capped.max(), 1), "<- capped at the 95th percentile")

Output:

87.1 <- capped at the 95th percentile

Summary

  • Know why data is missing: MCAR, MAR or MNAR.
  • Drop rarely; fill by group where it makes sense; add "was missing" flags.
  • Find outliers with IQR fences (robust) or z-scores (for bell-shaped data).
  • Errors get fixed, real rare values get kept or capped, and signals are never deleted.
